payload.title: werk: people and agents build software through one repeating pipeline, aligned through a decision map
payload.why: The person brings judgement and drive. The agents bring knowledge and speed. Each pass through plan, build and validate feeds the next pass, so the tool must carry the state between the steps that a stateless prompt loses.
payload.body: The pipeline is a loop, not a line: what validate finds goes back into the next plan. The tool keeps the state between the steps, so the person never has to repeat what an earlier step settled.

kill.text: The person uses the pipeline to build werk itself and one other app, for example an iOS music player. If the result is disappointing for any reason, revisit this decision.

payload.title: The principles hold for every part of werk
payload.why: A principle holds for every part of werk, so a card in any area that breaks one is wrong, not a trade-off to weigh.
payload.body: werk coaches the person's judgement and never decides for them: an agent proposes, and only the person accepts (#map-proposal).

payload.title: The decision map is the record of a project's decisions
payload.why: A map of cards joined by typed links, folded from an append-only log, holds what the work has established. The transcript is disposable; the map is not.

payload.title: Agents work on the map through werk's command line and one set of instructions
payload.why: Every agent that can write to the map reads the same instructions and acts through the same commands, in any project. The rules live in a program, so they hold whichever agent writes.

payload.title: A chat lets a person talk to a live agent that changes the map in the same turn
payload.why: Decisions settle in conversation, and a map that someone fills in afterwards misses them. A chat beside the map, with the open card sent along, lets the agent write what the talk settles while it replies. A conversation lives across many messages, so the agent keeps what it already read.
payload.body:
The chat pane sits in the right pane of the screen, beside the views. A conversation lives across many messages, page reloads and server restarts. A message goes to the agent together with the card the person has open, so "this card" needs no id (#chat-open-card). The agent runs the message as a live turn: it reads the code and the map, runs commands, and writes cards and notes. Its reply streams into the pane while it works (#chat-stream).

The page never writes to the map itself. Every change comes from an agent turn through the map's command line. When the log changes, every open map redraws (#map-views-read). The chat log never triggers a redraw. Only a request that carries the server's token can start a turn (see #proj-serve-trust).

Example. The map holds the card "Checkout retries", which says two tries.

1. The person opens "Checkout retries", types "Make it three tries", and presses Enter. The message goes out with that card.
2. The agent turn starts. The reply streams in while the agent reads the card.
3. The agent changes the card through the command line. The log grows, the map redraws, and the card says three tries.
4. A page on another site sends a message to the server. It has no token, so no turn starts and the map does not change.

```
 person ──(message + open card)──▶ server ──▶ agent turn
   ▲                                           │
   │                                           ├─ reads code and map
   └──── reply streams into the chat ◀─────────┤
                                               └─ writes log ──▶ every map redraws
```

payload.title: The browser shows the map and the work as views that a person reads and acts on
payload.why: The person acts in the browser, not in a terminal. Each view answers one question about the project: the cards, the tickets, the flow of work, the measures, the product's parts.

payload.title: We align on intent before building
payload.why: A wrong build costs more than a question. The agent shows real options side by side, built when prose cannot show the difference, and the person picks.

payload.title: Work runs in three stages, plan, build and validate, and a person approves at the end of each
payload.why: Today's models do not plan, build and validate reliably from one instruction. Stages give a checkable output between the steps and a point where a person approves: G1 closes plan, G2 closes build, G3 closes validate.
payload.body:
Plan turns a decided subtree into a spec and tickets (see #plan-stage). Build turns each ticket into merged code (see #build). Validate checks the result with what the builder never sees (see #val-stage).

Each stage ends at a gate: a pause where a person approves the result before the next stage counts on it.

```
PLAN:      decided subtree -> spec -> tickets                 [G1]
BUILD:     builder loop per ticket -> merge loop              [G2]
VALIDATE:  held-out set after each merge -> measurement       [G3]

G1  what will be built is right, judged on a prototype or on the plan
G2  the main line holds the subtree's tickets, every held-out step green
G3  the measurement of the released product holds up
```

Every gate waits for a person. The stages overlap: validate starts with build, and a project repeats all three in small slices (#pipe-iterative).

kill.text: A new model generation arrives. Give it one high-level instruction on a real decision and see whether it plans, builds and validates with checkable output. Or a build of a whole project with this pipeline fails for reasons that come from the stage structure: agents stuck on technical limits, agents that follow a dead end, agents that wait for permissions, or agents that cannot deliver what the decided cards define.

payload.title: werk measures its pipeline and its own tool
payload.why: A product measure says whether one feature works, not which stage, gate or model to change, so the pipeline measures itself. A measure card says what is recorded and how it is counted, and it holds for every way the numbers are read.
payload.body:
The pipeline records the cost, the failures and the outcome of each ticket it builds, the effort trend across tickets, and the time each ticket waits. Every measure is a fold over logs that the pipeline writes anyway (see #ms-store). How a change to the pipeline is compared on a fixed replay set of tickets is still open (#ms-replay).

The tool measures itself the same way: the fold time, the unit test runs, and the reviews of stale cards.

payload.title: One werk works on many projects, and ships as a product
payload.why: werk runs on any project's folder, keeps one map per project, and installs as one program per platform.

payload.title: werk's build rules: how its code is written, tested, run and released
payload.why: A project's build rules are cards in its own map. These are werk's: they describe the werk v0 repository.

payload.title: werk v0 is a rebuild of werk from scratch, by werk's own pipeline
payload.why: The prototype proved the design. v0 rebuilds it in a new repository from the decided cards, in an order that lets each part be built and checked on its own.

payload.title: A card is a decision with a reason, and options, sources and excerpts are nodes beside it
payload.why: A decision is read cold, so it carries its own reason and its own proof. A rejected choice and a piece of evidence are kept and can be shared, so each is a node of its own, not text inside a card. A source that many cards cite then exists once and cannot drift between copies.
payload.body:
A card holds a title, a why, a body, who decides, and a status. Three other kinds of node sit beside a card and never in the tree:

- An **option** is a choice weighed against one card, with the reason it lost. It belongs to that card through its alternative_to link.
- A **source** is evidence with its finding. Many cards can cite one source, each by a supported_by link.
- An **excerpt** is a verbatim quote from a conversation, extracted from the transcript and never written from memory (see #map-excerpt). It is quoted for the one card that cites it.

A card's page shows its proof: its excerpts, the findings of its sources, its depends_on links with their reasons, and its options. "What else rests on this source?" is a query over the supported_by links, not a text search.

A source can turn out to be wrong. To avoid a third kind of mark, the map keeps no state for a doubted source. A person lists the cards that cite it and asks of each one whether it still holds without that evidence. A card that does not hold is reopened by hand, and the marks of a reopen follow (#map-marks). A card that holds is left as it is.

kill.text: Read a card cold with its options and sources beside it. If its reason or its rejected choices cannot be found without searching the log, revisit.

payload.title: A card is written for a reader who opens it cold, long after the conversation
payload.why: The reader must act on the card's subject without the conversation that wrote it. The title says what the card is about, the why gives most of the understanding, and the body holds the detail for the reader who acts. Session facts and code names go stale while the decision still holds, so a card holds neither.
payload.body:
**Three layers.** The title is one plain sentence with a subject and a verb, about this card's own rule. It names no tool, no other decision, and no count that a later change can make wrong unless it names every member. The why gives about 80% of the understanding in two or three sentences of plain causal steps, with no card references and no commands. The body states the problem, then the answer ("to avoid X, the map does Y"), with references, examples and pictures. When a layer grows too long, its content moves down one level: title, why, body, then a child card.

**About its subject.** A card does not narrate the session: no "Eryk said", no "as discussed", no stage of the conversation. It does not tell its own edit history or where its text came from, because the log records that. A reversal is stated as a fact about the subject. Attribution lives in who decides and in the log.

**At the level of the decision.** A card names behaviour and concepts. It names no source file, function, constant, line or internal address, because those change with every refactor; the code points to the card. The form of a command lives on one command-line card, and every other card names the operation. A card states rules, not one module's results: a module's behaviour list or test plan lives in that module's tests.

**No copies.** A card does not list its children, because the tree draws them and a copy goes wrong when a child moves. Where a sentence states a fact that a child expands, it names the child in parentheses. A card points at a depends_on target and does not restate it.

**Every term defined.** A word is plain English or defined by a decided card. A new term gets a plain definition where it first appears. A coined phrase that a reader must ask about breaks this rule.

**A mechanism shows an example.** A card that says what happens when someone acts carries one worked example: a few named things with plain titles, then numbered steps with one action and its result each, including the case where nothing happens. An ASCII picture with the same names follows, with every symbol labelled. The example shows the rule as it holds now, never two versions side by side. A card that names a thing or fixes a layout needs no example.

```
WRONG  title: Four facts gate decided, each with a written escape hatch
       why:   A silent default hides a missing fact. An escape hatch turns the gap into a record.
RIGHT  title: A card needs four facts before it is decided
       why:   A missing fact must not hide behind a default. A fact can be waived, but the waiver is written down.
```

kill.text: Cards written under these rules still get requests to reword a cryptic title or a long why, or a mechanism card with an example still leaves the reader asking what happens when they act.

payload.title: The wording rules reach every agent that writes card text, and the person's read before accept is the only check
payload.why: Card text drifts back to narration and code names when its writer does not see the rules. The rules travel inside the agent instructions, so every agent that can write a card gets them and no other agent does. No program checks the words, because a phrase check misses narration in other words and a reviewer model costs a call per card.
payload.body: The wording rules are part of the agent instructions, so they reach exactly the agents that get that text (see #agents-instructions). The person reads every proposed card before the accept.

kill.text: A periodic sweep counts the cards that break the wording rules among cards written after the rules reached the prompt, against cards written before. No drop in the rate means the prompt is not enough.

payload.title: Cards relate through four typed links: refines, depends_on, supported_by, alternative_to
payload.why: Each link type causes one action, so a program can derive what a change affects from the links alone. A small set stays easy to get right in a live conversation. The links are the map's model, so they mean the same in every view and in the command line.
payload.body:
```
  child  --refines-------> parent   part of it; places the card in the tree; a change marks the children
  card   --depends_on----> card     uses what the other card decided; a change marks it, one hop
  card   --supported_by--> source   its evidence; carries no mark
  option --alternative_to> card     a rejected choice, kept so a reopen can bring it back
```

refines is where a card sits, and depends_on is what a card needs. They are two graphs over the same nodes: the tree (#map-tree) and the basis (#map-depends). An option has exactly one link, alternative_to; a refines link as well would list it twice, under the children and under the options. A source and an excerpt take no parent.

kill.text: Models read the relations between cards from prose reliably, and a program can still police them. Test it by having an agent derive the affected cards from the prose alone and compare with the links.

payload.title: Every real card sits under one chain of real parents up to the root
payload.why: The map draws only the cards in the tree below the root, and an accept walks up from a ghost to the first real card. Both need every chain of parents to end at the root through real cards, without a loop. So a change that would break the chain is refused before it is written, and a card added with no parent goes under the root.
payload.body:
A card has at most one parent. Every operation that sets a parent (an add under a parent, a refines link, a move, a drag in the map) refuses in two cases and says which: a real card under a ghost, which is a proposed card that nobody accepted, and a loop, where a card would go under a card that sits below it. A ghost under a ghost, or under a real card, is allowed.

A loop of depends_on links is allowed. A change marks only the next hop, so two cards that use each other mark each other once and the mark stops there.

Every map has two top cards with the same ids in every project: `what` holds the requirements and `how` holds the build rules. Both are created decided with the map, so a card under a top card always has a basis, and every tool finds them without a lookup. An add that names no parent puts the card under `what`, in the same event, so no card is in the log but on no page. The person moves it lower by request (#agents-place-cards). Options and sources take no parent.

Example:
- X "We charge per seat" is a real card under the root.
- G "The invoice lists each seat" is a ghost under X.
- Y "Seats are counted each month" is a real card under X.

1. The agent moves Y under G. Refused: Y is real and G is a ghost. Y stays under X.
2. The person accepts G. The same move now succeeds.
3. The agent moves X under Y. Refused: Y sits below X, so the move closes a loop.
4. The agent adds Z with no parent. Z sits under the root.

```
  step 1             step 2             step 3
  root               root               root
   +- X               +- X               +- X  --move under Y--x loop
      +- G (ghost)       +- G               +- G
      +- Y --move--x        +- Y               +- Y
  (ghost) = proposed, not accepted     x = refused, nothing written
```

kill.text: Propose a ghost and move a real card under it; in a second test move a card under its own child. If either move succeeds, revisit.

payload.title: A depends_on link says in one sentence what the card takes, and never points up or down its own branch
payload.why: A reader who must clear a mark needs to judge whether the change reaches the card, and the reason on the link is the only place that says so. A link to an ancestor or a descendant repeats what the tree already says, because a change already marks a card's children and a decided parent already counts as a basis. Such links only hide the links that cross subtrees.
payload.body:
A depends_on link without a reason is refused. The reason says what this card takes from the other card, not what the other card is. Linking the same pair again with a new reason replaces the reason, and the trace of every mark shows the reason of the link it passed (#map-trace).

A depends_on link to the card's own ancestor or descendant is refused, and the refusal says why. A move that turns a link into one removes that link. The rule holds while a card is a ghost too: a ghost's link to its proposed parent is refused, so an accept never puts a lineage link into the map.

```
  A1 --depends_on--> B1    ok   another subtree
       why: "A1 places its labels on the grid that B1 defines."
  A1 --depends_on--> A     x    ancestor: refines already says it
  A  --depends_on--> A1    x    descendant: same reason
```

kill.text: A sweep of all depends_on links finds links that make no sense although they have a reason, or a link to a parent is accepted, or a move leaves such a link in place.

payload.title: The map is folded from an append-only log of events, and the log is the record
payload.why: Every change is one event added to the end of the log, and nothing is deleted. The map on screen is the fold of the whole log, so every view and every rule sees the same state. The order of events also says what changed after a card was decided, which is what the marks need.
payload.body:
A turn that rewrites a card adds an event, and the fold shows only the result. Each meaning has its own event type, so a reader of the log sees the fact in the type alone and the fold keeps one branch per meaning. A card added under a parent is one event: its place is part of what was added. A removal is one more event, so the card can come back.

```
  log (only grows)              map (the fold)
 +----------------------+      +-----------------------------+
 | 1 added    #a        |      | #a "Use an append-only log" |
 | 2 added    #b under a| fold |    decided                  |
 | 3 retitled #a        | ---> |  +- #b "Cards fold from it" |
 | 4 decided  #a        |      +-----------------------------+
 | 5 removed  #b        |
 | 6 restored #b        |
 +----------------------+
```

Event 3 replaces the title, so the map shows only the new one, and the old title stays in the log. Events 5 and 6 cancel out.

The fold also derives the marks with their traces (#map-marks), the rollups (#map-rollup), and the held links of ghosts. A rule that checks a write reads the folded map and nothing else, so the marks are derived in one place and every rule and view sees the same ones.

The log is committed with the project. The chat transcript is a separate file with a shorter life, and nothing in the map depends on it.

kill.text: Change one decided card. If a program cannot list the cards it affects from the links alone, or a reader needs the chat to learn why a card holds, revisit.

payload.title: Every read replays the whole log, and no snapshot of the map is stored
payload.why: A full replay keeps the log the only state. A full fold of about 7,400 events took 13 to 20 ms, so a snapshot would only add a second copy that must agree with the log and be rebuilt when the fold logic changes. Each fold records its time, so the kill criterion has data.
payload.body: Each read folds the log from the first event to the last, and the fold time grows with the log. The fold time is recorded as a measure (see #ms-fold-time).

kill.text: metric: the median time of a full fold. When a read can no longer afford it, the fallback is a stored snapshot.

payload.title: A write refuses an event that breaks a map rule, and the fold sets such a line aside and names it
payload.why: One bad line in a committed log must not hide the whole map, because a merge can bring one in. A new write must not add a bad line, and a click that takes several nodes must take all of them or none. A set-aside line that nobody sees stays forever, so every read names it.
payload.body:
A write checks its events against the folded map, in order, and appends all of them or none. An event that breaks a rule, such as an unknown node, a second parent, a link from an option other than alternative_to, or a refines loop, is refused with the rule it breaks. An accept or a discard that takes several nodes writes one event per node in one write, in the order the rules need: a parent becomes real before its child, and a child leaves before its parent.

The fold applies the same rules. An event that breaks one is not applied, the events after it still fold, and the log is never rewritten to remove the line. Every command that reads the map prints one warning per set-aside line, with its line number and the rule, before its own result, and still does its work.

kill.text: A committed log with one bad line still shows every other card, and the warning names the line.

payload.title: Every view draws the fold of the log, and a log change tells each open view to read it again
payload.why: The map is a view of the log, so a second way to change it would be a second store to keep in step. A control in a view appends an event and never edits the drawn card. The change signal carries no data, so a page has one way to get the map: the same full read it makes on first load.
payload.body:
When the log grows, the server sends a bare signal on the live channel to every open page, and each page reads the whole fold again and redraws. A page never patches its copy from the signal. A page also reads the whole map each time its live channel connects, on the first load and on every reconnect after a server restart, so a write made while the server was down is drawn too. The server starts to watch the log before it accepts a connection, and no timer polls the log.

The pipeline log has its own bare signal. A view that shows measures reads only the measures again, and the map is not read for it.

Example:
- Tabs T1 and T2 show the map with card #a. The server is running.

1. The agent adds card #b from the command line. The log gets one event.
2. The server sends the signal to T1 and T2. Each reads the whole fold and shows #a and #b.
3. The server stops, and a command adds #c. No signal is sent.
4. The server starts. T1 reconnects, reads the map, and shows #c.
5. Nothing is written. No signal comes, and no tab reads again.

```
 agent --add #b--> log --grows--> server --signal (no data)--> T1, T2 --read fold--> redraw
 server restarts                  T1 connects ------------------------> read fold --> redraw
```

kill.text: Open the map in two tabs and add a card from the command line; then stop the server, add a card, and start it. If a tab does not show the new card within a second, without a manual reload, revisit.

payload.title: A card moves through proposed, open or proto, decided, reopened and removed
payload.why: Each state change is one event in the log and has its own check. Kept in one place, the rules cannot disagree about what a state means.
payload.body:
```
  proposed --accept--> open, proto or decided (the status the ghost had)
     |
     +--discard--> gone
  open / proto --decide--> decided --reopen--> open
                           decided --amend---> decided
  a real card --remove--> removed --restore--> back where it was
```

A status is about the card's own claim, not about its subtree: a decided card can have open cards below it, and progress over a subtree is the rollup (#map-rollup). A status describes the decision, not the build: a decided card with nothing built yet is not a contradiction. Out of scope is not a status (#map-out-of-scope). proto marks a card that only a built artifact can settle.

kill.text: The proto and reopened states are the most doubtful parts. If either proves unhelpful or a problem in use, revisit.

payload.title: Every change to a card's words is a proposal that the person accepts or discards
payload.why: The agent never applies a change to a title, a why or a body directly. It proposes the change, the map shows it as a diff, and the person accepts it or asks for a correction. So nothing the person has not read enters the map.
payload.body:
A proposal is staged on the card and shows as a pending change beside the current words. A card has at most one pending change: a change to its words or a removal (#map-remove), never both. The accept commits it and the discard drops it. An accept from the command line refuses unless it states that the person asked for it; the accept button in the map is the real path, and both commit the same events.

The proposing agent describes the new body as operations on the blocks of the old body: each block is kept, elaborated into new text, or removed, and new blocks are added (see #align-diff). The program checks every quoted old block against the real body before it shows the diff, and shows a quote that does not match as a plain removal and addition. Every block of the current body must appear in an operation, so a block never disappears on accept without a struck-through line in the diff. A list that leaves a block out is refused and prints the blocks at risk. A block is a run of text between blank lines outside a code fence, so a list or a fenced code block is one block, and two equal blocks need one operation each.

payload.title: A proposed node is a frozen ghost until the person accepts it
payload.why: A card that nobody accepted is fuzzy, and once in the log it looks the same as a decided one. So every new node, whether card, option, source or excerpt, enters as a ghost that derives nothing. A ghost's words cannot change, so the accept commits exactly what the person read.
payload.body:
A ghost is in the log and drawn in the tree under its proposed parent with the look of a new card (see #align-diff-look), apart from the mark of a pending change on a real card. It is in no rollup, no mark and no count. Every kind stages, because the reason an option lost is agent-written content of the same kind the gate exists to catch.

Frozen means the words. A second add with the same id, and any change to the title, the why or the body, is refused. The only correction is a discard and a new proposal (#map-ghost-thread). A link, a status, who decides and a kill criterion still work on a ghost. Each link of a ghost is held: it is drawn, and it goes live by itself once both ends are real, with no second event. The decide check counts held links, so a ghost can be decided before its accept, with its basis and its options held, and the accept commits it as one unit.

The accept takes one ghost at a time, by the button on it, and there is no batch accept. What an accept and a discard take along with the ghost is #map-ghost-carry.

payload.title: An accept takes a ghost's ghost parents and attachments with it, and a discard takes what only that ghost held
payload.why: A card that commits without its options or its evidence shows no proof, and its links stay held. A ghost child left under a discarded parent hangs nowhere. A source can support many cards, so dropping one card must not drop what another card still cites.
payload.body:
**Accept.** The accept of a ghost card also makes real its ghost refines ancestors up to the first real card, so a click cannot orphan a card, and the ghost options, sources and excerpts of every card it commits. It never takes a ghost that the card depends on, because that is another card with its own words.

**Discard.** The discard of a ghost card also drops its ghost descendants, the ghost options of each card it drops, and each ghost excerpt quoted for one of them. It drops a ghost source only when no remaining card, real or ghost, cites it. A real node is never dropped. Either one writes one event per node, all in one write (#map-log-refuse).

Example:
- C "We charge per seat", a ghost card, with C:ex0, a ghost excerpt quoted for it.
- S "Pricing survey", a ghost source cited by C and by D.
- D "The invoice shows the seat count", a second ghost card.
- T "Churn study", a ghost source cited only by C.

1. The person discards C. C, C:ex0 and T leave the map.
2. S stays a ghost, because D still cites it.
3. The person accepts D. D and S become real together, and D shows S as its proof at once.

```
before                       after discard C       after accept D
C (ghost) --> C:ex0 (ghost)  (gone)                (gone)
C (ghost) --> T (ghost)      (gone)                (gone)
C (ghost) --> S (ghost)      S (ghost)             S (real)
D (ghost) --> S              D (ghost) --> S       D (real) --> S
-->  supported_by
```

kill.text: Propose two ghost cards that cite one ghost source, discard the first, then accept the second. If the source is gone after the discard, or still a ghost after the accept, revisit.

payload.title: A corrected ghost keeps the thread of notes that led to its new words
payload.why: A ghost is corrected by a discard and a new proposal with the same id, and the notes on it are the reason for the correction. The thread belongs to the card id, so the new ghost shows those notes. A marker shows where the new words begin, so each note is read against the words it was about.
payload.body:
A discard takes the ghost out of the map and leaves the thread of its id. When the id is proposed again, the thread shows a marker at that point, and a note above the marker was about the earlier words. The inbox shows no markers, so it labels each such note as written about earlier words. An id reused for an unrelated card carries the old thread, so a new idea takes a new id.

Example:
- X is a ghost card, "Export is its own command".
- N1 is a note on X: "Say what the export writes."

1. The person writes N1 on X. The thread of X shows N1.
2. The agent discards X. X leaves the map, and N1 stays with the id.
3. The agent proposes X again as "Export writes every order as one file". The thread shows N1, then the marker. The inbox labels N1 as about earlier words.
4. The person writes N2 on X. The thread shows N1, the marker, then N2, and N2 has no label.

```
step  map          thread of X
1     X (ghost)    N1
2     -            N1                    (kept, out of sight)
3     X (ghost)    N1 | proposed again
4     X (ghost)    N1 | proposed again | N2
|  = the marker: notes above it were about the earlier words    -  = no node with the id
```

kill.text: Write a note on a ghost, discard it and propose it again. If the note is gone, or the marker is missing, revisit.

payload.title: The person writes a note on any node's thread from its page, in the person's own name
payload.why: A ghost is corrected through the notes on its thread, so the person must be able to write there. A note sent through the chat is written in the agent's name, and the inbox cannot tell it from the agent's own notes. So the page sends the note itself, behind the same token that guards every other write.
payload.body: The card page has a note box under the thread of every node: a card, a ghost, an option, a source or an excerpt. The server checks the page's token and the request's host (see #proj-serve-trust), then appends one note in the person's name; without the token it refuses and writes nothing. A note changes no words, so a frozen ghost takes notes too. Each entry shows who wrote it, and every open page draws the thread again when the log grows (#map-views-read). The agent writes its own notes from the command line.

payload.title: A decided card is frozen, and a change to it is an amend: a reopen and a decide in one step
payload.why: Other cards depend on a decided card because of what it says. If its text could change without a mark, those cards would not learn of the change. An amend runs the decide check again and marks the next hop, so an edit works the same way as a reopen. A depends_on link is part of what the card says: it names why the card holds, so a link changes only by an amend too.
payload.body:
Frozen on a decided card: the title, the why, the body, its depends_on links, who decides, and a waiver of a decide fact. Free: its place in the tree, options, sources, kill criteria and their state, and notes. A change to a frozen field is a proposal (#map-proposal), and its accept is the amend. The card stays decided, so the map never shows it open, and the next hop is marked with the change "amended" and the proposal's sentence (#map-marks). An amend has no event of its own: the accept of a proposal on a decided card is the amend.

The amend runs the decide check (#map-contract) on the new version, and a change to a frozen field must leave every fact in place. It fails when the change removes a fact, or when the card was decided before a fact became required and still lacks it. A free change is refused only when it takes away a fact the card had, such as its last option, so a missing fact can always be added first, and an option is removed one at a time while another remains. Removing a card that this card depends on is not a change to this card.

An open or proto card is not frozen. It changes through a proposal and marks nothing, because no card can be decided on it.

Example:
- Q "We charge per seat" is decided, who decides is you, with one option O and a kill criterion. Card D depends on Q.
- R "Seats are counted each month" was decided before kill criteria were required, and has none.

1. Someone removes O. Refused: Q would have no option.
2. Someone adds option O2, then removes O. Both pass, and nothing is marked.
3. Someone proposes "who decides: me" on Q, and the person accepts. Q stays decided, and D goes stale with the trace "amended".
4. Someone proposes a new body for R. The accept is refused: R lacks a kill criterion.
5. Someone records a kill criterion on R, then the accept passes.

```
 change                       on   result
 remove O                     Q    refused (no option left)
 add O2, remove O             Q    allowed, nothing marked
 who -> me, accepted          Q    amend: Q decided, D stale
 new body, accepted           R    refused (no kill criterion)
 add kill criterion           R    allowed; then the body amend passes
```

kill.text: Amend decided cards on a real map and watch the reviews of the cards they mark. If most reviews confirm the marked card unchanged, the freeze adds no safety, and an edit to a decided card can mark nothing.

payload.title: A card becomes decided only when a program check of four facts passes
payload.why: The map's rules about who decides, the basis, rejected options and kill criteria stay prose without a check. The check runs in the command line at the move to decided, so it holds for an agent, a script and a person alike. A missing fact must not hide behind a default: a fact can be waived, but the waiver carries a written reason.
payload.body:
The check reads the log, not the prose. The four facts, in the order a refusal lists them:

1. **Who decides** is set. It cannot be waived.
2. **A basis holds.** The basis is the card's parent and every depends_on target. At least one exists, and each one is decided and not stale. While one is open, proto or stale, the card waits (#map-wait), and a waiver does not end the wait. A paused basis still holds, because its content is still true. A root card is decided from the moment the map is created, so a card under a root always has a decided parent. A real card counts only a real basis; a ghost counts held links too.
3. **An option was weighed** when who decides is you or not set yet: an option exists, or the author states that none was weighed. That statement, "unchallenged", is a recorded fact and is never inferred from the data, because the data cannot tell "no option weighed" from "weighed and never written down". A card decided by me or by a prototype needs no option.
4. **A kill criterion** is on record (#map-kill).

The check runs at the move to decided and at an amend (#map-frozen), not at creation, because a new card has no links yet; a card cannot be added already decided. A refusal lists every missing fact at once, each with the command that fixes it and the card id filled in, so the agent fixes the card in one pass with no person reading the error. A waiver of the basis or the option needs a non-empty reason, which prints wherever the card prints.

Example:
- X "We charge per seat" has a title and a body, and nothing else.

1. The agent decides X. Refused, with four entries: who, basis, option, kill criterion.
2. The agent sets who to you, links a decided basis, adds an option, and records a kill criterion.
3. The agent decides X again. It passes.
4. Had the agent set who to me, it could skip the option.

```
decide X   who MISSING | basis MISSING | option MISSING | kill MISSING   => refused, 4 entries, one refusal
fix all four
decide X   who ok | basis ok | option ok | kill ok                       => decided
```

kill.text: Decide a card with no who, no basis, no option and no kill criterion: the refusal must name all four at once. Waive the basis with an empty reason: refused. If either result flips, revisit.

payload.title: A reopen states whether the card is wrong or only waits: invalidated, rejected or postponed
payload.why: A reopened card is open again for one of two kinds of reason. Invalidated or rejected means the content is wrong, so the cards that use it need a review. Postponed means the content still holds and only its work waits, so the cards below it wait too but need no review.
payload.body:
The test: would you build it unchanged if you had the time? Yes means postponed; no means invalidated or rejected. A reopen that names no reason is invalidated. Invalidated and rejected put a stale mark on the next hop (#map-marks). Postponed puts the postponed mark on the card itself and a paused mark on every card downstream (#map-paused). Out of scope is a postponement (#map-out-of-scope).

Only a decided card or a postponed card can be reopened, because an open card has nothing to reopen. A postponed card stays open, carries the postponed mark, and is left out of the search for work. Deciding it again is the resume: it ends the postponed mark and every paused mark it caused, and nothing else. A later reopen with another reason also ends the postponement, and its own reason marks the cards as that reason's rule says.

kill.text: Postpone a card, then decide it again: its downstream paused marks clear. If a mark from another postponed card also clears, revisit.

payload.title: A card can be removed from the map, and nothing leaves the log
payload.why: A map with a few wrong cards is not a broken map, and cleaning up one card must not mean rewriting it into something else. A removed card leaves every view, so it stops taking space and attention. A removal is one more event, so a restore brings the card back.
payload.body:
A removal takes the card and its refines subtree. With the reparent choice, the direct children move up to the card's parent instead, for a bad parent over good children; a card with children and no parent cannot be reparented, and the top card `what` cannot be removed. The removal also takes the options and excerpts of every card it takes, because one left behind is an orphan no view can reach. A source stays while any card that cites it stays. A removed card makes nothing stale, counts in no rollup and cites nothing.

A removal names a real card or an option. A ghost is not removed; it is discarded.

An agent never removes a card. It proposes the removal, the card shows the pending removal in red, and the person's accept takes the card out with the same events as a removal the person made, so a restore undoes it the same way (#map-restore). A discard drops the pending removal, and the card stays.

Example:
- Card L "Legacy importer" is decided and has no children.

1. An agent proposes the removal of L. L stays in the map, drawn in red.
2. The person accepts. L leaves the map.
3. The person restores L. L is back, with no pending change.
4. Had the person not accepted, nothing would change: L waits in red.

```
step  event                  L
1     removal proposed       in the map, red
2     accepted               out of the map
3     restored               in the map, no pending change
```

kill.text: Propose a removal as an agent, accept it, then restore the card. If the card does not come back exactly as it was, revisit.

payload.title: A restore is the exact undo of one removal
payload.why: A remove followed by a restore must leave the map as it was, which is the promise that a removal is never final. So the removal names only the card, the fold works out what it takes and keeps that record, and the restore brings back exactly that set. Links of a removed card wait instead of being deleted, and its id stays taken.
payload.body:
A restore names the card that a removal named. It brings back every node the removal took, and the children that the reparent choice moved go back under the restored card. A node that went out with another card comes back only through that card. Each removal is undone on its own, so the order of restores does not change the result. A restore of a card whose parent is still out is refused and names the parent to restore first.

The fold keeps removed nodes, the record of each removal in force, and the links with an end out apart from the live map, so a read that knows nothing of removals sees none of them. A link with an end out waits, and goes live again the moment both ends are in. A link that comes back is the old link, so its marks come back with it.

While a node is out, every new write that names it refuses and names the restore: a new link, an add under it, a change to its words or facts, a decide, an accept or a discard. An add that reuses the id refuses too, because the log still holds the old card's history under that id.

Example:
- Card `login` depends on card `session`.
- Card `session` has the child `session-ttl`.

1. A person removes `session`. `session` and `session-ttl` leave the map. The link from `login` waits.
2. An agent tries to add a new card with the id `session`. Refused: restore `session`.
3. A person restores `session`. Both cards come back, and the link is live again.

```
step  live nodes                    out                   waiting link
0     login, session, session-ttl   -                     -
1     login                         session, session-ttl  login -> session
2     login                         session, session-ttl  login -> session   (add 'session' refused)
3     login, session, session-ttl   -                     -
```

kill.text: Remove a card with reparent, link and remove a second card, then restore both in the opposite order. If the tree, the links and the rollups differ from the state before the removals, or an add with a removed id succeeds, revisit.

payload.title: A change marks the next hop only: the cards that depend on the changed card, and its children
payload.why: A reopen or an amend can make the cards that use the changed card wrong, and only the links say which ones. Marking one hop keeps the marks few: a review that leaves a card unchanged stops the mark there, and a review that changes it is a change too, so the mark moves one hop more. A program walks the links, because a model asked which cards a change affects recovers only a small part of the chain.
payload.body:
A mark is derived from the log and never written. A card is stale when a card it depends on, or its parent, was reopened as invalidated or rejected, or amended, after the link existed, and the card has had no review since (#map-review). supported_by and alternative_to links carry no mark.

A mark holds only while the link it passed over is the same link. A link made after the change carries no mark from it, because it was written against the current text; a card linked to a stale or open card waits instead (#map-wait). A link removed and made again is a new link, so an old mark does not come back. A link made again with a new reason is the same link and keeps its mark.

A postponement marks in a different way: a paused mark, at any distance (#map-paused). Every mark shows a trace (#map-trace). The marked cards list in fix order: a card comes after the marked cards it depends on, so no card is fixed against a basis that is still wrong.

Example:
- A "We charge per seat".
- B "The invoice shows the seat count", depends on A.
- C "The invoice PDF has a seat column", depends on B.
- K "The seat count is rounded up", a child of B.

1. A is reopened. B goes stale. C and K stay clear, because they are two hops away.
2. B is reviewed and confirmed. B clears, and nothing else is marked.
3. Had B been amended instead, C and K would go stale.
4. A new card N links to A after step 1. N carries no mark; it waits until A is decided again.

```
 C --depends_on--> B --depends_on--> A  <-- reopen
 K --refines-----> B
 N --depends_on--> A   (link made after the reopen)

 after reopen A:     B STALE    C, K clear    N waits, no mark
 after confirm B:    B clear    C, K clear
 after amend B:      B clear    C, K STALE
```

kill.text: metric: the share of reviews that clear a stale mark with no change to the card. A high share means the marks send reviewers to cards that hold.

payload.title: A postponement pauses every card downstream, at any distance
payload.why: A postponed card's content still holds, so the cards that use it need no review; they only wait with it. A paused card is never reviewed, so a pause that moved one hop at a time would stop at the first card. The pause therefore reaches every card downstream at once, and ends when the postponed card is decided again.
payload.body:
At the postponement, one walk over the links in the map at that moment marks every card that reaches the postponed card through refines children or depends_on dependents, at any distance. Each card is marked once, along a shortest path, and its trace names that path. A card linked later takes no paused mark.

The postponed card itself carries the postponed mark, and every card downstream carries the paused mark: only the origin was postponed, and the trace shows the distance.

A paused mark is not stale. It leaves the status colour in place, and a paused card is still a basis that holds, so work that only reads its content goes on. A review clears only stale marks and leaves paused ones. When a pause and a stale mark reach one card, the card reads stale, so a real invalidation never looks calm. A card shows one mark word, the first that holds of stale, postponed, paused and waiting, and its page keeps every trace.

Example:
- P "Invoices are in EUR only".
- M "Invoice prices use the EUR format", depends on P.
- Q "The PDF footer states the currency", depends on M and on X.
- X "We charge per seat".

1. P is postponed. P reads postponed. M and Q read paused.
2. X is reopened. Q also goes stale, and reads stale. Its page shows both traces.
3. Q is reviewed and confirmed. The stale mark clears, and Q reads paused again.
4. A new card N links to M. N has no mark and can be decided, because M still holds.
5. P is decided again. M and Q have no mark.

```
 M --depends_on--> P (postponed)       word shown on Q
 Q --depends_on--> M                   1: paused
 Q --depends_on--> X                   2: stale  (paused + stale)
 N --depends_on--> M (made later)      3: paused
                                       5: (none)
```

kill.text: Postpone a card, link a new card to a paused card downstream, and decide it. If the new card shows a mark or cannot be decided, revisit.

payload.title: A card whose basis does not hold waits; it is not stale
payload.why: A card linked to an open or stale card was written against the current text, so a review of it has nothing to check. It cannot be decided until its basis holds again. If the basis is confirmed unchanged it can be decided at once; if the basis is amended, the amend marks it and it is reviewed.
payload.body: Waiting is derived from the log, and nothing writes it. A card waits while it is not decided, carries no stale or paused mark, and stands on a basis that is open, proto or stale (the basis fact of #map-contract). The marks list names each waiting card with the basis it waits for, after the marked cards. A review skips a waiting card.

kill.text: Create a card that depends on a stale card. If it is marked stale at creation, or cannot be decided once its basis is confirmed unchanged, revisit.

payload.title: A review of a stale card ends in a confirm or an amend
payload.why: A confirm says the card holds unchanged, and it must show that each link reason was read, so it lists the targets it read, and a list that leaves an older link out is refused. An amend changes the card, which marks the next hop. The agent that made a change reviews every card it marked in the same turn, so marks do not pile up unread.
payload.body:
**Confirm.** The confirm lists every depends_on target whose link is older than the card's newest stale mark; a link made after it needs no entry, and a target with no link from the card is refused. A refusal names each unread link with its reason and prints the confirm again with the full list. A confirm also fails while the card's basis does not hold. The confirm clears the card's stale marks, and the mark stops there.

**Amend.** The card changes through a proposal (#map-frozen). Its accept clears the card's stale marks, and the amend marks the next hop like any other change.

**Who reviews.** After a change, the agent that made it reads each marked card, the changed card and the reason on each link between them, before the turn ends. It confirms a card that holds and proposes an amend for one that does not. It never amends a card that the person decides without the person's accept. It skips a card that waits and leaves paused marks as they are. A review is never a bulk clear.

Example:
- A "We charge per seat".
- B "The invoice shows the seat count", depends on A.
- D "Invoices are in EUR".
- C "The invoice PDF has a seat column", depends on B and on D.

1. B is amended. C goes stale.
2. A confirm of C that lists B only is refused, and the refusal names the link C to D with its reason.
3. A confirm of C that lists B and D passes. C clears.
4. Had the reviewer amended C with "The PDF now shows usage units", the cards that depend on C would go stale with that sentence.

```
 C --depends_on--> B --depends_on--> A
 C --depends_on--> D
 confirm C [B]      refused: the reason of C -> D is not confirmed
 confirm C [B, D]   C clears, nothing else marked
 amend C            C clears, cards on C STALE ("amended")
```

kill.text: metric: the share of the person's reviews of a stale card that end in a confirm with no change to the card.

payload.title: Every mark shows its trace: which change, with what reason, along which link, and why
payload.why: A mark alone says only that something near the card changed. The trace names the change, its kind and date, the text typed with it, and the link with its reason, so the reader can judge the mark without a log query. A paused mark can sit far from its origin, so its trace also names the cards between.
payload.body:
A mark from a reopen names its reason: invalidated, rejected or postponed. A mark from an amend says amended and shows the proposal's sentence. A stale trace is one link long. A paused trace names each card between the postponed card and this one, nearest to the origin first, and the link type of the last hop. The marks list and the card page print the same trace.

```
 STALE from #X, invalidated, 2026-10-10
   Charging moves to usage.
   Y -> X: <the reason on the link>

 PAUSED from #P, postponed, 2026-10-10
   via Q, R (nearest to P first)
   last hop: depends_on
```

kill.text: A reader still asks why a card is marked after reading its trace.

payload.title: Every decision records what must become true to revisit it
payload.why: The author sets the revisit trigger when the decision is made, so a later challenge only checks that trigger and costs little socially. A decision with no stated reason is the warning sign, not a decision with no metric, so an answer is required and a metric is not. The decide check blocks until an answer is on record, so the question is always asked.
payload.body:
The agent asks while the card is open: what must become true to change this decision? The answers, from best to weakest:

1. A metric: a data source, a metric, a threshold, a time window and a minimum sample. The agent drafts the query and the author confirms it. If the metric does not exist yet, building it joins the decision.
2. A manual test by the author.
3. No metric, with a reason: an unclear hypothesis (the agent pushes back once, then accepts), not worth measuring, slow or noisy (a proxy and a review date), taste or values (a link to a principle), or a constraint (an event on its source).
4. Revisit at any time.

A criterion can name a rejected option as its fallback, so the alternative is on the map when the criterion fires. A refused decide drafts one to three criteria from the card's hypothesis and its options. A criterion can be added to a decided card at any time. The history of fired and unfired criteria is data about decision quality.

payload.title: A program watches each kill criterion, and a fired criterion proposes a replacement card
payload.why: A metric needs a scheduled check, some criteria fire on an event, and a review date catches the rest. A watch that fails must never read as "not met". When a criterion fires, the author keeps the judgement: the agent brings the evidence and the fallback option as a proposal and changes nothing itself.
payload.body:
Three triggers: a metric checked on a schedule by an agent, an event such as a new decision on the same subject or a launch in a new market, and a review date as the fallback. Time windows and minimum samples keep one bad day from firing a criterion. A query that errors or returns no rows marks the criterion unmonitored.

When a criterion fires, the agent proposes a new card that supersedes the decision, with the evidence and the fallback option (#map-ghost). The old card stays, marked superseded, and is reopened with a reason (#map-reopen). A decision that cannot be undone and reaches widely is never reverted automatically.

payload.title: Every card shows a rollup of its refines subtree
payload.why: A card's status answers for one card, so a person cannot tell whether a subtree is finished or barely started. The rollup counts the card and everything below it. One definition on the server feeds the map and the command line, so the two never disagree.
payload.body:
The rollup counts the cards, the open, proto, decided and postponed ones, the stale ones, and the unchallenged ones. Unchallenged and stale cut across status and would break the sum, so they are counted apart from the statuses and never drawn in the same row (see #ui-counts). The command line prints the same rollup as one line, and again on each child, so a branch can be ranked before it is opened.

Unchallenged counts only decided cards that the person decides and whose author stated that no option was weighed (#map-contract). A card the agent decides is a reversible call, so an option on it is noise, and counting every card put the number near its maximum, where it ranks nothing.

A subtree is finished when no card in it is open or proto (#map-finished), and drained when it is also free of unchallenged cards. Drained has no colour of its own: it is the two numbers read together.

payload.title: An agent records a card's depends_on links and its rejected options in the turn that settles it
payload.why: Only the author knows, at creation, which other card this one needs and which alternatives it beat. A change marks only the links that exist when it happens, so a link added later leaves the card looking current when it is not. An option written down later cannot be told from a decision made with no contrast.
payload.body: When a card is added, its depends_on links are written in the same step, each with its reason (#map-depends). When a decision comes from real contrast, which means a named alternative and a reason it lost, the alternative is added as its own option with that reason and linked to the card in the same turn. A single-hop model check recovers only 6% to 11% of an invalidation chain, so the links cannot be rebuilt later.

kill.text: Reopen a card that others depend on. If a card written because of it is not marked, revisit.

payload.title: The agent places each card in the tree, and the person corrects the placement by request
payload.why: The agent's placement is usually right, and a correction costs one request, so placing cards by hand would be work for no gain. A parent with a single child is a sign that the two are one decision.
payload.body: The agent decides the parent of every card it writes, and whether to promote or demote it, without asking first. The person asks for a move in the chat, and the agent runs it. The agent does not build a chain of single-child cards: it merges the child into the parent, or puts it beside the parent, unless the child is a separate decision that will get siblings soon.

kill.text: Count the parents with exactly one child card and compare with 42 of 110 in the source. If the share has not fallen, or the person moves cards by hand often, revisit.

payload.title: Find lists the cards an agent can work on now: open or proto, and carrying no mark
payload.why: An agent looks for a card it can work on now. A proto card is still work. A postponed card and every card a mark holds back wait, so listing them would make the agent filter again.
payload.body:
Find lists real cards whose status is open or proto, in the refines subtree of one card, breadth first, the card itself included; with no card named it reads each tree of the map. It leaves out a card with a stale or paused mark and a card with the postponed mark. A card reopened as rejected is open work again and is listed. Options, sources, excerpts, ghosts and removed cards are never listed. Find never lists a decided card: an agent that needs a decision for context searches the decided cards by their words.

```
 Product            open                   listed (the card itself)
 +-- Billing        proto                  listed
 +-- Login          decided                left out: found by search
 +-- Export         open, paused           left out
 +-- Reports        open, stale            left out
 +-- Archive        open, postponed        left out
 +-- Search         open, rejected         listed
```

kill.text: Postpone one card and mark another stale, then run find on their parent. If a marked or a decided card is listed, or an open, a proto or a rejected card is missing, revisit.

payload.title: A project's build rules are cards in its own map
payload.why: werk's prompts are the same for every project, and the requirement cards say what to build, but neither says how this project is built: its commands, conventions, domain words and test policy. Without one home for these rules, each agent guesses them again from the code, and two agents can guess differently. As cards, the rules get reasons and links like any decision, and a changed requirement marks the rule that serves it.
payload.body:
The build rules sit under a second top card, `how`, beside `what`, the top card of the requirements, so werk finds them the same way in every project and the tree shows the split. A card is a build rule when it holds only for this project's own repository: its stack, tooling and conventions. A card is a requirement when it states what the product does for its users, even when it names a technology. When the product builds software, a rule it applies to every project it builds is a requirement, and the way its own repository follows that rule is a build rule that depends on it.

A build rule depends on the requirements it serves. A domain word is a build rule too, so the project needs no separate glossary. An agent that werk did not start reads the project's instruction file, which tells it to list the build-rule cards from the map and follow every one; the file points to the rules and copies none of them, so the map stays the only source. werk adds the rule titles to the agents it starts (#agents-build-rule-titles).

A rule that a program can check becomes a linter, a test or a hook that the agent cannot edit. A card holds only what no check can hold and what an agent cannot infer from the code. Generated or generic rules do not help an agent, so a build-rule card is decided with an option weighed against it, like any other card.

kill.text: Builds in a project with build-rule cards break those rules as often as builds in a project without them, or agents that werk did not start keep ignoring the pointer in the instruction file.

payload.title: werk puts the titles of the decided build-rule cards into the prompt of every agent that gets its instructions
payload.why: An agent cannot follow a build rule it does not know exists. The titles are short, so all of them fit in every prompt like a table of contents, and the agent opens a card in full only when its task touches that rule. werk adds the titles itself, so no agent has to remember to look.
payload.body:
The list holds only decided cards: an open or proposed card is not a rule anyone agreed to, while a decided card below an open one still counts. The list goes to the agents that get the werk agent instructions (#agents-instructions), and to no other. With no decided build rule, the prompt holds no list.

Example:
- R "An order export holds every order", a requirement.
- B "Tests run against a real database", a decided build rule.
- D "Use one log per service", an open build rule, with E "Each log line is JSON", decided, under it.

1. A build pass for R starts. Its prompt lists B and E.
2. The ticket writes a query, so the builder opens B in full and writes the test against a real database.
3. 
4. The person decides D. The next pass lists B, D and E.

```
map                        prompt of a build pass
root   R ...               werk instructions
how    B  decided  ------> build-rule titles: B, E
       D  open  (left out)
         E decided ------>  (opens B in full when the task needs it)
```

kill.text: Cards that are both a requirement and a build rule keep landing on the wrong side, so an agent misses a rule it needed.

payload.title: werk must be able to become a standalone product
payload.why: The agent terminal that runs werk today is a temporary harness. Whatever werk proves must move out of it without a rewrite. This constraint decides where werk's logic lives.
payload.body: werk is built around an existing agent command line for now, but nothing in werk may depend on living inside it. A rule that exists only as a prompt file cannot move into a product, so the rules live in a program (#prin-logic).

payload.title: Logic lives in a program, and Markdown holds prompt text only
payload.why: An agent follows a rule in prose most of the time, but a product needs it followed every time. A prompt file also runs only inside one agent harness. So every rule that must give the same result for the same input is code, and a prompt holds only the work that needs judgement.
payload.body:
A step goes in the program if the same input must always give the same result: a state change, a staleness walk, a contract check, a retry cap, a time limit, a merge. A step goes in a prompt if it needs judgement: writing a spec, grading against a rubric, reviewing a diff, classifying a stuck agent. The program builds the prompt, sends it, parses the answer and decides what happens next. A prompt holds no control flow: "if the checks fail, retry three times" is a loop, so it is code.

A skill file, where one exists, is a thin wrapper that names the command to run and holds no rule of its own.

The closest prior art is a planning skill that charts an effort as a map of decision tickets in a tracker. It shares the idea of a plan as a map of decisions worked one at a time. As a prompt file it cannot do what needs a program: walk a truth edge to mark dependent decisions suspect, keep a rejected alternative with its reason, and refuse a decision that lacks a required fact. Those three are why werk's map is a program.

Example: the decide check refuses a card with no basis or no kill criterion and prints the command that fixes it. As prose in the agent instructions, the same rule was skipped twice.

kill.text: Revisit only if the standalone-product constraint is dropped.

payload.title: A written rule about a record is enforced by a check when the record changes state
payload.why: A rule that exists only as prose is forgotten without anyone noticing, and the records drift. A check at the state change catches it at the one moment the rule applies, and a printed fix lets the agent correct itself.
payload.body:
A check has three parts. It runs when the record moves to the state the rule guards, not when the record is created, because a new record cannot yet meet the rule. Every refusal prints the exact command that fixes it, so the agent corrects itself with no person. Every rule has an escape hatch that writes a reason to the record, so a check never skips a rule silently.

Example:

- Ticket T-12, with the rule "a ticket moves to done only with a linked pull request".

1. An agent moves T-12 to done.
2. The check finds no linked pull request and refuses the move.
3. The refusal prints the command that links a pull request to T-12.
4. The agent links one and moves T-12 again. The move passes.
5. A research ticket with no pull request moves to done with a written reason. The reason stays on the record.

```
move T-12 to done ──▶ check: linked pull request?
                        ├─ yes ──▶ moved
                        ├─ no  ──▶ refused + prints the fix command ──▶ agent runs it ──▶ retry
                        └─ waiver with a reason ──▶ moved, reason recorded
```

payload.title: Every agent that werk starts and that can write to the map gets werk's agent instructions
payload.why: An agent follows only the rules it reads. A build pass runs in the project's own repository, whose instruction files know nothing about the map. So werk gives one instruction text to each agent it starts, added after the agent's own system prompt so the agent keeps its base rules for its tools.
payload.body:
werk keeps one instruction text for agents: how to keep the map current, how to propose and word a card, how to review marked cards, and how to tag who decides. The text is about any project, not about werk. werk adds it to the system prompt of the chat agent, each build pass and the plan writers. Every command in the text starts with the word werk (#agents-cli-name).

werk appends the text to the end of the agent's own system prompt and never replaces it. The agent's base prompt holds the rules for its tools, and the werk text does not restate them. The project's own instruction files load as they do without werk.

An agent with a narrow contract does not get the text, because the text would contradict that contract. The product-diagram agents edit the diagram, which the text forbids. A model call with no tools cannot act on the map at all.

When the project is werk itself, its own instruction file already includes the text, so werk does not add it a second time.

kill.text: A build pass or the chat agent proposes a card that breaks the wording rules it was given.

payload.title: The agent instructions write out every rule they use and cite no card of werk's own map
payload.why: An agent in another project reads that project's map, not werk's. A card id from werk's map points at nothing there, so the rule behind it must be written in the text itself.
payload.body: Every rule that the instructions or a shipped subagent rely on is written out in plain words where it is used. An example names no real card and uses a made-up id, such as #checkout-retry. The rule holds for werk's own map too: the text reads the same in every project, and a change to a werk card does not change what an agent is told until the text changes with it.

kill.text: An agent in a target project fails because a rule it needs is missing from the text.

payload.title: The subagents that the agent instructions name travel with them into every project
payload.why: An instruction to use a subagent that the project does not have fails at the moment the agent needs it. So the subagent definitions go wherever the instructions go, and each prompt goes out as written because every werk command in it starts with the word werk.
payload.body: The instructions tell an agent to use subagents that a project does not define: one that builds the options of a fork (#align-build-options) and one that classifies a module before its tests are written. werk ships their definitions with the instructions, and each agent that gets the instructions also gets the subagents. Inside a werk checkout the project already defines the same subagents, so werk adds nothing.

kill.text: A build pass in a target project asks for a subagent that is not there.

payload.title: A chat reply names the map operation, not the command line that runs it
payload.why: The person reads a reply in the chat pane and acts in the map, not in a terminal. A full command line with its path and flags tells them nothing they can use. The name of the operation, such as decide or accept, tells them what comes next.
payload.body: The chat agent names an operation by its plain name when it tells the person what it did or what to do next, for example "Next: accept #checkout-retry". The agent still runs the full command itself. A full command line appears in a reply only when the person must run it in a terminal.

kill.text: A person must copy a command out of the chat to finish a step that the map cannot do.

payload.title: An agent reads an image directly, and uses a subagent only for a long image loop or a short text fact
payload.why: Reading an image gives the model a native image block of at most about five thousand tokens, because large images are scaled down first. A large context comes from text and tool output, not from a few images. A subagent that reads the image for the agent returns text, which loses overlaps, spacing and colours.
payload.body: The default is a direct read. A subagent reads the images in two cases only: a render-and-check loop that will read more than about ten images in one session, so the images stay out of the main context, and a task that needs only a short text fact from the image. A subagent gets a list of what to check, because a subagent with no list reports only what it finds notable.

payload.title: Every question to the person shows at least two contrasting options
payload.why: One option turns a decision into a rubber stamp, because judgement needs contrast. A person builds a preference faster from options that differ along one feature than from an explanation of the feature, so showing variants aligns intent better than asking open questions.
payload.body:
When the agent needs the person to choose, it shows at least two options. The options differ along the one dimension in question, the set stays small, and each option carries a short rationale. Every option is a real reading of the requirement; the agent never adds a filler option such as "I do not care".

The agent builds alignment with the person by talking, by asking about one fork at a time, and by showing prototypes when prose cannot show the difference (#align-build-options).

payload.title: The chat agent writes the options of a question itself, with no subagent before it
payload.why: A subagent that judged whether to sample before each question found nothing to sample in a month of use, because most forks are rules that two sentences of prose state fully. Writing the options directly saves one subagent call per question.
payload.body: Before the agent asks the person to choose between readings of a requirement, it writes the contrasting options itself. When the person can judge an option only by looking at a built result, the agent has each option built first (#align-build-options), and the question carries the results.

kill.text: The person rejects every written option of a question as missing the reading they meant, three times in one month.

payload.title: A prototype is thrown away, and only its screenshot, its patch and a short note survive
payload.why: Prototype code has prototype quality. If production started from it, the review would have to fight that quality. So the production build starts from the brief and the decision, and the prototype leaves only a record.
payload.body: An option that must change tracked files is built in its own throwaway copy of the project; any other option writes only into its own artifact folder. The build leaves a screenshot, a short note on the trade-off and, when it changed tracked files, a patch file. These attach to the option as evidence and outlive the run. The copy is deleted, even when the build fails or runs out of time. The patch is a record, not code to merge.

payload.title: Named options are built side by side, one artifact per option, for the person to compare
payload.why: A person often cannot choose between versions described in prose, but chooses at once between versions they can look at. So the options are named first and each one is built separately and at the same time, so one option's changes never reach another option's result.
payload.body:
The person asks for options by name, or the agent names them before a question. A prototyper subagent gets the fork and its options. It first asks whether two sentences of prose make the difference clear; if they do, it answers that no build is needed (#align-build-tier). Otherwise it makes one call to werk, which builds every option at the same time. The unit is an option: one artifact per option.

Each build is a one-shot headless agent process with its tools allowed up front, not a chat conversation, because nobody answers its questions. A build may not ask a question; where the brief is open, it picks a reading and says so. The count of builds and their wall-clock time are capped. Each build leaves a screenshot and, for a source change, a patch (#align-ephem). werk records each result as evidence on its option. The main agent writes the option cards; the prototyper only reads and builds.

Parallel builds run in werk's program, not as nested subagents, because a subagent cannot reliably start subagents of its own and the build noise would fill the main agent's context.

Example:

- Brief "Show the open card's sub-cards", option A "A grid of tiles", option B "A compact list".

1. The person asks to build A and B.
2. werk starts two builds at the same time.
3. Each build leaves a screenshot on its option. A layout changes no tracked file, so neither build copies the project.
4. The person opens both screenshots and picks A. B stays as a rejected option, with its screenshot as the reason.
5. If build B fails or runs past its time limit, B shows the error and A still completes.

```
A "A grid of tiles" ──▶ build A ──▶ screenshot A ─┐
                                                  ├──▶ person picks A
B "A compact list"  ──▶ build B ──▶ screenshot B ─┘
        (A and B run at the same time)
```

kill.text: Over one month, the person picks from the prose of the options without opening the built versions in most comparisons.

payload.title: An option is built only as far as its difference needs to be seen
payload.why: A built option costs an agent run and often a copy of the project, and most choices are rules that two sentences state fully. A build pays only when the person must look at the result, such as a layout, a wording or a timing, and a copy of the project pays only when the option must change tracked files.
payload.body:
Three steps, each only when the one before is not enough. If two sentences of prose make the difference clear, nothing is built: the agent writes the options and asks. If the difference must be seen but no option changes tracked files, each option writes its artifact into its own private output folder and reads the project as it stands; distinct folders cannot collide, so the builds run in parallel with no git operation. If an option must change tracked files, it gets its own throwaway worktree, and the diff becomes its patch.

Example:

- Q1 "Where does the remove button sit on a card?", A "top right corner", B "bottom of the card".
- Q2 "Does a removed card keep its id?", A "the id stays taken", B "the id is free again".

1. For Q1, prose does not show which looks right, and a mockup needs no change to tracked files, so each option gets a mockup in its own output folder.
2. For Q2, two sentences state each option fully, so nothing is built and the agent asks.

```
question ──▶ does prose show the difference?
               ├─ yes ──▶ write the options and ask              (Q2)
               └─ no  ──▶ must an option change tracked files?
                            ├─ no  ──▶ one output folder per option   (Q1)
                            └─ yes ──▶ one worktree per option, diffed to a patch
```

payload.title: Every proposed change to a card is shown as marks inside the one card, never as a before and after pair
payload.why: Reviewing a change to a brief is much faster than reviewing a rewritten brief. A before section next to an after section is a rewrite in two pieces that the reader must compare by eye.
payload.body: Every change to a card's words goes through a staged proposal (#map-proposal). The agent never writes a before section and an after section, in the card or in the chat, and never sends a rewritten card as plain text. The person always sees one card with the changes marked inside it (#align-diff-look).

payload.title: A proposal marks each changed word in blue, a new card is blue all over, and a removal is red
payload.why: A reader must find every change in one scan, without reading word by word, and must tell at once what the accept will do. A blue highlight shows every change; a whole blue card says the card is new; red says the accept takes a card out of the map.
payload.body:
The marks are the same in the title, the why and the body. Added text has a blue highlight. Removed text has a blue highlight and a strikethrough. There is no plus sign and no before or after label. A list or a heading is marked line by line: old and new list items pair up one by one, so one added, removed or reworded item is marked alone.
