Only a block that changes kind, such as a paragraph that becomes a list, shows the old block removed and the new block added. Inside a reworded block only the changed words are marked.

A new card has a blue border and a blue background. An edit to a card has a blue border only. Both carry the badge "proposed", and so does the tile of a card with a pending change. A proposed removal uses the stale colours instead: a red border, a red background tint, a red badge and a red accept button, because its accept takes the card out of the map.

kill.text: The person reads a real proposal and cannot find every change at a glance, cannot tell a new card from an edit, or confuses a removal with a stale card.

payload.title: werk keeps no record of how the person decides
payload.why: A standing preference lets an agent settle a repeated trade-off without asking the person again. Each decision on the map settles a different trade-off, so such a record would hold entries that nothing reads a second time.
payload.body: A decision profile would record how the person decides, not what to build: preferences that hold across work items, such as "fewer dependencies over a faster build". An agent would check it before a question and apply a matching entry. The profile pays only when a kind of trade-off comes back, and none has. When one does, the profile starts from the portable decision-profile format in the evidence.

kill.text: The same kind of trade-off comes up a second time, and a standing preference would have answered it.

payload.title: Out of scope is a postponement, and the map has no third state and no destination node
payload.why: Work ruled out of scope means we do not build it now, not never, because plans change after a few passes. A postponement already says that, and it pauses every card that needs the postponed one. A destination node is not needed either, because the root claim is never reached and the rollup already says when a subtree is finished.
payload.body:
A ruled-out card is postponed with one sentence that says why. Every card that depends on it is paused, because nothing that needs it can be built either. A postponed card still counts as open in the rollup, which is correct: it has something left to decide later. The rollup draws the postponed share inside each status band.

A decision that something must never be built has two existing shapes: a reopen with the reason rejected, when the content is wrong, or a decided card that states the opposite and keeps the original as a rejected option.

werk's map outlives every effort, so it has no per-effort finish line or destination. The stopping rule is a reading of the rollup per subtree (#map-finished).

payload.title: A subtree is finished when its rollup has no open and no proto card, and buildable when only postponed ones remain
payload.why: A written finish line is an arbitrary stopping point, because discussion always finds more detail. So no bar is written. Finished is read off the rollup, and the build reads the same with postponed cards left out, because postponed work is deliberately not being done.
payload.body:
Finished means every card in the subtree is decided and every card that needs a prototype has been built and judged. Buildable is the same with postponed cards left out. Both are readings of counts the rollup already has; neither needs a field or a new count.

Finished is weaker than drained on purpose. Finished answers whether any work is left. Drained also requires that no decision by the person went unchallenged, and answers whether the decisions were contested.

payload.title: werk ships as one executable file per platform, with the runtime and the built client inside
payload.why: A user should install werk without first installing a runtime of the right version. The runtime compiles the server, its packages, itself and the built client into one file. So the user gets one file that starts werk, and every user runs the same runtime version that the checks ran on.
payload.body:
Each release builds one executable for macOS and Linux, each on ARM and Intel. Windows is out until a user needs it. The file holds the server code, its packages, the runtime and the built client, and werk serves the client from inside the file. The agent command line stays a separate install, because werk starts it as a child process and the user logs in to it.

Inside the executable there is no source folder, so two rules hold in a checkout too, and the same code runs in both. First, werk never finds a part of itself by listing a folder: the list of its own commands, client files, prompts and subagents is written when the bundler reads the code, and the release embeds those files. The user's files, such as the map and the repository, are read from disk. Second, werk never starts itself through a runtime and a source path: a child process and an agent prompt name werk (see #agents-cli-name). The executable has no source to reload, so it serves with no hot reload.

A user installs the file through one channel (#proj-channel), and a person releases it (#proj-release).

kill.text: The release check installs the file on a clean machine of each platform, starts werk, opens the map and runs one chat turn. If that fails on a platform and a fix needs changes to werk's code, fall back to a package.

payload.title: Users install and update werk through a Homebrew tap
payload.why: Homebrew is on most macOS developer machines and runs on Linux. It downloads the right file for the platform, checks its checksum, puts it on the path and updates it with the user's other tools. So werk needs no installer or update command of its own.
payload.body: werk's project owns a tap, a git repository of formulas. The formula points at a release's executables and their checksums, and each release updates it. Each release also attaches the files for direct download, for a machine without Homebrew; a direct download gets no automatic update. Homebrew does not set the untrusted mark that a browser download gets, so the tap needs no platform signing. Signing becomes necessary only if direct download becomes the main channel.

kill.text: Revisit when users without Homebrew ask for werk.

payload.title: A person releases a version by tagging a green commit on the main line
payload.why: The merge loop merges many tickets a day, and a subtree is often half built. A release on every merge would ship half-built features and a new version every hour. A person picks the commit, and automation does every step after it, so a release is one action.
payload.body: A release starts when a person puts a version tag on a commit of the main line. The tag is refused unless that commit's clean-machine run is green. The tag starts an automated run that builds the executable for each platform, attaches the files and their checksums to a release, and updates the Homebrew formula. The release notes list the cards that became decided since the previous tag. The version follows semantic versioning: major for a change that breaks the map files or a command, minor for a feature, patch for a fix.

kill.text: Releases happen less often than once a month because nobody tags.

payload.title: werk publishes its state one way to an external issue tracker that each project configures
payload.why: A tracker lets a person read the plan on a phone, keeps the record after the branch is gone, and allows queries across past work items. werk's own log stays the source of truth, so the tracker is only a publish target, and the tracker differs per project.
payload.body:
werk publishes the current state and republishes it from the current log whenever the log changes. It never reads the tracker back: an edit made in the tracker does not reach the log, and the next publish overwrites it. Simplicity wins over a second editable interface, and offline work keeps working. Each project picks its tracker, for example Linear for work and GitHub Issues for side projects. One adapter with a small fixed set of operations hides which tracker it is, so no prompt knows which tracker it talks to and a new tracker costs one adapter.

A ticket description is plain text, a field that every tracker has (#proj-tracker-format). werk uses no vendor-only agent-session interface, so there is no live progress in the tracker while an agent runs; the ticket updates when the agent ends.

payload.title: Each card is one tracker ticket, linked to the others, and the gates are mirrored from werk
payload.why: A ticket does not have to stand alone, because the tracker is only a publish target. One ticket per card with links needs no rule for how deep to walk a subtree or what to inline. A gate is triggered in werk and only mirrored to the tracker, because werk never reads the tracker back.
payload.body:
A related card becomes a separate ticket, linked. A dependency uses the tracker's native blocking relation where one exists, in both Linear and GitHub. A rejected option and evidence have no native match, so they go into a plain links section of the description. How to publish the tree placement of a card is not settled.

The person approves a gate in werk's own interface, which also works on a phone. werk records the gate in its log first, then sets the matching tracker state or label. A ticket carries a kind: a buildable ticket passes through the gates, and a decision ticket closes when its card is settled, with no in-progress phase.

Open: does a new link republish every ticket it touches, or only the two tickets at its ends?

payload.title: Build runs a builder loop for each ticket and a merge loop for each run
payload.why: One ticket is built alone in its own worktree, and a run merges many tickets into one tree. The two jobs stop for different reasons, so they are two loops.
payload.body:
Build turns the tickets of a planned subtree into merged, checked code on the target repository's main line. The builder loop takes one ticket to green in its own worktree (#build-ticket). The merge loop takes the green tickets one at a time onto the main line and runs the held-out set after each merge (#build-merge).

The per-ticket step is called check, not validate. Validate is the stage that holds what the builder cannot see.

payload.title: Two rubrics are built into the tool: one for prototypes and one for production code
payload.why: A loop needs a stop condition. The bar differs by whether the output is thrown away or merged, not by work item, so the tool ships two fixed rubrics and never derives one per run.
payload.body:
A rubric is the stop condition of a loop. A loop uses the prototype rubric when its artifact is thrown away after it answers a question (#pipe-rubric-proto), and the production rubric when its code merges.

A rubric has up to three sections. Checks are deterministic: a command and its exit code, with no model (#pipe-rubric-checks). Judgements need an agent, because no exit code answers them: the grader (#pipe-grader) and, for production code, the quality review (#pipe-review). The held-out set is withheld from the builder and belongs to validate (see #val-heldout). The prototype rubric has no held-out section: held-out exists to stop a builder gaming a bar it can see, and a throwaway builds up nothing worth gaming.

A builder pass clears the checks itself. The judgements run after green checks, and the held-out set runs after the merge.

A rubric is written once, not per work item. A rubric derived per run needs an approval per run, and that recurring input is what the rubric exists to remove. The rubrics name roles, not tools, so the same rubric fits every project: each project binds the check names to its own commands.

kill.text: A project needs a bar that binding the check names to its own commands cannot express.

payload.title: A rubric line is a check when one command's exit code decides it, and a judgement otherwise
payload.why: A check and a judgement fail in different ways and are fixed in different ways. One test for the dividing line stops each borderline line from being argued twice, once when it is written and once when it fails.
payload.body:
Every rubric line belongs to one of two layers.

A check is one command that decides the line the same way on every run. Its exit code is the whole verdict. A threshold counts, so a coverage percentage is a check. A check names its command, not the property it wants: a type-check command, not "the types are right". Its output is for the agent: the agent runs it, reads the failure, fixes the code and runs it again. No person reads a check, and nothing grades or negotiates with one.

A judgement is an agent that reads the diff against one decided card and returns a score and the gap (see #pipe-grader).

The dividing line: if pass or fail needs someone to weigh the output, the line is a judgement. If a command can decide it, the line is a check, even when it looks like a quality question. Example: "no new public function without a doc comment" is a lint rule, so it is a check. Which checks the builder sees is a separate question from which layer a line is in.

payload.title: A check line calls a make target of the project, not a tool
payload.why: A tool name in a rubric binds it to one toolchain. A make target lives in the project beside its code, so the rubric line means the same thing in a web, backend or mobile project, and a change of tool is a one-line edit in the project.
payload.body:
Every check line is a make target, such as `make test`, `make lint` or `make typecheck`. The rubric holds the name, and the project holds the command behind it: a Node project, an iOS project and an Android project each answer `make test` with their own tool.

A check is only as strong as the target behind it: a lint target with no configuration passes. A project with no such target gets one. A missing target is work to do, not a reason to call a tool directly.

payload.title: Every project builds in a git repository of its own, outside werk
payload.why: werk is a product that builds other projects, so where werk keeps its own data says nothing about where a project lives. This also holds when the project is werk.
payload.body:
Each project names one git repository as its target. The worktrees, the checks, the merges and the held-out runs happen there, on its main line (#build-merge). werk keeps the project's map, board, specs and tickets in its own store, never in the target. There is no default target: a project with no target cannot start a build. The werk under construction is a target project like any other (#prin-product).

The target is one fact of the project, recorded in the project's board log; the latest record is the current target. A path is accepted as a target only when all of these hold: it does not overlap werk's store, it is the top folder of a git repository and not a folder inside one, and the repository has a main line. A main line is a branch named main or master, or, in a repository with no commit yet, the branch that HEAD names when that name is main or master.

kill.text: Build a project whose map lives in werk's store: only the target repository's main line moves, and a project with no target refuses to build.

payload.title: Each builder pass is a fresh agent, and the repository is the only memory between passes
payload.why: A long agent context degrades, and it keeps the memory of a failed attempt. The file system and git do not degrade, so a fresh agent per pass that reads the branch history works from the true state.
payload.body:
No agent lives longer than one pass. Each pass gets the brief, the decided cards it needs, the rubric and the last failure, does one unit of work and exits.

1. The loop makes one worktree for the ticket.
2. Pass n starts a fresh agent in the worktree. Its prompt holds the brief, the decided cards in the ticket's closure, and the last failure: the failed step and the end of its output, cut to about 4,000 characters.
3. When the agent exits, the loop commits the worktree as pass n. The next agent reads the history with git and gets nothing else from earlier passes.
4. The loop runs its own verdict steps. The loop's run is the verdict, even if the agent ran the checks itself.
5. All green: stop. Red: keep the failure and go to step 2. At the retry cap: stop and keep the branch.
6. Each pass is recorded as a started and an ended step in the pipeline log, with its results, time and cost (#ms-store).

The loop has no long-session mode. The long session is the fallback of the kill criterion and is built again only if it fires.

kill.text: metric: builder passes and tokens per ticket, per story (see #ms-trend-size). The planned comparison against one long session on real tickets has not run.

payload.title: The builder loop runs fresh passes on one ticket until its checks, grader and review all pass
payload.why: A fix is a new pass with the failure in its input, so the loop needs no separate fix step. The cheap verdict runs first, and a grader or reviewer that breaks must never let a pass through.
payload.body:
One ticket, one worktree. A pass has four steps:

1. Implement. A fresh builder agent does one unit of work toward the ticket (#build-implement).
2. Check. The ticket's checks run in order and stop at the first red one (#pipe-check-layers).
3. Grade. Only on green checks, a grader scores the diff against each decided card of the ticket's closure; a card it leaves out scores 0 (#pipe-grader).
4. Review. Only on a passing grade, one reviewer per quality area reads the diff (#pipe-review).

A red step, or a grader or reviewer that breaks or goes silent, fails the pass with the reason in the next brief, and a new pass starts at step 1. A retry cap stops the loop (#build-retry-cap).

The worktree starts from the main line's tip. The next build of a ticket continues from the branch of its earlier build when that branch sits on top of the main line's tip; otherwise it starts again from the tip. So a conflict at the merge, a stop or an archive leaves work that the next build reuses.

payload.title: The implement step runs the project's implement skill on the whole ticket
payload.why: The implement skill already holds the implement process, so werk keeps no second copy that drifts. The loop still gives the verdict, so the skill's own tests only help the agent.
payload.body:
Each pass starts with the /implement skill and then gives its input: the ticket (title, what to build, acceptance criteria), the spec lines of the stories it delivers (#plan-ticket), the decided cards it cites with their rejected options and the reason each lost, the ticket's checks, the build's card obligation (#build-card-obligation), and the last failure if there is one. The first pass is told that nothing is done yet.

Three rules are added to the skill: do not weaken, skip or delete a test to make a check pass; ask no questions; propose a card for each decision that no card gives, at the moment it is made (#build-missing-decision). The loop commits any change the agent left uncommitted.

A ticket names no file paths, so the agent explores the code itself in every pass.

payload.title: A builder that meets a question no card answers searches the map, then proposes a card and builds on it
payload.why: A gap in the map looks like a failing ticket: the builder fixes one symptom per pass, the reviewer finds the next, and the cap parks the ticket and all that need it. Searching the whole map first stops the builder from deciding again what another branch already decided; a proposal it builds on keeps the run moving, and the person rules later.
payload.body:
Each pass gets the id and title of every decided card. Before it decides a question that no cited card answers, it searches the map for the terms of the question and reads every match. A decided card that answers the question binds the pass like a cited card.

Only when the search finds no answer does the pass become a decision pass. The gap shows when the next pass names the last failure's cause a spec gap (#ms-fail-cause), or when the grader or reviewers raise findings in one area in two passes in a row and no cited card answers the question behind them. The builder states the question, picks an answer by a fixed guideline, and proposes a card with its options and depends_on (#map-ghost). The guideline picks the answer that is safest when wrong and easiest to undo: deny by default, least privilege, the smallest interface, no data deleted; on a tie, the answer that changes the fewest decided cards. Who decides is the person; no agent accepts it.

From that pass on the ticket cites the proposal, the grader and reviewers judge against it as if decided, and the ticket may merge on it. An accept leaves everything as it is. A discard, or an amend that changes the answer, files a rework follow-up for every merged ticket that cited it, the way a changed card blocks an open ticket (#plan-ticket-watch). The run's end report lists every builder proposal first. A ticket still red after its decision pass parks as usual (#build-stuck-park).

kill.text: metric: share of builder proposals from a decision pass that the person discards or changes

payload.title: A ticket's retry cap counts its failed passes across all its builds, except spec gaps and conflicts
payload.why: The cap must stop a ticket that keeps failing for its own reason, but not spend passes on causes outside the ticket. A spec gap needs its decision pass, a conflict means another ticket merged first, and a person who retries a stuck ticket after a fix needs passes to run.
payload.body:
Each build starts with a retry cap (default 5), recorded at its start. The cap counts failed passes across every build of the ticket, so it also bounds the trips between the builder and the merge queue. A silenced, looping, timed-out or dead pass counts.

Three kinds of pass do not count. A pass whose cause is a spec gap (#ms-fail-cause), or a grader gap that a person must settle: the decision pass after it always runs, and once the ticket cites the proposal, later failures count, so a ticket gets one free pass per open question. A pass that fails on a conflict with the main line: a conflict at the merge queue (#build-conflict), and up to three clashes with the tip inside one build (#build-tip-in). And when a person moves a stuck ticket to ready or building, the budget starts again at the full cap; the spent passes stay in the record. A ticket that leaves blocked only because the ticket it waited on merged keeps its spent passes.

Example, cap 5: passes 1 to 4 fail on builder errors (count 4). Pass 5 fails on a spec gap (count stays 4). Pass 6 is the decision pass and fails a check (count 5): the ticket parks.

kill.text: A decision pass runs and the pass after it names a spec gap again for the same question.

payload.title: Each pass merges the main line's tip into the ticket's branch before its checks run
payload.why: Module names cannot catch every shared file, so two tickets can each be green alone and clash at the merge queue after a full pass. Merging the tip first turns the clash into a failure of the pass, where the builder is already working, and makes the checks see the tree the merge queue will check.
payload.body:
Right after the builder commits and before any check, the pass merges the main line's current tip into the branch. When the main line has not moved, nothing is merged.

A clean merge: the checks, grader and review run on the merged tree, and the tip becomes the base of the grader's diff, so the grader sees only this ticket's changes. A conflict: the pass fails with the conflict as its failure, the merge stays open in the worktree, and the next pass resolves it (#build-conflict). Up to three such conflict passes in one build cost no retry; after that each counts.

kill.text: metric: share of merges that end as a conflict at the merge queue

payload.title: On the last counted pass, small grader gaps merge and become a follow-up ticket
payload.why: A ticket whose only problems left are small gaps in cards it did build would park at the cap with all its work unmerged and every later ticket waiting. Merging it and filing the gaps as their own ticket keeps the work moving and keeps each gap visible.
payload.body:
A small gap is a failed grade line on a decided card that the diff builds, scored one point under a pass, that no person must settle. An unmet acceptance criterion, a behaviour out of scope, an unrecorded decision, a plain contradiction, or a gap only a person can settle still fails the pass.

Before the last counted pass, a small gap fails the pass as usual. When the pass that would use up the cap fails only on small gaps, it counts as green and the review still runs. If the review is green, the ticket merges and a follow-up ticket is filed: it cites the cards of the gaps, quotes each gap as the grader wrote it, and waits on the board until the source ticket is done. The follow-up passes the same ticket checks as any ticket, so file paths in a quoted gap are cut to the bare file name; a follow-up that still fails them is not filed.

kill.text: Follow-ups for deferred gaps pile up unbuilt, or a deferred gap turns out to break a user path.

payload.title: Archiving a building ticket ends its build, and nothing of that build merges
payload.why: A build runs from the merge loop or from a single build command, and only the builder loop is present in both. When the builder loop itself watches the board, an archive ends every build the same way, with no second process to notice it.
payload.body:
While a build runs, its builder loop reads the board about once a second. When it finds its ticket archived, it stops the pass's agent, commits nothing of that pass, runs no checks, records no retry, and ends. An archive during the checks or grade of a pass also ends the build: nothing merges, even a pass that ended green. The worktree goes and the branch stays.

The archive ends one build. It is not a stop of the merge loop: the loop merges nothing of that ticket and goes on with its other tickets, and no other ticket moves back to ready.

kill.text: Archive a building ticket during a run: if any of it merges, its branch is gone, or another ticket moves back to ready, revisit.

payload.title: The building column holds only tickets that a live session builds
payload.why: A ticket left in building after its session ended looks like work in progress when none runs, and a person must move it by hand. So every way a build or a loop ends moves its tickets out of building, by how it ended.
payload.body: A green build of one ticket moves it to merging, with the branch that holds the green work; the build does not merge it, because the merge loop owns every change to the main line, and its next run on the subtree merges that branch before any new build. A single build red at its retry cap, or a build that breaks for a reason other than a red pass, moves the ticket back to ready with the reason; the worktree goes and the branch stays. Inside a run, a ticket red at its cap parks in blocked as stuck instead (#build-stuck-park). A merge loop that stops for any reason (stuck, a cap, a deadlock, a person's stop) moves every ticket it left in building or merging back to ready, with the stop reason, and its next start builds those tickets first. An archive takes the ticket out of the columns (#build-archive-ends).

kill.text: After a build or a run ends, the board shows a ticket in building that no session builds.

payload.title: The server restarts a build whose process died, as a fresh pass from the ticket's branch
payload.why: A build runs in its own process, apart from the server, and that process can die from a kill, a crash or a machine sleep. Nothing inside a dead process sees its own death, so the server, which already checks whether each build process is alive, writes the end and starts a fresh pass from the committed work.
payload.body:
A build is dead when the board log has its start, no end, and its process is gone. The server looks for dead builds when a build process it started exits and when the server itself starts; while the server is down, nothing watches. For each dead build the server:

1. Writes the end with died as the reason, and records the dead pass as a red pass, with zero wall time and no cost, because the dead process cannot report them.
2. Starts a fresh pass of the same ticket from the last commit on its branch, with the death as the last failure in the brief. Work the dead pass did not commit is lost, at most one pass.
3. Gives the fresh pass the retry cap the dead build started with, and counts the death against it, so a build that dies on every pass still stops.

The fresh pass runs as its own process group through the build's public command and outlives the server. It continues the dead build: same build identity, same card obligation. A build whose process is alive is left alone, whichever server started it.

kill.text: A restarted build dies again on most of its passes: the restart only burns the cap.

payload.title: Every pipeline agent starts through one runner, whatever its role
payload.why: Each role needs the same launch work: a time limit, a session log, its model, its environment and the overseer. If each role started its own agent, a fix to one launch would miss the others. One runner makes every role share each fix.
payload.body: A role differs only in its prompt, its tool list, its model and the reply it parses. The runner does the rest of the launch: it holds the overseer (see #build-overseer), picks the model from the role (see #pipe-model-per-role) and writes the session file (see #ms-store-detail). Start and end records belong to a step, which may run several sessions, so the steps write them. The chat conversation is not a pipeline agent: it has its own child and takes the same launch options for its role.

kill.text: A pipeline role starts its agent without the runner and lacks the time limit, the session log or the overseer.

payload.title: A plain-code overseer inside the agent runner ends every pipeline session that is stuck
payload.why: The pipeline runs without a person, so a stuck agent stops the run until someone looks. Most liveness questions have an answer without a model, and a watcher that is itself an agent can stall like the agents it watches.
payload.body:
The overseer watches each agent session that the pipeline starts: builder passes, graders, reviewers, the held-out binder and the plan writers. It acts on four signs: a permission ask that nobody answers (#build-overseer-asks), no new event for too long (#build-overseer-silence), a tool call that is frozen (#build-overseer-inflight), and a session that loops (#build-overseer-loop). It is the safety control that makes auto-merge possible.

The overseer is plain code: a timer inside the runner that starts each session, reading the session's event stream. It starts a model only for a question that needs judgement, as a short classification call that it waits on with a timeout like any tool call. Nothing watches the overseer, and it has no model inside it to stall. Every overseer act is a line in the session log.

Chat-pane and terminal sessions have no overseer; a person watches them.

kill.text: A chat-pane or terminal session stays stuck and nobody sees it for a long time.

payload.title: The overseer answers a builder's permission ask itself, and no verdict means deny
payload.why: The loop runs without a person, so an ask that waits for one stops the agent until someone looks. A classifier that does not answer must never widen a permission.
payload.body: A builder session runs in the automatic permission mode with the standard edit tools plus make and git allowed. Any other call that the agent's own permission engine cannot settle is an ask. The overseer sends the ask to a classification call with the tool, its input and the ticket. If the ask makes sense for the ticket, it is allowed. Otherwise it is denied, with a comment that says why; the agent reads it and continues without the call. No verdict means deny. Every answer and its comment goes into the session log, for a person to read later.

payload.title: A session that writes no event for 60 seconds is cancelled, and the builder starts a fresh pass
payload.why: The named signs cover known causes, but an agent can also stall for a cause nobody named, such as a retry storm or a rate limit. One silent pass is no evidence that the ticket cannot be built, because such a stall goes away on a new session.
payload.body:
The silence clock measures the time between two events of a session. It starts at the agent's first event, because start-up time grows under load; before that, only the wall-clock cap applies (#build-overseer-loop). Every piece of text the model generates counts as an event, so a long file write is not silence; these partial messages only keep the clock armed and are not written to the session log. A running tool call is not silence: the in-flight rule decides about it (#build-overseer-inflight).

The limit is 60 seconds, a starting value. The held-out binder gets 3 minutes, because it starts the product and runs long test commands that print nothing until they end.

A silent builder session is cancelled and the loop starts a fresh pass whose brief says the last pass went silent; the silenced pass commits its edits, skips the checks, and counts against the cap. A silent grader or reviewer fails its step with silence as the reason.

kill.text: metric: silence cancels per 100 agent sessions

payload.title: The overseer tells a working tool call from a frozen one by its process and its stream
payload.why: A test that waits on a promise that never resolves looks the same from outside as a long build. Only the process tree and the event stream show the difference, and a fixed wall-clock limit on calls would cancel long work that is still going.
payload.body:
A tool call that has started and has no result is in flight. While it runs, the overseer samples the call's process tree for CPU time, and watches its output and the agent's event stream: while a call runs, the agent itself is quiet, so any new event comes from the work in flight, such as a subagent. A call is working while its CPU time or its output grows; flat for the silence limit (#build-overseer-silence) it is frozen. A subagent call has no process tree of its own, so its events are its only sign of work.

A frozen call is cancelled and the agent gets the cancel, with the evidence, as the call's result and continues. A frozen call with no process of its own cancels the session, like silence.

A probe that cannot read the process table gives no evidence: the sample counts as unknown, adds nothing to the flat time, and cancels nothing. Only a read that ran can report that a call has no process. During a probe failure a real stall runs to the wall-clock cap; that cost is accepted over cancelling a pass that may be working and charging the ticket for a fault in werk's probe. Each failed probe is recorded, and each pass records its count of samples and of failed samples.

kill.text: metric: share of process probe samples that failed. Also revisit when a looping subagent holds a session open to its wall-clock limit.

payload.title: A classifier judges every 5 minutes whether a session loops, and its verdict decides whether the wall-clock cap extends
payload.why: Progress has no fingerprint a program can compute: a loop that changes one character each pass looks new to any hash, so whether work moves forward is a judgement. The same verdict lets a fixed cap tell a long healthy job from a stuck one.
payload.body:
Every 5 minutes the overseer asks a classifier whether each running session is looping. The input is the ticket's brief and the tool calls since the last verdict, not the whole log. The output is looping or not looping, with a one- or two-sentence reason. The classifier is skipped when there is no new tool call since its last verdict. No verdict counts as not looping. On looping, the overseer cancels the session and a fresh pass starts with the reason in its brief.

Every session also has a wall-clock cap, a parameter of the build. Every command that runs agents reads its caps through one shared clamp: a cap of at most 900 seconds and at most 5 agents at once. When a session reaches the cap with a last verdict of not looping, it gets another stretch as long as the cap, up to three stretches in all, so a wrong classifier cannot keep a session alive without end. A session with no verdict, or a looping one, ends at the cap. A builder session that ends at the cap commits what it left, skips the checks, and fails its pass with the reason; the pass counts against the cap.

Example, cap 600 s: pass A edits and tests and is judged not looping at 300 s, so at 600 s and 1200 s it gets new stretches and ends at 1800 s. Pass B is judged looping at 300 s and is cancelled then. Pass C makes no tool call, has no verdict, and ends at 600 s.

kill.text: metric: share of build sessions that end at the last stretch of the cap

payload.title: The merge loop merges green tickets straight onto the main line, one at a time, then runs the held-out set
payload.why: Each ticket is green alone. Only a check of the main line plus the ticket shows whether they are green together, and one merge at a time keeps the main line from moving under a merge. No run entity owns a plan's output, so nothing would own an integration branch, and one line to merge onto is the simplest start.
payload.body:
Starting the merge loop on a planned subtree is the trigger for its tickets; starting it again resumes. The loop schedules builds (#build-parallel) and takes green tickets through a merge queue, one at a time, straight onto the main line with no integration branch:

1. Merge the ticket's branch with the main line's tip in a temporary worktree.
2. Run the ticket's checks there, once each. A red check does not stop the merge (#build-merge-red).
3. Move the main line, but only from the value it had when the merge started, so a main line that moved in between is never overwritten. A checkout of the main line follows by fast-forward; a checkout whose local changes block that stops the loop, and nothing moves.
4. Start the held-out set on the new commit (#build-heldout-beside). This step belongs to validate (#val-stage).

A conflict sends the ticket back to the builder (#build-conflict), and so does a guarded move that fails because something else moved the main line. werk assumes one werk instance per repository and takes no lock. Build ends when every ticket is merged and G2 opens (#val-heldout-g2).

kill.text: A run reports a failed guarded move of the main line, or a person wants two werk instances in one repository.

payload.title: A red check at the merge does not stop the merge, and files a follow-up ticket to fix it
payload.why: The ticket's checks already ran on the ticket merged with the main line's tip, so a check red at the merge is rarely the ticket's fault and most often flaky. Merging anyway keeps the work moving, and the follow-up makes every red check, flaky or broken, a visible task; a rerun would hide a flaky check for the next ticket.
payload.body:
The merge queue runs each check once on the temporary tree and never again. A red check does not stop the merge: the main line moves, and the merge record names each red check. The queue then files one follow-up ticket for that merge. It names each red check with the tail of its output, cites the cards the merged ticket cites, has the red checks as its own checks, and waits on nothing. The builder that takes it decides whether the check or the code is wrong.

A conflict still sends the ticket back, because there is no merged tree to check. A stage after the checks that fails, such as a follow-up's own step gate (#build-followup-gate), still stops the merge. A red check inside a builder pass still fails that pass.

kill.text: Merge follow-ups for red checks are mostly real breakage, not flaky checks: the main line then carries broken code between a merge and its fix.

payload.title: A merge conflict is resolved on the ticket's own branch, costs no retry, and that ticket merges next
payload.why: A conflict means another ticket merged first, not that this ticket is wrong. A fresh rebuild takes as long as the first build, and the main line moves again meanwhile, so a ticket that touches a busy file would conflict again and again.
payload.body:
When git cannot merge a ticket, the next pass starts from the ticket's own branch with the main line's tip merged into it. The builder gets the conflicted files and the conflict output, resolves them, and runs the checks. The pass does not count against the retry cap. A ticket that comes back green from a conflict pass goes to the front of the merge queue, so no other merge can move the main line under it first.

A ticket whose merge conflicts ten times in a row is parked as stuck (#build-stuck-park). The limit is high because several tickets build at once, and a ticket that adds a line to a file most tickets change can lose the race several times.

kill.text: metric: share of conflict passes whose next merge conflicts again

payload.title: Up to 3 tickets build at once, and two tickets build together only when they touch no module in common
payload.why: The ticket blocking edges give the order, and the modules each ticket touches give the overlap. Serial builds make a run as long as the sum of its tickets, and two tickets that edit one module at once conflict at the merge queue.
payload.body:
A ticket can start when every ticket in its blocked_by list is merged and no failed set check holds it (#plan-ticket-checks). The run builds up to 3 such tickets at once, each in its own worktree off the main line's tip at the moment its build starts.

Each ticket names the modules it changes, by concept and not by file path (#plan-ticket). A ticket starts beside the ones already building only when their module names share none; otherwise it waits until the other has merged. The compare is of the names alone, trimmed and in lower case, with no agent. A list can still miss a shared file, which the tip merge in each pass catches (#build-tip-in). The cap of 3 is a first guess, and the merge queue still takes one ticket at a time.

kill.text: Merge conflicts send more than 1 ticket in 4 back to the builder over a run, or builds hit the rate limit or the machine cannot keep up with 3.

payload.title: A stuck ticket stops only itself and the tickets that need it
payload.why: If one stuck ticket ends the whole run, every independent ticket waits for a person, often overnight.
payload.body: A ticket that hits its retry cap or its conflict limit moves to blocked with the stop reason. Every ticket that needs it, directly or through others, stays blocked behind it. The merge loop goes on with every other ticket. The run ends only when nothing can build or merge, and then it reports each stuck ticket and what waits on it. A person who moves a stuck ticket back to ready gives it a new budget (#build-retry-cap).

kill.text: metric: share of tickets built after a park in the same run that also go stuck

payload.title: Red held-out steps become one follow-up per source ticket, and a source has at most one open follow-up of each kind
payload.why: One follow-up per source ticket lets each fix build, fail and stop on its own, so one step no builder can pass does not hold back other fixes. One open follow-up per kind takes later problems into itself, so several tickets do not change the same code at once and conflict.
payload.body:
Each held-out step comes from the brief of one source ticket. A red held-out run groups its red steps by source and files one follow-up per group; it cites the cards of its source and has its own retry cap. A red step that an open follow-up already carries files nothing.

A merged ticket has at most one open follow-up of each kind, for every kind: the step follow-up, which makes red held-out steps green; the rework, which brings the code in line with a decision that changed (#build-missing-decision); the check follow-up from a red check at the merge (#build-merge-red); the gap follow-up from grader gaps deferred on the last pass (#build-grade-defer); and the decision follow-up from a step that contradicts its cards (#val-heldout-contradiction). When a later problem of a kind arrives: with no open follow-up, a new one is filed; with one still in ready or blocked, it takes the new problem into its text and list; with one already building, its text does not change under the builder, so a rework files a new ticket, and every other kind files nothing, because the next held-out run, check or grade finds the problem again.

Nothing limits the number of follow-ups in a run. A step that no builder can make green gives a run that never reaches G2; that cost is accepted until a run shows a bug-fix loop.

kill.text: A run files follow-ups for the same held-out step more than once, or one merged ticket still has two open follow-ups of one kind.

payload.title: The held-out set runs beside the merge queue, and the next merge does not wait for it
payload.why: The held-out set grows with every merged ticket. While the merge queue waits for it, the green branches behind it age and conflict.
payload.body: After a merge, the held-out set starts on that merge's commit in the background, and the queue takes the next ticket at once. A red step files a follow-up for its source ticket (#build-followups). When a newer merge lands while a run is going, the older run is not stopped: each result belongs to its own commit, and only the result on the main line's final tip opens G2.

kill.text: metric: share of held-out runs that end with a step not run

payload.title: A step follow-up merges only when its own red steps pass on its merged tree
payload.why: A follow-up's checks never run the steps that made it, so it could merge with them still red and the next held-out run would file another. Running those few steps in its merge gate makes done mean the steps pass, and a step no builder can pass stops at the cap instead of looping.
payload.body: After the checks pass on the temporary tree, the binder runs the red steps that the follow-up carries, and only those, on that tree. All pass: the follow-up merges. A step ran and is red: nothing merges, and the ticket goes back to the builder with the step's text and what the binder saw (#val-heldout-feedback); the cap applies. A step the binder could not run does not block (#val-heldout-notrun). The whole held-out set still runs beside the queue; this gate waits only for one follow-up's steps.

kill.text: metric: merged follow-ups whose step is red again at the next held-out run

payload.title: A run refuses to start while a run is in progress on its subtree or an ancestor
payload.why: An agent starts runs from the command line, not from a button. If only the board disabled the start, an agent could start a second run, and two runs would write overlapping tickets and build against the same code. So the rule sits where every run starts, and the board only shows it.
payload.body:
A run is in progress while its process is alive. Every way to start a run, resume, restart or plan over a subtree checks the same rule: a run in progress on the same subtree or on any ancestor makes the start fail, and the refusal names the blocking run and where to find it. A run on a descendant is not covered. The board shows the same fact as a disabled control.

A restart ends the unfinished work of a subtree first (#ui-build-resume). From the command line, a restart says that it ends that work and lists each build it cancels and each ticket it archives, and waits for a confirmation, so an agent cannot restart by accident.

payload.title: The builder loop's effort per ticket is tracked across tickets, and a rise raises an alert that blocks nothing
payload.why: A per-change gate judges one diff, but rot is a cost that grows over many diffs, and with auto-merge no person sees it grow. When a codebase rots, the same size of ticket needs more work from the loop, so that effort is the outcome to watch; code metrics only predict it.
payload.body:
For each ticket the loop records the builder passes until the checks, grader and review pass, the tokens, the wall time, and the grader and review fails. The loop does this work anyway, so the numbers cost nothing extra and apply to every project. Effort is measured per story (#ms-trend-size).

Secondary signals show rot earlier and point at the cause: check runtime and the number of flaky tests, the count of non-blocking review findings per ticket (only their trend shows them adding up), and drift between the project's agent docs and its code, which only a judgement can read.

For each metric the measure compares the project's first 10 tickets with its last 10, and raises an alert when the current window is 20% or more above the base. Both numbers are a first guess. An alert is information only: it blocks no merge and stops no build.

payload.title: Ticket size is the number of spec stories the ticket delivers
payload.why: A large ticket needs more passes than a small one, so without a size a run of large tickets looks like rot. The size must come from the plan, because any size taken from the build grows with the rot it must show.
payload.body: The measure divides each ticket's effort by the number of spec stories it delivers (#plan-ticket). The stories are fixed before the build starts. One story can be small or large, so the count is rough; the trend only needs it measured the same way on every ticket. A ticket with no story, such as a refactor, counts as 1.

payload.title: werk is tested at two seams, the command line and the browser, and the agent runs every test itself
payload.why: The agent builds werk but cannot see the result unless a test shows it. The command line is the only write path to the map and the build's own seam, and the browser is the only place the views exist, so tests at these two seams cover the behaviour with no lower seam.
payload.body:
The command line, run against a temporary project and a temporary git repository, covers every write to the map, because the map changes only through the command line (see #map-views-read), and the whole build pipeline (see #how-pipeline-seam). The browser, through a real werk server on a copy of a fixture project, covers the views, card rendering, the chat pane and the board (#how-test-browser). Both seams put one scripted fake agent in place of the real one (#how-test-fake).

Pure code also gets unit tests under a coverage gate (#how-test-coverage). That gate measures coverage; it is not a third seam for behaviour. I/O code gets named behaviours (see #pipe-test-scope).

This card is a requirement. No alternative was weighed against having tests.

kill.text: A bug reaches use that a test at neither seam can catch, only a test below them.

payload.title: The build pipeline is tested at its command line, with a scripted fake agent
payload.why: The build goes wrong in the process spawns, the pipes and the git calls. Only a seam above all of them sees those failures.
payload.body: Tests run the build commands against a temporary git repository, with the scripted fake agent (see #how-test-fake) in place of every agent the pipeline starts: the builder, the grader, the reviewers and the overseer's classifiers. Every time limit is a parameter, so a test sets the overseer's limits to milliseconds. A test checks what a person sees: the exit code, the branch and its commits, the merged tree, the session and pipeline logs, and the board. It does not check internal calls. One seam covers the builder loop, the merge loop, the overseer and the trend report.

payload.title: A test never reaches a real external service or the real data of the person who runs it
payload.why: A real service costs money and time and answers differently on each run, and a write to real data damages the work of the person who runs the tests.
payload.body:
Each external service that a test could start or call is replaced by a fake with fixed answers, and every setting that points at real data is removed before the first test. The guard covers every process a test starts, because a child process inherits the settings of the shell that started the run. A harness that cannot confirm the fake is in place refuses to start.

There is one fake per service, and every harness uses it: the command-line tests, the server tests and the browser tests. A fake with no script for the current call fails at once with an error and never invents an answer.

kill.text: A test run calls a real external service, or writes to real data of the person who runs it.

payload.title: One fake agent replays a script of ordered steps per role, and records every launch
payload.why: A test must control what the agent says and does and in what order, and check what werk asked it. One ordered list of events and file edits keeps them in the order a real agent makes them. A build runs many fresh passes of one role, so each launch of a role plays that role's next reply.
payload.body:
The fake is found first in the program search list under the real agent's name (see #how-test-env). A launch names its script and its role through its environment (the role travels outside the prompt, see #how-agent-role); a launch with no script or no role fails at once and names what is missing.

The script holds, for each role, a list of replies and an exit code. A reply is an ordered list of steps: an event, printed as one line of the agent's output stream, or an edit, a file written relative to the folder the fake was started in. A chat agent lives across many messages, playing one reply per message, and ends when its input closes. Any other role reads one message, plays the reply for its launch number (first launch, first reply), and exits with the script's code. A launch with no reply left fails with an error that says how many replies the role has.

An ask step prints the permission request and does not wait: the next steps play at once, so a test can script an ask followed by a stall, repeated tool calls or a crash. When an ask settles, the fake prints a tool result with the ask's id, an error result for a denial. An ask still open when the input closes, or at the end of a turn with no input, settles as denied. A crash with an ask open exits with no result, as a real agent that dies.

An edit whose path leads outside the starting folder, also through a link, fails the launch and writes nothing. Each launch and each chat message is recorded beside the script, with the arguments and the role, so a test can check what werk asked.

kill.text: A test needs an agent behaviour that an ordered list of events and edits cannot express; or the fake behaves differently from the real agent when an ask is open; or a scripted edit changes a file outside its folder.

payload.title: Every agent the pipeline starts carries its role in its environment, not in its prompt
payload.why: One fake agent stands in for every agent in a test, so it must know which job each launch does. Prompt text changes often, so a fake that reads the prompt gives the wrong reply after a rewording; a role value in the launch environment stays fixed, and the real agent ignores it.
payload.body: A role is a short fixed word for the job, such as builder or grader. The pipeline sets it on every agent process it starts, in production and in tests alike. The fake reads it and plays the reply the test scripted for that role. A new kind of agent gets a new role when it is added. Reviewers run at the same time, one per quality area, so each reviewer's role names its area as well (reviewer-security, reviewer-design and so on), and a test can script a finding for one area only.

kill.text: Reword one agent prompt and run the pipeline tests: if a fake plays a reply scripted for another role, revisit.

payload.title: Plan, build and validate repeat in small slices
payload.why: What gets built changes what gets decided next. A plan made before any build runs is a plan made without that information.
payload.body: A project does not decide everything, then plan everything, then build. A person decides part of the map, plans part of it, and builds part of it, and each part can start before the others end. So a ticket can be built while other cards are still open, and new tickets can join the board during a run.

payload.title: Each pipeline agent runs on the model that its role needs
payload.why: Most of the pipeline's cost comes from the agents that run many times per ticket: builder passes, reviewers and held-out runs. The strongest model stays where one mistake spreads to every later step or where a result is judged: the plan and the grader. The builder gets the cheaper model with the strongest as an advisor, and the narrow or mechanical roles get the cheaper model alone.
payload.body:
To keep cost down without weakening the gates, the pipeline picks the model of each agent from its role, not from one default.

| Role | Model |
| --- | --- |
| Spec writer, ticket writer | Opus |
| Grader | Opus |
| Builder | Sonnet, with Opus as advisor |
| Reviewers of each quality area | Sonnet |
| Held-out binder, step author | Sonnet |
| Overseer classifiers | Sonnet |

A role that is not in the table, such as the chat agent, keeps the default model of its own setting.

A weak builder result does not pass unseen: the checks and the grader on Opus still judge it. A weak plan has no such gate after it, so the planners stay on Opus.

kill.text: The share of tickets that go green on the first pass, or the share that reach the retry cap, gets clearly worse than in the runs with an Opus builder.

payload.title: A prototype is judged only on whether it answered its question
payload.why: A throwaway artifact is worth building only while it is cheap. Every production habit it carries makes it slower without making it more useful.
payload.body:
The prototype rubric has checks and judgements, and no held-out section.

The checks: the artifact exists where the build said it would, and its entry point exits 0, if it has one.

The judgements: the artifact answers the question the fork asked, and nothing more. Where the brief was silent, the build states in one line the reading it chose. A build with no person cannot stop at a question, so it picks and says so, and a prototype that picked silently is worth less. Nothing was written outside the prototype's own worktree or scratch folder.

Not checked, on purpose: coverage, lint, doc comments, naming, dead code, commit hygiene. Without this exclusion a builder carries production habits into a throwaway, and the prototype stops being cheap, which removes the only reason to build one instead of arguing.

payload.title: Pure code gets a coverage number, and I/O code gets a list of named behaviours
payload.why: A wrong line in pure code gives a quiet wrong answer and is cheap to test, so a high number pays. Covering an I/O line means faking the live thing, so a percentage rewards the fake; a list of named behaviours aims at the real risk.
payload.body:
The rule holds for any module in any project werk builds.

To classify a module, ask one question: does a wrong line fail loudly (throw, hang, crash), or does it quietly give a result that looks correct? A quiet wrong answer means the module is pure. A loud failure means it is I/O: it holds something live, such as a child process, a socket, an open file or a network call.

A pure module gets a high line-coverage threshold. The project decides the number once, for all its pure code.

An I/O module gets one list of named behaviours and no percentage. One agent reads the module and the code that calls it, against one brief: name what breaks the tool if this is wrong, one sentence each. Each behaviour is a responsibility, not a location: "a crash never loses the message in flight" stays true after a rewrite, "line 326 throws" does not. So the list needs a new reading only when the module's job changes. Each doubt is a fact question or a design question. A fact question asks what the code does: the agent reads the source and settles it. A design question asks what the code should do: only a person decides it, with at least two contrasting options. The settled list becomes the module's named test cases, and only an open design question becomes a card.

Example. The module manages the chat agent's process.

1. The agent reads it and writes six behaviours, such as "a crash never loses the message in flight".
2. It is unsure whether a restart sends the waiting message again. That is a fact question. The source shows that it does, so the behaviour goes on the list.
3. It is unsure whether an idle process should stop after 30 or after 60 minutes. That is a design question, so it becomes a card with both options for the person.
4. The seven behaviours become the module's named test cases.

```
module --> one reading --> behaviours ---------------------------------> named test cases
                      \--> doubts --+-- fact question --> read the source --'
                                    '-- design question --> card with options --> person decides
```

A read-only subagent ships with the agent instructions and runs this rule on demand, when the build reaches a module with no test policy. It classifies and lists, reports a missing threshold instead of inventing one, and never writes to the map. The main agent writes the result into the module's own tests.

payload.title: The production checks are named roles: unit tests, coverage, typecheck, lint and end to end
payload.why: A check that names a tool fits one project. A check that names a role fits every project werk builds.
payload.body:
The roles are the unit tests; the same tests with the project's own coverage threshold enforced; the strongest static type pass the language offers; the style and static-analysis pass; and the product driven end to end against a real build.

Each project binds each role to a make target of its own (see #pipe-check-make). A role with no command behind it is work to do, not a check to drop. A ticket that lists no checks of its own runs all five.

The coverage number stays out of the rubric. One blanket percentage over a project is wrong (see #pipe-test-scope), so the threshold and the modules it covers live in the project's coverage configuration, where a non-zero exit enforces them.

payload.title: In every project, the builder agent sees the result of its change by itself
payload.why: The builder agent works alone in its worktree, and no person looks at each pass. It can fix only what it can see. So every project gives it two ways to see: tests over the code that it runs itself, and the real product that it can start, open and inspect.
payload.body: A pass that cannot see its result reports success on code that does not work, and the error reaches the merge or the person. To avoid that, every project werk builds has a test command that the agent runs alone and reads by its exit code, and a way to drive the running product end to end, for example a browser it can open and screenshot. Neither needs a person. The production checks name both (#pipe-rubric-checks). Each project chooses its own tools for them, as one of its build rules (see #agents-build-rules).

kill.text: Builder passes keep reporting success on changes that a person or the held-out set then finds broken.

payload.title: The grader scores a diff against its ticket's criteria, the cards it rests on, and its scope
payload.why: Done means the diff meets its ticket and breaks no decided card. Only an agent can read a card against a diff. Because the lines come from the ticket and its cards, the same grader works for every project.
payload.body:
The grader runs after the checks are green. It scores three kinds of line, and none comes from a fixed list.

A delivery line for each acceptance criterion of the ticket: does the diff meet it?

A contradiction line for each decided card in the ticket's dependency closure, cited or not: does the diff do something this card forbids, or do it differently? A part of a card that the diff does not build yet passes, because the set checks make some ticket cite every decided card (see #plan-ticket-set-checks).

One scope line: does the diff build a behaviour that no acceptance criterion and no story of the ticket asks for? A builder pass that fixes a failure builds whatever the failure names, so without this line a diff grows past its ticket and decides questions that other cards own. The gap names each such behaviour, so the next pass removes it. A follow-up ticket has no spec stories, so the full text of each of its held-out steps stands in for them. A contradiction line never asks for a missing part of a card, so it cannot push a diff out of scope.

Each line gets a score from 1 to 5, where 3 passes, and a gap: the unmet criterion, the contradiction or the out-of-scope behaviour, with the file, line or test that shows it. The gap is the output that matters. On a fail, the next builder pass gets it with the brief. A score with no reason gives the builder nothing to fix.

kill.text: The scope line fails diffs that a criterion does ask for, or misses a diff that builds a behaviour nobody asked for.

payload.title: A later grade of a ticket checks the earlier gaps and regressions, not a fresh reading
payload.why: A grader that reads each pass fresh finds a new small detail every time, so a ticket fails pass after pass on gaps nobody saw before. When the first grade names every gap at once and each later grade checks only those gaps plus anything newly broken, the passes move toward green.
payload.body:
The first grade of a build names every gap it finds on a line in one answer. Each later grade in the same build gets the lines that failed before, with their gaps. A line that failed before fails again only while its gap is still open. A line that passed before fails only for a regression: something that worked at the earlier grade and that the later changes broke. A gap that was there at the earlier grade and was not named then does not fail a later pass. A new build of the ticket starts with a fresh first grade.

A line that the grader's reply leaves out scores 0 and fails, also at a later grade, so a silent grader never passes a line. A low score on a line that passed before fails only when the grader flags it as a regression.

Example:

- Ticket T "Paste a screenshot" rests on card A "A message carries its images" and card B "The composer shows a menu".

1. Pass 1: the grader fails A, gap: an empty list is still sent. B passes.
2. Pass 2: the builder fixes the empty list. The grader checks A's gap: closed. It checks B for a regression: none. The pass is green.
3. If pass 2 had broken B's menu, B fails as a regression.
4. If the grader now notices a small detail in B that pass 1 already had, B does not fail.

```
pass 1 grade:  A fail (empty list sent)   B pass
                     |
pass 2 grade:  A: is that gap closed?     B: did pass 2 break it?
               yes -> pass                no -> pass
```

kill.text: Held-out steps or later tickets often find a gap that the first grade of a ticket should have named.

payload.title: Reviewers, one per quality area, read the diff after the grader passes
payload.why: The grader asks only whether the diff does what the decided cards say. Nothing then catches a problem that no card names: duplication, weak tests, escape hatches, a new dependency.
payload.body:
The reviewers ask whether the change is good code, not whether it is the right change, which is the grader's job (#pipe-grader). The two stay separate, so each has one source of lines. Prototype code gets no review.

The review is fixed and built into the tool, the same for every project. It has five areas: design (module boundaries, coupling, error handling, fit with the code around it); maintainability (duplication, complexity, dead code, escape hatches such as suppressions and skipped tests); tests (assertions that fail without the change, edge cases, failure paths, and any test the change made weaker); security and dependencies (input validation, secret handling, each new dependency and its reason); and performance (extra work, expensive queries, unbounded loops on the input).

Each area gets its own reviewer with a fresh context, and all run at the same time, so a reviewer does not anchor on another area's findings. The cost is about five times that of one agent. A finding must point at the diff or at code that the diff directly affects.

Each finding has a severity (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW), a file and line, the impact, and a fix. CRITICAL or HIGH fails the pass, and the findings go into the next builder pass like a grader gap. MEDIUM and LOW do not block: the loop records them, and their count per ticket goes into the trend report (see #ms-trend). A finding with a missing severity, or one the rubric does not name, is recorded as written and does not block, because a block on an unknown word fails a pass on a typo.

A failed review starts a new builder pass, which runs the checks, the grader and every reviewer again. A fresh reviewer can find a new HIGH issue on each pass, so the retry cap is what stops a loop that does not converge.

payload.title: A judge agent can only read, and it cannot ask for more tools
payload.why: A judge must not change the code that it judges. If a judge could ask for a write tool, a model would decide each ask, and a write can look reasonable for the ticket. A fixed list of read tools makes the limit certain and costs no model call.
payload.body:
A judge agent is the grader (#pipe-grader) or a reviewer (#pipe-review). A builder asks for a tool when it needs one, and the overseer sends that ask to a classifier (see #build-overseer-asks). A judge does not use that route.

The loop starts each judge with a fixed tool list: tools that read a file, search the text of files and find files by name, and the git operations that show a diff, the commit history and one commit. The agent runtime refuses every other call at once, and the judge continues without it. No ask reaches the overseer, so the classifier never runs for a judge. The overseer still watches a judge session for silence and for loops.

Example:

- B: the builder session of pass 2. It can ask for any tool.
- G: the grader session of pass 2. It has the read list only.
- O: the overseer of the build pass.

1. B asks to run the test command. O sends the ask to the classifier, which allows it, and B runs the tests.
2. G reads the diff and two source files. Each call is on its list, so it runs with no ask.
3. G tries to edit a test file. The runtime refuses the call. O sees no ask.
4. G returns its scores. The edit did not happen, so G judged the code that B wrote.

```
  B --ask: run tests--> O --> classifier --allow--> B runs tests
  G --read diff------> on list --> runs, no ask
  G --edit test------> not on list --> refused by the runtime (O sees nothing)
  G --scores---------> loop
```

kill.text: Start a grader on a pass whose prompt tells it to fix a failing test. If the working tree has any change after the grader exits, revisit.

payload.title: Validate holds what the builder never sees, and it runs beside build
payload.why: Validate is everything the builder cannot see. The held-out set is the first part of it, and it runs at each merge to catch a break where it starts.
payload.body:
Validate is defined by who can see it, not by when it runs. Build holds what the builder sees and runs: its own tests, the checks, the judgements. Validate holds what the builder never sees: the held-out set first (#val-heldout), and the measurement of the released product later (#val-measure).

So validate starts with build. The step author starts when the builder starts, the merge loop runs the held-out set after each merge, and a red step reaches a builder while build is still running. The gates keep their order: G2 still closes build and G3 still closes validate. Only the stages overlap.

payload.title: Validate ends by measuring the released product and analysing the result
payload.why: Some failures show only with real users. G3 needs a measurement of the released product, and an analysis that says what it means for the next intent.
payload.body: What the measure step and the analyse step each produce is not decided, nor what analysis adds beyond reading the measurement. Both work on a released product, so they wait for the first release to users.

kill.text: The first release goes to users.

payload.title: A held-out set of user-path steps, which the builder never sees, runs after each merge
payload.why: A builder optimises whatever it can see, so part of the merge bar stays out of its sight. A whole path through the product is harder to fake than one function, and the bugs that unit tests leave are in the connections between parts.
payload.body:
Each held-out line follows one path through the whole product, the way a user does. It never tests one part alone: unit tests already do that, and each part can pass alone.

Three agents make and run the set, and none of them is the builder. A step author writes the steps of each ticket while the builder builds (#val-heldout-steps). A binder turns the steps into tests on the merged tree (#val-heldout-binder). The merge loop runs them after each merge, on a tree that no single builder controls.

The steps are stored in werk's own store, outside every builder worktree. Known gap: a builder can still read them by an absolute path. The steps are out of the builder's worktree, not out of its reach.

Each step ends green, red, or not run (#val-heldout-notrun). A red step files a follow-up ticket for the ticket whose step went red (see #build-followups), and the red badge stays on the merged ticket after its follow-up goes green. A follow-up ticket gets no step author: its steps are the red steps. A binder error files no follow-up. The set runs once more at the end of the run, and a binder error that stays ends the run and waits for a person.

payload.title: A step author writes plain Given/When/Then steps from the brief, while the builder builds
payload.why: The steps need only the brief and the decided cards, not the code, so they can be written while the code is. Written before the UI exists, a step can name only what the user sees and does, so it stays valid when the implementation changes.
payload.body:
The step author is a separate agent with no tools, one per ticket. It starts when the builder starts, from the same brief, and never reads the code.

A step is plain text in Given/When/Then form. There is no Gherkin runtime: the steps are input for the binder, which writes the real tests. A step names a user action or a thing the user sees, never a selector, file or function. Most steps are end to end, but that is not what makes them held out: a step is held out because the builder does not write it and cannot read it.

Examples for werk:

```
Given the map is open with 50 cards
When a card is added from the command line
And the user searches for its title
Then the new card is in the results
```

```
Given cards A, B and C, where C depends on B and B depends on A
And all three cards are decided
When A is reopened from the command line
Then B and C show as stale in the map
When C is rederived
Then B still shows as stale and C does not
```

payload.title: A held-out step written before its source card changed is rewritten before it can file a follow-up
payload.why: A step tests the product against what its cards say, and the cards keep changing after the steps are written. A step is a fair test only while it says what its cards say now, so keeping steps in step with the cards makes every red step point at work the map still asks for.
payload.body:
Each steps file records the version of each card its steps were written from (a card's version is defined in #plan-ticket-watch). Before the held-out set runs on a merged tree, every step whose source card changed since then goes back to the step author. The author rewrites the step from the current card, or drops it when the card no longer asks for that behaviour. A step never files a follow-up while its source card is newer than the step.

Example:

- Card B "A person stops a build only by archiving its ticket" replaced the earlier rule that a drag back into ready stops a build.
- Step S "A person stops a build by a drag back into ready" was written from B before that change.

1. The held-out set is about to run. S records B at its old version, and B has a newer one.
2. The step author reads the current B. B forbids the drag, so the author drops S.
3. The held-out set runs without S, and no follow-up asks for the drag.
4. A step whose source cards did not change runs as before.

```
steps file:  S  <- written from B (version 1)
map:         B  now at version 2
                 |
before run:  version 1 != version 2 -> step author rewrites or drops S
run:         only fresh steps run; only a fresh red step files a follow-up
```

kill.text: Follow-up tickets stop at the retry cap while a red step contradicts a decided card.

payload.title: A red step is checked against its source cards before it files a follow-up, and a contradiction files a decision follow-up
payload.why: A step that misread its card fails after every build, because no code can satisfy both the step and the card. Checking a red step against its cards keeps such a step out of the build tickets, and a decision follow-up settles it without a person waiting.
payload.body:
A held-out step can contradict a decided card that never changed: the step author misread the card when it wrote the step. A step that is out of date because its card changed is a different case (see #val-heldout-fresh).

To avoid a follow-up that cannot succeed, the step author reads every red step against its source cards before the step files anything. If the step agrees with its cards, it files a build follow-up as usual. If it contradicts a decided card, no build follow-up is filed. A decision follow-up is filed for the source ticket instead. It builds no code at first. It judges whether the card or the step is right, by the guideline for a missing decision (see #build-missing-decision): the answer that is easiest to undo, and when two are equally safe, the one that changes the fewest decided cards. It proposes a card with its answer, its reason and the options it weighed. An agent never accepts that proposal. The step stays out of the set, as not run, until the step author rewrites it from the cards and the proposal. If the judgement changed the card, the follow-up then builds the code that the proposal asks for. Nothing in this path waits for a person, who rules on the proposal later.

Example:

- Ticket Q "A quote becomes an excerpt" is merged.
- Card E "A message position counts from zero, hidden lines included".
- Step S "The excerpt's message position is 3". The chat log in S has three lines, so the last line has position 2.

1. The held-out run turns S red.
2. The step author reads S against E. E gives 2, S says 3: a contradiction.
3. A decision follow-up D is filed for Q. No build follow-up is filed.
4. D judges that E is right: it changes no decided card. D proposes a card that confirms E for this case.
5. The step author rewrites S to position 2, citing E and the proposal. S runs again and is green.
6. If S had agreed with E, step 3 would be a build follow-up, as usual.

```
S red -> author reads S against E
           |-- agrees ------> build follow-up for Q
           '-- contradicts -> decision follow-up D -> proposed card P
```
