```
                                                        |
                              S rewritten from E and P <'  -> S runs again
```

kill.text: Held-out steps file a second build follow-up after the check passed them.

payload.title: A binder agent turns steps into tests, and never makes a test pass
payload.why: The binder reads the code. If it may change a test until it passes, it fits the test to the code, and the held-out set checks nothing.
payload.body:
The binder reads the merged code, finds the elements each step names, and writes the tests for the project's stack. It binds every step of the run in a temporary worktree, and its tests never reach the main line.

The binder cannot change step text. It only maps each step to user actions and assertions. It does not make a test pass: when a step fails, it records the failure and stops. It fixes only its own errors, for example a typo in a locator. "Element not found" can be a binder error or a missing feature, so the binder reports which one it judges it to be.

Example of what the rule stops: search does not update live. A binder that may make tests pass adds a page reload before the search. The test passes and the feature is still wrong.

The rule is enforced after the session, not trusted. A binder that changed any file outside its own test folder has fitted the product to the test, and its whole report is void. Everything the binder and its test runner write inside that folder is its own, screenshots, traces and result folders included. A path is compared as stored, never in a display form that quotes unusual characters, or the binder's own output reads as a change to the product.

Accepted risk: a binder writes a wrong test, and a correct feature fails. This is fixed when it happens, not prevented.

payload.title: On a held-out failure, the builder gets the text of the failed step
payload.why: The builder needs a reason to fix the code. The step text gives one in user terms and holds no test code.
payload.body:
The next builder pass gets the failed step, word for word, with the brief. It does not get the test code or the other steps.

Accepted risk: each failure shows the builder one step, so after many failures the builder has seen most of the set. This is watched and fixed if it happens.

payload.title: A held-out step that the binder could not run is not run, not red
payload.why: A binder that timed out or failed says nothing about the product. Showing it as red reports a break that nobody found.
payload.body:
After a merge, each held-out step ends green, red, or not run. A step is not run when the binder session failed, hit its time limit, or could not bind the step.

A not-run step files no follow-up ticket. On the board it shows as a grey badge on the done ticket, apart from the red badge of a step that ran and failed (see #ui-board-columns). G2 still waits for it, because it is not green, and the held-out run after the next merge tries it again.

The binder's time limit grows with the number of steps it binds, so a large set does not time out where a small one would pass.

kill.text: A red held-out badge comes from a step that did not run.

payload.title: A held-out step that needs a capability another unmerged ticket builds is not run, not red
payload.why: A step author writes from the brief, so a step can need an operation, a screen or a log field that a later ticket builds. Such a step fails for the missing capability, not for the ticket's code, and its follow-up could only build another ticket's work. Ending it as not run keeps every red step pointing at merged code.
payload.body:
A capability is anything a step reaches the product through: an operation of the command line, a screen or route, a field or kind of event in the log, a behaviour of an agent. The binder reports the capability a step needs when the main line does not provide it. If a ticket that is not merged yet owns that capability, the step ends as not run and files no follow-up. If the step's own source ticket owns it, the ticket forgot to build it, and the step is red.

A follow-up that holds only such steps cannot be fixed by any change inside it. A builder pass on it checks two facts for each step: another unmerged ticket owns the missing capability, and the seam behind the step has unit tests that state the step's outcome and pass on the main line. When both hold, the pass ends with no code change and the follow-up closes. When a step has no such unit test, the pass writes it. The steps stay in the set, G2 still waits for them, and a step that goes red once its capability exists files a new follow-up then.

Example:

- Ticket R "Every agent werk starts gets the agent instructions" builds the prompt builder, with unit tests, and is merged.
- Ticket B "A build pass runs on one ticket" builds the operation that starts a build pass, and is not merged.
- Step S of R: "When the person starts a build pass on a ticket, then its prompt begins with the build agent's own instructions".

1. R merges. The product has no operation that starts a build pass, and B owns it. S ends as not run, with a grey badge on R. No follow-up is filed.
2. A follow-up F for R that holds only S finds that B owns the operation and that a passing unit test at the prompt builder states S's outcome. F closes with no code change.
3. B merges. The next held-out run tries S through B's operation. S is green, or S is red and files a new follow-up for R.
4. If R itself was meant to build that operation, S is red at step 1.

```
merge:   R                                    B
S:       not run (capability owned by B)  ->  green | red -> new follow-up for R
F:       closes, no code change (unit test at the seam passes)
```

kill.text: A step is filed more than once for a capability another ticket owns; a step stays not run after its owning ticket merged; or a follow-up closed with no change while its step stayed red after its capability merged.

payload.title: The held-out run after a merge holds the steps of merged tickets only
payload.why: A step whose ticket is not on the main line describes behaviour nobody has merged yet. Its red result reports a break nobody made and files a follow-up that builds another ticket's work.
payload.body: The set that runs after a merge holds the steps of the subtree's tickets that are merged onto the main line, and nothing else. A ticket's steps join the set in the merge that brings its code, so that merge's own run already includes them. Steps of a ticket that is still building or merging stay out, even when the step author has finished them. Steps of an archived ticket leave the set with the ticket, and a restore brings them back. A red step therefore always points at code on the main line: the ticket's own code, or a later merge that broke it. When every ticket of the subtree is merged, the set is complete, so G2 still waits on every step of every live ticket.

kill.text: A break reaches G2 that a step left out of a merge's held-out run would have caught.

payload.title: G2 opens only when every held-out step is green on the main line
payload.why: A held-out step is a user-visible failure the pipeline already found. A main line that carries one asks the person to approve a known break.
payload.body:
The held-out set does not block the merge queue (see #build-heldout-beside). A red step files a follow-up ticket, and build goes on.

G2 belongs to the tip of the main line for the tickets of one planned subtree. It opens when every ticket of the subtree is merged and every held-out step is green, and a later merge opens it again for the new tip. A not-run step is not green, so G2 waits for it too.

So build ends later when held-out steps fail, but it never ends with a known break in front of the person. Cost accepted: the main line can be red on a held-out step until the follow-up ticket is built.

payload.title: Plan turns one decided subtree into one spec, then splits the spec into tickets
payload.why: A subtree holds many decisions, not one statement of the work. A spec puts the problem, the user stories and the test seams in one agreed place, and the tickets then split one whole.
payload.body:
The plan runs two writers in order, each an agent with no person behind it. The spec writer writes one spec over the subtree: the problem, the solution, a numbered list of user stories, and the decisions about implementation and testing. The ticket writer splits that spec into tickets (#plan-ticket). One subtree gives one spec, and one spec gives one or more tickets. A plan reads every card in its scope in full (#plan-scope).

The writers' templates stop to ask a person whether the test seams are right, how fine the tickets are, and which tickets block which. In the pipeline an agent answers each question, from the decided cards of the subtree and the map around it. An answer that no card gives becomes a proposed card, never only text in the spec (#plan-answers).

The spec and the tickets live in werk's own store for the project, never in the repository being built. A spec with no numbered user story stops the plan.

payload.title: The plan scope is the subtree plus every decided card it depends on, followed down and never up
payload.why: A decision two links away, under a card the subtree links, reached the planner only as a title, and the planner filled the gap itself. Following every dependency and every card below it hands the planner each decision the subtree rests on. Stopping at parents and at undecided or postponed cards keeps the scope to what the subtree needs.
payload.body:
The plan reads every card in the scope in full. The scope starts with the subtree. Then, until nothing new comes in, each card in the scope adds every card it depends on, together with that card's own subtree. The walk never goes from a card to its parent, because the way up leads to the whole map.

Only decided cards are in the scope. The walk stops at an open, proto, stale or postponed card and does not go below it. To keep a feature out of a build, postpone it.

The scope has two tiers. The first tier is the subtree and every card that a subtree card links: a depends_on target, or a card id written in its title, why or body. An open or proto card in the first tier stops the plan before any agent runs, and every first-tier card must be cited by at least one ticket. The second tier is the rest of the scope. It is context: no ticket must cite it, and it never stops a plan. The prompt keeps the tiers apart, the first tier first.

Example. The subtree is #app "The app", with one child, #app-login "Login by magic link".

- #app-login depends on #mail "Mail goes through one provider".
- #mail sits under #infra "Infrastructure", next to #cdn "Static files on a CDN".
- #mail has two children: #mail-retry "A failed send retries three times", and #mail-bounce "Bounces unsubscribe the address", which is open.
- #mail-retry depends on #queue "Jobs run on one queue".

1. The scope starts with #app and #app-login. Both are first tier.
2. #app-login depends on #mail. #mail comes in as first tier, because a subtree card links it. #mail-retry comes in with it as second tier.
3. #mail-retry depends on #queue. #queue comes in as second tier.
4. #mail-bounce is open. It stays out, and the plan does not stop, because it is second tier.
5. #infra and #cdn stay out. The walk never goes from #mail up to #infra.

```
#infra                        out: a parent is never followed
 |- #cdn                      out
 '- #mail                     tier 1 (linked by #app-login)
     |- #mail-retry           tier 2 --depends_on--> #queue   tier 2
     '- #mail-bounce (open)   out, no stop
#app                          tier 1 (subtree)
 '- #app-login                tier 1 --depends_on--> #mail
```

kill.text: A plan must cite a linked card that the planned work does not change only to pass the coverage check, or a planner prompt grows past one context window because of linked cards.

payload.title: A plan writer returns each answer that no card gives as data, and the program proposes it as a card
payload.why: A person must see every decision the plan made that no card gave. An agent that adds cards itself can write a card nobody can trace to the plan, so the writer returns data that the program checks and then proposes.
payload.body:
Beside its output, each writer returns a list of answers. Each answer has a title, a why that names the question it settles, and a body. The program proposes each one as a ghost card under the root of the planned subtree, with the agent as the one who decides. An answer the program cannot propose, such as one whose id is already in the map, stops the plan with an error.

A writer never writes to the map. It may read any file, and it may write only the files that its own task names; every other write is refused, because no person answers in a pipeline run.

A missing answer list and an empty one mean different things. An empty list says that cards settled every question. A missing or malformed list says the writer did not finish, and the plan stops before the next writer starts.

kill.text: Most answer cards that several plans propose are nitpicks that add nothing to the map's decisions.

payload.title: A second plan over a subtree extends that subtree's spec and open tickets in place
payload.why: A second or interrupted plan over the same subtree would otherwise put a second full ticket set on the board beside the first. Keying everything a plan writes by the subtree, with no run entity, leaves one spec and one ticket set per subtree.
payload.body:
A plan over a subtree first looks for the spec and tickets that an earlier plan wrote for it. When they exist, the plan updates the one spec and changes the open tickets in place, under their own numbers. New tickets cover only the scope that the existing tickets do not.

Open means ready or blocked. A ticket that is building, merging or done stays as it is, because only the merge loop moves it (see #ui-board-control). If the writer changes such a ticket, the plan puts the old text back and reports it. If the writer's rewrite of an open ticket fails the ticket's own checks, the plan keeps the old text.

A story that still holds keeps its number, and a new story takes the next number after the highest, because built tickets list story numbers and cannot change. An open ticket that the new spec no longer needs is archived (#plan-archive). A plan over a subtree whose earlier tickets are all archived numbers its tickets after the highest number the board holds for the subtree.

No run entity owns a plan's output: the subtree is the key of the spec, the ticket folder and the ticket ids. A plan over a parent or a child of an earlier plan's subtree is an overlap, and that case is not settled.

kill.text: A second plan over a subtree that already has tickets leaves two ticket sets for it on the board.

payload.title: A plan archives an open ticket that the subtree's current spec no longer needs
payload.why: A ticket that no spec asks for must not stay buildable. The archive is reversible, so the person loses nothing.
payload.body:
The ticket writer lists the open tickets it drops, each with a one-sentence reason, apart from the tickets it writes. The plan archives each listed ticket that is open and ignores the rest. The archive names the plan as its actor and carries the reason, so a person can tell it from their own archive and see why the ticket left before they restore it.

A restore undoes any archive exactly: the ticket returns to the column it left, ready, or blocked with its old reason. A restore of a ticket that is not archived, or of a number the board does not hold, is refused and records nothing.

kill.text: A second plan over a planned subtree leaves a ticket buildable that its spec no longer needs, or a restore does not return a ticket to the column it left.

payload.title: A ticket, not a card, is the unit of build work: a thin end-to-end slice of decided cards
payload.why: A decided card is a constraint, not a task, and cards differ widely in size. A builder needs something narrow, complete and small enough for one fresh context, so a ticket slices across cards and carries the build state.
payload.body:
A ticket is a tracer bullet: a narrow but complete path through every layer the change touches, which can be shown working on its own and fits one fresh context. A slice usually crosses several cards in different subtrees. A cut along the refines tree gives horizontal layers instead, and decided cards range from one line of a function to a whole feature.

A ticket holds a title, the behaviour it makes work from the user's side, its acceptance criteria, the spec stories it delivers, the decided cards it cites, the tickets that block it, the modules it touches, and the checks that decide it, in one fixed structure (#plan-ticket-shape). It names no file paths: they go out of date before the build reaches the ticket, and the builder researches the code itself on each pass.

A ticket lists the numbers of the spec stories it delivers instead of copying them. The ticket writer assigns them, so every story is delivered by at least one ticket, and one story can need several tickets. When the build starts, the stories and the spec are frozen: a change to either is a change to the plan. A prefactor, a refactor or an internal fix delivers no story and gets no invented one. The stories give the ticket's size before the build (see #ms-trend-size) and the builder's definition of done from the user's side.

The tickets that block a ticket are the delivery order, and the planner decides it (see #plan-ticket-set-checks).

Build state lives on tickets. A decided card says that the argument is settled, not that code exists. The board shows each ticket in its column, and the build loop picks its next ticket from the board (see #ui-board-columns). A card has no built flag, and the map shows no build progress. A person decides which ticket is built, and when (see #ui-board).

kill.text: A build of tickets shows that most tickets cite exactly one card, so the card was the unit after all; or a person asks which decided cards have no code yet, and the board cannot answer.

payload.title: Every ticket shares one fixed structure: header lines, then three sections in a fixed order
payload.why: A fixed structure puts every field in the same place in every ticket, so a person reads tickets faster and a check reads every field without a model. A missing field is a plain failure, not a guess.
payload.body:
A ticket starts with five header lines, in this order: title, cites, blocked_by, stories and touches. Three sections follow, in this order: What to build, Acceptance criteria, and Checks. Cites, blocked_by and stories may be empty, and Checks may have no bullet. Every line and heading must be there.

Cites holds card ids. Blocked_by and stories hold numbers. Touches holds the names of the modules the ticket changes, as concept names and not file paths, because the scheduler compares them to decide which tickets build at the same time.

A ticket's number is the leading digits of its file name, so a file named 02-reopen is ticket 2, and the format needs no number line. A file with no leading digits cannot be a blocker. Two files with the same number both fail, and neither counts as a blocker.

```
title: A person can reopen a decided card from the map
cites: map-reopen, map-stale
blocked_by: 2
stories: 4, 7
touches: map view, decision log

## What to build

A person opens a decided card and presses reopen. The card goes back to open, and every card that depends on it shows a stale mark with the reason.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reopened card shows as open in the map.
- [ ] Each card that depends on it shows a stale mark that names the reopened card.

## Checks

- `make test`
- `make e2e`
```

kill.text: Tickets often fail their own checks only on structure while their content is sound.

payload.title: The ticket checks run as one operation, and a failure blocks only what it names
payload.why: A planner, a person and an agent that edits a ticket all need the same checks without a plan. One bad ticket or one uncited card must not keep every good ticket from being built.
payload.body:
One operation runs the own checks on every ticket of a folder and the set checks on the whole set (#plan-ticket-set-checks). Each failure names its ticket, the check and the field, so the reader finds the place to fix without reading the rest. A pass, a failed check and a call that could not run the checks are three different exit codes, so a broken call never reads as a pass.

An own check reads one ticket file and nothing else, so it runs as soon as the writer writes the file, and its failure names one ticket. A ticket passes when it has a title, every header line and section of the fixed structure, at most 4000 characters, text under What to build, at least one acceptance criterion, no file path anywhere, only make targets as checks, and module names that do not read as paths. Empty cites and stories pass: coverage is a property of the set.

A ticket that fails its own checks does not go on the board. Every other ticket goes on the board. A failed set check is reported and the plan exits with an error. A failed set check that names a ticket puts that ticket in blocked, with the check as its reason. Only the blocked_by check names tickets; the cards-cited and stories checks name none, so they block none. The reason clears when the tickets are fixed and the set check passes again.

kill.text: Builders often edit the wrong files because tickets name no paths, or a planner cannot tell a pass from a call that could not run the checks.

payload.title: Three checks on the whole ticket set: cards cited, stories delivered, blocked_by
payload.why: Coverage and order are properties of the set. No single ticket can pass or fail them alone.
payload.body:
The set checks read the tickets of one plan that passed their own checks, the decided cards of the planned subtree, and the spec's story numbers. A ticket that fails its own checks is not on the board, so its cites and stories do not count.

Cards cited: every decided card in the planned subtree is cited by at least one ticket. A failure lists the cards that no ticket cites. A proposed card does not count, also when it carries the status decided, because the plan proposes its own answers under the subtree. It counts after a person accepts it, on the next run of the checks.

Stories delivered: every story number in the spec is listed by at least one ticket, and no ticket lists a number that the spec does not have.

Blocked_by: every blocker is a ticket in the set, and the blocked_by graph has no cycle. A cycle is one failure that names every ticket on it; a ticket that names itself is a cycle of one. A failure of this check names only the tickets that must not start: the ticket that names a missing blocker, and the tickets on a cycle.

The order belongs to the planner. Blocked_by is the delivery order, and no check compares it with the depends_on edges between the cited cards. A decision edge and a build need often agree, but not always. A wrong order shows at the build, as a failed check or a merge conflict.

kill.text: After a build run, a ticket started before code it needed existed, or tickets waited for blockers they did not need.

payload.title: A change to a cited card blocks every open ticket that cites it
payload.why: A ticket is written against its cited cards as they were at the plan. If one changes before the build, the ticket can build the old decision and nothing says so. A program that compares versions marks it the same way every time.
payload.body:
When a plan puts a ticket on the board, the board records the version of each card the ticket cites. A card's version is the position in the decision log of its latest change that counts, and 0 when none does. A change counts when it can change what a ticket must build: a new title, why or body, a status change such as a reopen, a removal, a stale mark, or a depends_on edge added or removed. A note and a change of view do not count.

The watch is a program, not a model. It runs when the server opens the project and each time the decision log grows, so it sees every writer of the log. A change made while no server ran is caught at the next start, because the watch compares versions and does not need to see each event live. A failed run writes an error, marks nothing and does not stop the server; the next change runs it again. The watch is idempotent: a ticket already blocked for the same reason gets no second move.

Only an open ticket, ready or blocked, gets the mark. A marked ticket goes to blocked, and its reason names each changed card and the kind of change. The program cannot say whether the ticket still makes sense, only that it must be checked again. A marked ticket cannot be moved back to ready by hand. The mark clears when a plan over the subtree changes or keeps the ticket against the new versions (see #plan-extend).

A new card has no ticket to look up. A card added to the subtree of a plan with open tickets runs that subtree's cards-cited check again against the current map. The failure is reported and blocks no ticket.

Example. Ticket app/01 is in ready and cites #app-login at log position 40. No server runs.

1. A person retitles #app-login. The log grows to position 41. Nothing watches, so app/01 stays in ready.
2. The server starts. The watch runs once: #app-login changed after position 40, so app/01 moves to blocked, with a reason that names #app-login and the new words.
3. A note is written on #app-login. The log grows and the watch runs again. A note does not count, so nothing moves.

```
log position:  40 plan    41 retitle    (server start)    42 note
app/01:        ready      ready         blocked           blocked (no new move)
watch runs:    -          -             yes               yes
```

kill.text: Marks on open tickets come so often that re-plans become routine work and most marks change nothing in the ticket.

payload.title: Every build opens a card obligation, and the pass closes it with new cards or with the cards it followed
payload.why: The obligation is data in the log, so a pass that changes code and leaves the map untouched shows as an open obligation. A pass that made no new decision closes it by naming the cards its choices came from, so it never writes a card only to meet a quota.
payload.body:
The start of a build appends the obligation to the decision log before any code is written. It names the ticket and the cards the ticket cites. Each build of a ticket opens its own obligation, so a second build never inherits one that an earlier build closed. The open ticket shows what its builds proposed or followed (see #ui-board-drawer). No card in the map shows an obligation.

A pass closes the obligation in one of two ways. It proposes one card for each decision that no card gives: a pass that makes three decisions writes three. The agent places each card itself, its parent and its depends_on, because knowing what a decision refines is judgement. Or, when every choice in its diff came from a cited card or from a card its search found, it records "no new decision" and names those cards. The grader checks that record against the diff as it checks the cited cards, and a choice that none of the named cards gives fails the pass as an unrecorded decision. The cards this build proposed count as named, whether or not a person has accepted them yet, so a build never loops on a gap that only an accept could close. A list of values, a configuration or the inside of one helper is not a decision, so it is never a reason to write a card.

Example:

- Card A "Each agent carries its role outside the prompt".
- Ticket T "Show the role in the launch record", which cites A.
- Pass P builds T.

1. The build starts. The log gets obligation O for this build, and O is open.
2. P adds the role to the launch record. Every choice comes from A. P records "no new decision" and names A. O closes.
3. The grader reads the diff. Each choice traces to A, so the pass goes on.
4. If P also picks a new file format that A does not give and names only A, the grader fails the pass as an unrecorded decision. The next pass proposes card C for the format, and C closes O.
5. If P exits with neither a card nor a record, O stays open, and the ticket shows that no card was written.

```
build starts --> obligation O (open)
                      |
pass P --+-- a decision no card gives --> proposes card C --> O closed by C
         '-- every choice from cards --> "no new decision: A" --> O closed
                                               |
                       grader: a choice in the diff that A and C do not give --> pass fails

O = the card obligation of one build   A = a card the pass names   C = a card this build proposes
```

kill.text: A ticket ends at the retry cap on a gap that its own proposed card gives, or passes keep writing filler cards to close obligations.

payload.title: Every turn names the open card: the whole card when it changed, a one-line reminder otherwise
payload.why: The agent cannot ask which card is open, and a card announced once drops out of its context after a resume or a compaction. A one-line reminder on every other turn costs almost nothing and keeps the card named. A new agent has heard nothing, so its first turn always gets the whole card.
payload.body:
To keep the agent from working blind, every turn starts with a line about the open card. When the open card changed since this agent's last turn, the turn starts with the whole card as a compact block: the id and title, then one labelled line each for the kind, status and who decides, the why, the children and the depends_on targets, each line left out when the card has nothing for it. Every other turn starts with a one-line reminder that names the id and title. The agent's instructions say that "this card" or "current" means the card on that line, unless the person names another id. Navigating without typing sends nothing.

The last card heard belongs to one agent, not to the conversation, so a new agent always gets the whole block on its first turn, also when the card did not change. The map has no state with no card open: the whole tree is the home card's page, so a turn sent from the tree names the home card, and a message with no card names the home card too. An id that the map no longer holds still goes out: the line names the id and says the map holds no card with it, so the person's words are not lost.

Example:

- The page has #retry "Checkout retries" open.

1. The person sends "Make it three tries". A new agent starts. The turn starts with the whole block of #retry.
2. The person sends "And log each try". The turn starts with the reminder.
3. The agent exits. The person sends "Why did it stop?". A new agent starts, and the turn starts with the whole block again.

```
 turn  agent  first line of the turn
 1     a-1    [the map is now at #retry — Checkout retries] + block   (1)
 2     a-1    [still on #retry — Checkout retries]                    (2)
 -     a-1    exits
 3     a-2    [the map is now at #retry — Checkout retries] + block   (3)

a-1, a-2  the first and the second agent.  (n)  the step.
```

kill.text: The map gains a view of the whole tree that is not the home card's page.

payload.title: Each conversation keeps a chat log of what the agent was told, said and did, and the map stays the record
payload.why: A later reader of a conversation, and every quote taken from it, needs what the agent heard, what it said and what it ran. The log is not the record of decisions: what the talk settled must be on a card, so losing the log loses no decision. A streamed token is only an early form of a finished block, so it is not kept.
payload.body:
The chat log of a conversation is one file named after the conversation, in a folder beside the map's log, outside version control. It gets one line, in order, for the open-card line that starts a turn, the person's words, each finished text block of the agent, each tool call with its input, and each tool result. A streamed token, a status update and a turn start or end write no line.

Each line holds its speaker, person or agent; the time it was written; the agent session id; its kind; and its text. The kind is spoken, tool call, tool result, or tooling for text that the tooling adds, and it decides which lines can hold a quote (see #map-excerpt-pointer). A line that cannot be read, or has an unknown kind, still counts for the message position and holds no quote.

Each line records the session of the agent that heard it, because a quote points through the session at the wider context. A new agent names its session only in its first output, after the person's words are already in, so the lines of a fresh agent wait in memory until it names its session. An agent that exits before it names one leaves its lines with an empty session, so no message is lost. The conversation's name does not change when the agent restarts, so one log holds the whole conversation across agents and server restarts. A context clear does not delete the log (#chat-context-pie).

A conversation name is letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores and does not start with a dot, so a name never points outside the folder. Any other name is refused before a file is read.

If deleting the chat log ever loses something that matters, a decision failed to reach a card.

payload.title: Each part of a reply stays under the message that asked for it
payload.why: A person can send a second message while a reply still streams, and the pane draws that message at once. If new parts of the first reply land at the bottom, they read as the answer to the second message. A name on each turn lets the pane put every part where it belongs.
payload.body:
A turn is one message from the person and the whole reply to it, up to the end line with duration and cost. The page gives each message a short, plain turn name when it sends it, and the server refuses a name that is not short and plain, because the name goes into every event and into the page. The agent runs one turn at a time. The server keeps the sent turns that have not ended, in order, and each part of the reply belongs to the oldest. Every chat event on the live channel names its turn, and the start and the end of a turn are events of their own.

A message whose turn has not started shows a waiting mark: "waits for the reply above". The mark goes when its turn starts. A part that arrives with no open turn, for example when the agent writes on its own, opens a turn that the server names, and a page starts a new turn for it at the bottom. A message that the server refuses, or that never reaches it, leaves the thread, and its words go back to an empty composer with the error.

Example:

- Message A "Summarise the open cards" is sent. Its reply streams.
- Message B "Also list the ghosts" is sent while the reply to A streams.

1. The pane draws A, then the first part of reply A.
2. The person sends B. The pane draws B below reply A, with the waiting mark.
3. A second part of reply A arrives. The pane adds it under A, above B.
4. The end line of A arrives. The agent starts B, and the mark under B goes.

```
server order: [A, B]        pane
                            A  Summarise the open cards
  part 1 -> A                 a1
  part 2 -> A                 a2     <- step 3: lands above B
  end    -> A                 12s · $0.04
                            B  Also list the ghosts
                               ○ waits for the reply above   <- steps 2 to 4

○  the waiting mark.  a1, a2  parts of reply A.
```

kill.text: Send a second message while a long reply streams. If any part of the first reply appears below the second message, revisit.

payload.title: An exit of the agent ends every open turn, and a waiting message is not sent again by itself
payload.why: A message that waits behind a running turn has already gone to the agent, and the agent takes it with it when it exits. Sending it again by itself would start work at a moment the person did not choose, and an agent that exits at once would get it in a loop. One more send by hand is the safer cost.
payload.body: When the agent exits and werk does not start it again by itself (an early-exit retry or a replay into a new session, see #chat-crash-retry and #chat-resume), the running turn and every turn that waits behind it end. The server keeps no waiting message for the next agent, and the next agent starts only when the person sends a new message. The words stay in the thread and in the chat log. The pane tells the two ends apart: a turn that started says the agent exited before the reply ended, and a turn that never started says the agent exited before this message got an answer, so the person knows to send it again.

payload.title: The pane streams each turn as it runs and renders the reply as Markdown
payload.why: When only a tool call showed that the agent was alive, a person could not tell work from a hang. Streaming the text, the agent's state and the token count shows progress at once. A finished block replaces its streamed form, so only finished blocks are kept.
payload.body:
The agent runs with partial messages on, so the server gets each block while it streams. It sends three kinds of update on the live channel: a finished block, which the chat log keeps; a streamed token, which is never kept; and a status. A streamed block and its finished form share one id, so the finished text replaces what streamed.

The header row shows a pulse, the agent's state, the seconds and the tokens so far. The state is thinking during a thinking block, running a tool during a tool call, and writing during a text block. The turn ends with its duration and cost.

The reply renders as Markdown with the renderer of card text (see #ui-render), and an unclosed code fence still renders while a reply streams.

payload.title: A suggested next reply at the end of an agent message becomes a button
payload.why: The agent often ends with a suggested reply such as Next: say "merge it". Typing the phrase back costs the person a round of typing for words the agent already wrote. A button sends the phrase as a normal message.
payload.body: The pane reads the last line of each finished agent message. A line of the form Next: say "<phrase>" or Next: reply "<phrase>", with straight or curly quotes and optional bold, adds a button under the message labelled with the phrase. Text after the closing quote is ignored. A click sends the phrase as a normal message with the open card, and leaves the composer, its draft and its pending images as they are. The next message from the person removes every such button, so only the latest offer can be clicked. A message in another wording gets no button. An offer that is not clicked also signals the conversation as waiting for the person.

payload.title: Each conversation runs in a Claude Code process that werk starts and talks to over its streaming JSON input and output
payload.why: A session that a host application started holds its own input, so werk cannot write a message to it. A process that werk starts takes each turn as one line on its input, resumes by session id, and gives werk every built-in tool of Claude Code. The library form of the same agent would mean a rewrite with no defect to fix.
payload.body:
To give each conversation a real two-way channel, werk starts one long-lived Claude Code process for it and writes each turn of the person to that process's input as one JSON line. It reads the process's output as a stream of JSON events: blocks, tool calls, results and control requests. This is the same input and output setup that a host application uses for its own sessions, so it is known to work. The clipboard stays the way to hand text to a session that the person runs elsewhere.

The process inherits the environment of the shell that started the server, including its Claude Code login, not anything from the browser. When the agent cannot log in, the fix is to sign in to Claude Code in the shell that runs the server.

Of the other ways to run Claude Code, a hosted agent has no access to the local working tree, and the raw model interface would mean writing the whole tool loop again.

kill.text: Reopen if the host exposes a way to send a turn to its own session, if the spawned process stops taking input, or if reading the stream breaks against a new Claude Code version.

payload.title: A restart resumes the conversation's session, and only Claude Code's own no-such-session error clears it
payload.why: Editing werk means restarting werk, and a fresh session would contradict the transcript still on screen. Treating any early exit as a dead session once deleted a working conversation, so only the one error that proves the session is gone may clear it.
payload.body: The agent names its session id in its first event. werk stores it per conversation and resumes it on the next start. If the stored session no longer exists, Claude Code says so and exits before it names a session. Only that message clears the stored id: werk then starts a new session and sends again the message the person was waiting on. Any other early exit leaves the id alone, because losing a working conversation costs more than a retry (#chat-crash-retry). An error result that arrives before the session is named is not a finished turn, so it does not clear the message that waits to be sent again. A person can start a fresh conversation on purpose.

payload.title: A crash is retried once only when the agent wrote nothing yet, and the pane shows the whole error
payload.why: An agent that exits before it writes anything has done no work, so starting it again repeats nothing. After it names its session or writes any part of a reply, it may have run a tool or edited a file, and a second run would do that work twice. A failure such as a login problem or a bad flag fails the same way again, so a retry only doubles the wait.
payload.body:
werk sorts each exit that it did not cause. An exit is early when the agent wrote nothing of the turn: no session id and no part of a reply. An early exit gets one automatic retry on the same session, unless its error is one that a retry cannot fix, such as a login problem, a missing credential or a bad flag. A late exit is never retried: the stored session stays, the open turns end, and the oldest one shows the error.

The pane shows the whole error output of the agent, not its last lines, because the cause is usually in the first line. A long error folds behind a disclosure. Every stop of a send ends with the same line under the message: "Your message was not delivered. Send it again."

Example:

1. The agent exits with an unknown error before it names its session. One retry runs with the same message.
2. The agent exits with a login error before it names its session. No retry runs. The pane shows the whole error and the not-delivered line.
3. The agent names its session, edits a card, then exits with an error. Nothing runs again, and the turn ends with the whole error.

```
start ──> [nothing written] ──exit──> early: retry once, unless a retry cannot fix it
      ──> session named / reply part ──exit──> late: turns end, whole error, no rerun
```

payload.title: An agent that exits without werk stopping it marks its conversation dead until the next agent starts
payload.why: werk stops agents on purpose, and those exits must not read as deaths. Any other exit needs the person, who may be away from the pane when it happens, so the mark must be one they cannot miss and must stay until a new agent replaces the dead one.
payload.body: An agent is dead when it exits and werk did not stop it. werk stops an agent on purpose for an idle sweep, for a restart with a new model or a cleared context, and at server shutdown. An early crash that its one retry recovers is not a death; the conversation is dead only when the retry also fails or is not made (#chat-crash-retry). A death drops the agent's open asks and background agents, because no process is left to answer them. The conversation stays dead until its next agent starts, on the next message. While it is dead, the pane shows a red line that says so.

payload.title: The pane shows a line while a background task of the agent still runs
payload.why: A background subagent or shell command can run on after the turn ends, so the pane looks finished while work goes on. Claude Code's own marker for it does not reach werk's pane. The agent sends its whole task list on every change, so werk keeps only its length and never matches an end to a start.
payload.body: A background task is a subagent or a shell command that the agent starts and that runs on after its turn ends. Each time one starts or ends, the agent sends the full list of running tasks as one event. werk replaces the count with the length of the last list, and any other event leaves the count as it is. While the count is above zero, the pane shows a line pinned under the chat log, which stays in view while the log scrolls, and the conversation reads as running even with no turn open. When the agent exits, its tasks end with it and the count goes to zero.

kill.text: A conversation reads idle while one of its background tasks still runs, or reads running after its agent sent an empty task list.

payload.title: Claude Code's own auto permission mode decides which tool calls are safe, and werk classifies none
payload.why: Deciding which tool call is safe is the job of Claude Code's permission engine. A second classifier inside werk must copy that job, and every gap in the copy is a wrong question or a missed one. File edits are the agent's normal work, so they run with no question.
payload.body:
The chat agent runs in Claude Code's auto permission mode, fixed and not a setting. A default allowlist adds the file tools, the map's own command and a few interpreters, so a file edit never waits on a question; a server option can narrow that list. werk keeps no shell parser, no read-only list and no rule matcher. It only sees the calls the engine cannot resolve, and it asks the person about each (#chat-approval). The agent's instructions tell it to change a file with the edit tools, not by piping it through a shell script, because the edit tools need no question and show a diff.

Measured over nineteen calls in auto mode, only a network call stopped for a question, and it came with no suggested rule. So in practice the question bar is a last stop for network access, and the edit tools in the default list already let the agent change any file in the repository. The pane shows no diff of edits: version control does.

payload.title: A call the engine cannot resolve is asked in the pane, and the turn waits for the answer
payload.why: The agent runs without a terminal, so a call that needs a person would otherwise come back refused and the turn would go on without it. Asking in the pane keeps the turn open while the question waits. A refused or unanswered call must never widen a permission.
payload.body:
A call that the engine cannot resolve arrives as a control request on the agent's own output stream, and the agent stays blocked. The server puts the question in the pane over the live channel. The bar shows the tool, the whole call as a code block, and the reason Claude Code gave, as it was sent. Its buttons are Allow once, Always allow and Deny, and Always allow appears only when the request carried a suggested rule, which the button shows (#chat-always-allow). The answer goes back on the agent's input with the same request id, and the tool runs or does not.

One click disables the bar, and the server refuses a second answer to a question that is already closed, so a question is answered once. Every open page shows a question when it arrives and removes it when any page answers it, and a page that opens later reads the open questions first. Several open questions stack. Cmd+Enter allows and Escape denies the first one; one key press acts on one target, so the composer ignores Enter while Cmd or Ctrl is held. Escape denies from anywhere, which is the safe direction to be wrong in.

payload.title: A question from the agent is a form the person answers, and the answer goes back as the reason of a refusal
payload.why: A question shown as a raw tool call hides the question and gives no way to answer it. The permission channel has no field for an answer and a call is never changed on approval, so the answer travels as the text of a refusal. The pane and the log must not show that refusal as a failure, because a picked answer is a normal reply.
payload.body: The pane shows the agent's question in the question bar as a form. Each question lists its options as lettered choices with their descriptions, single or multiple choice as the question says, and one more free-text row takes an answer that is not listed. Submit answer sends the picks; Decline refuses the question. The answer reaches the agent as one line per question: For "<question>": <picked labels>. The pane does not paint that result as an error. The picks live outside the drawn page, so a redraw does not clear a half-filled form.

payload.title: Always allow stores the rule that Claude Code suggested, for that conversation only, and the next agent starts with it
payload.why: A permission given in one conversation must not apply to another, and it must survive a restart. werk stores the suggestion the CLI made and never writes a rule of its own, so it needs no rule matcher.
payload.body: An Always allow click applies the suggested rules and folders to the live agent and adds them, each once, to the entry of its own conversation in a local allow file. A restarted agent of that conversation starts with those rules as allowed tools and those folders as added directories. A missing or broken file counts as no choices. In auto mode the CLI attaches no suggestion to the questions it asks, so the button does not appear in practice; the path stays for a later CLI that does.

payload.title: Every answered question goes to a local ask log, apart from the map's log
payload.why: To find which calls keep asking, and which rules are worth adding to the defaults, there must be a record of each question and its answer. That record is local history, not a decision, so it stays out of the map's log.
payload.body: One line per answered question, appended and never rewritten: when, the tool, the call, the reason Claude Code gave, the decision, and the rules an Always allow added. The decision is allow, always, deny, or answer for a question the person answered, so a count of refusals does not include normal replies; a declined question is a deny. Only questions that reached the pane are written: a call the engine allowed by itself asked nobody. The log is outside version control.

payload.title: A run of tool calls collapses into one line that names the latest call
payload.why: Every read, edit and shell call at full length pushed the conversation off screen. Folding only long output still left several lines of tool calls per turn. One line per run clears the space, and naming the call's main input says what the agent does.
payload.body:
The pane groups each run of tool calls into one closed section. Its line shows the latest call's tool and the first line of its main input, the first non-empty of the command, the file path, the path, the pattern, the address, the query and the description, cut to about 80 characters, then the count of calls in the run. A call with none of these shows the tool name only. The line updates while calls stream in. Opening it shows every call with its input and output.

```
▸ Read src/a.ts · 1 call
▸ Bash werk show retry · 2 calls
▸ Task · 3 calls
```

payload.title: A page redraws the chat thread from the chat log every time its live channel connects
payload.why: The live channel keeps nothing for a page that is not connected, so a block finished while the page was away never reaches it. The chat log holds every finished block and survives a restart, so a read of it on each connect closes the gap. The gap matters only when an agent can run on while the page is away.
payload.body: On every connect of the live channel, the first one included, the page reads the conversation's finished blocks and redraws the thread from them. A block that still streams stays, and its finished form replaces it when it arrives, because the two share one id. Today a reload and a first view already read the log, and an agent on the same machine stops with the page's laptop, so this waits until agents run away from the page.

kill.text: Reconsider when an agent runs on a machine other than the page's.

payload.title: The chat header row sits directly above the composer
payload.why: The person types at the bottom of the pane. The turn state and the context fill must be in the same glance as the text box, so the person can see whether the agent works or is stuck.
payload.body: Top to bottom, the pane holds the chat log, the background-task line, the dead-agent line, the open questions, the chat header row, the composer, and last, when the project has tabs, the tab strip. The header row holds the turn state, the interrupt button, the context pie and the model selector, with a border above it. A popover from the header row opens upward.

payload.title: Opening a conversation shows its newest message, and new messages pull the log down only when the person is at the bottom
payload.why: A person opens or switches to a conversation to see where it is now, so the log scrolls to the end, also for a long one that loads for the first time. A person who scrolled up to read must not be pulled away by a new message.
payload.body: Every switch to a conversation scrolls its log to the bottom, for a log that loads for the first time and for one shown before. A scroll position from before the switch is not kept. While the conversation stays open, the log follows new messages only if the person is already near the bottom.

kill.text: A person loses their reading place by switching away from a conversation and back.

payload.title: The chat header picks Sonnet, Opus, or Sonnet with an Opus advisor, each pinned to an exact model id
payload.why: Switching to a stronger model for a hard card, or a cheaper one for routine edits, must not need a code change or a restart of werk. Exact model ids keep werk on a known version until someone repins it, instead of moving silently when an alias changes.
payload.body:
The selector offers three choices: Sonnet, Opus, and Sonnet with Claude Code's built-in Opus advisor, which the agent consults itself at decision points, such as before it commits to an approach or calls a card settled. Sonnet with the Opus advisor is the default. The ids are claude-sonnet-5-5[1m] for Sonnet and claude-opus-5-5 for Opus and the advisor, and the server refuses any other pair. If the advisor is not available, for example behind a gateway, the agent runs Sonnet alone without saying so.

The model takes effect only when the agent starts, so a switch stops the agent on purpose and starts it again on the same session: the conversation is kept, and the stop is not a crash. A switch and a context clear are refused while any turn is open, from the moment a message is sent until its reply ends, because a stop would drop a message that waits behind the running reply. The pane disables the selector for the same span, and the server refusal is the real guard. Every open page learns of a switch or a clear from the live channel.

payload.title: A pie beside the model selector shows how full the context is, and a clear ends the session but keeps the chat log
payload.why: Token use was invisible until the agent slowed down or failed near the window limit. The model reports both numbers, so the fill is no guess. A clear must make the agent forget, but the chat log is where every quote points, so a clear deletes nothing.
payload.body:
The pie shows the context in use over the context window. The use is the sum of the input, output, cache-read and cache-creation tokens of the latest single model call, because one call's usage is the size of the conversation at that call; the turn's final total adds up every call and would overstate it many times. The window comes from the final result of the turn, read from the entry of the conversation's own model, not the advisor's. The pie is blue under a third, yellow from a third, and red from two thirds.

A click opens a popover with the percentage and Clear context. A clear forgets in two places: the stored session goes, so the next message starts an empty context, and every open page empties its shown chat. The chat log on disk keeps every line, because a quote points at a message in it. The map is untouched. A clear is refused while a turn is open, like a model switch.

payload.title: A conversation keeps its model, advisor and context fill across a server restart
payload.why: The model choice and the context size belong to the conversation, not to the server process. Saved beside the conversation's session, they come back on a restart; without that, every restarted conversation falls back to the default model and shows a wrong fill.
payload.body:
The conversation saves its model, its advisor and its last context fill in a small settings file beside its session file, and reads them when it is rebuilt. A read of the conversation returns these settings with its messages, so the selector and the pie are right before any message. A missing or broken file means the default model and an empty pie. A clear keeps the model and advisor and resets the fill.

The window depends on the model, so before a turn reports it, a model marked as a million-token model counts a million tokens and any other two hundred thousand. A model switch resets the window to the new model's size until the next turn reports it.

payload.title: Typing a slash or a hash sign in the composer opens a menu of commands or cards
payload.why: Typing a command name or a card id by hand is slow and error-prone. A menu shows what can be typed while the person types it. A trigger inside a path, a URL or inline code is not a request for a menu, so only a clean word opens one.
payload.body:
The composer looks at the word that ends at the caret. It opens a menu when the word starts with a slash or a hash sign and the character before it is whitespace or the start of the text. A backtick right before the trigger, or a second slash, hash sign or backtick inside the word, opens no menu, so a path like /src/app and inline code stay plain text.

Both menus share one place and one look: a list above the composer, because the composer sits at the bottom of the pane. Arrows move, Enter or Tab chooses, and Escape closes. A choice replaces the word with the trigger, the chosen name and one space, and puts the caret after the space.

The slash menu lists the commands the agent knows (#chat-command-source) that start with the typed text, case ignored. The hash menu lists cards: the id matches first, in the order of the header search after a hash, with the exact id first; then cards whose title holds the typed text, up to the header search's limit. A bare hash sign lists nothing.

payload.title: The slash menu lists the commands that the agent names when it starts
payload.why: Only the agent knows its whole set of commands: the built-in ones, the project's, the user's and those of its plugins. It names them in the first event it writes, so the server keeps that list and the menu reads it. Before the first agent starts, the list is empty and no menu opens.
payload.body: The server keeps the command names from the start event of the most recent agent of the conversation. Each start replaces the list; a name is stored without its leading slash, and a start that names none empties it. The composer asks the server for the names each time a slash word opens the menu. That read changes nothing and starts nothing, so it needs no token.

kill.text: Open a fresh map and type a slash before the first message. If an empty menu there is a real hindrance, read the command folders as a fallback.

payload.title: A pasted screenshot uploads at once as a file, and the agent opens it by its path
payload.why: A screenshot shows a UI bug at once, where prose is slow. Uploading at paste time lets a wrong type or an oversized image show on its chip before the send. The agent opens each file with its own read, so the model sees the image itself and never its bytes.
payload.body:
The person pastes an image into the composer or drops it on the pane. The paste puts a token [Image #N] at the caret and a chip with a spinner above the composer; removing a chip removes its token and renumbers the rest. The page uploads the image at once. The server reads the size and the first bytes, and stores a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP image of up to 20 MB under a new name made of the time and a random part; it trusts neither the page's claimed type nor the file name. A refused image shows its reason on its chip and is not sent. The page also checks the size before the upload, so the chip can name the limit.

The send carries the text and the stored name of each image, and waits while an upload still runs. The server turns each name into a path, refuses a name it never stored, and starts the turn with one line per token that maps it to its path and asks the agent to open each image. The sent message shows each image under its number.

The images sit in an attachments folder beside the map's log, with its own ignore file so they stay out of version control: a screenshot is transcript, not map. The server serves only plain file names inside that folder. A removed chip leaves its file, which costs disk space only.

payload.title: One werk server process works on many projects, and only the interface is shared
payload.why: werk is a tool for any project, and a person moves between projects many times a day, so one place lists them and switches between them. One process holds every project, so one code reload updates all of them. Each project keeps its own map, conversations, agents and history, so work in one never touches another.
payload.body:
A project is a folder with a git repository and a map. The person adds a project once, and it stays on the list until they remove it (proj-list). The interface, its code and its display settings are shared (proj-display). The map, the conversations, the running agents, the builds and the history belong to one project.

There is one werk server per machine, on one port. It holds one context per project. A hot reload in dev mode replaces the code for every context at once, and the live agent sessions of every project survive it (see #how-runtime).

A switch to another project changes only what the browser shows. The chats, builds and other work of the project the person left keep running, and the switcher marks each project with a running agent turn.

Every feature of werk works in every project. No feature is limited to werk's own repository.

kill.text: manual: use werk on at least two real projects for a week. Switching between them never mixes their state.

payload.title: A request that changes state or starts an agent needs the server's token, and its Host must be a loopback name
payload.why: A chat request starts an agent that edits files and runs shell commands without asking, so whoever can send it can run code on the person's machine. A random token in the served page is something another site or another machine cannot read. A Host check closes DNS rebinding a second time for the price of one comparison.
payload.body:
The server uses the synchronizer token pattern from the OWASP guidance on cross-site request forgery. It makes a random token at each start and puts it in a meta tag of the page it serves. Every request that starts an agent turn, writes to a log, answers a question, uploads an image or moves a ticket must carry the token in a request header, or the server refuses it. The check runs before routing, so a route added later is covered without its own check. While the server listens on loopback only, it also refuses a request whose Host is not a loopback name.

The token never goes into a log, a transcript, or the environment of an agent the server starts, because that agent can read all three. A read-only request needs no token. A test or a tool that makes a changing request reads the token from the page the same way the page does.

payload.title: A failing request answers an error and never stops the server
payload.why: One request with an empty image name once made the server read a directory, and the uncaught error killed the whole process with every live agent in it. A guard around the whole request handler turns any such failure into one error answer.
payload.body: The server wraps its whole request handler, so a request that throws answers a server error and the server keeps running. Each route still checks its own input; the wrapper catches the class of bug that a route forgot.

payload.title: Several conversations run at once, each in its own tab
payload.why: One running turn blocks the chat pane, so a second topic waits for the first to finish. With tabs, each topic gets its own conversation and its own live agent, and the person moves between them while every turn keeps running.
payload.body:
Each tab is one conversation with its own agent process, its own session and its own chat transcript. The tab that exists before any fork is the main conversation. A forked or empty-started conversation has a home card (see #chat-home-card), and its tab carries that card's id. The feature gives two gains: throughput, because a turn in one tab runs while the person works in another, and tokens, because a new tab is a fork that shares its parent's cached prefix (#chat-tabs-fork).

The tabs build on the chat and the chat does not depend on them, so a project can have one conversation and no tabs.

payload.title: A conversation has a name and a home card, and the home card is a label, not a fence
payload.why: Several conversations need names that say what each is about, and a card id reads better than a number. A conversation crosses subtrees anyway, so a fence would block normal work or force a switch. The home card labels the conversation and never limits it.
payload.body:
A conversation that a fork or an empty start opens records the card it opened on as its home card. That card labels its tab and is the context of its first turn. The main conversation, the one that exists before any fork, has no home card. The home card is not a fence: the conversation may go anywhere, and every turn still names the card open at that moment (#chat-open-card).

Each conversation also has a short lowercase name that every request and every live event carries, so a page keeps the conversations apart and drops events of another. A missing name means the main conversation, named main. Every conversation keeps its own session and model settings.

payload.title: Tabs are a horizontal strip of card-id chips at the bottom of the chat pane
payload.why: A strip costs one row of height and never moves, so a switch is one click. Chips keep the order in which they were opened, so a key that selects a chip by its position always picks the same tab.
payload.body:
The strip is the last row of the chat pane, below the composer, and starts flush at the pane's left edge. A chip is drawn as a real tab attached to the pane above it. A chip shows the card id of its conversation, not the card title, and a dot for the tab's state (chat-tabs-signal).

The strip shows at most five chips (chat-tabs-park). Cmd+1 to Cmd+5 select a chip by its position. Cmd+[ and Cmd+] step to the previous and the next chip, and a step past either end wraps to the other end. A strip with one chip does not move on a step.

To keep positions learnable, chips stay in insertion order. Parking a chip closes its gap and never reorders the other chips.

kill.text: manual: step past the last chip several times in daily use. If the wrap lands on a tab you did not mean to open, change to a step that stops at the ends.

payload.title: The focused tab sets the map's position, not the other way round
payload.why: Every turn tells the agent which card the map shows. If a tab were focused while the map still showed another tab's card, its agent would hear the wrong subject and would follow it. So each conversation owns its card, and focusing a tab moves the map to that card.
payload.body:
The focused tab owns its position. Focusing a tab sets both the scope above the composer and the map.

Three rules follow. Navigation on the map inside a tab changes only that tab's position, and a switch away and back restores it. A fork is focused, so a fork moves the map to the fork's card (#chat-tabs-open). Text typed in the composer and not sent belongs to its tab and survives a switch, because it was written under that tab's card.

A page load whose address names a card opens that card in the focused tab. A page load whose address names no card opens the focused tab's own position.

payload.title: A new tab forks the session of the tab it comes from
payload.why: A fork starts with a full copy of its parent's history, so the agent keeps what the parent already read and understood. The model provider reads that shared prefix from its cache, so the fork's first turn costs little, while an empty start would read the same files and cards again on every later turn.
payload.body:
A fork resumes the parent's stored session in fork mode (see #chat-resume). The agent tool writes the fork as a new session with its own id; the parent's session gets no new turn. A measured fork of a 70,000-token conversation read the whole prefix from the cache and wrote only its own 61 new tokens.

A fork is a continuation, so it starts on the parent's model and advisor, not on the default. The fork's transcript opens with one line that names the parent, with a button that switches to the parent tab and shows the parent's last message before the fork. A fork that has not sent a message yet keeps its parent and home card across a server restart, so its first message still forks.

A tab that has never sent a message has no session to copy. A fork of it opens a new tab on the clicked card with no parent, and that tab's first message starts an empty session. An empty start on purpose is a second, explicit control for an unrelated topic (see #chat-tabs-open).

Example:

- tab A on "#map" has sent no message.
- tab C on "#map" has session s1.

1. The person forks A at "#fold". Tab B opens on "#fold" with no parent. Its first message starts an empty session.
2. The person forks C at "#fold". Tab D opens on "#fold" with parent s1. Its first message continues from a copy of s1, on C's model.

```
A "#map" (no session) --fork--> B "#fold" (parent: none) --first message--> empty session
C "#map" (session s1) --fork--> D "#fold" (parent: s1)   --first message--> copy of s1
```

kill.text: manual: fork a tab on a non-default model, check the model of the fork, and use the link back to the fork point.

payload.title: A Shift+click on a card forks a tab there and focuses it, and a plain click only navigates
payload.why: Both gestures land on the card that the person clicked, so the rule to learn is one rule. The only difference is whether a new conversation starts there. The tab that the person leaves keeps running its turn.
payload.body:
A plain click moves the map, and the focused conversation follows it. A Shift+click forks a new tab on that card and focuses it, so the map goes there too (#chat-tabs-follow). A Shift+click on a card that already has a tab switches to that tab and does not fork again.

The tab strip ends with a plus button. A short press forks the conversation on the open card: the new tab keeps the parent's history and takes the open card as its home card. If another tab already has that home card, the press switches to it; on the focused tab's own home card it forks that tab, so the button never looks dead. A long press or a right-click opens a small menu with Fork current conversation, in bold, and New empty conversation. An empty conversation opens a new tab every time, with no history and no agent until its first message.

Focusing the fork costs the ability to read the earlier tab while the fork starts. One key press returns to it (#chat-tabs-strip).

payload.title: A tab is parked, never closed, and a menu lists every conversation
payload.why: A strip with many chips is worse than no tabs, so the strip keeps at most five. The session of a conversation stays on disk, so hiding a tab loses nothing, and a separate closed state would behave the same as a parked one.
payload.body:
When a sixth tab opens, the least recently touched idle tab is parked. A tab with a running turn, an open ask or a running background agent is not idle and is never parked; if no tab is idle, the strip runs over the cap until one is. A close control on a chip parks that tab at once, ahead of the cap. The close control appears on hover in place of the state dot, so a chip never changes width. The last visible chip has no close control, so the strip is never empty.

A menu at the end of the strip lists every conversation, visible and parked, and marks the focused one and the parked ones. The list scrolls past ten rows and sorts by last use, oldest at the top, so the most recent sits next to the button that opens it. A row is described by the session's own title from the agent tool, so two tabs on one card read differently; a session with no title shows the first line of its first prompt. A click on a parked row brings it back to the strip.

Parking hides a tab; it does not stop its agent. A parked agent stops only after it stays idle (chat-tabs-reap).

payload.title: A parked conversation's agent stops after 30 idle minutes and comes back when the tab returns
payload.why: Parked agents that never stop make the memory of the server grow without end. An agent that stops only after it was idle does not lose a turn in progress, and its session stays on disk, so a resume brings it back with no visible difference.
payload.body:
A check runs at least once a minute. It stops the agent of a conversation that has been parked and untouched for 30 minutes. Any activity of the agent counts as a touch. The check never stops an agent with a running turn, an open ask or a running background agent. The 30 minutes are a starting value.

When a tab comes back from the menu, a conversation whose agent still runs keeps it, so it never gets a second process. A conversation whose agent was stopped, and that has a session, starts its agent at once on that session (see #chat-resume), so it is ready before the person types. A conversation with no session starts nothing until its first message.

Example: conversation B has session s-b; conversation A has never sent a message.

1. B is parked while its agent runs. The person brings B back. No process starts.
2. B is parked again and stays idle for 30 minutes. The check stops its agent.
3. The person brings B back. An agent starts at once and resumes s-b.
4. A is brought back. Nothing starts. A's first message starts its agent.

```
bring back B
  agent runs?  yes -> keep it, start nothing        (step 1)
               no  -> session known?
                        yes -> start now, resume s-b (step 3)
                        no  -> start nothing         (step 4)
```

kill.text: manual: bring back parked conversations in daily use. If the start at once leaves idle processes that nobody types into, or a conversation ever runs two processes, change to a resume at the next message.

payload.title: Each tab shows whether its agent runs, waits for the person, or is dead, and a waiting tab blinks
payload.why: A person runs several conversations but reads one. A permission ask or a dead agent stops its tab until the person acts, so those states must be hard to miss from any tab, while a running agent only informs.
payload.body:
Each chip carries one state dot. Running means the agent works, also when only a background agent of the tab still runs (see #chat-background-agents). Waiting means the tab needs the person: an open permission ask, an open question, or a next-action button that waits for a click (see #chat-next-button). Dead means the agent exited and werk did not stop it (see #chat-dead-agent). A waiting or dead dot blinks, in the color of the reason; when two reasons hold, the more urgent one shows, and dead wins over waiting.

An ask is answered only on its own tab, in that tab's own ask bar. It never shows inline in another tab, and the ask does not pull the focus to its tab. The focused tab's own dot blinks too, so its chip and its ask bar say the same thing.

A parked tab has no chip, so the menu button at the end of the strip blinks for every tab that is not focused, in the color of the most urgent one. The focused tab never drives that button.

A running conversation also marks its card on the map, so the person sees from the map which card a conversation works on. The main conversation has no home card, so its mark sits on the card that it is at now.

kill.text: manual: leave one background tab with an open ask and one with a dead agent, and check that each chip blinks in its own color. If you do not notice the blink, this card changes.

payload.title: A tab that needs the person shows a line in every other tab's pane, in the color of the reason
payload.why: A blink on a small chip is easy to miss while the person reads another pane, but a line in that pane is not. One pattern for every reason is learned once, and the color tells the person what the tab needs before they switch to it.
payload.body:
An attention bar sits in the chat pane between the chat log and the ask bar. It shows one line for each other tab that needs the person. The line names the tab and the reason, and its color matches that tab's blinking dot:

- Dead, red: the line gives the error.
- Permission, yellow: the line names the tool.
- Question, blue: the line gives the question.
- Offer, green: the line gives the action.

A line stays while its reason holds. It goes when the person answers or clicks, when the agent withdraws the ask, or when the next agent of a dead tab starts. A tab with two reasons shows only the more urgent one, in the order of the list. A click on a line focuses that tab. The focused tab shows no line for itself.

Example: tab #log is focused; the agent of #fold asks to run Bash; the agent of #map asks "Which layout?".

1. The #fold dot blinks yellow. The #log pane shows "#fold waits for permission: Bash".
2. The #map dot blinks blue. A second line shows: "#map asks: Which layout?".
3. The person clicks the #map line. #map gets the focus and shows its own question form. Its pane shows the #fold line and no line for #map.
4. The agent of #fold exits with code 1 before an answer. Its ask goes, and its line turns red: "#fold died: exited with code 1".
5. A tab whose agent runs and asks nothing shows no line and does not blink.

```
  #log pane (focused)
  +--------------------------------------+
  | chat log                             |
  | [Y] #fold waits for permission: Bash |  <-- attention bar
  | [B] #map asks: Which layout?         |
  | ask bar: asks of #log only           |
  +--------------------------------------+
  tab strip:  [ #log ]  [ #fold (Y) ]  [ #map (B) ]

  [x] = color of the line   (x) = color of the blinking dot
  R = red, dead   Y = yellow, permission   B = blue, question   G = green, offer
```
