kill.text: manual: revisit when the lines read as noise and do not lead to an action: an answer, a click, or a new start of that tab.

payload.title: A tab reads another conversation on demand, and no conversation is pushed into another
payload.why: Forks do not hear each other after the split, and that is normal. The map on disk holds the current state and an agent reads a card before it writes, so a stale context does no harm. What a sibling said is rarely needed, and werk knows each conversation's session, so an exact lookup costs less than a broadcast on every switch.
payload.body:
Two channels exist, and both are pulled. The state is the map, which every turn already reads. What was said is the transcript of each conversation, read with two operations.

The list operation shows every conversation with its home card, session, number of turns and last activity. The read operation resolves a reference to one transcript and prints it, filtered by case-insensitive patterns that must all match, with the messages around each hit. A reference is tried from the most specific kind to the loosest: an exact session id, a home card, a tab name, then the start of a session id. The first kind that matches decides, and two matches of that kind are an error, not a guess.

The default transcript is werk's own: it is clean, it is tagged with cards, and it hides tool calls unless asked. A second mode reads the agent tool's own transcript with werk's own reader of that format, for a tool call that werk's transcript shortens too much.

The agent's instructions name both operations and tell the agent never to answer that it has no access to another conversation.

kill.text: manual: in a forked tab, ask about a decision made in a sibling tab. The agent finds that conversation and quotes it. If it answers from its own context, or says it has no access, this card fails.

payload.title: Each conversation session is one line in an append-only conversations log
payload.why: A tab can get a new session under its old name, for example when its stored session no longer resolves. A store that keeps one current session per tab overwrites the old one, and that session drops out of the list. A log that only appends keeps every session listable.
payload.body:
The server appends one line each time a tab's agent reports a session. The log sits in the same folder as the map log. A line holds the tab name, the session id, the home card when there is one, and the parent session when the tab is a fork. No line is rewritten. The list folds the lines into one entry per session id, so a restart that resumes the same session adds no entry.

Example: tab main reports s-1; tab map-hash, a fork of s-1 on #map-hash, reports s-2.

1. The log gains "main s-1".
2. The log gains "map-hash s-2 home #map-hash parent s-1".
3. The server restarts and main resumes s-1. The list still shows one entry for s-1.
4. At the next restart s-1 does not resolve, and main reports s-3. The log gains "main s-3".
5. The list shows s-1, s-2 and s-3. Both s-1 and s-3 carry the name main.

```
step  event                       line appended
1     main reports s-1       -->  main      s-1
2     map-hash reports s-2   -->  map-hash  s-2  home #map-hash  parent s-1
3     restart, resumes s-1   -->  (no new entry)
4     s-1 gone, reports s-3  -->  main      s-3
list: s-1 (main)  s-2 (map-hash)  s-3 (main)
```

kill.text: manual: the list of conversations shows two entries for one session, or misses a session that a tab reported.

payload.title: An edit to the browser client never resets the tabs or a message in flight
payload.why: A conversation that edits werk's own client must not clear the tab strip or lose a turn in any other tab. Server hot reload keeps the server alive, but the browser still reloads the page on a client edit, so the client must keep or restore every tab's state across it.
payload.body: To keep tabs across a client edit, the client swaps a changed component in place, so the strip, each tab's open card and a turn in flight stay (see #how-stack-react). When an edit cannot apply in place, the page reloads and restores the strip, each tab's position, each draft and each half-filled question form from state saved in the browser.

payload.title: The project list belongs to the user and sits outside every project
payload.why: The list belongs to the person, not to a project, so no project folder holds it. A project stays on the list until the person removes it, and a removal never deletes the project's map. A list file that cannot be read is never taken as empty, because the next save would erase the person's projects.
payload.body:
The list is one file of folder paths, in order, in a per-user folder. A setting names another per-user folder, so a test or a second server never touches the real list. A folder is stored by its real path, so two links to one folder are one project. A save writes a new file and renames it over the old one, so a crash never leaves half a list. A file that does not parse is refused with an error, and nothing overwrites it.

Remove takes a project off the list. The folder and its map stay, so adding the folder again brings back the same map. A project with a running agent turn is removed only after the person confirms; werk names the running turns, stops them, and then removes the project. The dev checkout cannot be removed (proj-dev-self).

A listed folder that was moved or deleted shows as missing. It does not open, and the person can remove it. werk never removes a project from the list by itself.

payload.title: Adding a project opens the operating system's folder dialog
payload.why: A browser cannot give the server the full path of a folder, so the server opens the folder dialog itself. The server runs on the same machine as the browser, so the dialog appears in front of the person.
payload.body:
The last row of the project switcher adds a project and opens the macOS folder dialog. When the list is empty, opening werk shows one page with the same action. werk supports only macOS for now, and a setting replaces the dialog with another program for tests.

A folder with no map gets an empty map. A folder with no git repository cannot be a project yet: werk refuses it, says that git is required, and offers to create a repository there. werk creates the repository only after the person agrees, and then adds the folder. A path that is not a folder is refused.

payload.title: A project is named by its folder name
payload.why: The name shows in the switcher and in the address, so it must be short and readable. The folder name is the name the person already uses for the project.
payload.body: When two projects on the list have the same folder name, the later one adds its parent folder's name in brackets, for example "api (work)". When that name is taken too, the brackets hold the whole parent path, which no other folder shares. In dev mode, werk's own checkout is listed first, so it keeps the plain name. A project has no other name, and there is no rename.

payload.title: Every page and every request of a project carries the project's name in its address
payload.why: One server holds many projects, so a request with no project name cannot tell whose map it reads. A name in the address also lets a link or a reload open the same project.
payload.body: Every request that reads or changes one project carries the encoded project name (#proj-names), and a request for a name that is not on the list is refused. The project list has its own address, outside every project. The page addresses follow the same rule; their form, and where an address with no project opens, are in #ui-routes.

payload.title: In dev mode, werk's own checkout is always on the project list
payload.why: In dev mode the person builds werk with werk, so werk's own map must always be one click away. The entry is the checkout whose code runs, not the folder where the server started.
payload.body: The entry is added each time werk starts in dev mode, at the top of the list. It is never written to the stored list, so it is gone when werk runs outside dev mode, and it cannot be removed. The rule holds for any dev mode: the mode that runs werk from its own source.

payload.title: Display settings follow the person across projects, and each project keeps its own place
payload.why: Theme, panel widths, filters and sort order are how the person likes to read any map, so they are shared by all projects. The open card and the current view name a place in one map, so each project remembers its own.
payload.body: A switch to a project opens the card and the view that were open the last time the person was in that project. A project opened for the first time opens its home card on the map. The chat tabs and their drafts also belong to the project.

payload.title: One lock per project keeps a second server out, and one lock per machine lets a second start find the running server
payload.why: Two servers on one machine would clash on the port, and two servers on one project would share its chat state. A lock in the per-user folder stops the first, and a lock in each project folder stops the second, also for a server started another way. The machine lock also lets a second start find the running server.
payload.body:
The machine lock sits in the per-user folder and names the process and the port of the running server. Each project context takes a project lock beside that project's map log. A project whose lock another live server holds shows as locked: it is listed and does not open.

A start of werk while a server runs does not start a second server. The start reads the port from the machine lock, waits up to five seconds for a server that holds the lock and does not listen yet, adds its folder to the running server's list with a trusted request (see #proj-serve-trust), opens that project in the browser, and exits. A setting names the program that opens the browser, so a test opens nothing.

Both locks are taken the same way. A start creates the lock file in one step that fails when the file already exists, so of two starts at the same moment exactly one wins. The lock names the holder's process id, and its port once it listens. A start whose create fails reads the lock. A dead holder means a stale lock, which the start removes and takes. A live holder means another server: the start waits a few seconds, which covers a server that is still stopping, then refuses and names the holder's port and process id. A lock that does not parse counts as held during the wait and as stale after it. The lock goes on exit and on an interrupt or terminate signal. A second instance on purpose, such as a test, points at another directory.

The removal of a stale lock has no guard: two starts within milliseconds right after a crash can both run, and the lock accepts that risk.

kill.text: Two servers on one .werk directory, seen even once, reopen this: the unguarded removal of a stale lock is the first suspect.

payload.title: The product diagram is a second graph of the product's parts, drawn from the decided cards
payload.why: The map's nodes are claims and answer why the product is like this. A product diagram's nodes are parts of the built thing and answer what there is. One decision can create several parts and one part can sum many decisions, so no view of the map is a product diagram.
payload.body:
| | map | product diagram |
|---|---|---|
| node | a claim | a part of the built thing |
| question | why is it like this | what is there now |
| shape | history, append-only | current state, overwritten |
| goes stale | by propagation | when the decided cards change |

The parts live in their own graph, not as a node kind in the map. A part inside the map would count in the rollup, the staleness closure and the drained count as a claim that is settled or not, and a part is neither. The only edge between the two graphs runs from a part to the cards that decided it (#ui-diagram-file).

The diagram looks forward. It shows the shape that the cards decide, not the shape of the code, because the code of a prototype has a shape that nobody chose. A part with no code is decided and not built yet. Code with no card is scaffolding, not a hidden decision. So the diagram is never used to audit the code.

payload.title: An agent sorts each decided card as structural, behavioural or method, and only a structural card makes a part
payload.why: No card field says which part of the product a card touches or at which level, so the fold from cards to parts needs a reader's judgement. Most decided cards are not about a running part. Without the sort, the rules for keeping the map show up in the diagram as parts of the product.
payload.body:
A structural card names a running part and makes a node. A behavioural card constrains a part that is already drawn and adds its id to that part as a citation: delete the card, and the diagram keeps the same boxes and edges. A method card is about how the map is kept and makes nothing. A card is both method and structural when a running part carries the rule out, for example a contract check that the command line runs before every status change. So the class depends on whether a running part carries out the decision, not on the card's topic. No card field stores the class; the agent applies the sort on every run.

Connections also come from decided cards, not from the code. A depends_on link between two cards is not an arrow between two parts: it says that one decision needed the other first. A drawn connection marks a boundary between concepts. It can stand for several features and several code routes, if it names every card that decided one of them. A part splits into one part per channel when it serves separate channels and the diagram already groups its consumers by those channels.

A trap for a planning tool: when the product is itself the planning loop, the product's data flow and the card status loop coincide. A fold tested only on such a project looks correct for the wrong reason. Test it on a second project before trusting it.

kill.text: Two cold reads of one decided set, with no earlier diagram, put a part boundary in different places, or one read merges what the other splits. Then the first read is a decision of its own and needs review, because every later redraw inherits it. Also revisit when the diagram runs on a second project whose data flow mirrors its card statuses.

payload.title: A connection that no card decides is drawn blank and becomes a question on the map
payload.why: If the tool fills a missing arrow from the code, the gap disappears and nobody decides it. If it draws the arrow blank and asks how the two parts talk, it finds the missing decision without choosing the answer.
payload.body: The tool draws the parts, then asks about each blank arrow, for example "The chat pane and the agent runner are both parts. How do they talk?" The answer is a decision, so it becomes a card. A blank arrow is a real state, drawn as a dashed line with a mark, so the diagram can be incomplete on purpose instead of guessing.

payload.title: The diagram is one text file: a content section says what exists, a grid section says where it goes
payload.why: The fold writes judgement, and judgement is stored as text that a person or an agent can read, diff and edit in place. The picture is drawn from the text on every build and never edited by hand, so it cannot drift from the text.
payload.body:
The content section names each part with its title and description, each connection with its label, the groups and the colour classes, in a small Mermaid-like syntax. Each part line and each connection line ends with the ids of the cards that decided it, so the link back to the map sits on the line it explains. A connection can carry several ids, because several decisions can feed one drawn connection. The content never names a cell, and the grid never names a title (#ui-diagram-grid).

The card ids are the only edge between the diagram and the map. They answer why a box is there. They also bound a redraw once the diagram and the decided cards no longer fit in one agent read: then the elements whose ids a change reaches are the ones to redraw. That works only because each id is written when its element is drawn; it cannot be recovered later.

payload.title: A diagram element and the cards that decided it link both ways in one click
payload.why: The ids on the diagram answer why a box is there. In the file that answer needs a search; in the drawing it needs one click. The reverse question, what this card drew, comes from the same ids, so the browser needs no second copy of the mapping.
payload.body: From the map to the diagram: a card has a button that opens the diagram, highlights every element that names the card, and scrolls the first one into view. From the diagram to the map: a click on an element lists the cards that decided it, and each one opens that card on the map. A thin line gets a wider invisible copy under it, so it is a usable click target.

payload.title: The agent writes every cell of the diagram grid; a checker refuses a broken grid and a program sizes and draws it
payload.why: Every layout defect of auto-layout and of hand-drawn pictures was found by looking at the picture, never by reading the input. A grid that the agent writes cell by cell is a coarse drawing of itself, so its author can read it back before anything renders. Sizing columns and rows from the measured text is arithmetic, so a program does it.
payload.body:
The grid is topological: a cell is a column and a row, never a position in pixels, and each column and row takes its size from the text that lands in it. One cell holds one token, and the token set is the whole authoring language. A part's id fills a rectangle of cells; a part takes one cell unless several connections leave or arrive on one side in the same direction. A path cell names its connection by its two parts, in a form that no part id can contain. A label sits inline in its own connection's lane and splits the path; the line is drawn straight through, with a plate in the background colour under the text. A junction lets two connections cross straight on different axes, and the horizontal one hops over the vertical one in a small arc. A spacer keeps a column or row one lane wide, and an empty cell collapses. Group frames come from the bounding box of their members.

The build gives three answers. It refuses a grid that breaks a tile rule: a part that is not a filled rectangle, a connection that is not one unbranched path between its two parts, a label that does not split its lane, a crossing that is not two straight runs, or rows of unequal length. It warns and still draws when a legal grid reads badly: a connection that doubles back on itself, or a single connection that leaves a part away from the middle of its side. A hard-to-read route is a warning, not an error, because it is sometimes the cheapest legal route.

kill.text: Revisit if an agent cannot write a legal grid for the full set of decided cards in a few attempts, or if the grid reads worse than a hand-drawn picture of the same content.

payload.title: Text widths come from a table measured once in a real browser, for the one font the diagram uses
payload.why: Every column and row size comes from the width of the text in it. A guessed width per character was wrong, and no check could catch it, because the check used the same guess. A table measured by a browser makes the sizes exact wherever the diagram's font is the font of the table.
payload.body: A headless browser measures every printable character at each size and weight that the diagram uses, once. The table is checked in, so the build needs no browser. The table holds only for the system font of the kind of machine it was measured on. Embedding one font in the picture is the fallback when a reader views the diagram on another kind of machine or outside werk.

kill.text: Text overflows its box on a second kind of machine, or in a viewer other than werk.

payload.title: A coarser shape grid declares each group's cells, and every member must fit inside its group's shape
payload.why: A group frame drawn as the bounding box of its members reserves no cells for its header strip, and its rectangle can cover a card that is not a member. A shape grid in the card-grid syntax lets the author declare each group's shape as a checked artifact, so the checker, not chance, keeps members inside their group.
payload.body: The shape grid is one more section of the same diagram file, next to the grid it constrains. A group with no shape entry is not checked. A group nests in another when its shape cells sit inside the other group's cells; nesting is never declared in the content text, because containment is a cell fact. A parent's checked region is its own cells together with the rectangles of its nested groups, and that region must be a filled rectangle. Shape cells map to the real resolved bounds of the grid's columns and rows, not to a fixed scale, because the columns differ in width. The check compares the declared shape with the bounding box of its members' real cells.

kill.text: Revisit when a broken group frame makes the product diagram hard to read.

payload.title: Each redraw rewrites the whole diagram with the old drawing as input, and says whether it was a local edit or a restructure
payload.why: The scope of a redraw is a judgement: with the changed card and the whole diagram in view, the agent can tell a renamed box from a wrong grouping. The old drawing keeps the new one continuous with the reader's picture of the system. A whole rewrite can move anything, so the redraw must say which kind of change it made.
payload.body:
A local edit keeps the same parts and the same grouping and changes text or one connection, so the reader can trust their picture. A restructure moves a boundary, splits a part or re-forms a group, and gives the reason. A restructure means that one card showed the earlier reading of the cards to be wrong, so it reaches the map as a note on each card whose change caused it, and the diagram view shows the last outcome with its reason.

This holds while the diagram and the decided cards fit in one agent read. Past that size, the card ids on the diagram bound the redraw (#ui-diagram-file).

kill.text: Most one-card changes come out as a restructure, or the reasons of restructures do not point at the card that changed: then the old drawing carries no reusable structure. Also revisit when the diagram and the decided cards no longer fit in one agent read.

payload.title: The Measure tab shows the share of one-card diagram runs that stayed local
payload.why: The redraw rule is revisited if one-card changes usually come out as a restructure. Only a count over every run answers that; the diagram view keeps the last run only. So each run is logged and a gauge counts the share.
payload.body: Each finished run of the diagram job writes one event to the pipeline log: the result (updated, unchanged or failed), the declared outcome and its reason, the decided cards whose change started the run, the wall time and the cost. The gauge counts only updated runs that exactly one card started, because a batched run cannot say what one card does. Beside the share it shows the counts of batched, unchanged and failed runs, so a small sample is visible. Under the gauge, a list shows each restructure in the window with its reason and the card that started it, and a click opens the card on the map. The threshold, window and minimum sample come from the redraw card's kill criterion; with none set, the share shows in grey with no state.

kill.text: After 20 one-card runs, compare the gauge counts and the restructure list with the run events in the pipeline log, and check that the list lets a person judge each reason without opening the diagram.

payload.title: The diagram view opens fitted to the whole picture, and 100% is the largest zoom
payload.why: The full diagram is much larger than a pane, and the shape of the whole system is the first thing to read. Text is sized exactly at 100%, so a larger zoom shows only softer text.
payload.body: The view opens fitted to the pane, and a readout shows the fit percentage. Zoom resizes the drawing instead of scaling a raster, so text stays sharp. The control holds zoom out, the readout and zoom in, and the readout toggles between fit and 100%. A modifier key with the wheel zooms, and a plain wheel scrolls. The control is pinned in the panel corner while the drawing scrolls.

payload.title: Zoom levels of the diagram are a refines tree over parts, separate from the map's refines tree
payload.why: Levels from one box for the whole system down to one component are a refines tree, the same idea as the four levels of C4. The tree is over parts, not claims, so it lives in the diagram's own graph, and each project picks its own number of levels.
payload.body: A level is a depth in the tree of parts. A diagram at one level must draw an edge whose real endpoints sit deeper: when two leaf parts talk, their parents are drawn as talking. That edge rollup is the same operation as the status rollup over the map's tree, over a different graph. Each group then needs a collapsed or open state.

kill.text: Revisit when one screen no longer shows the whole diagram clearly.

payload.title: The werk server keeps the diagram in step with the decided cards in a background job that no chat shows
payload.why: A diagram update is not a topic of conversation, and the user can assume the diagram matches the decided cards after a short delay. A job started by a chat agent reports its result back into that chat, whatever its instructions say, so the job lives in the server, outside every chat.
payload.body: A change to the log starts the job, not the end of a chat turn. The job runs the two diagram agents (#ui-diagram-sync-agents) and shows its state only on the diagram view. The updater never hands a choice to the user: a leftover it finds inside the diagram file, such as a comment that quotes an old label, it fixes in the same run, and it drops anything else. A project with no diagram file runs no job.

kill.text: The diagram lags the decided cards by more than a few minutes, or a diagram update shows up in a chat.

payload.title: A read-only scout judges whether the diagram changes, and an updater edits the file and rebuilds it
payload.why: Judging the change is a slow read that needs judgement; applying it is an edit-then-build loop that a program can check. Split in two, the updater can retry safely without re-deciding what the scout settled, and each agent gets only the tools its job needs, because nobody is there to answer a permission prompt.
payload.body:
Only a card whose current status is decided may justify diagram content. When a decided card stops being decided, the scout drops its citation from each line, and removes a line that no other decided card justifies. A stale card that is still decided keeps its standing. The scout names the change and its kind, local or restructure (#ui-diagram-redraw), or says that no change is needed.

The scout may read files, search and show a card. The updater may also edit files and run the diagram build. Neither can run a command that writes the map. Both run headless with no saved session, so they never appear in the conversation list. Their prompts ship with the product and must work on any project's map, so they cite no card of one project and use an invented example system.

kill.text: Over 20 sync runs, read the scout verdicts. If the diagram gains a box for a behavioural or method card, or misses a structural one, more than twice, merge the two agents or change the scout prompt.

payload.title: A diagram run starts when the set of decided cards changes, after a short pause, one run at a time
payload.why: Only a decided card may justify diagram content, so the question is what changed among decided cards. Comparing the decided set before and after answers it directly, also for an accepted proposal or a removed card. One chat turn writes several events in seconds, so a burst gives one run, and two updaters never edit the file at once.
payload.body:
The job folds the log at the last checked position and at the end, and compares the decided, live cards in each. A change is a card that became decided, a card that stopped being decided (reopened, set open or removed), a retitle, a changed why or body, or an added or removed depends_on or refines edge of a decided card. Notes, open cards, proposals, options and sources change nothing. Each change becomes one line of the scout's brief.

The job waits 5 seconds after the last log change. A change during a run queues exactly one more run, which covers everything since the last checked position. The position is stored beside the log, so changes made while the server was down are checked on the next start. With no stored position, the current end of the log is the baseline, and history is not replayed.

payload.title: A diagram run keeps its result only when the build passes, and a failed run keeps the last good diagram
payload.why: The updater's report is model output, so a claim of 0 errors is not proof, and a half-edited file must never stay on disk. A failure is information about the diagram, so it shows where the diagram is. A failure that comes from the input repeats on a timer, so the retry waits for new input.
payload.body: Before the updater runs, the job copies the diagram source and the picture. After it, the job runs the build itself and reads the error count. On any count but 0, on an updater failure or on a crash, it puts both copies back. A failed run does not move the checked position, so the next change to a decided card retries the same changes with the new ones. The diagram view shows a red mark with the reason on hover until a run passes, shows that a run is going, and reloads the drawing when a run updates it.

kill.text: The failure mark shows on the diagram view often. Then read the reasons, debug them, and revisit how a failed run behaves.

payload.title: The Flow tab counts the map's cards from the log, for the whole map or for one subtree
payload.why: Counts of the map need one place to read and compare them. Statuses, marks, edges and the status loop all belong to cards, so one card scope narrows all of them together. Measures of passes, runs and conversations belong to no card and live in the Measure tab.
payload.body:
Flow shows the status loop (#ui-flow-loop), a breakdown by subtree (#ui-flow-subtrees) and a flat list of all cards (#ui-flow-list). Tiles at the top count cards by status and by mark, and a tile sets the list filter. The scope is `what` by default.

Every flow table has two click targets on a row. A click on the id or the title opens that card on the map. A click anywhere else on the row makes that card the scope of the tab. On hover the row gets a background, and the id and title get their own highlight and an underline, so the user sees which action a click starts. In a narrow pane the tables hide the title and keep the id, which then is the link, and the row shows the title on hover; the number columns keep their width.

payload.title: The card status loop is drawn as three boxes with one counted arrow for every move between statuses
payload.why: Every status change is one timestamped event in the log, so the loop open, proto, decided can be counted instead of drawn by hand. A bare number between two boxes does not say what it counts or which way it goes; an arrow says the direction and its label says the count.
payload.body:
Each box shows the median time a card holds that status, how many finished stays the median covers, and the median age of the cards in it now. Neighbour moves sit between the boxes. The two long moves run around them: open to decided with no prototype, and the reopen from decided back to open, drawn in the stale colour because it says the plan was wrong. An arrow's reasons, such as postponed or rejected, sit on a second row under its count. Each box also has an arrow in for the cards born at that status, or the arrows do not add up. A note says that a number on an arrow counts moves, not cards, because one card can make a move more than once.

The loop is always fully in view: a wide pane puts the boxes in a row, a narrow pane in a column, by the width of the pane, not the window. A hidden arrow would read as zero traffic.

payload.title: Flow breaks its counts down by subtree and counts the depends_on edges that cross between subtrees
payload.why: A total for the whole map hides where the work is stuck, because one subtree can hold all the open and stale cards. A depends_on edge between two subtrees couples them, since a reopen in one marks cards in the other, so the crossing count shows which subtrees are tangled.
payload.body:
Each row is one subtree of the scope, with its count of cards per status, its stale and paused counts, and the loop numbers limited to it. A toggle sets the rows to the direct children of the scope or to every card with children.

A crossing edge is a depends_on edge between cards in different subtrees; a refines edge never counts, and the held edges of a proposed card do not count until it is accepted. The top of the tab shows the total for the scope: an edge counts when its two ends sit under different direct children of the scope, the scope card counts as one more part, and an edge with one end outside the scope does not count. For direct-children rows only, each row shows an in and out column, where an edge that leaves the scope counts too.

kill.text: If the crossing count and the in and out column are not used to find coupled subtrees, remove the metric.

payload.title: Flow lists every card flat, with filters for status, for marks and for removed cards
payload.why: The tree hides a card under its parent. A flat list shows all cards at once, and a filter answers one question: what needs me now. The map shows its current state only, so a removed card needs one place outside every card page where a person can find and restore it.
payload.body:
One row per card shows its id, title, status, marks and last move. Pills above the list filter by status (open, proto, decided) or by mark: stale, postponed, or proposed (a new card or an edit that waits for acceptance). The tiles at the top of Flow set the same filter, and a click on the active tile clears it. The headers sort by card, status or last move, in the natural order of the column, and a second click reverses it; a card with no move sorts last both ways. The list opens sorted by last move, newest first, and sorting works with the filters and the search.

Under the removed filter, each row is one removed card with its id, title, removal date and a restore button. A removed card shows under no other filter, so the counts cover only cards in the map. No card page lists removed cards, and the home card has no lists of stale, postponed or proposed cards, because two copies of a list drift apart. An open card still shows its own banner for each mark.

kill.text: Change this if a person looks for a removed card and does not find it in Flow.

payload.title: The Measure tab shows what belongs to no card, under one time window and no card scope
payload.why: Passes, runs, folds and conversations belong to no card, so a card scope would hide their panels or mean nothing to them. A tab of their own, with one time window, keeps the scope of Flow and the window of Measure simple. A measure and its drawing change for different reasons, so every panel, gauge and report draws a measure that a measure card defines, and depends on that card; no measure card depends on a view.
payload.body:
Measure shows what is counted from the pipeline log, the conversations and the background jobs: cost, failures, waits, the health of the tool, and the gauges of metric kill criteria (#ui-measure-gauges). One window of 7 days, 30 days or all applies to every panel and gauge. A rail lists the panel questions in groups, with a red dot on a panel that has a mark outside its band. The main column opens with the row of gauges, then the panel groups.

Every panel answers one question, which is its title. It shows a fold over the logs, not raw events: a value per unit of size, a distribution, a window or a ratio. It names its marks, lines and band in a legend. A mark outside the reference band (#ui-measure-ref) has its own colour, so a person finds it without a click. A mark opens the items behind it, such as tickets, cards and transcripts, and a card opens on the map by the click rule of Flow. A panel redraws when the pipeline log or the decision log gets an event. A panel never proposes a change: the person decides after the drill-down. A panel that compares two pipeline variants waits for a fixed replay set.

payload.title: Each panel draws a reference band learned from the measure's own history, until a person sets a threshold
payload.why: No threshold is known before data exists. A band from the measure's own history shows what is normal now, and a person turns a line into a threshold when the data supports it. A band or a threshold only marks a point; it never blocks, stops or changes the pipeline.
payload.body: The band runs from the median to the 90th percentile of the base window, behind the data, labelled as learned with its sample size. The band is learned from the whole history, so a short window does not shrink it. Below the base window size, the panel draws the data with no band and says how many items are missing. A person can turn a line into a fixed threshold, stored as a metric kill criterion on the card it guards; the panel then draws the threshold instead of the band.

payload.title: Measure opens with one gauge for every metric kill criterion on the map
payload.why: A metric kill criterion says when to revisit a decision. One row of gauges answers which decision to revisit now, with no search through the panels.
payload.body: A gauge shows the current value, the threshold, the decision it guards, and its live state (see #ms-kill-state) as a colour: red fired, green holds, grey not enough data. A grey gauge also shows its sample count against the minimum sample. The row comes from the metric kill criteria on the map, not from a fixed list; each gauge takes its source, threshold, window and minimum sample from its criterion. A criterion whose source the tool cannot read shows a grey gauge that names the source, so the gap is visible.

payload.title: The share of a person's stale reviews that confirmed a card unchanged is measured from the log
payload.why: Staleness propagation is revisited when most of a person's reviews change nothing, because then the marks are noise. An agent's unchanged confirm is the normal case, so it is shown but not counted. The number comes from the log, not from a hand count.
payload.body: A review counts only if the card was stale at that moment and a person made it. An amend counts as changed, and a confirm counts as unchanged. The threshold, window and minimum sample come from the kill criterion of staleness propagation. It counts over the whole map, with no share per subtree.

kill.text: Compare the number with the unchanged confirms by a person in the log. If they differ, or a confirm by the agent is counted, revisit.

payload.title: The cost panel shows the window's total and splits it into groups of work and the rows of a chosen unit
payload.why: A total, then bars that split it by the unit a person asks about, answer where the money went before any trend does. Big bars compare the groups, small bars show each row's share inside its group, and a click opens the sessions behind a row.
payload.body:
The header shows the total for the window. There is one group for each kind of work: plan chats, terminal turns on the map, and the pipeline, whose rows are its roles. A group's big bar is its share of the largest group. Each row has a small bar for its share of the group, its dollars and its percent of the total. A selector switches the rows between roles, chats, tickets, specs and cards, and the total stays the same in every unit. In a unit with many rows, the six largest get a row and the rest form one row, other, with its count. A row above its own band in earlier windows of the same length takes the outlier colour once it has ten earlier windows. A row opens the chats, tickets or transcripts behind it.

Example: window last 30 days, unit role, pipeline builder $60 and reviewers $20, plan chats $20.

1. The header reads $100.
2. The pipeline bar is full, because it is the largest group; plan chats is a quarter of it.
3. The builder row's small bar is 75% of the pipeline group, and the row reads 60%.
4. A click on the builder row lists its tickets, largest first. A group with no cost in the window shows no rows.

```
$100  (last 30 days)
Pipeline     ████████████████ $80 · 80%
  builder    ████████████     $60 · 60%   [bar = 60 / 80]
  reviewers  ████             $20 · 20%
Plan chats   ████             $20 · 20%
```

payload.title: The stage panel shows the cost of each stage over a period as lines, a daily share or a pie
payload.why: A total cost does not say which stage to change. Lines show the largest stage and the one that grows, but one spike hides the other lines. A bar of equal height per day shows how the split moves, and a pie of the period shows the final split at a glance.
payload.body:
Lines is the default view: one line per stage, one point per hour, six hours, day or week, by the period (24 hours, 7 days, 30 days or all). The legend on the right lists each stage with its sum for the period; a click hides or shows a stage, a command-click shows only that stage, and a second command-click shows every stage but it. A line whose last point is above the median-to-90th-percentile band of its earlier points is drawn heavier, once it has ten of them. A point opens the tickets or plan turns of that stage in its span.

The share view draws one bar per day (per hour for 24 hours), each 100% tall, with one segment per stage; the hover shows the stage's value and the day's total. The pie view draws one slice per stage for the whole period, largest first clockwise from the top, with a percent on slices of 5% or more; it has no outlier mark, because it has no earlier points. A stage keeps its colour in every view, the legend works in every view, and hiding a stage re-scales bars and slices to the stages still shown.

payload.title: The stage and effort panels switch their unit between dollars, tokens and wall time
payload.why: Work can grow costly without growing slow, or slow without growing costly, and the stage that costs the most money is not always the one that holds up every ticket. One switch on the same chart shows each unit with the same marks, legend and drill-down.
payload.body:
Dollars is the default. The band, the alert line and the medians are computed again from the values in the chosen unit, so an alert in one unit says nothing about another. Wall time counts only the time that steps ran: a ticket that waits in a column, for a person or for its turn, adds nothing, and a wait for a person is measured by the waits panel. Tokens sum every token kind, and the hover shows the breakdown, because a cache read costs about a tenth of a fresh input token, so tokens can rank work differently from dollars. A stage keeps its colour across units, and an opened mark shows dollars, tokens and time side by side.

Example: in one week the build stage cost $40 over 6 hours, and the grader $12 over 9 hours.

1. The stage panel opens in dollars. The build line is the highest.
2. The person switches to wall time. The grader line is now the highest, and the legend shows 9 h beside it.
3. A ticket waits two hours in the todo column. No line rises for those two hours.

```
 unit:  ( $ )  tokens   time          ( ) = the unit in use

 $  │   build ●───●            time │        grader ●───●
    │  grader ●───●                 │   build ●───●
    └──────────────                 └──────────────
      wk 1   wk 2                     wk 1   wk 2
```

payload.title: The effort panel plots each finished ticket's effort, adjusted for its size, against a band and an alert line
payload.why: Rising effort for the same size of work is the first sign of rot, and it hides in a list of tickets. Adjusting for size keeps a run of large tickets from reading as a rise.
payload.body: One dot per finished ticket, in build order. Lines show the reference band over the base window, the alert line and the median of the current window. A dot above the band takes the outlier colour, and a dot above twice the band's top a stronger one. The alert line compares two window medians and often lies inside the band, so it marks no single dot. A dot opens its ticket, its passes and their transcripts.

payload.title: The failure panels split failed passes by cause, one bar per check and one bar per judging gate
payload.why: A fail that is not the code's fault needs a fix to the check or to the judge, not to the builder. Only a split by cause shows which: a check can fail from its own infrastructure or from flakiness, and a judgement can point at the builder, the spec or the judge itself.
payload.body: The checks panel draws one bar per check, split by the check causes; a check with fails from its own infrastructure or from flakiness gets a note that the check needs the fix. The judgement panel draws one bar per gate, the grader and each review area, split by the judgement causes; a gate whose false-finding share is above its threshold gets a note that its prompt needs a fix. A segment opens the failed passes with their check output, or the findings with the cards or specs they name.

payload.title: The waits panel shows how long the build stops for a person, by kind of stop
payload.why: Each stop is a place where the pipeline is not autonomous, and the longest stops show which kind to remove first.
payload.body: The panel draws the stops and their waits that the interventions measure defines (#ms-outcome-interv), one row per kind of stop; chat-pane questions are not stops and have their own panel. One dot per stop sits in its kind's row on a log axis, with the window's median per row; an open stop counts up to now and is drawn as a ring. A dot above its row's reference band takes the outlier colour; a row with too few stops says how many more it needs. A dot opens the ticket, run or gate where the build stopped, with the reason the log holds.

payload.title: The fold panel plots each full fold's time against the log size and the threshold that reopens the replay-on-read rule
payload.why: The fold runs on every read, and its time grows with the log. The panel shows how close the fold time is to the limit at which replaying the log on every read must be revisited.
payload.body: One dot per full fold, at its time against the log size in events at that fold, with a line for the window's median. The threshold, window and minimum sample come from the kill criterion of the replay-on-read rule, so the panel draws that threshold instead of a learned band. A dot above the threshold is coloured, and the median line turns the stale colour when it crosses it. A dot names the read that ran the fold: the view or the command, the log size and the time.

payload.title: The tests panel draws, per unit test, the runs it failed and how many were timeouts
payload.why: Seeing a test that breaks under load apart from a real defect lets a person fix the right thing.
payload.body:
One bar per run, oldest first, is red when a time limit broke a test, amber for any other failure and grey for a clean run. Tiles show the runs in the window, the share with a timeout, the share with any failure and the count of failed tests. A table lists each failed test with the share of runs it failed in, how many were timeouts and its last message, timeouts first. Only a timeout puts a dot in the rail, because a plain failure is a defect to fix, not a measure to watch.

Example, three runs: A clean; B where one classifier test hit its time limit; C where the same test timed out again and a plain assertion failed.

1. The tiles show 3 runs, 2 with a timeout, 2 with any failure, and 2 failed tests.
2. The table lists the classifier test first: failed in 2 of 3 runs, both on a time limit.
3. The plain assertion is second: 1 of 3, no timeout.
4. A window with only clean runs shows grey bars, no table row and no dot in the rail.

```
runs   A    B    C        bar: [ok] [timeout] [timeout]
       .    T    T
table  classifier test   2 of 3   timeouts 2
       plain assertion   1 of 3   timeouts 0
```

kill.text: Revisit if a test that fails on load no longer shows as a timeout, because its failure message names no time limit.

payload.title: A 3D force-directed graph is a second view of the map that draws every link type
payload.why: The refines tree shows only parent and child, so a depends_on, supported_by or alternative_to link that crosses subtrees is invisible in it. A 3D graph plots every node once and draws every link type, so a cross-subtree link is as visible as a tree edge.
payload.body: A node keeps the colour of its status and kind. A postponed node keeps its real status colour with the same diagonal hatch that the rollup bar uses, not a flat grey. A click on a node marks it with a white glow and a larger size, keeps its colour, and fades every other node and edge toward the background by its hop distance over any link in either direction, so direct neighbours stay sharp. The panel that opens on selection carries the node's colour on its border. A locate button on the open card jumps into the graph, centred on that card, so the two views link both ways.

payload.title: A card goes to a tracker as plain text plus a picture that werk renders fresh, never as a format the tracker must render
payload.why: Trackers render different formats: GitHub renders Mermaid and Linear does not, so a format that needs the tracker's renderer breaks on one of them. Plain text never depends on the tracker, and a picture that werk renders looks the same everywhere. A stored picture goes stale when its text changes, so only text is stored and the picture is drawn again when it is needed.
payload.body: The decision log never holds a rendered image. A picture is drawn from the current text each time it is posted to a tracker or shown as a preview, so a picture never disagrees with its text.

payload.title: The map is a picture that each turn overwrites, not a transcript that grows
payload.why: A chat only grows, so the current answer sits under every turn that led to it and the whole picture gets lost in side paths. A picture that is replaced each turn shows only what holds now. A person who thinks visually reads the state of the work at a glance.
payload.body:
The visual artifact is the primary medium of the work, at every stage. When a turn changes a decision, the card changes in place. The map does not add a second card beside the first, so a reader sees one answer per question, not the path to it.

The history is not lost: the event log keeps every edit, and the chat keeps every turn. The map is the current view of both.

payload.title: The screen is two panes side by side, each with its own controls
payload.why: A view redraws while the reply streams in, so the view and the chat must both stay in sight. Each pane keeps its own controls, so neither moves when the other changes.
payload.body:
The left pane has a sticky header over a scrolling body. Header row 1 holds the scope, what is open, from left to right. Header row 2 holds the controls, with a left side and a right side pushed to the right edge. The body shows one view at a time. The right pane is one full-height slot for the chat, with its own controls.

This card names the slots only. Each part of the header names its own slot and depends on this card, so one postponed or reopened part does not pause the whole layout. The width of the left pane, not of the window, decides how a view adapts.

```
+- left pane -------------------------------+- right pane -+
| header row 1   scope, left to right       |              |
| header row 2   left side ...  right side  |  one slot,   |
+-------------------------------------------+ full height  |
| body           one view at a time         |              |
+-------------------------------------------+--------------+
```

kill.text: Send a message that edits a card. If the redraw is out of view while the reply streams, revisit.

payload.title: The header reads one small index of the map from the server
payload.why: The breadcrumbs, the search and the counts all need each node's title, status and parent. One read of a small index serves all three, so the page never loads every card's text or folds the log itself.
payload.body: The index lists each real node in map order with its kind, title, reason, status, its stale and postponed flags, and its parent, plus the counts of every card. A ghost is left out. The page reads it each time it reads the open card. A read changes nothing, so it carries no synchronizer token (see #proj-serve-trust).

payload.title: The project switcher in the header shows the open project and opens another
payload.why: A person may work on several projects in one werk server. A switcher in every view says which map they edit, and one menu opens any other project.
payload.body: The switcher sits at the left of header row 1, before the breadcrumbs, because the project is the widest scope. It shows the open project's name with a menu arrow. The menu lists every project, then a divider and "Add project…". A project with a running agent turn has a busy dot. A project whose folder is gone is grey, says missing, and does not open. A remove control shows on hover, except on werk's own checkout in dev mode. Opening another project leaves the turns of the first one running.

payload.title: Breadcrumbs show the path from the root to the open card, one line high
payload.why: A card sits deep in a tree, so the path says where the reader is and gives one click to any level above. The header is the one place that stays on screen in every view. A fixed height keeps the layout still at any depth.
payload.body:
The breadcrumbs sit in header row 1 after the project switcher and take the rest of the row. The path starts at Home and ends at the open card, which is bold and does not click; every segment above it opens its card. A view with no card in its address keeps the last card named.

The line never wraps. The last two segments always show, and a third shows when the left pane is at least 700 pixels wide. An ellipsis stands for the hidden ancestors, and each segment is cut with an ellipsis. Hovering the line opens the full path as an overlay just under the line, layered over the rest of the header, so the line stays visible under the pointer. The pointer can move into the overlay and click a segment there. A path of two segments or fewer has no overlay.

kill.text: Open a card five levels deep. If the header height changes, or the hover path hides a segment, revisit.

payload.title: View tabs switch the left pane, and each project remembers its last place
payload.why: A person moves between the views of one map many times in a session. One row of tabs that is always on screen makes a switch one click. The last place belongs to one person in one browser, so the browser keeps it, once for each project.
payload.body:
The tabs sit first on the right side of header row 2. The tab of the view in use is highlighted. A click opens that view at its own address, so Back returns to the view before. The map view opens at the card last open on the map; every other view opens at its last scope or the root.

The browser stores the last place under a key that holds the project name, so two projects never overwrite each other. A Map tab click and a reload with no place in the address read it back; a project with nothing stored opens the home. The served page carries the project name in its head, so a reload finds the stored place before its first draw and never draws the home first and then jumps.

kill.text: Click each tab, then Back. If a view does not open at its own address or Back does not return to the view before, revisit.

payload.title: The header search box opens any node by its id or its words
payload.why: A person often knows a word or an id but not where the card sits. One box in the header opens it from any view, so nobody walks the tree to find it. A leading # means the person knows the id, so the exact id must come first.
payload.body:
The box sits on the right side of header row 2, after the tabs. A result is any card, option, source or excerpt whose id, title, reason or finding holds the typed text, case ignored, at most twelve, in map order. A query that starts with # matches ids only: the exact id first, then ids that start with it, then ids that contain it. The arrows move the selection, Enter opens it in the map, Escape clears the box; a click opens a row too.

A row shows a dot, the title, and the id in a small grey monospace label. The dot uses the status colours; a stale card's dot is red; a postponed card's dot is split diagonally, status colour and grey. An option, a source or an excerpt has no status, so its dot takes the colour of its kind.

```
 search: #how-stack
 1 werk-stack            exact id   <- Enter opens this
 2 werk-stack:opt0       id prefix
 3 vi-werk-stack-notes   id contains
```

kill.text: Type a word from a card title and the # form of a known id. If Enter does not open that card, revisit.

payload.title: Each view and each card has its own address, under its project
payload.why: With the view kept outside the address, Back in one view jumps to a card in another, and a reload or a shared link opens the wrong view. One server holds many projects, so every address must also say which project it belongs to.
payload.body:
Every address starts with a fixed prefix and the project name. The view and the card follow: the map with a card open, the map with no card for the home, Flow with or without a card scope, and the other views. The card id is URL-encoded, so an option or source id makes a valid address. An address that names a card not in the map, or removed, opens a page that says so.

Back and Forward move through these addresses. A view switch adds one entry. Filters, sort order and similar display settings stay out of the address: they are settings, not places. A card link written in a card keeps a short form; a click opens that card in the current project and adds one entry, and a click with a modifier key acts as the browser would. An address with no project opens in the last project used. The server answers the address of every view that is built with the app; the address of a view that is not built yet is not found (see #how-stack-view-with-route).

kill.text: Use Back and Forward in each view. If a step lands somewhere unexpected, revisit.

payload.title: A card looks the same wherever it is drawn, and status and marks use separate channels
payload.why: A reader learns the marks once, so the page of a card and its tile use the same ones. Status partitions the cards and adds up; stale, unchallenged and postponed cut across status. If both kinds share one channel, a stale card hides its status and the numbers stop adding up.
payload.body:
Every card is a box with a coloured left edge that always carries its status, or the kind for a source or option. A stale card tints the whole box red; the edge keeps its status colour. A postponed card, and every card it pauses, keeps its status colour and gets faint grey diagonal stripes, in a tile and on its page, with a grey tag that reads postponed on the postponed card and paused downstream; the tag explains on hover that the work waits and the content still holds. A proposal adds its own marks on top of this look (#align-diff-look).

The who label reads "you decide", "I decide" or "build it first". The unchallenged mark is a hollow ring beside the who label. A pulsing planning mark shows while a plan of the subtree runs. Wherever cards are counted, status uses filled dots and marks use hollow rings in the same line, never a row or a bar segment of their own (#ui-counts).

kill.text: Revisit when a reader misreads a status or a mark on either the page or a tile.

payload.title: Counts use dots for status and rings for marks, short in the header and labelled on the card
payload.why: One scheme means a reader learns it once. Status numbers add up to the total and marks do not, so they need different shapes. The header row is narrow and always on screen; the card has room for a word after each number.
payload.body:
Both places count the open card and everything below it; a card with no children shows no counts and no bar. The order is the total, then the dots (open, proto, decided), then the rings (unchallenged, stale, postponed). A zero is left out. The postponed ring counts the postponed cards and those they pause, but not a card that is also stale.

The header strip sits on the left side of header row 2 and shows bare numbers; each has a hover title, and the unchallenged title gives the ratio to the decided cards. The card page shows the rollup bar, with decided, open and proto as widths and a postponed card's width hatched grey, and under it a line with the scope label "this card and everything below it", the total, and every number followed by its word.

kill.text: Open a card with open work below it. If the counts match the root's counts, or a number cannot be read without its hover title, revisit.

payload.title: One view is one card: its detail on top, its sub-cards below
payload.why: A side panel splits attention and changes shape with depth. One page per card, with the same shape at every depth, lets a reader learn the layout once and go deeper by opening a sub-card.
payload.body:
Every card, the root, a leaf and a source included, has one page of one shape. The detail is on top and the sub-cards follow. A leaf has no sub-cards, so its detail fills the page. The address names the open card, so a view can be shared and stays after a reload.

The page reads, in order: the hero (#ui-card-hero), the kill criteria (#ui-kill-rows), the sub-cards with their count (#ui-subcards), the neighbour lists with the explanations of its marks (#ui-card-links), and the card's thread of notes.

payload.title: The open card is a hero box that spells every mark as a word and shows its full text
payload.why: The open card is the one being read, so it names each mark in words and shows all its text. A tile shows only enough to choose.
payload.body:
The box opens with a row of tags: the id, which copies itself on a click, then the kind, the status, each mark as a word (stale, postponed or paused, proposed, no option weighed, planning) and the who label. The title is a heading that shrinks with depth to the third level. The why and the body render as Markdown with live references. Under the body come the rollup bar and the count line (#ui-counts). The top right corner holds the actions, such as accept and remove.

A backtick span in a title renders as code wherever the title is a heading or a row: the tree, the hero, tiles, link lists and breadcrumbs. Search results, the browser tab title, confirmations and the diff of a pending title show it as plain text.

payload.title: A card page lists every neighbour with the reason on its link, and explains each of its marks
payload.why: A reader of one card must see where it sits, what it rests on and why it carries a mark, without opening another card. A depends_on target can read open and still never have flagged anything, so the reopen behind a flag must show inline. A link row with no reason makes the reader open the other card to learn why it is linked.
payload.body:
Below the sub-cards, the page shows one list for each link type and direction the card has: Refines (the parent), Alternative to (for an option), Options, Evidence, Depends on, Depend on this card, and Cited by. A row shows the other node's #id, its title and the reason on the link; an evidence row shows the node's own text in place of a reason. A row whose link is held, because one end is a ghost, carries a pending mark. A list with no rows is left out. Children and options show as tiles (#ui-subcards), and the children get no second list.

Before the depends_on lists, the page explains each mark. For each stale or postponed depends_on target it shows the reopen's reason, date and why, or a link to trace the chain when the target was not reopened directly. For the card's own stale or paused mark it prints the trace, one block per mark.

```
page of I "The invoice shows the seat count"
REFINES      #app The app
DEPENDS ON   #S We bill per seat
             Counts seats            <- the link's reason
```

kill.text: If a reader still opens linked cards only to learn why they are linked, revisit.

payload.title: Kill criteria render as the first section after the hero, one row per criterion
payload.why: The criteria say how the decision ends, so a reader sees them before the lists. A criterion has several fields and fires on its own, so each needs a row, and the state sits at the left edge so a reader scans all states down one column.
payload.body:
Each row has two lines. Line 1: the ring, the state chip, the trigger chip, and on the right a link to the rejected option the criterion falls back to. Line 2: the criterion in plain words; for a metric, source, metric, threshold, window and minimum sample; for a review date, the date. A fired row adds when it fired, the value and the sample size; an unmonitored row adds why the check failed.

Fired uses the stale red, unmonitored the paused grey, monitored the neutral border. A decided card with no criterion shows the unchallenged ring and says nothing marks when to revisit it. An open card with no criterion shows dashed suggested rows.

For a metric criterion, the row shows the live state (see #ms-kill-state), the same state as its gauge on the Measure tab. A fired row offers one click that records the criterion as fired.

payload.title: A sub-card is a tile in a grid that shows enough to rank a branch without opening it
payload.why: The sub-cards section is where a reader picks the next card to open. The tile is one link to its card, so nothing inside it can be a link, but code and emphasis must still look as they do on the page.
payload.body: The heading gives the count of sub-cards and, when there are any, of proposed ones. Tiles fill as many columns as the width holds; real sub-cards first in log order, proposed ones last. A tile shows the title, the why line and one meta row: the id, the count of cards below, the count of evidence, the who label with its ring, and the planning mark. Status shows only as the edge colour. The why line renders inline Markdown; a link or image shows as its text and a reference reads as #id without linking. An option uses the same tile under Options.

kill.text: Revisit when a reader opens the wrong sub-card because the tile did not show enough to choose.

payload.title: The home view shows the requirements and the build rules side by side
payload.why: Every map has two top cards: `what`, the requirements, and `how`, the build rules. A person who opens the map must find both without the build rules crowding out the requirements. The root itself is a normal card with no parent, so its page has the shape of any card page.
payload.body:
The home is the first screen. It has two equal columns: the root with its title, why, counts and children on the left; the build-rules card the same way on the right. When there is no build-rules card, or it has no children, the right column shows only the empty card. Every breadcrumb starts at Home.

The map address with no card shows the home; every card, the two top cards included, opens at its own card address, so Back moves between the home and a card page. The page of the root lists only the cards that refine it, nothing else. The bare project address opens the home unless the project remembers another place. The home has no tab; the Map tab opens the card last open on the map.

kill.text: Revisit when the half-width columns hide so many requirement cards that people stop using the home to find a requirement.

payload.title: Accept is a button on the card, and discard is a typed correction
payload.why: Accept ends the review and needs no words, so a click is enough. A bad proposal needs a reason, so the person tells the agent what is wrong and the agent proposes again; a discard button would skip that.
payload.body: A ✓ sits in the top right of a card with a pending proposal. A click asks the server to accept; the server checks that the proposal is still pending and appends the same accept as the command line does. The request carries the synchronizer token. A click redraws the map from its own answer; the live channel is a second trigger, so a channel that stops firing does not hide the result.

payload.title: Remove is a button on a real card, and its one confirmation names what goes
payload.why: Cleanup happens while reading, when the judgement is already made. Removal is reversible, so one confirmation is enough. A bad parent over good children is a normal case, so the confirmation must also offer to keep the children.
payload.body:
The ✕ sits in the hero corner of a real card and of a real option, which has no other way out. The person's ✕ appends the removal at once after one confirmation drawn inside the card; an agent only proposes a removal and waits for the ✓.

For a card with children, the confirmation has three answers, each with its count: remove the card and its whole subtree; remove only the card and move its direct children up to its parent, named; or cancel. A card with no parent offers only the subtree answer. A card with no children keeps one plain question.

A proposed card has no ✕, because discarding is a typed correction; it shows the ✓ alone. A pending removal on a real card is accepted by its ✓.

kill.text: If a reparent from the ✕ needs undoing several times in a row because moving children up one level is too blunt, remove the move-up answer.

payload.title: Card text renders as Markdown with safe links and boxed, highlighted code
payload.why: Cards hold prose, commands and code, and a reader must tell them apart. A link scheme that runs code must never become clickable. A wrong grammar misleads more than no colour, so an unknown fence tag renders plain.
payload.body: A Markdown link becomes a link only for a web, mail, in-site path or in-page address; any other address renders as written, brackets included. A fenced code block renders in a box with sideways scroll and syntax colour, the same as in chat. The fence tag picks its grammar by any common name in any letter case; a tag with no grammar, or no tag, renders the full code as plain text in the same box. The tag shows as a small corner label. The renderer does not reformat code: the writer indents it.

payload.title: A card id in any text links to that card when the map can open it
payload.why: The map is a graph, but a reference in prose was a dead string the reader had to search for. A link must always open a card, so only an id the map can open now links, and a whole token links or none of it does.
payload.body:
References render in the body, the why, the finding, notes, and both sides of the chat; not in a tile. With a #, any known id links; without it, an id links only if it holds a hyphen or a colon, because a bare single word is as often English as an id. A code span links when it holds only an id; a command in a code span stays code. A fenced block, a heading and a URL fragment never link.

A reference starts only where a token starts: a word character, slash, second #, hyphen, colon or ampersand before it keeps it text. Trailing full stops, colons, underscores and hyphens drop one at a time until the rest is a known id, and stay as text after the link.

A known id is a node in the map now, a ghost included. A removed card, or one taken out with its parent, is plain text until a restore; a discarded ghost is plain text. Every link shows as the id with a # in front, in monospace, whatever form it was written in.

kill.text: Write --al-diff, ##al-diff, a bare al-diff and a removed card's id in a note. If the first two or the removed id link, or the bare id does not show as #al-diff, revisit.

payload.title: A ticket board is a view beside the map, with one column per ticket state
payload.why: Tickets are units of build work, not decisions, and a person reads them as columns to move through, not as a tree. The board is where a person watches the build run, not only where the plan is approved.
payload.body:
A small board in the style of Trello: one card per ticket. Clicking a ticket opens a drawer under the board (#ui-board-drawer). A ticket that has retried, or waits on unfinished tickets, shows a small count next to its title. A building ticket with a running session pulses; the pulse means a session runs now, not that the ticket sits in building. A line above the columns shows the gate state of each run, waiting or passed, and names the operation that passes it; the board has no approve button.

The board redraws on a live-channel signal when the board log grows. It also reads the board again every few seconds, because a builder that dies writes nothing to the log, and the poll makes its pulse stop.

payload.title: The board columns are blocked, ready, building, merging and done
payload.why: Before the build every ticket is in the same state, so a board of the gate alone cannot show the build as it runs. One column per ticket state follows each ticket through the whole run.
payload.body:
Building is the builder loop: implement, check, grade, retry. Merging is the merge queue, where the checks run on the main line plus the ticket; a red check there does not stop the merge and files a follow-up ticket, and a conflict sends the ticket back to building (see #build-merge). Done means the ticket is merged. The held-out run follows the merge and moves no ticket: a red held-out step is a state of the run, shown as a badge on the done ticket whose merge it followed, linked to the follow-up ticket in ready.

Each column keeps a minimum width of 200 pixels and shares any extra width. A screen narrower than five columns scrolls the board sideways.

kill.text: Use the board on a laptop screen. If the sideways scroll hides columns that a person must watch together, let the columns shrink.

payload.title: A ticket card on the board keeps one small size
payload.why: A long title makes one card many times taller, so a column holds fewer tickets and cannot be scanned. A live dot inside the title row takes a slot the narrow card needs for its title and counts.
payload.body:
The card shows the title up to two lines; a longer title ends with an ellipsis, a hover shows it in full, and the drawer header always shows it in full. The live dot is pinned to the card's top-left corner, outside the row. Only the first title line moves a few pixels right so the dot covers no letter, and moves back when the session ends.

```
+------------------------------+
|*  Import ticket files from   |   * = the live dot
| the plan folder and skip...2 |   2 = a count
+------------------------------+
```

kill.text: Work through a run with a four-line title on the board. If you open the drawer only to learn which ticket a card is, or the dot covers a letter, revisit.

payload.title: A ticket's drawer shows its brief, its relations, its live log and the cards its builds proposed
payload.why: A person opens a ticket to read what it asks, watch its build, and learn what its builds gave the map. An alarm on the map for each unclosed build obligation names ticket numbers and asks for no action, so the ticket shows the result instead.
payload.body:
The brief sits in a main column; a sidebar holds the cited cards, blockers, retries, files and checks, and a click on a cited id opens it on the map. The header has two lines: the id, the running dot and the controls, then the full title. Archive is a button in the header. While the drawer is open, each column shrinks to two cards and scrolls, so the drawer sits close under the board. The sidebar folds to a rail, and the log can hide the sidebar and double its height; both choices persist.

For a building ticket, a fixed-height log above the brief shows one summarised line per stream event, overseer lines included, each with its full time. Leaving building drops the log.

A Decisions section lists each card a build of the ticket proposed, marked proposal, accepted, or gone when the map no longer holds it. When no build proposed one, it says "No new card" and names the cards a build recorded it followed. A ticket no build has started shows no section.

kill.text: Revisit if a build changes code with no card and no record, and nobody notices because the map shows no alarm.

payload.title: A person reorders, archives and triggers one ticket at a time, and never edits it on the board
payload.why: Build order stays a person's choice while the process is iterative, and a manual trigger keeps it in their hands. Every other move belongs to an agent or a loop, so the board does not let a drag fake one.
payload.body:
A person can reorder ready tickets; archive a ready, blocked or building ticket after a confirmation that says an agent can restore it; and trigger a ready ticket inside an active run, by the trigger icon or a drag into building. Archiving a building ticket is the one way to end its build, and keeps its branch. The drag into building is the only manual column move: an agent moves tickets between ready and blocked with a reason, and the loops move them through building, merging and done.

Nothing builds before a person starts the run; inside a run, a trigger starts one ready ticket early through the same merge queue. A person changes a ticket by asking an agent, which runs the ticket checks again.

payload.title: A plan is a lasting card below the board columns, coloured by its state
payload.why: A plan runs two agents for minutes and writes no ticket until the end, and afterwards nothing ties its tickets together. A lasting plan card shows that a plan runs, why it failed, and how far its tickets are.
payload.body:
Each subtree has one plan card in a row below the columns; a second plan of the same subtree uses the same card. The card names the subtree and links to it, is at most four lines high, and shows the running step or the ticket count. It is creating while its agents run, and pulses with the current step; building while a ticket is not done; done when every ticket is done or archived; stopped, with the reason, when it ends with an open card in scope, an agent error or an invalid spec, or when its process is gone with no end. A plan ends ok, failed or stopped.

Each ticket links to its plan card. Clicking the plan card opens the drawer with both writers' logs, the spec it wrote, its tickets and how it ended. While a plan runs, the subtree's root card on the map carries a planning marker that links to the plan card.

kill.text: Run a plan with the board open. If the card does not show the current step live and the result after the end, or finished cards clutter the row, revisit.

payload.title: One press on a decided map card plans its subtree and then runs it, with no pause between
payload.why: A build over a whole subtree runs for hours, so it must start from the app, outlive the server, and need nobody between the plan and the run.
