payload.body: A map card carries a Build button. It works only when the plan's scope holds no open and no proto card; otherwise it is grey and names the cards that block it. One press starts the plan and then the merge loop over its tickets, as one detached process with no time limit that outlives a server restart. The press is the person's start of the run, so the tickets build with no review between plan and run. The plan card on the board shows the progress and holds the stop, which ends the whole process.

kill.text: Revisit if an unattended build spends its passes on tickets that the person rejects on first reading after the run.

payload.title: A subtree with unfinished work offers Resume or a confirmed Restart, never a second run
payload.why: A second ticket set beside an unfinished one, or a plan that changes tickets under a running build, creates races no rule settles. Resume continues the same work and a restart ends it first, so a subtree has one set of unfinished tickets. The map and the board show the same state, so neither place offers a press that starts a second run.
payload.body:
A subtree has unfinished work when one of its tickets is ready, blocked, building or merging, whether its run is alive or stopped. Then Build is replaced by Resume, the default, which starts the merge loop again over the same tickets, and Restart…, a smaller action whose confirmation lists what it does: cancel every running build and keep its branch, archive every unfinished ticket, keep the done ones, then plan and run from the current spec.

Every start action of the subtree is disabled while a run is in progress on the subtree or an ancestor (#build-run-guard); the disabled control stays visible, names the blocking run and links to its plan card. The map card and the plan card show the same state and the same actions.

Example: Billing has a running run; its child Invoices has tickets 3, 4, 5 left from a killed run.

1. Invoices shows Resume and Restart… disabled, "Blocked by the run on Billing".
2. Billing's run ends; both enable.
3. Resume restarts the merge loop over 3, 4, 5; the controls disable while it runs.
4. Every ticket is done; the card shows Build.

kill.text: Press Build on a subtree with a killed build, and look at a child of a running subtree. If a press starts a second run, or the child's controls do not name the parent run, revisit.

payload.title: Ticket state is its own append-only log beside the decision log
payload.why: A ticket is a unit of build work, not a decision. Putting its moves in the decision log would mix build churn into the record of what was decided, and every ticket move would refold the whole map. One pure fold of a separate log lets the server, the command line and the loops read the board the same way.
payload.body:
The board log has the same line shape as the decision log. A ticket's text stays in its ticket file; the log holds only where the ticket is and what happened to it. Event names are the record and the past-tense action, so a fold takes its own events and passes over the rest. Ticket events cover planning, moves, reorders, archive and restore, builds and passes, merges and held-out results; run events cover gates, and run start and end. A run start names the process that holds the run until its end.

To avoid a guessed data shape, the fold applies an event only when the change that writes it also defines its payload and its effect. It keeps every other line and passes over it, so a later fold that knows the event reads it from the first line. A replan, a mark from a changed cited card, and a re-run cards-cited check are events of their own, so a view can say why a ticket changed.

The record holds milestones only: a work item entered the build loop, a check or judge passed, it is blocked, it is done. A log of every machine cycle stays in the agent's own session. The record is stored outside every branch's working tree, so deleting a branch or a worktree without merging it loses nothing.

payload.title: A ticket moves only along a move that a card names, and every other move is refused
payload.why: The board log takes moves from a person, an agent, the builder loop and the merge loop, and each names only its own moves. A move no rule names has no owner, and allowing it would let a bug show a ticket as merged. Refusing by default, at a write and in the fold, keeps each column a fact.
payload.body:
Allowed moves: blocked to ready and ready to blocked, with a reason, by an agent, a failed set check, the cited-card watch, or the merge loop once every blocker has merged; ready to building, by a trigger, only with no open blocker; building to merging on a green build; building or merging back to ready when a loop stops or a single build ends red at its cap; ready or building to blocked for a stuck ticket; merging back to building when the merge cannot finish: a conflict, a failed follow-up step gate, or a main line that moved during the merge; merging to done on a merge, also when a check was red there (#build-merge-red). A done ticket never moves. The command line makes only the agent's moves.

Archive is how a person ends a running build, so a ready, blocked or building ticket can be archived, and a merging or done ticket cannot. An archived ticket keeps its column and reason and does not move until it is restored, and a restore puts it back where it was. An archive of an archived ticket, or a restore of one that is not, is refused and writes nothing, so each archive pairs with one restore.

```
blocked <-> ready -> building -> merging -> done
ready, building    -> blocked    a stuck ticket
building, merging  -> ready      a loop stops, or a single build ends red at its cap
merging            -> building   a conflict, a failed step gate, or a main line that moved
```

payload.title: A second plan rewrites an open ticket's words and never moves it
payload.why: A plan over the same subtree again rewrites its open tickets under their own ids. Only the words change: where a ticket stands is a fact of the board, and a plan does not move tickets.
payload.body: A planned event for an id already on the board is a replan, with the same type and payload as the first. For a ticket in ready or blocked, the fold replaces its title and blockers and keeps its column, reason and archive state. For a ticket in building, merging or done, the fold sets the event aside and a write refuses it, because only the loops change such a ticket.

payload.title: A builder session runs only while the board log says it started and its process is alive
payload.why: A builder runs in its own process and can die without a word, so a flag in a log alone would say it still runs and its ticket would pulse forever. Checking the process too makes a dead builder stop at once. The agent's many lines go to a log of their own, so the board log stays a short record.
payload.body:
The board log records a session's start, naming its process and its session log, and its end. A session counts as running only while it has a start with no end and its process is alive. When a builder exits while the server watches it, the server writes the end for it; a builder killed from a terminal, or started before a server restart, fails the process check.

Each session writes the agent's stream to its own session log, one line per event with its time; the live log in the drawer reads the last lines of it. A relative session log path is read from the folder that holds the logs.

```
board log          process   session log   ticket
S started (P, L)   alive     200 lines     pulses
(no change)        killed    (no change)
no end for S       dead      (no change)   no pulse
running = started, no end  AND  process alive
```

kill.text: Start a build, kill its builder from a terminal. If the ticket still pulses after the next board refresh, revisit.

payload.title: An excerpt is extracted verbatim from a conversation's chat log, never written from memory
payload.why: A quote written from memory is a paraphrase that nobody can check. Extracting the exact words with a pointer to the message makes the provenance of a decision verifiable, so 'how did we arrive here' needs no trust in an agent's memory.
payload.body: The quote operation takes a citing card, a conversation and the words. It finds the words once among the spoken messages of that conversation's chat log, and proposes an excerpt node with its pointer, which the citing card cites by a supported_by link. Text that is not an exact match, or not unique, fails instead of guessing (#map-excerpt-unique).

payload.title: Only a quote makes an excerpt, as one change with its link, and nothing changes it after
payload.why: An excerpt is proof of what someone said. If an agent could write or edit its words, a real quote could not be told from a paraphrase. Writing the excerpt and its link as one change means there is never an excerpt that supports no card.
payload.body:
A plain add of an excerpt refuses, because it has no transcript match behind it. The quote writes one event of a type only it writes, holding the excerpt id, the citing card, the words and every pointer part; the fold stages the excerpt as a ghost with the supported_by link held, and the two accept or discard together. An event with a missing or malformed pointer part, or a taken id, is set aside. The excerpt id is the citing card's id, a colon, ex and the first free number.

An excerpt is its own node kind, not a source: a source holds a finding that can be disputed, an excerpt only words. Every proposed change to an excerpt refuses, before and after the accept; a note still works. The excerpt is decided from the start, so a ghost excerpt adds no open card and no unchallenged count. The map refuses an excerpt whose span length differs from the length of its words.

kill.text: Quote a message, accept the excerpt, then try to retitle it and to add a second excerpt by hand. If either goes through, or the excerpt appears without its link, revisit.

payload.title: An excerpt points at one spoken message, and through its session at the wider conversation
payload.why: A reader must open the same message later and find the same characters. A position that moves with a view filter, or a match in text nobody said, breaks that. The session leads from the quote to the conversation around it, and the kept words survive on a machine without the chat log.
payload.body:
A pointer holds: the conversation; the agent session id, which leads to the raw transcript when it is still on disk; the message position among all lines of the chat log, counted from zero with hidden lines included; the span, the start and end character inside that one message; the speaker; and the time the message was written. A quote never crosses into the next message.

Only a spoken message, text that the person typed or the agent wrote, can hold a quote; tool calls, tool results and text the tooling adds never do. When the one match lies in a message with no speaker, time or session, the quote refuses and writes nothing. The excerpt keeps the quoted words as its own text.

Every place that shows a position, the printed card, the quote's report, a test or a scenario, shows the stored zero-based number; nothing adds one.

```
excerpt                  chat log of "pricing"
conversation pricing --> line 11 person ...
message 12          --> line 12 person "seats are the unit we bill" (span 0..26)
session 6ae61be7 --+     line 13 tool   (prints line 12)  <- never a match
                   +--> raw transcript, when on disk
```

kill.text: Quote a sentence, open the chat log at the stored position and cut at the span. If the result differs from the quote, or the session does not lead to the transcript when it exists, revisit.

payload.title: A quote must occur exactly once in the conversation, counting every start
payload.why: An excerpt points at one span. When the words occur twice, the program would have to pick one, and the citer did not choose it; a repeat inside one message is as much a guess as a repeat across two. Quoting more of the sentence makes the quote unique and keeps it readable.
payload.body:
The quote counts every character position where the words start in a spoken message, also where two occurrences overlap. It writes an excerpt only when the count over the whole conversation is one. Otherwise it writes nothing and says which case it found: no exact match; a match in several messages, with their number; or several matches inside one message, with their number.

Example: M3 is "We pick a grid.", M7 is "the grid wins, and the grid is faster."

1. "pick a grid" occurs once, in M3: excerpt, span 3 to 14.
2. "grid" is in M3 and M7: fails, 2 messages.
3. "the grid" occurs twice in M7: fails, 2 matches in M7.
4. In a message "aaa", "aa" starts at 0 and at 1: fails, 2 matches.

kill.text: Cite ten real quotes from past conversations. If a quote cannot be made unique by quoting more of its sentence, revisit.

payload.title: The server renders every chat text to HTML with the ids the map can open, and the page only places it
payload.why: Only the server knows which ids the map can open now, so only the server can decide which reference in chat becomes a link. A streamed update that carries the whole block so far renders on its own, also with an unclosed code fence, so the page replaces blocks and never joins text.
payload.body: The person's message and every reply block go through the same Markdown renderer as the cards. Sending a message is one request with the words and the page token; a blank message is refused and reaches no agent, and the answer is the message as HTML. The reply streams on the live channel: each update holds only the block id and the whole block so far as HTML, and the page puts it in the block with that id, or adds a block. A finished block replaces its streamed form. A finished block with no streamed form gets an id of its own, so it never overwrites another block of the same message.

payload.title: The command line is the agent's only interface to the map
payload.why: An agent has a shell and no view of the map. So every read and every write of the map is a command, and a card that needs an operation names the operation and points at its card, not at a command.
payload.body:
The command line reads and writes the decision map, the board and the pipeline log of one project. Its help prints every verb with its flags.

The rules of an operation live on the card that defines it. The form of a group of related verbs — the verbs, their flags and their output — lives on one card under this one. A form card depends on the cards that define its operations. No card outside this subtree depends on a form card, so a change to a flag never marks a design card stale. A new operation gets its design card first, then a line on a form card.

kill.text: A card that needs an operation cannot name it by pointing at a card, with no verb name in its text.

payload.title: Every verb reads its arguments and reports its result the same way
payload.why: An agent copies ids out of card text as they are, and it reacts to an exit code more reliably than to a message. One convention for all verbs lets the agent learn it once and saves the turn that a failed retry costs.
payload.body:
A card id is taken with or without one leading hash sign, in every positional id and in every flag whose value is an id. A ticket id follows the same rule. An argument that holds text — a title, a why, a body, a why-not, a note — keeps its hash sign as written.

A call that the command line cannot read exits 2 and prints the usage line: a missing or unknown flag, an unknown subverb, a missing id. A well-formed call that a map, board or contract rule refuses exits 1, prints the rule it broke, and appends nothing. A call that succeeds exits 0.

Output is plain text that a person and an agent read in the same way. A report verb may also print JSON on request.

Every verb takes an actor, and the default actor is the agent. The verbs that only a person may run refuse unless the call names the person as the actor. That flag is a claim that the person asked for the call.

kill.text: Run show with a #-prefixed id and link with #-prefixed ids on both ends. If either reports no node, or a title given with a leading # loses it, revisit.

payload.title: Every agent prompt and every printed command names the command line by the plain word werk
payload.why: werk gives its instructions and subagents to agents in every project, so the text must name the command line the same way everywhere. A path into werk's own source exists only in werk's repository.
payload.body:
Every instruction, subagent and permission rule writes the command line as `werk`. werk keeps a launcher named `werk` in a folder of its own and puts that folder first on the PATH of every agent it starts. In dev mode the launcher runs the command line of the checkout whose code is running, so each call uses the current code. In production it runs the installed program. The person's own terminal does not get it.

A `werk` command acts on the map of the nearest folder at or above the current folder that has a map, and fails with an error when there is none. An agent starts in its project's root folder, so its commands reach its own project's map.

A printed command is one that werk shows to copy: the next step after a refused change, or a usage line. werk starts every printed command with the word werk and does not read the name of the file that runs, from an install and from a source checkout alike. An agent prompt and a child process use the same command from one shared source. A person who keeps the file under another name places it on the path as werk.

Example: Maria installs werk and opens a change that werk refuses. werk prints "werk accept checkout-retry", she pastes it and it runs. From a checkout, the printed line is the same.

kill.text: People often paste a printed command and the shell does not find werk.

payload.title: Writing the map: add, link, unlink, move, retitle and edit
payload.why: Every new node and every edge enters the map through these verbs, so the ghost rule and the link rules are checked at the moment of the write, for every kind of node.
payload.body:
```
werk add <id> --title "..." [--kind card|option|source] [--why "..."] [--body "..."]
         [--parent <id>] [--status open|proto] [--who you|me|prototype]
         [--no-basis] [--unchallenged] [--why_not "..."] [--url ...] [--finding ...]
         [--obligation <id>]
werk link <from> <to> --type refines|depends_on|supported_by|alternative_to [--why "..."]
werk unlink <from> <to> --type <t>
werk move <id> --parent <id>
werk retitle <id> "new title"
werk edit <id> [--body "..."] [--why "..."] [--who ...] [--no-basis "<why>"] [--unchallenged "<why>"]
```

An add proposes a ghost of every kind and prints that it is proposed. It refuses the decided status, because a card reaches decided only through the decide check. A second add with the same id fails. A rejected option is two calls: an add of kind option with its why-not, then an alternative_to link to its card.

A depends_on link needs a why, and linking the same pair again replaces the reason. A depends_on link to the card itself, an ancestor or a descendant is refused with the reason. A link on a ghost is held until the ghost is accepted. An unlink takes one link out of the map; the log keeps it. A printed card shows each link's reason under the link, and marks a held link.

A retitle and an edit of the body or why change the words of an open or proto card with one event each. On a ghost they refuse and say to discard it and propose it again. On a decided card they refuse and name the proposal that stages the change. An edit that changes words and also sets who or a waiver is refused, so one call writes one event. A waiver flag takes its reason as its value, and a bare waiver flag is refused with the form that works.

kill.text: Propose a card, an option and a source, then link them. If one does not show as a ghost, refuses a word change, or a forbidden link is not refused with its reason, revisit.

payload.title: Deciding and reviewing: status, kill, reopen, rederive and stale
payload.why: Deciding is the one state change that the contract gates, and the reason of a reopen decides which mark its dependents get, so both are typed at the call that makes them, where a refusal can name its fix. The agent has no Flow tab, so the list of marked cards and the confirm that clears a mark are commands too.
payload.body:
```
werk status <id> decided|open|proto
werk kill <id> --form metric|manual|no-metric|revisit
     [--source ... --metric ... --threshold ... --window ... --min-sample N]
     [--text "..."] [--reason unclear|cheap|slow|values|constraint] [--review-date YYYY-MM-DD]
     [--fallback <opt-id>] [--clear]
werk kill-state <id> <n> monitored|unmonitored|fired [--detail "..."]
werk reopen <id> [--reason postponed|invalidated|rejected] [--why "..."]
werk rederive <id> [--confirm <id>,<id>...] [--status decided]
werk stale [<id>] [--kind stale|paused|waiting]
```

A move to decided runs the decide check (see #map-contract). Each missing fact fails the call and names the command that fixes it, with the card id filled in. A card that waits fails the call with the basis it waits on, and marks nothing (#map-wait). A status change never changes the words of a card.

A kill call adds one criterion in one form (#map-kill). A form that lacks its words is refused. The printed card lists the criteria in the order they were recorded. The state of a criterion is recorded on its own, by its number.

A reopen's reason defaults to invalidated, and its why is the text the trace shows. The mark that each reason leaves is #map-reopen.

A rederive clears the mark of one card. The confirm list names each depends_on target whose link reason the reviewer read; a list that leaves out an older link is refused and the full command is printed again (#map-review). A card with no mark writes nothing and exits 0. With the decided status the rederive also runs the decide check. An amend's sentence travels with the proposal that stages it.

The stale list covers the whole map, or one card and its refines subtree. One line per card gives the kind, the id and the title, and a second line gives the origin, the reason and the date of the mark. The order is fix order (#map-marks). Each waiting card names the basis it waits on. The list writes nothing, and says so when nothing is marked.

kill.text: Decide a card with one missing fact: the call must fail with the exact command that fixes it. After a reopen, run the list: it must tell what needs attention and in what order without opening a card. If either fails, revisit.

payload.title: Staging changes: propose, accept, discard, remove and restore
payload.why: A change to a decided card, a new card and a removal all wait for the person. Each needs one verb to stage it, one to commit it and one to drop or undo it, and the buttons in the map run the same events.
payload.body:
```
werk propose <id> [--title "..."] [--why "..."] [--ops '[{"tag": ...}]'] [--who ...]
             [--no-basis "<why>"] [--unchallenged "<why>"]
werk accept <id> --actor you
werk discard <id>
werk remove <id> [--reparent]
werk restore <id>
werk removed
```

The ops are a list of tagged edits: elaborated (old and new), new, and removed (old). Every block of the current body must be the old of an op, or the call fails and prints the blocks at risk. An old that does not quote a real block is shown as removed plus new, never trusted. A waiver in a proposal takes its reason as its value, as in an edit.

An accept needs the person as the actor; the check button in the map appends the same event. Accepting a ghost also accepts its ghost refines parents, options and sources. A discard of a ghost takes its ghost children with it.

An agent's removal is a staged change that the person accepts. A removal takes the card and its refines subtree out; with the reparent flag the direct children move up first. A restore undoes one whole removal. The removed verb lists what is out. A refused removal or restore prints the rule and appends nothing.

The printed card shows a pending change as one inline diff: removed text in [- -] and added text in {+ +}, block by block, so a terminal reader sees one diff and not two copies.

kill.text: Stage a change, accept it in the map, and compare. If the diff does not match the ops or a block is lost, revisit.

payload.title: Reading the map: show, search and find
payload.why: The agent has no map view, so it reads cards, searches the map and lists open work through commands. A builder searches the whole map before it decides a question that no cited card answers.
payload.body:
```
werk show [<id>]
werk search ["term" ...] [--status decided|open|proto] [--under <id>]
werk find [<id>] [--status open|proto]
werk events [-n 20]
```

A show prints one card with its why, body, links and the reason on each link. The rollup prints as one line — the card count, then only the counts above zero — and again after each incoming refines row, so a branch can be ranked before it is opened. A ghost prints no rollup. A flagged depends_on row carries the reopen reason, and each mark prints its trace. With no id, a show prints the first real card that refines no other. A show of a removed card fails and names the removal and the restore that brings it back.

A search with no term prints the index: one line per decided card with its id and title. A builder pass gets this index. Each term is a case-insensitive pattern, and a card matches when every term occurs in its title, why, body, or an option's why-not. Matches print as id, status and title, most hits first. The status filter defaults to decided with no term and to every status with a term. A ghost or a removed card never matches.

A find lists the open and proto cards that can be worked on in a subtree, the card itself first, breadth first, one line each in the shape of a search match (see #agents-find). An id that is not in the map is refused.

kill.text: Run show on a stale card. If you cannot tell why it is marked without opening the map, revisit.

payload.title: The printed card shows the words of its options, excerpts and sources
payload.why: An agent reads a card only in its printed form. If the printed card names an option without its why-not, the agent skips the extra query and later proposes a choice that was already rejected for a reason.
payload.body:
After the links, the printed card ends with up to three sections. Options lists each option with its title and its why-not. Say lists each excerpt that supports the card, with its speaker and its words. Ev lists each source with its title and its finding. A ghost item carries the word proposed. An empty section is not printed.

Example:

- Card `price` "We charge per seat".
- Option `price:opt0` "We charge per project", why-not "Projects vary in size too much".
- Excerpt `price:ex0`, speaker you, words "Seats are what the buyer counts".

1. The agent prints `price`.
2. The output gives the card, its links, then the sections.
3. The agent reads the rejected option and its reason with no second query.

```
card price  [decided]
We charge per seat
  ...links...
Options
  price:opt0  We charge per project
    why not: Projects vary in size too much
Say
  price:ex0  you: "Seats are what the buyer counts"
```

kill.text: Print a card with an option, an excerpt and a source. If you cannot state the option's why-not or the excerpt's words from the output alone, revisit.

payload.title: Notes and other conversations: say, inbox, convos, recall and quote
payload.why: The agent answers on the card that the person reads, and it reads other conversations to recover what was said there. werk stores each conversation's session, so recall goes straight to the right transcript, and quote extracts words instead of writing them from memory.
payload.body:
```
werk say <id> "..."
werk inbox [--since <seq>] [-n 20]
werk convos
werk recall <card|session|name> [--grep "term" ...] [--context 2] [--tail 20]
            [--max-chars 2000] [--tools] [--thinking] [--raw]
werk quote <card-id> <conversation> "the words"
werk quote <card-id> <conversation> --text "the words"
```

A say appends one note to the thread of a card that is in the map, a ghost included. The inbox prints the notes of the person and of the agent, each with its card and its log position, oldest first, cut by a start position and a count. A thread belongs to the id, so a marker shows where the id was proposed again.

The convos list prints one line per conversation: name, home card, session, turn count and last activity. A recall resolves a session id, a card id, a conversation name or the start of a session id, in that order; a reference that fits two conversations fails as ambiguous. Grep terms are case-insensitive and all must match; context adds the messages on each side. Tool calls and thinking stay hidden unless asked for, and the raw form reads Claude Code's own transcript.

A quote takes the citing card, the conversation and the words, as the last argument or with the text flag but never both. Words that do not occur exactly once in the conversation are refused, and nothing is written (#map-excerpt-unique). On success it prints the new excerpt id, the message position and the span.

kill.text: Ask the agent about another conversation. If it does not find and quote the right message with these verbs, revisit.

payload.title: Prototypes: one command builds every option of a fork
payload.why: Parallel runs, caps and isolation live in code, so the agent makes one call per fork and never nests subagents.
payload.body:
```
werk prototype --fork <question-id> | --fork-file <path> [--tier output|worktree] [--timeout 600]
```

A prototype builds one artifact per option in parallel and proposes each result as a source on its option. The number of options caps at 5 and the timeout at 900 seconds, in code.

kill.text: Run a sample and a prototype on one fork. If a run leaves its tier or its caps, revisit.

payload.title: Running the pipeline: target, plan, loop, build, run, restart, gate, followed and change-request
payload.why: Each stage is one command that a person, an agent or a board button starts, so a stage runs the same way from every place. The records a build and a chat agent owe the pipeline are commands too, so they stay structured.
payload.body:
```
werk target [<path>]
werk plan <subtree-id> [--timeout 600] [--silence 60]
werk loop "<brief>" --check "..." [--brief-file <path>] [--card <id> ...] [--cap 5] [--timeout 600]
werk build <ticket-id> [--cap 5] [--timeout 600] [--silence 60] [--check-timeout 300]
           [--progress 300] [--classify-timeout 60] [--inflight 60] [--probe-every 5] [--no-asks]
werk run <plan-run> [the flags of build]
werk restart <subtree-id> [--yes]
werk gate <plan-run> [approve --actor you]
werk followed <obligation-id> --cards <id>,<id>...
werk change-request <ticket> --class plan|build --found review|after-merge --why "..." [--catchable yes|no] [--of <n>]
werk change-request <ticket> --list
```

A target sets the one target repository of the project, or prints it. It refuses a path that is not a folder, has no main line, or lies inside or holds werk's store. A build, a run and a gate refuse without a target and name the target verb.

A plan turns a decided subtree into a spec and tickets and exits 1 when a set check fails. A loop builds one brief in a throwaway worktree. A build runs the builder loop on one ticket; the cap is its retry cap. A run drives the merge loop over a planned run, and running it again resumes. A restart without its confirm flag prints what it would end and changes nothing. A gate approve needs the person as the actor.

A followed call closes one card obligation with the record "no new decision" and names the decided cards the pass followed. It refuses a ghost, a removed or an unknown card, and an unknown or closed obligation. The record is a fact, so it needs no accept.

A change-request appends one record about a done ticket to the board log, as an event of its own. A build miss needs the catchable answer, and a plan miss refuses it. A correction names the number of an original record; a correction of a correction is refused, and originals and corrections share one numbering per ticket. The list prints each record with the correction in force.

kill.text: Plan, build and run one small subtree with these verbs. If a stage does not start from one command and stop where its card says, revisit.

payload.title: Every board operation, the ticket check included, is a subverb of werk ticket
payload.why: An agent changes the board only through the moves a person also makes, each with a reason, and needs to see where a ticket stands after each change. The ticket checks run on their own so a plan and a person get the same verdict.
payload.body:
```
werk ticket list [--run <id>]
werk ticket move <id> blocked|ready --reason "..."
werk ticket archive <id>
werk ticket restore <id>
werk ticket import <plan-run>
werk ticket check <folder> [--cards a,b] [--spec <file>]
```

A ticket id is the full `<subtree-id>/NN`, because each subtree numbers its tickets from 01. A restore also takes the number after the slash when exactly one archived ticket ends in it, and refuses a number that fits more than one.

An agent moves a ticket only to blocked or ready, with a reason that is not empty. An archive takes a ready, blocked or building ticket that is not archived yet, and the ticket keeps its column. A restore puts an archived ticket back in that column. Each write prints one line with the column after the change, such as `werk/04 is in blocked` or `werk/04 archived from blocked`. The list prints each column with its tickets in plan order and the archived tickets last, and reports each board log line that the fold set aside. An import puts a plan run's ticket files on the board, and leaves out a ticket that fails its own checks or is on the board already.

Every ticket operation is a subverb of ticket, so one help entry lists them all. The check takes a folder, not a ticket id, because it reads ticket files, often before they are on the board. A ticket check prints one line per failure as `<ticket file>: <check>: <field>: <message>`, with `ticket set` as the ticket part of a set check, then a count line. It exits 0 when nothing fails, 1 when a check fails, and 2 when it cannot run.

kill.text: Run a restore on an archived ticket. If it does not return to its old column, or a refused call exits 0 or appends to the board log, revisit.

payload.title: The command line prints the measures as text reports: fails, rework and cost
payload.why: A person or an agent must see where the pipeline fails and what it costs without reading events. Each report is a read-only command over the logs, and a slow one runs only on demand.
payload.body:
```
werk fails [--json]
werk rework [--json]
werk cost [--top 15] [--json]
```

The fails report reads every build in the pipeline log and prints the build count, the first-pass green rate, the cap-hit rate, the passes per build as median, 90th percentile and maximum, the fails by cause, one row per gate key with its causes, and the signals over a threshold.

The rework report reads the board log, the decision log and the target repository. It prints one row per ticket with rework, the totals, the merges whose window is still open, and the merges whose commits the repository no longer holds. It asks the repository, which takes seconds, so no other read of the measures runs it.

The cost report prints plan cost per card and per day. The reports write nothing.

payload.title: Starting the server: serve
payload.why: The server holds the port, the conversation and the tool allowlist, so its flags set those and nothing else. A setting that only a second instance or a test needs comes from the environment.
payload.body:
```
werk serve [--port 4000] [--allow "Read,Edit,Bash"] [--new]
```

Without the new flag, the server resumes the stored conversation. The allow flag narrows the tools of the pane's agent. No flag sets the permission mode. A second serve on the same project refuses to start. Start the server in a shell where the agent is logged in.

kill.text: Start the server twice on one project and once with the new flag. If the lock or the fresh start does not behave as written, revisit.

payload.title: One append-only pipeline log holds every step's start, end and cost
payload.why: The measures and the debugging trace come from the same facts: when each step started and ended, what it cost, and how it ended. One event log with one fold serves both, in the same shape as the decision log and the board log.
payload.body:
The pipeline log is one append-only file per project, one event per line, in the shape of the decision log. Every step of every stage writes a started event and an ended event: a plan, the spec, the tickets, each build, each builder pass, each agent session, each check, the grader, each reviewer, a merge, the held-out set. The events of one plan or build share one run id. An ended event carries the wall time, the cost and its token breakdown, the result, and for a red step its gate and cause. A later correction event can replace a session's cost; the original stays in the log and the fold takes the latest.

Every measure of a step is a pure fold over this log. No measure is stored as a summary that can disagree with the events. The fold sets aside an event that fits no started step, and names it with its position and a plain reason.

The board log keeps where a ticket is and what happened to it; it holds no step events. The pipeline log does not copy a ticket's moves, so a measure of where a ticket waited folds the board log.

kill.text: Revisit if a measure needs something the layout cannot hold: a fact outside step events, a fold too slow to run, or a measure that needs a transcript.

payload.title: Transcripts and check output are untracked files beside the tracked pipeline log
payload.why: A transcript or a full check output is large, and only debugging reads it, so in the log every fold would read it. The log holds every measure and is small, so git tracks it and losing a laptop or a worktree loses no history.
payload.body:
Each agent session writes its full transcript, with the overseer's acts in it, to one file beside the log. Each check run writes its full output to one file; the log event keeps only the exit code and the time. The ended event of the step names its file. The files sit in fixed folders beside the log, so a later step finds a file from its event.

Git tracks the pipeline log like the decision log. Git does not track the detail files: the first write to the log adds the ignore rules if they are missing, in any project. A lost detail file loses debugging detail, not a measure.

kill.text: Measure the size of the pipeline log after 100 tickets. If it is over 50 MB, stop tracking it and keep it local.

payload.title: Each plan keeps a copy of the spec and the tickets it wrote, beside the pipeline log
payload.why: A plan updates the spec and the open tickets of its subtree in place, so the next plan erases what the last one wrote. A small copy per plan lets a person compare what two plans produced, and it changes nothing that the build reads.
payload.body:
When a plan ends, it copies the spec and every ticket it wrote or changed into one folder per plan beside the pipeline log, and the plan's ended event names that folder. The copy is a record, not a second source: no plan or build reads it. A ticket that the plan left as it was is not copied; the plan lists it as kept. A kept ticket is a ready or blocked ticket, not archived, whose file has the same text before and after the plan. A done or archived ticket is not part of the plan. Git does not track the copies, like the other detail files.

Example. #app is planned twice.

1. Plan 1 writes the spec and tickets 01, 02 and 03. Its copy holds all four.
2. Ticket 01 is built and goes to done.
3. Plan 2 changes the spec and ticket 02, adds 04, and leaves 03 as it was.
4. Plan 2's copy holds the spec, 02 and 04, and lists 03 as kept.

```
plan 1 copy:  spec   01   02   03
plan 2 copy:  spec*       02*  03=  04+
              * changed   = kept   + new   (01 done, not part of plan 2)
```

kill.text: After five plans, compare two copies of one subtree. If a needed copy was lost with a worktree, let git track the copies.

payload.title: A plan's start event lists the scope cards it reads, with their tier and version
payload.why: Two plans of one subtree can differ because their input differed, not because the planner did. A list of card ids, each with a position in the append-only decision log, is small and recovers the exact text that the planner read.
payload.body:
When a plan starts, its event holds the scope as a list. Each entry has the card id, its tier, and the position in the decision log of the last change to that card. A fold of the decision log up to that position gives the card text that the planner read. The event also holds the size of the input: the number of cards in each tier and the length of the scope text in the prompt. The token count is in the cost of the step, so the event does not repeat it.

Example. A plan of #app reads #app and #app-login in tier 1, and #queue in tier 2.

1. The plan starts and lists #app-login at tier 1, log position 812.
2. #app-login changes later, at position 905.
3. A second plan lists #app-login at 905.
4. A comparison shows that only #app-login changed between the two inputs.

```
plan 1  start  [app@790 t1] [app-login@812 t1] [queue@611 t2]  2+1 cards
plan 2  start  [app@790 t1] [app-login@905 t1] [queue@611 t2]  2+1 cards
@N = position in the decision log   t1, t2 = tier
```

kill.text: After two plans of one subtree, fold the decision log up to each listed position and compare with the prompt the planner received. If a card's text differs, store the text in the event instead.

payload.title: Each stage records its cost in dollars and wall time, at the finest grain it can attribute
payload.why: Tokens alone mislead: a cache read costs about a tenth of a fresh input token, and models have different prices. Dollars add up across stages and models, and token counts do not.
payload.body:
The unit is dollars, with input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens as the breakdown, and wall time beside it. Card refinement in plan costs per card: each conversation has a home card and each turn names the open card, so each turn goes to one card, and a turn with no card goes to its day. The spec and tickets cost per spec. A build costs per ticket, and the merge loop per run. Each cost is also shown per unit of size: per decided card in plan, per spec story in build.

The shape is a distribution — median, 90th percentile, maximum — not a mean, because one runaway ticket hides in a mean. There is no threshold at first; the first 10 tickets and the first 30 days of card refinement set the base. A session that ends before it states its cost, because it stopped or crashed first, is recorded as zero cost and zero tokens, so the log is always written; a measure cannot tell that zero from a true one.

kill.text: After 10 tickets and 30 days of plan turns, check that every stage has a cost per item. If per-card plan cost cannot be told apart for a card, report a daily total instead.

payload.title: A plan turn's cost is written to the pipeline log when the turn ends
payload.why: Claude Code deletes old session transcripts, after 30 days by default. A plan cost read back from transcripts later is lost for every turn older than that.
payload.body:
When a chat-pane turn ends, the pane appends one event with the turn's cost and tokens, its conversation, and the card open on that turn, or no card. Subagents that the turn started count in its cost. A background task can wake the agent after the turn ended, with no new message from the person; each wake appends the turn's next part with only the responses since the part before. A part is known by its conversation, its turn and its number, so the live record and a later backfill never count one twice. A reader adds the parts into one turn.

Example. A turn ends at 10:00 for $2. At 10:09 a background subagent wakes the agent for $1, and at 10:20 another for $0.50.

1. 10:00 — part 0: $2.
2. 10:09 — part 1: $1.
3. 10:20 — part 2: $0.50.
4. A later backfill finds all three parts and adds nothing.
5. Read back, it is one turn on the open card, $3.50.

```
prompt ──► result 10:00 ─ wake ─► result 10:09 ─ wake ─► result 10:20
           part 0  $2             part 1  $1             part 2  $0.50
read:      1 turn, $3.50
```

kill.text: After a week of chat turns, compare the turns in the pipeline log with the transcripts. If more than 5% of turns are missing, read cost back from the transcripts as well.

payload.title: Past plan cost is rebuilt from the agent transcripts that past sessions left on disk
payload.why: Plan ran for weeks before cost recording existed. The transcripts still hold each response's tokens, model and time, so a backfill writes the same turn events now and the base need not wait 30 more days.
payload.body:
The backfill reads the transcripts once and appends one plan-turn event per finished turn, the same event a live turn writes. Every reader folds the log and never reads a transcript. A turn already in the log is skipped, so the backfill runs again at any time; the last turn of a session written to in the last 15 minutes waits for a later run. A response split into blocks counts once, and a subagent counts toward the turn that started it.

The event holds facts, not shares: the open card, the cards the turn wrote, how many responses wrote to the map and how many changed code, the cost, tokens and wall time. The counting rule runs in the fold, so a change to it needs no rewrite of the log.

Dollars are tokens times the price for that model and token kind; a cache write is priced by its lifetime, and fast mode costs twice the rate. Each event names the date of its price table. A subscription session did not pay these prices, so the result is an API-equivalent cost, not a bill. A model with no price counts as zero and is named. Wall time runs from the person's message to the last response; a gap of more than 15 minutes is idle and does not count.

A chat-pane turn is plan cost for the card open in that turn. A terminal turn is plan cost only when it wrote to the map, split equally over the cards it wrote; a turn that only changes code is not plan cost. Inside a plan turn, a response that changed code is prototype cost, the prototype step of plan, and a response that wrote to the map is refinement; the other responses follow that ratio. The background runs that keep the product diagram in step write no card, so they are not plan cost.

kill.text: After the first backfill, read 20 terminal turns at random. If more than 4 are classified wrong as plan or not plan, count only chat-pane turns.

payload.title: A pipeline session's cost includes every subagent and fork it started
payload.why: A session's own record holds only its main thread, and each fork or subagent bills in a record of its own. Summing the whole tree when the step ends, and writing the sum to the log, keeps the true figure after the transcripts expire.
payload.body:
When a pipeline session ends, its cost is the sum of the main thread and every subagent and fork under it, split by token kind, with the count of records it covers. A response that appears in two records counts once.

A past session that the log holds at its main-thread cost is rebuilt the same way from the transcripts its temporary worktree left, found by the build's id. The rebuild appends a correction event; the original stays, and the fold takes the latest. A rerun skips a session that has a correction, and a session with no transcript left keeps its old figure and is listed as not rebuilt.

Example. A builder session's main thread costs $3 and its two forks cost $2 each.

1. The step-end figure from the main record alone is $3.
2. The tree sum is $7 over 3 records, and the log holds $7.
3. A rerun of the backfill finds the sum and adds nothing.

```
session T ─┬─ main thread  $3
           ├─ fork 1       $2   ──► logged cost: $7, 3 records
           └─ fork 2       $2
```

payload.title: Every cost breakdown adds up to one total of the project's own spend
payload.why: A cost per stage cannot say what the project cost in all. One total that adds plan turns and pipeline sessions, each counted once, answers it, and every breakdown can be checked against it. Spend on other projects is not this project's cost.
payload.body:
The total for a window is the sum of plan turns (chat turns and terminal turns that wrote to the map) and pipeline sessions (builder, grader, reviewers, held-out binder, overseer, spec and ticket writers), each at its tree sum. A build's own rollup event is not added, because it repeats its sessions. A session with no price for its model counts as zero and is listed beside the total. Sessions that belong to other projects are not read.

The same events add up per chat, per ticket, per spec and per card. A chat is one conversation with its home card and turn count; a conversation that started over is one chat. A ticket holds every session of every build, green or red, and its merge sessions. The held-out binder works for a set of tickets, so it is a row of its own. A spec holds its writer sessions and its tickets. Each unit has dollars, tokens by kind, wall time and the count of sessions, and its rows add up to the total, with a row for events that name no unit.

```
total = plan turns + pipeline sessions
      = chats + terminal turns + (builder + binder + reviewers + grader + others)
```

payload.title: The time a ticket spends in each board column is a measure, folded from the board log
payload.why: Cost says what a ticket cost, not where it waited. A ticket that waits two days in ready and one that builds for two days look the same in wall time. The board log already gives every move a time, so the measure needs no new event.
payload.body:
A visit to a column runs from the move into it to the move out of it. A ticket that enters a column more than once adds its visits, and the count of visits is kept beside the total. The first visit starts when the ticket is planned. Done is not timed. An archive stops the clock. Per column, the measure is the median, the 90th percentile and the maximum. A ticket still in a column counts up to now and is marked open, so a stuck ticket counts before it moves.

Example. Ticket 01 "Login by magic link".

1. 10:00 — planned into ready.
2. 10:30 — to building. Ready: 30 min.
3. 10:42 — a check fails, to blocked. Building: 12 min.
4. 14:00 — a person moves it to ready. Blocked: 3 h 18 min.
5. 14:05 — to building. Ready: 5 min more.
6. 14:15 — to merging. Building: 10 min more.
7. 14:17 — to done. Merging: 2 min.

If step 4 has not happened yet, blocked counts up to now and is marked open.

```
10:00   10:30   10:42                         14:00 14:05 14:15 14:17
  |ready  |build |blocked ....................  |rdy  |build|mrg |done
  [ 30m  ][ 12m ][         3h 18m             ][ 5m ][10m ][2m ]
ready = 30+5 (2 visits)   building = 12+10 (2 visits)   blocked = 198   merging = 2
```
Times in minutes.

kill.text: Fold the column times for the tickets on the board and check ten against their move history. If a total is wrong because a move lacks a time or a column, write each move into the pipeline log instead.

payload.title: Each failed pass records which gate failed it, and the cause
payload.why: A pass count says how often the loop failed, not what to fix. A fail from a spec gap needs a plan fix, and a fail from a flaky check needs a check fix; neither is a builder mistake.
payload.body:
**Gate.** Each fail names its gate: a check by name; the grader, with the card the diff failed against; a review area, with the finding's severity; or the merge loop, for a conflict. A gate that judged nothing — a silent or looping pass, a broken step — is named too, and has no cause.

**Cause.** Each fail gets one cause. Builder error: the code was wrong and the spec was clear. Test is wrong: the test asserts old behaviour and the diff is right. Spec gap: the spec does not say what the diff should do. False finding: the finding passes on the next pass with no change to the code it names. Check infrastructure: the check crashed, timed out or lacked its tool, and the code did not run. Flaky: the check passes on a rerun with no change. Conflict: the ticket clashes with work merged after it was built; only a merge fail has it.

A pass that an archive of its ticket stopped is no evidence about the ticket: its ended event is marked, and it counts no retry and is not the last failure.

**Derived numbers.** The first-pass success rate, the cap-hit rate, the passes per build as median, 90th percentile and maximum, and the fails by cause and by gate. A build is one run of the builder loop over one ticket; a ticket that the merge loop sends back builds twice.

**Starting thresholds.** These are guesses until data exists, and each needs a minimum sample. A cap-hit rate above 10% over at least 10 builds points at ticket size or spec quality. One gate key that fails three builds in a row becomes a check or a rubric line. A false-finding share above 20% for one judge, over at least 5 of its fails, means its prompt needs a fix. Any flaky or check-infrastructure fail is a fix to that check.

kill.text: After 20 builds, read the fail report. If a threshold never fires, or fires on builds that needed no change, adjust it. If most fails land in builder error with no pattern by gate, the cause set is too coarse.

payload.title: A rerun of the red check sets the flaky cause, and the next builder pass names the other causes
payload.why: The next pass already reads the failure and the code to fix it, so it knows the cause with no extra session. Only flakiness and a broken check need no judgement, so a program sets those. A check that fails and then passes on the same commit gives no stable verdict, so it does not cost the ticket a pass.
payload.body:
A red check runs once more on the same commit. Green on the rerun gives the cause flaky, and the green rerun is the verdict: the pass goes on to the next check, the grader and the review. The pass record keeps the flaky cause, so the measure counts flaky checks on green passes too. Red on the rerun leaves the pass red.

A check that fails on a crash, a timeout or a missing tool before the code ran gets the check-infrastructure cause from the check run itself, and is not run again. A stop by the person is not such a fail.

For every other cause, the next pass names one cause of the last failure, with one sentence of reason, at the end of its work. The cause is stored on the pass that named it and attributed to the pass before. A fail at the retry cap has no next pass, so its cause stays unknown.

Example. Ticket T has the checks type check, unit test and lint, in that order.

1. Pass 2 runs the checks. The type check is green and the unit test is red.
2. The unit test runs once more on the same commit and is green, so its cause is flaky.
3. Lint, the grader and the review pass, so pass 2 is green.
4. Had the rerun been red, pass 2 would be red and pass 3 would name the cause.

```
pass 2:  type ✓  unit ✗ → rerun ✓ (flaky)  lint ✓  grader ✓  review ✓  → green
pass 2:  type ✓  unit ✗ → rerun ✗                                    → red, pass 3 names the cause
✓ green   ✗ red
```

kill.text: After 20 builds, read the fails by cause. If the next pass names a cause that contradicts the failure it was given in more than a few cases, switch to a separate classifier.

payload.title: The pipeline measures what it gets wrong and where it needs a person
payload.why: A software factory promises working software from a decided plan. How often it delivers that is a measure on a separate axis from cost, and an event not recorded when it happens cannot be recovered later.
payload.body: The pipeline counts the outcome events of each build: the defects it let through, the points where it needed a person, and the work asked for or undone after it finished. Each count is a fold over records that the board log, the decision log and the repository hold already, and it is recorded from the start, not when something first reads it.

payload.title: Escapes are defects that passed the builder loop, counted by where they were found
payload.why: Each escape is a missing check or rubric line, and the place where it was found shows which gate should have caught it. Two places are check results the board log holds already and two are follow-ups, so no escape needs a record of its own.
payload.body:
An escape is found in one of four places. In the merge loop, a check is red on the ticket; a conflict is not a defect of the ticket, so it is not an escape. In the held-out set, a step goes red after the ticket's merge. At review, the person finds it before passing the run's gate. After merge, the person finds it later. The first two are folded from the merge and held-out results on the board log. The last two are build-miss follow-ups, whose record says whether a check could have caught the defect.

The number is escapes per ticket, by place. An escape that a check could have caught adds that check; there is no window and no threshold.

Example.

1. app/01 goes red in the merge loop on the unit tests: merge loop.
2. app/02 merges, and a held-out step fails afterwards: held-out set.
3. A week after app/03 merges, the person finds a wrong expiry, recorded as a build miss a check could catch: after merge.
4. app/04 conflicts in the merge loop: not counted.

```
              merge loop   held-out   at review   after merge
app/01            1
app/02                        1
app/03                                                1 (check could catch)
app/04        (conflict: not counted)
```

kill.text: After 30 merged tickets, compare the escapes by place with the follow-ups and red results on the board. If an escape the person knows of is missing from every place, add the place it came from.

payload.title: A change request is a person's request after a finished build, recorded as a plan miss or a build miss
payload.why: Plan has no exit code. A change request, a request to change what a finished build delivered is the clearest sign of what the plan or the build got wrong, and only the chat agent that receives it has the request and its reason at hand.
payload.body:
A change request is a request from the person to change work that a finished build delivered. The chat agent records it in the same turn, before it starts the work, as a fact about the ticket in the board log. The record names the ticket, the class, where the problem was found and one line of reason. A correction is a new record for the same follow-up, and the last one counts.

A plan miss: the build did what the plan said, and the plan was wrong or silent. A build miss: the plan was right and the build got it wrong; a build miss is also an escape, so its record says whether a check could have caught it. A change request is found at review, before the run's gate passes, or after merge. A request about a ticket whose build has not finished is not a change request.

Early signals of plan misses come before the person sees the build: the cards a builder proposes when no cited card gives a decision, and the spec-gap fails. The numbers are plan misses, build misses and builder proposals per ticket; they must go down over time, and a rise raises the trend alert.

Example. Ticket app/01 "Login by magic link" is done.

1. The person writes "the link expires after 1 minute, make it 15".
2. The agent reads #app-login, which says 15 minutes: a build miss found after merge, which a unit test could have caught.
3. The agent records the change request, then fixes the code.
4. The person says the card never said 15; the agent records a correction: plan miss.

```
chat turn ──► change request app/01   build miss  after merge  check could catch: yes
          ──► correction app/01  plan miss                (the last record counts)
```

kill.text: After 20 follow-ups, read each record against its chat turn. If more than 4 have the wrong class, the person classifies each follow-up.

payload.title: An intervention is a stop where the build waits for a person, read from structured facts
payload.why: An autonomous pipeline that often waits for a person is not autonomous. Each stop leaves a structured fact in the board log or the pipeline log, so the count and the wait are a fold, and reworded reason text never moves a count.
payload.body:
A stop is a place where the build cannot go on until a person acts: a gate that waits; a ticket held in blocked by a failed check, as stuck, because a cited card changed, or with no check; a merge loop that stopped; a merge that was red or conflicted on the main line; a build at its retry cap; a restart of unfinished work. A builder's question is not a stop, because the overseer answers it. A gate has no reject: a person who does not accept a result asks for a change, which is a change request (#ms-outcome-followup).

The kind comes from the facts the build writes with each stop, never from the reason text. A move written before those facts existed has only its reason, and for that move alone the start of the reason decides the kind. A wait runs from the stop to the next event that moves the work on, so it measures the stop, not a person's response time; an open stop counts up to now.

The numbers are stops per ticket and per card, by kind, and the total wait. They must go down over time, and a rise raises the trend alert.

Example. Ticket app/02 "Add an item".

1. 10:00 — a check fails, and the ticket moves to blocked with the check named.
2. 11:30 — the person moves it to ready. The stop lasted 1 h 30 min.
3. 12:00 — the run reaches the gate and waits; the stop counts up to now.

```
app/02   10:00 [blocked: check] ── 1h30 ── 11:30 ready     12:00 [gate] ── open ──► now
```

kill.text: After 20 stops, check each kind against the board. If a stop has no structured fact and falls back to its reason text, add the fact to the event that writes it.

payload.title: A chat-pane wait runs from a pending question or an unclicked next-action button to the person's answer
payload.why: A chat-pane turn that hands a question to the person stops work until the person answers. The pane already knows both kinds of hand-off without reading prose: a question form with no answer, and a next-action button with no click.
payload.body:
A wait starts when a chat-pane turn ends with a structured question that has no answer, or with a next-action button that has no click. It ends when the question is answered, the button is clicked, or the person sends the next message in that conversation. A question written in free text starts no wait. Every wait is recorded, with no minimum length. The record holds the conversation, the card the map was at, the start and the end.

The numbers are the median wait per conversation and the total wait per day, and an open wait counts up to now. Button waits come from each conversation's chat history, a resolved question's wait from the ask history, and an open question's wait from the live ask queue, because the ask history gets a line only when the ask resolves.

A chat-pane wait is part of a conversation the person leads, so it is not an intervention and raises no trend alert.

kill.text: After 30 days of use, check whether the waits ever led to a change, such as answering sooner or asking fewer questions. If they never did, remove the measure.

payload.title: Rework is a cited card reopened, or merged code changed, soon after a build
payload.why: Work undone soon after it is done costs twice, and rework shows it even when no one filed a follow-up. Both kinds fold over records that exist already, and the repository answers the code question at read time.
payload.body:
A cited card reopened: a decided card is reopened after a ticket that cites it started to build. The reopens come from the decision log and the cited cards, with the time they were cited, from each ticket's cite records. A reopen that postpones a card is not rework, because the decision still holds.

Merged code changed: a later commit changes or reverts a line that a ticket's merge added, within 14 days of that merge. The fold reads the merge commit that the board log holds for each ticket and asks the repository when the measure is read; nothing new is recorded at merge time. The 14 days are a first guess.

The number is rework events per ticket, by kind.

Example. Ticket app/01 cites #app-login and merges on 1 May as commit 9f2c.

1. 3 May — #app-login is reopened: card rework.
2. 6 May — a commit rewrites two lines that 9f2c added: code rework.
3. 20 May — another commit changes a line of 9f2c. That is past 14 days, so it is not rework.

```
1 May merge 9f2c ─┬─ 3 May reopen #app-login   ── rework (card)
                  ├─ 6 May commit edits 9f2c   ── rework (code)
                  └─ 20 May commit edits 9f2c  ── past 14 days, not counted
```

kill.text: Review the 14-day window once 30 tickets have merged and their code is older than 14 days.

payload.title: Pipeline variants are compared on a fixed replay set of tickets
payload.why: Tickets from two periods differ in size, area and difficulty, so a cost difference between them says little about the pipeline. The same tickets run through both variants isolate the pipeline.
payload.body: The set is 10 to 20 finished tickets, each with its spec and its starting commit, chosen across sizes and areas of the code. A variant, for example a different model per stage, builds every ticket in the set. The comparison reads cost, fails by cause, and escapes against the held-out set. Each ticket builds at least 3 times per variant, because one agent run varies a lot from one try to the next. Production data shows the trend over time; the replay set is the experiment that compares variants.

kill.text: Metric: the spread of cost and fails across repeats of one ticket on one variant, against the gap between two variants.

payload.title: Every change to werk passes the production checks before it merges, and again on a clean machine after
payload.why: An agent writes most of werk's code, and nobody reads every line. Automated checks are the only review that runs on every change. A run before the merge turns every red check into a follow-up ticket at the merge that caused it, and a run on a clean machine after the merge shows that a pass does not depend on local state.
payload.body:
werk gives each production check name a real command: the linter for lint (#how-lint), the type checker for typecheck (#how-typecheck), and the test commands for test, test with coverage and end-to-end (#how-tests).

A change to werk merges through the merge loop, not through a hosted pull request. The merge loop runs the checks on the main line plus the change. A red check there does not stop the merge: it becomes a follow-up ticket (see #build-merge). A hosted CI service then runs the same checks after the merge, from a clean install (#how-ci).

Every check first installs the locked dependencies, with no change to the lock, and installs again only when the package file or the lock file changed. So a check gives the same verdict in the merge loop's temporary tree, on a fresh clone and on a working checkout.

This card is a requirement. No alternative was weighed against having checks.

kill.text: werk must become a product that agents change without a person reading every line. Checks stay as long as that holds. Revisit the install step if a check gives a different verdict on a fresh clone than on a working checkout.

payload.title: GitHub Actions runs every check again on a clean machine after each merge to the main line
payload.why: On the builder's machine, installed packages, local files and a warm cache can hide a problem. A run on a clean machine starts from the lockfile alone, so it finds what only a new user would hit. It runs after the merge, so it adds no wait to the merge loop.
payload.body:
Each push to the main line starts a GitHub Actions run. The run installs the pinned Bun and the locked packages, runs every production check, builds the executable for one platform (see #proj-dist), and starts it once to see that werk serves its map. The run is the gate for a release (see #proj-release), not for a merge.

A red run is handled like a red held-out step: the merge stands, the failure becomes a follow-up ticket, and that commit cannot be released. A pull request that a person opens gets the same run, and merges only on green.

**Example**

- Ticket T "Card titles wrap at the card edge"
- Commit M, the main line after T merges

1. The merge loop runs the checks on the main line plus T. A red check does not stop the merge; it becomes a follow-up ticket. A conflict sends T back to its builder, and nothing merges.
2. T merges, and the main line moves to M. M is pushed.
3. GitHub Actions installs from the lockfile, runs every check, builds and starts the executable.
4. Green: M can be released. Red: a follow-up ticket gets the failure, and M cannot be released.

```
 builder's machine                  GitHub Actions (clean machine)
 checks on main+T --red--> follow-up ticket, T still merges
 merge: main = M --- push M ---> install, every check, build, start
                                    green: M releasable | red: follow-up, M not releasable
```

kill.text: metric: share of main-line runs that are red while the merge loop's checks on the same commit were green

payload.title: Biome lints and formats all of werk's code with one configuration
payload.why: An agent runs the linter after every edit, so the linter must be fast and its fixes must apply without a person. Biome lints and formats TypeScript, JSX and JSON as one program with one configuration, so no two tools have overlapping rules, and one command fixes what it can.
payload.body:
The lint check runs Biome over the server, the client and the tests. The formatter and the linter share one configuration, so a format fix never breaks a lint rule. The rule set is Biome's recommended set plus its React rules, which check hook dependencies and hook order (React comes from #how-stack-react). A rule turns off only in the shared configuration, with a reason beside it. A comment that turns a rule off for one line also needs a reason.

Biome has fewer type-aware rules than typescript-eslint. The type checker (#how-typecheck) covers type errors. The one known gap is a promise that nobody awaits. If that gap causes a real bug, ESLint for type-aware rules only is the fallback.

kill.text: A change of linter is one configuration file and one automated rewrite. Revisit when an unawaited promise causes a real bug that Biome did not report.

payload.title: TypeScript 7 checks all of werk's code in strict mode, as a separate check
payload.why: Bun and Vite remove the types and run the code without checking it, so a type error runs until it breaks at runtime. A separate strict pass of the compiler finds it before the merge. TypeScript 7 is the native compiler, about ten times faster than the JavaScript one, so the check stays cheap enough to run after every agent change.
payload.body:
The typecheck check runs the TypeScript 7 compiler over the server, the client and the tests. It only checks and writes no output, because Bun runs the server source and Vite builds the client. werk calls no compiler interface from its own code, so the unstable programmatic interface of TypeScript 7.0 does not matter.

Strict mode is on, and so is the rule that a read from an array or a map can return nothing. That rule finds the most common runtime error in agent-written code: a lookup that is assumed to succeed. A type that says nothing (any) is not allowed, and the linter reports it.

One configuration covers all the code. A part that needs other settings extends the shared one, and the check runs all of them.

kill.text: Revisit if the check on array and map reads makes agents add empty guards more often than it finds real bugs, or if a tool werk adopts needs the TypeScript 6 compiler interface.

payload.title: werk runs on Bun, and in development an edit reloads the changed module without killing live agent sessions
payload.why: An agent edits werk's own source while a chat agent runs inside werk. A restart on each save kills that agent mid-turn. Bun's hot reload keeps the process and its global object, so a guard kept there can hold the server and its children across an edit. Bun can also compile werk into one executable.
payload.body:
To let an agent edit werk while a live conversation runs inside it, the server runs under Bun's hot reload. One guard, kept on the global object, records that the server already runs in this process. A reload that runs the start-up again finds the guard and reuses the live server, its port, its live-channel connections and its child processes (#how-runtime-swap).

The one correctness objection to Bun was an open Bun issue: the close event of a server-sent stream does not always fire when a client disconnects. A direct test on werk's own live-stream handler, on the pinned Bun version, saw close fire on a clean and on an abrupt disconnect every time. Two more reasons decide for Bun. Its compile step gives the one-executable release (see #proj-dist), which Node's single-executable support, still marked as in active development, does not match as cleanly. Its fast breaking-change cadence costs little when agents do the upgrades, and the pinned version (#how-toolver) contains it.

payload.title: A hot reload keeps the live server and swaps in the new request handler
payload.why: The guard must keep every long-lived thing, but an agent that edits a route handler also needs to see that edit without a restart. Bun reloads only after the program's first evaluation ends, so the start-up must not wait for the serve verb, which runs until the server stops.
payload.body:
The guard keeps the listening server, its port, the open live-channel connections and the long-lived children on the global object. Each hot reload evaluates the start-up again. The guard puts the new request handler in place of the old one and logs that it reuses the live server. It never listens a second time and never starts a second child. So an edit to a route handler is live after the reload, and only an edit to the start-up code itself needs a restart.

The command line's start-up loads the verbs, starts the chosen verb and ends. It does not wait for the verb's result. When the verb ends, a callback exits with the verb's exit code. If the start-up waited for the serve verb, its first evaluation would never end, and no edit would ever reload.

**Example**

- The server runs under hot reload. The chat child C runs a turn.

1. The start-up loads the verbs, starts serve, and ends.
2. An agent saves an edit to a server module. Bun evaluates the modules again.
3. Serve finds the live server on the global object and swaps in the new handler. C keeps its turn.
4. The person stops the server. Serve ends, and the callback exits with its code.

```
start-up:  load verbs -> start serve -> end      (no wait on serve)
edit:      evaluate again -> swap handler        (C keeps its turn)
stop:      serve ends -> callback -> exit with serve's code
```

kill.text: An edit to a route handler is saved, and the next request after the hot reload still runs the old handler; or a hot reload crashes the server or leaves it unable to answer.

payload.title: The serve verb runs itself again under hot reload, and the child stops when its parent dies
payload.why: A person starts the server with the plain serve verb, and hot reload is a runtime flag that a running process cannot turn on. So the verb starts one child with hot reload on, and the child alone holds the lock and the port. A child that outlives its parent would keep the lock with nobody to stop it.
payload.body: The serve verb starts a child process with hot reload on and waits for it. The child carries a marker that names its parent, so it never starts a child of its own. The parent passes the stop signals to the child and exits with the child's exit code. The child checks twice a second that its parent is alive, and stops itself when the parent is gone. A person who starts the verb under hot reload by hand gets the server directly. The executable has no source to reload, so it serves in its own process.

kill.text: Start a plain serve, kill the parent with SIGKILL, and see the child stop and the lock go. Revisit if a stopped server ever leaves a process or a lock behind.

payload.title: In development, one werk process serves the API and runs Vite for the client, and a reload after a client edit keeps the composer draft
payload.why: One process and one port let the lock and the hot-reload guard cover the client too. Vite applies most client edits in place. An edit it cannot apply reloads the page, and the person may be in the middle of a message, so the draft must survive.
payload.body:
The dev task starts the server from source with dev mode on. The server starts Vite in middleware mode inside its own process and hands each client request to it, so the browser talks to one port. A client edit that Vite can apply in place updates the page and keeps its state. An edit that Vite cannot apply becomes a reload signal on the live channel the page already listens to. The page stashes the composer draft in the tab's session storage, reloads, and restores the draft. The open card is in the address and the transcript is on the server, so nothing else in the page needs keeping.

Dev mode is on only when the dev task asks for it and werk runs from source. The executable never starts Vite: it serves the client it carries (see #proj-dist). In dev mode werk's own checkout is on the project list (see #proj-dev-self).

kill.text: Edit a client file in dev: the page updates in place, or reloads and keeps the composer draft of each tab. If the draft is lost or the server restarts, this is wrong.

payload.title: werk's client is built from components on one framework
payload.why: Hand-written rendering grows with every screen, and each screen solves layout, state and live updates in its own way. A component framework gives every screen one way to do this, so an agent changes one small part at a time and a change in one part does not break another.
payload.body: werk builds its client from components on one framework (#how-stack-react), not from hand-written rendering. The client renders the one-view-per-card layout (see #ui-card-page). React mounts only where state lives (#how-stack-islands), and progressive loading is a shape of the read interface, not a framework feature (#how-stack-api).

payload.title: The client is React, transformed by Vite running inside werk's Bun server
payload.why: Two criteria decide it: a component hot reload that keeps state, and how well agents write the framework. React Fast Refresh keeps hook state per component, and agents know React best. No runner-up wins either criterion back.
payload.body:
React with Vite. Vite runs as the client transform in middleware mode inside werk's Bun server; it is not the process host. One process: Bun serves the read interface and the live stream and hot-reloads its own modules, and Vite transforms and hot-reloads the client.
