The chat pane holds a live stream and a turn in flight, so a component remount on save is the failure that the state-keeping hot reload prevents. The criteria of component structure, progressive loading and partial hydration do not separate the candidates (see #how-stack-islands and #how-stack-api).

payload.title: React mounts as small islands inside server-rendered HTML, with no Astro and no server components
payload.why: The server already holds the fold and can render card HTML directly. Mounting React roots only where state lives gives partial hydration without a page-per-navigation model, which would cut the chat pane's live stream on every move.
payload.body: Islands as a pattern, not a platform: several small React roots inside server-rendered HTML. The chat pane, the header controls, the ask bar and the board are islands. The card text, rendered Markdown, the evidence and depends-on lists, breadcrumbs and rollup bars are server-rendered HTML that never hydrates. The page reads the open card's HTML from the server on each connect and each change signal and puts it in the view slot, so there is one read path for card text. The server puts the synchronizer token into the page before any script runs.

payload.title: A move between view addresses happens inside the page, so the chat pane stays open
payload.why: The chat pane holds a live stream and a turn in flight, and a page load cuts both. So a plain click on a view link changes the address and the view without a page load, and Back and Forward do the same. A link that the browser must follow itself still loads a page.
payload.body:
The client changes the address in the browser history and redraws only the view, with no page load. Which clicks add a history entry and which the browser follows itself comes from #ui-routes. Back and Forward open the view of the history entry they reach. Each move starts a new card read, and only the newest read may land, so a slow read of an earlier card never covers a later one.

**Example**

- Card retry "Retry a failed payment once" links to card root "Ship the checkout".

1. The person clicks the link to root. The address becomes root's, one history entry is added, the view shows root, and the chat pane keeps its stream.
2. The person presses Back. The view shows retry. No page load.
3. The read of root lands after step 2. Nothing happens, because a newer read started.
4. A command-click on the link opens root in a new tab. This page does not change.

```
 history            view     chat pane
 [retry]            retry    open
   | (1) click
 [retry][root]      root     open  (no page load)
   | (2) Back
 [retry] root       retry    open  (no page load)
   (3) late read of root -> dropped
```

payload.title: Progressive loading is a shape of the read interface: one card at a time, plus a shape of the whole map with no bodies
payload.why: Sending the whole map with every card body on load and on every change costs more each time a card is added, and no component framework makes that cheaper. Views need every node only for structure, and the body of one card at a time.
payload.body:
Two problems hide behind 'the map is too big to load at once'. The whole map ships on every change, which is transport. Every card body ships whether or not it is read, while one view shows one card (see #ui-card-page). A measurement on a map of 418 cards gave a 503 KB payload, 28% of it card bodies.

The card read returns one card with its body and its direct neighbours' titles and ids. The shape read returns every node's id, kind, status and marks, every edge, and each card's rollup, with no bodies; it serves the tree, the rollup bars and the graph. No read of the whole map with bodies exists. The change signal carries no ids (see #map-views-read), so a view reads the shape again on each change. A card read of an id that the map does not hold answers with the server's not-found page, so the client keeps no copy of that page.

React's part is small: a boundary per card view makes the card-scoped fetch natural to write. The saving is in the read interface.

payload.title: The client lives in its own folder beside the server code, and Vite builds it into a separate output folder
payload.why: The server is TypeScript that Bun runs directly. The client is code that Vite transforms. One folder per runtime keeps each tool on the files it owns.
payload.body:
The client source sits in a folder of its own at the top of the repository, apart from the server source: one HTML page and one React root. One Vite config sits at the top of the repository and gives absolute paths, so the server can start Vite from any project directory. In dev the server asks Vite for each client file and nothing is written to disk (see #how-dev-loop). The build step is the only writer of the output folder, which is not committed, and the release build puts the built client inside the executable (see #proj-dist). The type check covers client and server in one run.

```
repo/
  <server folder>/   TypeScript that Bun runs as it is
  <client folder>/   one HTML page + one React root (Vite transforms these)
  <output folder>/   the built client, not committed
  <Vite config>      one, at the top, with absolute paths
```

kill.text: Hot reload does not work well for the client or the server with this layout; or the layout needs extra configuration, folders or build steps to keep working; or code that the client and the server both need cannot be shared across the two folders.

payload.title: The client builds its screens from shadcn/ui components
payload.why: An agent writes most of the client, and it writes faster and more consistently when it picks from a small set of known components. shadcn/ui is the React component set that agents know best, and the client owns its source, so a change is a plain edit.
payload.body:
Every button, input, dialog, menu, tab, tooltip and layout comes from one component set: shadcn/ui. Each component is a Radix primitive, which gives keyboard focus, roles and screen-reader labels, styled with Tailwind. The component files are copied into the client as its own source, not installed as a package, so the set is small and fixed, and a change is an edit to one file. Tailwind compiles to static CSS, so no style work runs in the browser on each render.

A screen changes a component only through its variants and class names. A look that more than one screen needs becomes a new variant in the shared component file. A screen never edits a shared component for its own case.

kill.text: A tested agent pipeline that builds client screens with these components gives poor results, or its agents invent props or variants, mix in other styling methods, or edit shared components for one screen.

payload.title: A view's address enters the client in the same change that builds the view
payload.why: An address with no view behind it shows an empty or placeholder pane, and that placeholder is a screen nobody decided. So each address is added by the work that builds its view, and the client answers only the addresses of views it has.
payload.body:
The client and the server know only the addresses of views that are built. An address of a view that is not built yet is answered as not found, like any other address that is not a view address. The work that builds a view adds its address, its page title and its tests in the same change.

**Example**

1. The map view is built and the board view is not. A browser opens the board address. Result: not found.
2. The change that builds the board view adds the board address. The same address now opens the app with the board.

payload.title: werk's modules are single-purpose and small, so independent tickets touch different modules
payload.why: Two tickets build at the same time only when they share no module, so large shared modules turn independent tickets into a queue.
payload.body: Each module does one thing and is named for that thing. A behaviour that more than one feature needs is a module of its own. A shared list, such as the commands, the routes or the views, holds only the entries; each entry's code lives in its own module. A ticket names the modules it changes, and small modules keep those names few and precise.

kill.text: Count how many ticket pairs of a plan share a module, and how many merges conflict.

payload.title: Each command-line verb lives in its own module and registers itself, so a new verb edits no shared list
payload.why: Which module a new verb changes decides whether two tickets that add verbs can build at the same time. A verb that registers itself from its own module makes those tickets share nothing.
payload.body: The command line finds its verbs by registration. A ticket that adds a verb adds one module in the verbs folder and changes nothing else. The list of verb modules comes from that folder, gathered when the code is bundled, and the printed verb list comes from the registered verbs. A second registration of a name replaces the first, so a hot reload of one verb module works. A call that the command line cannot read is refused before any verb runs, with an exit code apart from that of a verb that fails, so an agent can tell a wrong call from a failed operation.

kill.text: Add two verbs in two tickets. If both need an edit to one shared module, or the printed verb list misses a registered verb, drop this decision.

payload.title: A person or an agent can start work on werk from the repository and the map alone
payload.why: An agent starts every session with no memory, and a new person starts with no context. Both need how to run the project, where each decision is recorded, and which command does each task. When the repository answers these, nobody has to ask and an agent does not guess.
payload.body:
werk's repository gives every newcomer one path in. The README says what werk is and how to install and start it. The agent instruction file says how to work on the code (#how-devex-agents). The map holds every decision and its reason (#how-devex-docs). One list of task commands covers everything a person or an agent runs (#how-devex-tasks), on a pinned tool version (#how-toolver).

This card is a requirement. No alternative was weighed against it.

kill.text: werk is built mostly by agents that start each session cold. The requirement holds as long as that is true.

payload.title: One agent instruction file, AGENTS.md, holds only what an agent cannot learn from the code or the map
payload.why: Each line in an instruction file is read at the start of every agent session, so a long file costs attention and drifts from the code. A short file that says how to run, check and find things stays true. Most agent tools read AGENTS.md, so werk is not tied to one of them.
payload.body:
werk's repository has one instruction file at its root, AGENTS.md. A tool that reads another name, such as Claude Code with CLAUDE.md, gets a one-line file that imports AGENTS.md.

The file holds what the code and the map cannot say: how to start werk in development, which task runs each check, where the server and the client code live, and the rule that a decision goes on the map. It includes the shared werk agent instructions (see #agents-instructions). It tells the agent to list the build-rule cards and follow every one before it changes code, and copies none of them.

A line goes into the file only after agents got the same thing wrong more than once. A rule that a program can check becomes a check and leaves the file. The file has no list of modules or files.

kill.text: Revisit when agents ask the same question about the code in more than one session, which shows a missing line.

payload.title: The map is werk's design documentation, and the code points to the card that explains it
payload.why: A design document beside the map would be a second record of the same decisions, with no staleness marks, so it drifts without a sign. The map already holds each decision, its reason, its rejected options and what depends on it.
payload.body: werk's design lives on the map and nowhere else. The repository has a README with what werk is, how to install it and how to start it, and no folder of design documents. A code comment says why only when the reason is not visible in the code; if a card holds the reason, the comment names the card id and does not copy it. A card never names a file or a function, so the link goes one way, from the code to the card. A term is defined on the card that introduces it.

kill.text: A person new to werk tries to find how one feature works from the README, the map and the code only. If they cannot find the overview they need, add a document for that one gap.

payload.title: Every task a person or an agent runs on werk is a make target, and the Makefile lists them all
payload.why: The checks are already make targets, so the Makefile is the one place a newcomer looks. When every other task is a target too, one list holds everything that can be run, and an agent never guesses a tool's flags. A target's one-line description prints in the help list, so the list cannot drift.
payload.body: The Makefile has a target for each task: start werk in development, run each production check, run all checks in the merge loop's order, apply the safe lint and format fixes, build the executable, and print the list of targets, which is also what a call with no target does. Each target calls a script in the package file, which holds the real command, so a change of tool edits one script and the target name stays (see #pipe-check-make). The fix target lets an agent repair style problems in one call before it runs the checks.

kill.text: Revisit if agents call package scripts or tools directly more often than the targets.

payload.title: The repository pins one Bun version, and every task stops on a different one
payload.why: Bun ships breaking changes in minor releases, so the same code can pass on one version and fail on another. A pinned version makes every machine, CI and the release build run the same Bun, and a clear stop on a mismatch turns a confusing failure into a one-line fix.
payload.body: The repository holds a file with the exact Bun version. CI installs that version and the release build compiles with it. Every make target first compares the installed version with the pinned one; on a mismatch it stops and prints both versions and how to install the pinned one. An upgrade of Bun is a ticket of its own, and the merge loop's checks decide whether it merges.

kill.text: Revisit if Bun keeps compatible behaviour across minor releases for a year.

payload.title: werk's repository configures Claude Code for speed and safety, and never for a rule
payload.why: Claude Code is a temporary harness, so a rule that lives in its configuration stops working when werk runs outside it. The configuration may still make an agent faster and safer inside it. Every rule it helps with is also enforced by a check or by the werk command line.
payload.body:
The Claude Code configuration in werk's repository holds no rule of its own. It decides which commands run without a question (#how-cc-perms), gives feedback after an edit (#how-cc-hooks), and links the subagents the instructions name (#how-cc-subagents). A repeated workflow becomes a command, not a skill (#how-cc-skills).

The test for any new entry: if Claude Code ignored it, would a rule break? If yes, the rule belongs in a check or in the werk command line, and the entry may only repeat it earlier.

kill.text: It holds while the Claude Code harness is temporary for werk. If werk becomes a Claude Code plugin only, the configuration may hold rules.

payload.title: One hook formats and lints each file right after an agent edits it
payload.why: An agent that learns about a lint error only when the checks run must find the file again and fix it in a second pass. A hook after each edit fixes the format at once and shows the remaining errors while the file is still in the agent's context. The lint check still runs before every merge, so a skipped hook breaks nothing.
payload.body:
After an agent writes or edits a source file, the hook runs the formatter and the linter on that file only, applies the safe fixes, and returns the errors that remain. On one file it finishes well under a second. It does not block the edit and does not run tests or the type check; those run in the merge loop's checks.

**Example**

1. An agent saves file F with wrong indentation and an unused import.
2. The hook formats F and removes the import as a safe fix. Nothing remains, so the agent goes on.
3. If an error remained, such as a missing hook dependency, the agent reads it and fixes it in its next edit.
4. If the hook did not run, the lint check before the merge reports the same errors.

kill.text: Remove it if it makes an edit wait noticeably or if its output distracts the agent from the task.

payload.title: The shared Claude Code settings allow the task commands and werk's command line, except the operations only a person may do
payload.why: An agent that stops for a question on every check run is slow, and a person who approves the same command many times stops reading the questions. The make targets and the werk command line are safe and run on every ticket. Accepting, removing and restoring a card are a person's decisions, so these still ask.
payload.body:
The settings file that the repository shares allows every make target and the werk command line. Accepting, removing and restoring a card stay behind a question. An ask rule in the shared file wins over an allow rule in a personal file, so a personal entry cannot turn these questions off. A command outside the list gets Claude Code's normal permission question.

An entry for a person's own tools goes into the personal settings file, which the repository's own ignore list names. The shared file allows no command that writes outside the repository or reaches the network, so a person can accept it without reading every line.

kill.text: Revisit when the same question about a command outside the list comes up in most sessions.

payload.title: werk's repository has no project skills or MCP servers, and a repeated workflow becomes a command
payload.why: A skill is a prompt file that runs only in Claude Code, and its steps are rules that no program checks. A workflow that agents repeat is cheaper and safer as a make target or a werk command: it runs the same way every time, in any harness, and a person can run it too.
payload.body: werk's repository defines no Claude Code skills and no MCP servers of its own. When agents repeat the same sequence of steps, it becomes a make target or a werk command, and the agent instruction file names it. A person may use personal skills while working on werk; the repository does not depend on them, and no card or instruction names one.

kill.text: Revisit when a workflow needs judgement at most of its steps, so that a command would only wrap a prompt.

payload.title: A subagent that werk ships has one definition, and werk's own repository links to it
payload.why: werk ships some subagent definitions into every project, and its own repository needs the same subagents. Two copies drift. When the repository's subagent folder links to the shipped files, werk's own agents run the prompt that users get, and a check makes a copy fail before it merges.
payload.body:
Each shipped subagent (see #agents-subagents) is defined once in werk's source, as the markdown file Claude Code reads: a header with the name, the description and the allowed tools, then the prompt. werk's repository folder for Claude Code subagents holds a link to each file, not a copy. When werk starts an agent in another project, it reads the same file and hands the agent that definition; it writes nothing into the project's own subagent folder. A command in a prompt starts with the word werk, so the prompt needs no change between projects (see #agents-cli-name).

The lint check ends with a small program that compares the shipped subagents with the folder. It fails when a shipped subagent has no entry, when its entry is a plain file, or when its link points elsewhere. A subagent that only werk's development uses is a plain file there, and the program ignores it. Because it runs inside the lint check, it runs in the merge loop, on the clean machine and on demand with no new check name.

A subagent definition holds a prompt only. A step that a program can do is a werk command that the prompt names.

kill.text: Revisit if links fail on a platform or in a tool that werk must support, or if the check fails with no real copy or missing link behind it.

payload.title: Bun's test runner runs everything in-process, and Playwright's test runner runs everything in a browser
payload.why: Each runner drives a different thing, so a new test has one obvious home. Bun's runner comes with the runtime. Playwright's runner gives the trace viewer, fixtures, retries and parallel workers that browser tests need.
payload.body:
Server code and React components run under Bun's test runner, components with a browser-like DOM (see #how-test-globals). A second component runner such as Vitest stays out until a Vite-specific transform makes a component behave differently under Bun than in the app. Browser flows run under Playwright's test runner (#how-test-browser).

The unit run uses four parallel workers and a default per-test limit of 15 seconds instead of the runner's 5. Run in one process, the suite takes most of the time that the build loop gives one check, so a slow machine would fail it for time alone; with parallel workers the machine is shared, so a test that starts many processes needs the longer limit. A hanging test still fails, only later. The coverage run is the same run with coverage on, then the gate (#how-test-coverage); a plain test run does not check coverage.

kill.text: A unit-test check fails for time as check infrastructure, or a test fails on the parallel workers and passes alone.

payload.title: A browser test file has a suffix of its own, and only the browser runner loads that suffix
payload.why: Two runners share one repository, and each must find only its own files. The unit runner loads every file that ends in .test or .spec, so a browser test with either suffix would run under the unit runner and crash. A suffix of its own keeps the two sets apart by name, wherever the file sits.
payload.body: A browser test file ends in .e2e.ts, and the browser runner loads only that suffix. The unit runner loads only .test and .spec files, so it never sees a browser test and needs no list of folders to skip. A unit test file ends in .test.ts, beside the code it tests. A misnamed file fails loudly: a browser test named .spec.ts is loaded by the unit runner, and the browser runner's test function throws there.

payload.title: The coverage check judges each pure file on its own against 90% of its lines, and a pure file with no test fails
payload.why: One percentage over the whole project mixes pure and I/O lines, so well-tested I/O code can hide an untested pure file. A file that no test loads is missing from the coverage report, so a check that reads only the report lets it pass.
payload.body:
Only pure code gets a coverage number (see #pipe-test-scope), and the rule covers every pure module in werk. The check works from an explicit list of pure files, not from whatever the report contains. It compares each listed file, by itself, with a threshold of 90% of its lines, so one file far above cannot lift another below. A listed file with no entry in the report counts as 0% and fails. A listed file with no executable lines, such as type declarations, passes. The check prints one line per listed file and fails when any file is under the threshold.

The gate can only judge a whole file, so pure logic inside an I/O module moves into its own file to join the list. The change that adds a pure file also adds it to the list. The list is a set: a merge that conflicts on it keeps every entry from both sides, and a file leaves the list only in a change that deletes the file or makes it impure and says so.

kill.text: A pure file with no test, or under the threshold, passes the coverage check; or a merge of two branches that each add a pure file leaves one of them out of the output; or keeping the list current costs more than the bugs it catches.

payload.title: A pure file's coverage counts only the lines that its own test file runs
payload.why: A test for one pure file often calls other pure files, so a file can reach the threshold with no test of its own, and its own tests can be deleted with no sign. Counting only the file's own test closes that gap.
payload.body:
A pure file's own test file sits in the same folder, with the same base name and the unit runner's test suffix. The coverage run runs each own test file alone, with coverage on, and keeps only the result for its pure file; the results join into one report for the per-file check. A listed pure file with no own test file counts as 0%, and the check names the missing test file. The ordinary test run still runs the whole suite. The cost is one coverage run per pure file, so the coverage run grows with the list.

**Example**

- Pure file R renders text, with own test R-test. Pure file K finds card links, with own test K-test. R calls K.

1. The coverage run runs K-test alone. K is at 100%.
2. Someone deletes K-test. R-test still runs every line of K.
3. The coverage run runs R-test alone and counts only R's lines.
4. K has no own test file, so the check sets K to 0%, names K-test as missing, and fails.

```
R-test --calls--> R --calls--> K
   +-- K lines run, NOT counted --+
```

kill.text: Delete the own test file of a pure file that another pure file's test also runs, then run the coverage check. If it passes, revisit.

payload.title: The test run cleans the environment once, by setting family, for every process a test starts
payload.why: A test that starts an agent must find the fake one, and a test must never write to a real project's log. Editing the program search list inside the test process does not guarantee either, because Bun's spawn, program lookup and shell read the environment the process started with.
payload.body: Before the first test, the run removes every setting of werk, of the agent and its account, and of git. It removes them by the start of their names, so a setting added later is removed too. It gives the run a fresh, empty home folder, so no tool reads the person's own configuration. Every other variable stays, so the tools the tests need still run. It puts the fake agent first in the program search list, and makes Bun's spawn, program lookup and shell default to the cleaned environment, so a process a test starts inherits it. The browser test server checks the same rule at start-up and refuses to start when the fake agent is not first.

kill.text: A test run starts the real agent, or writes to a real project's log, although the run cleaned the environment.

payload.title: Each test writes to its own fresh project and its own copy of the app source, removed when the test ends
payload.why: A test that shares a store with another test reads what that test wrote, so its result depends on the order of the run. In werk the store a test writes is a project, and a test of hot reload must also edit the source, so both are copies that the harness removes, also when the test fails.
payload.body:
The harness gives a command-line test, a server test and a browser test the same thing: a fresh directory with a git repository and an empty map. The map is the fold of the project's own log (see #map-log), so a fresh project is a fresh map. The test writes its map with werk commands. A browser test serves it on a port of its own. When the scope of the test ends, the harness removes the directory and stops the server.

A test that edits werk's source, such as a hot-reload or client-reload test, edits a copy. The harness copies the server source, the client source and the build and type configuration into a temporary folder and runs the app from there. The copy links to the installed packages of the checkout, except the Vite dependency cache, which each copy keeps for itself: a cache shared by two app roots makes Vite optimize again and reload the page, which a reload test would read as its own result. A test server never takes the lock of a real project, because the settings that point at a real log are removed.

kill.text: Two tests pass alone and fail together; a test directory, server or app copy is still there after a test ends; a failed reload test leaves the checkout dirty; or a reload test fails because of the copy itself.

payload.title: Server tests and component tests share a process, so the DOM is registered once and the runtime globals are put back
payload.why: Server code and component code expect different globals, and one test process holds both kinds of test. React finds a DOM only if one exists when it first loads. A DOM that replaces the runtime's network function makes a server test fail for a reason outside its own code.
payload.body:
A global is a function or object the runtime gives all code without an import: the network function, streams, timers, a document. In each test process, one browser-like DOM is registered before any test file loads, so React finds it. The runtime's network, stream and timer globals are then put back, so a server test uses the real network function. Each component test removes what it rendered, also when it fails. A run on parallel workers has one test process per worker, and each registers its own DOM.

**Example**

1. The setup registers the DOM, which replaces the network function with its own.
2. The setup puts the runtime network function back. The document stays.
3. Component test C renders a button, checks it, and removes it.
4. Server test S calls the network function and reaches a local test server.
5. Without step 2, S gets the DOM's network function, which follows browser rules, and fails.

kill.text: A component test fails because React found no DOM, a server test uses the DOM's network function, or one component test sees what another left rendered. Revisit if every kind of test runs in its own process.

payload.title: Browser tests drive a real werk server through Playwright, pass on structure, and keep the screenshot as evidence
payload.why: Only a real browser against a running werk exercises the whole product: its server, its live stream and its agent child. Assertions on the page structure fail for a reason a person can read in one line. A pixel comparison on a UI that changes every commit teaches the agent to accept diffs rather than read them.
payload.body:
A browser test boots werk the way a person does: a real werk server on a copy of the fixture project, the real routes, the real live stream, with the fake agent first in the program search list. It opens Chromium, navigates, clicks, asserts, and writes a screenshot to a folder. The cost is a heavy dependency, a browser binary.

A browser test passes on structure, never on pixels. The assertions run over the page and its accessibility tree: the card title is present, the stale mark is on the right card, the chat pane shows the expected messages. The screenshot is evidence, not a verdict: nothing compares it. To judge how something looks, the agent reads the screenshot (see #agents-images). So a red test always names a broken structure, and a look that is wrong but structurally correct is found by looking, not by failing.

payload.title: The product's browser test run also finds the tests in the binder's folder
payload.why: The binder turns each held-out step into a browser test and writes it into a folder of its own. If the product's browser run looked only in its spec folder, a held-out step would never run, and never go green, whatever the product does. Reading both folders gives a held-out test the same server, fake agent and fixture project as a product spec.
payload.body:
The browser test run looks for tests in two folders: the product's browser spec folder and the binder's folder (see #val-heldout-binder). The binder's folder exists only in the temporary checkout where the binder works (see #val-heldout), so a builder's run finds only the product specs.

**Example**

1. The binder writes the test for step S1 "The list updates while the person types a search" in its folder and starts the browser run on that file. The run finds it, starts the real server on a fixture copy, and S1 ends green or red by what the product does.
2. A builder starts the browser run in its own checkout. There is no binder folder, so no held-out test runs.

kill.text: A builder's browser test run finds a held-out test, or a held-out browser step fails because the run did not find its test.

payload.title: werk v0 is the map, the board and the chat over the log, with the inner build loop and werk's own build rules
payload.why: v0 is the smallest visual layer over Claude Code that a person can use while building it. Three views and a build loop that turns decided cards into merged code are enough to build the rest of werk with werk.
payload.body:
v0 holds three views, the map, the board and the chat, over the log and its fold. It includes the chat pane beside the map, the command line as the only write path, extracted excerpts, card rendering, the card wording rule, new cards as proposals, the contract check at decided, the reopen reasons, many projects from one server, compilation into one executable, the ticket board (#v0-board), the inner build loop (#v0-loop), and werk's own build rules. Each included item is a card elsewhere on the map, and a depends_on edge records the inclusion.

Outside v0: the product diagram, the 3D graph, the Flow and Measure views, the tracker export, the validate stage, pipeline self-measurement, and the install channel and release steps. v0 records kill criteria and watches none, so each criterion shows the state recorded, in the neutral look; the fired and unmonitored looks arrive with the watch that sets them.

The prototype's behaviour sets the bar. A gap between v0 and the prototype is first a missing or unclear card, not a reason to copy prototype code.

kill.text: Run the prototype's browser test paths against v0. Each path that passes on the prototype and fails on v0 is one gap. Reopen v0 when the gap count is too high.

payload.title: v0 is built from scratch in a new git repository whose main branch starts with zero files
payload.why: The prototype was iterated on to find the right shape, and its code carries every shortcut of that search. A clean build in a repository of its own tests whether the decided cards are enough to rebuild the behaviour, and shares no files, history or map state that a build could start from by mistake.
payload.body:
The main line of every v0 build is the main branch of a new git repository, separate from the prototype's (see #build-merge). Its first commit holds no files. The spec and the first tickets set up the project from that empty tree: the package files, the build and test targets and the folder layout, all at the root of v0's own repository. Nothing in v0 imports from the prototype.

The spec is the decided cards, not the prototype code. The prototype stays in its own repository as a reference: a builder may read it to see how a decided behaviour looks, but does not copy it, no build starts from it, and nothing merges into it.

kill.text: Build v0 from scratch and compare it with the prototype. If v0's behaviour is too far from the prototype's, reconsider and extend the prototype instead.

payload.title: v0 runs the whole inner build loop on a decided subtree
payload.why: A selected subtree of decided cards becomes merged, tested code. v0 covers build and test only.
payload.body: v0 includes at full scope the plan with a spec and tracer-bullet tickets, the builder loop with the checks, the grader and the quality review, the merge loop with the held-out set, the overseer, stateless passes, and the command-line pipeline tests. Each is a pipeline card that v0 depends on. Every gate waits for a person. Trend reports are not in v0.

payload.title: In v0, alignment before building is the accept gate, the plan's proposed answers and the build gates
payload.why: v0 builds no separate alignment feature. Three mechanisms that v0 builds anyway already put every agent answer in front of the person before code.
payload.body: Every card, option, source and excerpt an agent adds waits for the person's accept (see #map-ghost). Every answer that the spec or ticket writer gives and no card gives comes back as a proposed card before the build (see #plan-answers). Every build gate waits for the person (#v0-loop). The rest of alignment, such as building options side by side, is out of v0.

kill.text: Build with v0. If an agent builds the wrong thing because a reading of a requirement was never shown, and none of the three mechanisms caught it, v0 needs more of alignment.

payload.title: v0 builds the whole ticket board, and the command line gives the same ticket operations
payload.why: The first build run needs the whole board, columns and actions both, so v0 does not build a subset. An agent must move and archive tickets as the board does.
payload.body: v0 builds the board design of #ui-board in full: all its columns and all its actions. The command line carries the same ticket operations as the board's controls (see #agents-cli-tickets). There is no import, because a v0 project has no ticket files from before the plan recorded its tickets.

payload.title: In v0, each project has one conversation, and v0 builds no tabs
payload.why: v0 is the smallest layer that lets werk build the rest of itself, and one conversation per project is enough for that. The tabs, forks, parking and idle stop are decided and built in the prototype, but they stay out of v0 to keep its scope small.
payload.body:
v0 builds one continuous conversation per project (see #chat), with no tab strip, no fork and no park. A dead agent (see #chat-dead-agent) has no other tab to show its mark, so the mark sits in the chat header row beside the turn state, and the pane shows the whole error. A dead agent in a project that is not open shows a dead mark on that project's row in the project switcher (see #ui-switcher).

**Example**

1. The agent of the conversation of project P "checkout" exits with an error a retry cannot fix, while the person looks at project Q.
2. The switcher row of P shows the dead mark.
3. The person opens P. The header row shows the dead mark and the pane shows the error.
4. The person sends a message. A new agent starts, and the mark goes.

payload.title: v0 builds a part before the part that calls it, and shows it working alone first
payload.why: When a caller and the part it calls are built together, a red result can come from either. A part shown working alone on hand-written input gives its caller a tested base, and the caller reuses it with no second implementation.
payload.body: Three orders follow. The held-out set is built and gated on the run's tree first: the step author, the binder, the run, the feedback to the builder and the gate refusal while a step is red (see #val-heldout, #val-heldout-g2). The merge loop then adds the run after each merge and the follow-up ticket on a red step. The ticket check operation is built and shown on a folder of hand-written tickets before the plan step, which then calls the same operation (see #plan-ticket-checks). The quote operation is built before the chat pane and tested on a hand-written chat log; it defines how a chat log holds a message, and the chat pane then writes its log in that form, so quoting a real conversation needs no second reader.

kill.text: If a part built first cannot be shown working on its own, the order gives nothing and both parts can be built together. Run the ticket checks on a folder with one bad ticket; if they do not name the ticket and the field, or the plan cannot call the same checks, drop that order.

payload.title: v0 writes every build step to the pipeline log and builds no report over it
payload.why: The builder loop needs a record of each pass, its gate and its cause, and a test of the loop reads that record. The pipeline log is the one place for it. Reports over it are additive, so v0 writes the facts and reads them only where the loop needs them.
payload.body:
v0 writes the whole pipeline log of #ms-store: the start and the end of every step, with its cost and result, and for a red step its gate and cause. Transcripts and full check output are files beside the log (see #ms-store-detail).

The builder loop reads the log only where a rule needs it: the retry cap skips a pass that ended on a spec gap (see #build-retry-cap), and the next pass reads the last failure. The fail report, the Measure view, the trend report and the cost of chat plan turns are not in v0.

kill.text: A report over the log is additive: it reads events that v0 already writes, so adding one later changes nothing that exists.

payload.title: A metric kill criterion has a live state, computed from its source over its window
payload.why: A recorded state goes out of date as soon as the data moves, so a fired criterion can sit unseen. Computing the state from the measure each time it is read gives the real state wherever the criterion is read.
payload.body: The state of a metric kill criterion is read from its source over its window: fired when the value is past the threshold, holds when it is not, and not enough data while the sample is below the minimum sample. A criterion whose source werk cannot read has no live state and says which source is missing. A criterion that is not a metric, such as a manual test or a review date, keeps the state that a person records.

payload.title: Every unit test run is recorded, and a failure on a time limit counts apart
payload.why: A test that fails only when the machine is busy looks like a code bug and costs a pass to chase. Recording every run, and counting timeouts apart, marks a test that breaks under load as that, not as a defect.
payload.body: Every run of the unit test command leaves one record: when it ended, how many tests ran and which failed. A failure is a timeout when the runner ended the test on its time limit or the message names a time limit. The measure counts runs on one machine's checkout, not the checks of a build in its own worktree.

payload.title: Every full fold records its time and the size of the log
payload.why: Replaying the whole log on every read holds only while the fold stays fast. Recording each fold gives the kill criterion of that rule its data.
payload.body: Every full fold appends its time, the number of events and the read that ran it to a file beside the log, outside the log itself. A failed write of that line never stops the read. A fold over part of the log, to see a past state, is not a read of the map and is not timed.

payload.title: Recording past cost: cost import
payload.why: A turn or a session that ended before its cost was logged must still count, and the agent transcripts expire. One command adds what the pipeline log lacks, so it is safe to run again.
payload.body:
```
werk cost import
```

The import appends every finished turn that the pipeline log does not hold yet, and corrects each pipeline session whose cost left out its subagents. It is safe to run again.

payload.title: Conductor's own Claude Code integration (inspected 2026-09-01)
payload.finding: Conductor drives Claude Code as a child process over stream-json on unix sockets. No terminal, no paste. Events land in a per-session append-only outbox file.
payload.body:
Inspected on 2026-09-01 from the process table and Conductor's application-support directory.

**How it runs Claude Code.** Conductor starts its own pinned claude binary as a child process, through a sidecar runtime. The child's stdin, stdout and stderr are unix sockets to the sidecar, not a terminal. One user turn is one JSON line written to stdin, in stream-json format. Conductor never pastes text and never simulates keystrokes. Because the sidecar owns that stdin, no other program can write into a Conductor session.

**How it stores events.** Each session has one outbox file. The file holds a version, the session id, a next-sequence counter and a list of pending events. Each pending event wraps the raw stream-json payload with a session id, a turn id and a user-message id. The queue drains into a SQLite database.

**What it confirms for werk.** The outbox is an append-only event log with a sequence number, and the database is a projection of it. werk's log and fold have the same shape, so a production app reached the same design independently. Conductor also drains the queue, which works like a snapshot. werk has no snapshot yet (see #pr-log-snapshot).

payload.title: Start the fold from a stored snapshot of the map
payload.why_not: A snapshot is a second copy of the state that must agree with the log and be rebuilt when the fold logic changes. At 13 to 20 ms per full fold, that cost buys nothing.

payload.why: takes the link rules that a write and the fold check

payload.title: Fail the whole fold on the first event that breaks a rule
payload.why_not: A committed log can receive one bad line from a merge. A failed fold shows no map, so the reader cannot see or fix the card the line is about.

payload.title: Send the new events or the new fold on the live channel
payload.why_not: The page then gets the map two ways, from the full read and from the push. The two can disagree, and a page that misses one push keeps a wrong map.

payload.title: Poll the log on a timer as well as watch it
payload.why_not: A poll adds a second trigger and an interval to tune. The read on each connect already covers every write the watch can miss.

takes the rule that each state change is one event in the log

payload.title: Deterministic word-overlap matching pairs the old and new sentences

payload.title: dev-pipeline-research-semantic-diff.md: topic-level diff, beyond word/line
payload.finding: No shipped product or paper diffs a short document at topic level. arXivEdits (arXiv 2210.15067) does sentence+span alignment plus a trained edit-intention classifier — too heavy for one brief. Lightest buildable path: reuse the LLM that proposes the edit as the classifier. It tags each new-body sentence against the old body as elaborated / new, and lists unmatched old sentences as removed. Verify its quoted old-sentence match against the real text in code before rendering, so a wrong LLM tag cannot silently produce a wrong diff. Render: word-level diff only inside elaborated pairs; plain add/remove markers for new/removed sentences.

payload.title: Prototype: option A, agent-supplied ops verified against the real body
payload.text:
Ran against #al-diff-cli's own real body (read-only, nothing written to the log).

I supplied 3 ops in one call: elaborate a real sentence, add a new one, and — deliberately — elaborate a sentence I paraphrased instead of quoting exactly. The verifier caught the bad quote on its own and demoted it to a plain new+removed pair instead of rendering a false elaboration:

REJECTED (quote not found verbatim): "agent.ts has no existing path for a headless model call — only the interactive session."

Rendered on the card (elaborated pair with word-diff, new lines, and the demoted removed line):

==CLI verbs: propose <id> --title/--why/--body, accept <id>, discard ~~<id>.~~ **<id>** **—** **propose** **takes** **ops** **directly,** **not** **just** **flat** **new** **text.**==

==+ A prototype of this exact mechanism ran at al-diff-cli:ex0.==

==+ agent.ts has no existing path for any second model call, headless or not.==

==~~agent.ts has no existing path for a headless model call — only the interactive session.~~==

A second, real bug the prototype caught in itself: node.bodyEdited stores the new value at payload.patch.body, not payload.body. My first pass read the wrong field, silently rendered a stale body, and produced a false verification failure — found only by checking the actual event, not by trusting the assumed shape. Fixed before this result. Script was throwaway, per #al-ephem — deleted after this note.

payload.title: Spike on the werk prototype: Bun 1.4.1 compiles werk into one executable that runs with no checkout (Oct 2026)
payload.finding: The prototype server, its client files and its prompt files were compiled with Bun 1.4.1 into one executable and run from an empty git repository, with the source folders moved away. It added and showed cards, served the client from inside the file (byte counts equal to the source files), kept a live event stream open and survived a client disconnect, and started a fake Claude Code child that called the executable back to propose a card. Size per platform: 63 MB on macOS ARM (26 MB compressed), 70 MB macOS Intel, 82 MB Linux Intel and ARM; the werk code adds almost nothing to the runtime. A native build takes under a second; all other platforms cross-build from one Mac. The first build crashed at start, because the code read a folder of its own modules and its client files from disk at run time. Seven files changed to make it run: every file the code reads became a file listed at build time, and every place where werk starts itself, in a child process or in an agent prompt, had named the runtime and a source path instead of the executable. About forty messages shown to a person still printed the source form of the command. A file imported both as code and as an embedded file is refused by the compiler. Werk's own split, produced by running #werk-test-scope's method against werk's current code.

**Pure — 90% line threshold.** src/fold.ts, src/permission.ts, src/log.ts, src/types.ts. fold.ts derives stale and needsReview; a wrong fold renders a wrong map that looks entirely correct, so a bug here is invisible without a hard number.

**I/O — a named behaviour list, no percentage.** src/agent.ts, src/server.ts, src/cli.ts, src/convos.ts. Each holds something live: a claude child process, an SSE stream, the append-only log on disk. The four lists are #werk-test-behaviours-agent, #werk-test-behaviours-server, #werk-test-behaviours-cli, #werk-test-behaviours-convos.

This card is evidence, not the rule. When werk's client is rebuilt at #werk-stack, or any of these four files is split or renamed, re-run #werk-test-scope's method against the new code — do not hand-edit this card to chase the refactor.

payload.title: Applied to werk today: one brief across four files, three forks, all settled from source
payload.body:
Werk's own run of #werk-test-behaviours's procedure.

One brief covered all four modules at once. Three independent samples from the sampling runner. All three agreed almost word for word on every module's list — no fork needed for most of it.

Clustering surfaced three real forks, all fact questions about existing code, each settled by reading source rather than asking:

```
#werk-test-behaviours-ambiguous-convo-ref-attribution   convos.ts owns it, cli.ts is a thin wrapper
#werk-test-behaviours-model-switch-during-turn          setModel/clearContext throw, never kill mid-turn
#werk-test-behaviours-always-rule-mechanism              both halves are true at once, not a choice
```

Four resulting lists: #werk-test-behaviours-agent (9), #werk-test-behaviours-server (8), #werk-test-behaviours-cli (8), #werk-test-behaviours-convos (6).

payload.title: A judge asks for tools like a builder, and the classifier denies each write
payload.why_not: The classifier allows an ask that makes sense for the ticket, and a write can look sensible to it. Each ask also costs a model call that a fixed list does not need.

payload.title: The held-out set runs one time, after build, on the finished tree
payload.why_not: A break is found late, not at the merge that caused it, and the builder is no longer running to get the failed step.

payload.title: The step author writes browser tests directly, with role and text locators
payload.why_not: The author works before the UI exists, so it guesses the roles and labels, and the tests tie the set to one tech stack.

payload.why: It compares card versions, the log position of each card's latest counted change, as the cited-card watch defines them.

payload.title: Check each red step against the decided cards only after the run went red
payload.why_not: For a card that changed, a version comparison is a fact that needs no model, and it acts before the run instead of after. The model check stays for a step that misread an unchanged card (#val-heldout-contradiction).

payload.title: Put a step that contradicts a card in front of the person as a question
payload.why_not: The person would rewrite a step that the step author can rewrite from the current card, and the run would wait for the answer.

payload.why: It adds a check before the per-ticket filing of follow-ups, and a second kind of follow-up beside the build follow-up.
A step that waits for its rewrite shows as not run, which files no follow-up and keeps G2 waiting.

payload.title: A step that contradicts a card stops the run until a person rules
payload.why_not: A run that waits for a person stalls every ticket behind it, and the question has a safe default by the guideline for a missing decision.

payload.why: The binder maps the plain Given/When/Then steps, which name only what the user sees, to real tests.
The builder can get step text without test code because the binder keeps the steps as text and binds them separately.
The failed step goes to a fresh pass with the brief, as every pass starts with no memory of the last.

payload.title: The builder gets the failing test code
payload.why_not: The test is then no longer held out, and the builder can fit the fix to that one test.

payload.title: The builder gets a written description of what the user saw and expected
payload.why_not: Some agent must write it for each failure, and its detail varies. The step text is already in user terms.

payload.why: It tells a step that failed from a binder that could not run it, which the binder reports.

payload.title: A binder error or timeout counts as a red step
payload.why_not: In the first build run of werk-v0, every one of the 8 merged tickets showed red because the binder hit a fixed 10-minute limit, so the red badge carried no information.

payload.why: Closing a follow-up with no change is safe only because a step that goes red later files a new follow-up.

payload.title: Build the missing capability inside the follow-up ticket
payload.why_not: The capability is the scope of another planned ticket. A follow-up would build it out of order, touch that ticket's modules, and collide with it when it builds.

payload.title: Block the follow-up on the tickets that build the missing capability
payload.why_not: It needs a new blocking link across subtrees, and the held-out run already rechecks the steps after those tickets merge, so the block is a second record of the same wait.

payload.title: Archive the follow-up as not needed
payload.why_not: An archive says that the spec no longer needs the ticket, which is false: the steps must still pass. It also takes the wait off the board.

payload.why: An archived ticket takes its steps out of the set, and a restore brings them back.
Steps are written per ticket at build start, which is why they exist before the ticket's code is merged.

payload.title: Run the whole set after each merge, and show a step of an unmerged ticket as not run
payload.why_not: The binder still binds and runs steps that cannot pass at every merge, and the grey badges say nothing about the main line.

payload.title: Keep the steps of an archived ticket in the set
payload.why_not: A later plan that archives a ticket covers its scope with new tickets that carry their own steps. The old steps then fail against a main line built differently, each as a follow-up ticket.

payload.title: G2 does not wait for the held-out set, and a red step is fixed after approval
payload.why_not: The main line keeps a user-visible break that the pipeline already found, and the fix has no gate to hold it.

payload.title: The held-out set also blocks the merge queue, and a red step sends the ticket back to building
payload.why_not: One red step would hold back every ticket behind it in the queue. As a signal for the whole subtree it files follow-ups and lets merges go on.

payload.title: An agent writes the tickets directly from the subtree, with no spec
payload.why_not: The tickets then split a set of separate decisions. Nothing states the problem, the user stories or the test seams once, for all the tickets.

---
name: to-spec
description: "Turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the project issue tracker: no interview, just synthesis of what you've already discussed."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

This skill takes the current conversation context and codebase understanding and produces a spec. Do NOT interview the user; just synthesize what you already know.

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

## Process

1. Explore the repo to understand the current state of the codebase, if you haven't already. Use the project's domain glossary vocabulary throughout the spec, and respect any ADRs in the area you're touching.

2. Sketch out the seams at which you're going to test the feature. Existing seams should be preferred to new ones. Use the highest seam possible. If new seams are needed, propose them at the highest point you can. The fewer seams across the codebase, the better - the ideal number is one.

Check with the user that these seams match their expectations.

3. Write the spec using the template below, then publish it to the project issue tracker. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label - no need for additional triage.

<spec-template>

## Problem Statement

The problem that the user is facing, from the user's perspective.

## Solution

The solution to the problem, from the user's perspective.

## User Stories

A LONG, numbered list of user stories. Each user story should be in the format of:

1. As an <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>

<user-story-example>
1. As a mobile bank customer, I want to see balance on my accounts, so that I can make better informed decisions about my spending
</user-story-example>

This list of user stories should be extremely extensive and cover all aspects of the feature.

## Implementation Decisions

A list of implementation decisions that were made. This can include:

- The modules that will be built/modified
- The interfaces of those modules that will be modified
- Technical clarifications from the developer
- Architectural decisions
- Schema changes
- API contracts
- Specific interactions

Do NOT include specific file paths or code snippets. They may end up being outdated very quickly.

Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it within the relevant decision and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts, not a working demo, just the important bits.

## Testing Decisions

A list of testing decisions that were made. Include:

- A description of what makes a good test (only test external behavior, not implementation details)
- Which modules will be tested
- Prior art for the tests (i.e. similar types of tests in the codebase)

## Out of Scope

A description of the things that are out of scope for this spec.

## Further Notes

Any further notes about the feature.

</spec-template>
````

# To Tickets

Break a plan, spec, or conversation into a set of **tickets**: tracer-bullet vertical slices, each declaring the tickets that **block** it.

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

## Process

### 1. Gather context

Work from whatever is already in the conversation context. If the user passes a reference (a spec path, an issue number or URL) as an argument, fetch it and read its full body and comments.

### 2. Explore the codebase (optional)

If you have not already explored the codebase, do so to understand the current state of the code. Ticket titles and descriptions should use the project's domain glossary vocabulary, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

Look for opportunities to prefactor the code to make the implementation easier. "Make the change easy, then make the easy change."

### 3. Draft vertical slices

Break the work into **tracer bullet** tickets.

<vertical-slice-rules>

- Each slice cuts a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests): vertical, NOT a horizontal slice of one layer
- A completed slice is demoable or verifiable on its own
- Each slice is sized to fit in a single fresh context window
- Any prefactoring should be done first

</vertical-slice-rules>

Give each ticket its **blocking edges**: the other tickets that must complete before it can start. A ticket with no blockers can start immediately.

**Wide refactors are the exception to vertical slicing.** A **wide refactor** is one mechanical change (rename a column, retype a shared symbol) whose **blast radius** fans across the whole codebase, so a single edit breaks thousands of call sites at once and no vertical slice can land green. Don't force it into a tracer bullet; sequence it as **expand–contract**. First expand: add the new form beside the old so nothing breaks. Then migrate the call sites over in batches sized by blast radius (per package, per directory), each batch its own ticket blocked by the expand, keeping CI green batch to batch because the old form still exists. Finally contract: delete the old form once no caller remains, in a ticket blocked by every migrate batch. When even the batches can't stay green alone, keep the sequence but let them share an integration branch that all block a final integrate-and-verify ticket; green is promised only there.

### 4. Quiz the user

Present the proposed breakdown as a numbered list. For each ticket, show:

- **Title**: short descriptive name
- **Blocked by**: which other tickets (if any) must complete first
- **What it delivers**: the end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work

Ask the user:

- Does the granularity feel right? (too coarse / too fine)
- Are the blocking edges correct: does each ticket only depend on tickets that genuinely gate it?
- Should any tickets be merged or split further?

Iterate until the user approves the breakdown.

### 5. Publish the tickets to the configured tracker

Publish the approved tickets. **How** depends on the tracker `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` configured; the tickets are the same either way, only the shape of the blocking edges changes:

- **Local files** → write one file per ticket under `.scratch/<feature-slug>/issues/<NN>-<slug>.md`, numbered from `01` in dependency order (blockers first). Each file's "Blocked by" lists the numbers/titles it depends on. Use the per-ticket file template below: one ticket per file, never a single combined file.
- **A real issue tracker (GitHub, Linear, …)** → publish one issue per ticket in dependency order (blockers first) so each ticket's blocking edges can reference real identifiers. Use the platform's native blocking / sub-issue relationship where it has one; otherwise set each ticket's "Blocked by" to the blocking issues. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label unless instructed otherwise; the tickets are agent-grabbable by construction.

Work the **frontier**: any ticket whose blockers are all done. For a purely linear chain that means top to bottom.

Do NOT close or modify any parent issue.

<local-ticket-template>

# <NN>: <Ticket title>

**What to build:** the end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work, from the user's perspective, not a layer-by-layer implementation list.

**Blocked by:** the numbers/titles of the tickets that gate this one, or "None (can start immediately)".

**Status:** ready-for-agent

- [ ] Acceptance criterion 1
- [ ] Acceptance criterion 2

</local-ticket-template>

<issue-template>

## Parent

A reference to the parent issue on the tracker (if the source was an existing issue, otherwise omit this section).

## What to build

The end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work, from the user's perspective, not layer-by-layer implementation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Criterion 1
- [ ] Criterion 2

## Blocked by

- A reference to each blocking ticket, or "None (can start immediately)".

</issue-template>

In either form, avoid specific file paths or code snippets: they go stale fast. Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts, not a working demo, just the important bits.
````
payload.finding: Each ticket is a vertical slice that fits one fresh context, with blocking edges, a 'What to build' from the user's side, and acceptance criteria. No file paths. Wide refactors use expand-contract.

payload.why: The scope leaves out a postponed card and everything below it, so postponing is how a feature stays out of a build.

payload.title: The subtree, or the subtree and the cards it links one hop out, with other cards by id and title
payload.why_not: A decision under a linked card reaches the planner only as a title, and the planner invents its content.

payload.title: Linked cards in full, as context only: not gated and not cited
payload.why_not: A linked card is often the work itself. As context only, no check makes sure that a ticket covers it.

payload.title: The first tier in full, the rest by title, with map search
payload.why_not: A title in the index does not make the planner open the card.

payload.why: The program, not the writer, adds the cards, because rules live in a program and not in a prompt.
Each answer enters the map as a ghost proposal, as every new card does.
A rewrite of an open ticket stays only when it passes the ticket's own checks.

payload.title: Each plan writes a new run with its own spec and a full ticket set
payload.why_not: A second or interrupted plan puts a duplicate ticket set on the board, and the person must find it and archive it.

payload.why: An archive is one of the ticket moves, and a plan is a second actor that may make it.

payload.title: The plan moves the ticket to blocked with the reason "not in the current spec", and the person archives it
payload.why_not: The person must clear each such ticket by hand after every re-plan, and the archive is reversible anyway.

payload.why: A ticket can be built while other cards are still open because plan and build repeat in slices.
A ticket must fit the one fresh context that each stateless builder pass starts with.

payload.title: Build decided cards or subtrees directly, with no ticket
payload.why_not: A card is a constraint on a thing, not the thing, and a subtree groups by decision, not by layer. A pass then follows the luck of depth and body length, builds a horizontal layer, and a parent pass and its child passes rewrite each other's work.

payload.title: Tickets hold the build state, and the map derives a built mark per card
payload.why_not: A card is built when every ticket that cites it is merged. That needs new fold logic, and the board already shows the progress.

payload.finding: A spec has a Problem Statement, a Solution, a long numbered list of user stories in the form 'As an <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>', Implementation Decisions, Testing Decisions, Out of Scope, and Further Notes.

payload.title: A free-form ticket: the same fields, in any order and format
payload.why_not: A reader cannot find a field in the same place in every ticket, and a check must search for each field or ask a model, so a missing field becomes a guess.

payload.why: The verdict is the exit code of one command, as every check gives it.
The check lines of a ticket must be make targets.
The shape check fails a ticket that lacks a header line or section of the fixed structure.
A blocked ticket cannot move to building, which is how a failed set check holds a ticket back.

payload.title: A ticket may name file paths as hints for the builder
payload.why_not: No benefit is expected: the builder researches the code itself on each pass.

payload.title: The set checks read every ticket with a title line, also one that failed its own checks
payload.why_not: A ticket that is not on the board would count as coverage, so the checks would pass for a card or story that nothing will build.

payload.title: A ticket must list every ticket it waits for directly
payload.why_not: A blocker of a blocker already holds the ticket back. The direct-only reading fails a correct set and makes each ticket repeat its blockers' blockers.

payload.title: A blocked_by failure also names the ticket that should be waited for
payload.why_not: That ticket is not wrong. On the first plan of werk-v0 it put ticket 1, which has no blockers, in blocked, so no ticket could start.

payload.title: Blocked_by must agree with the depends_on edges between the cited cards
payload.why_not: A decision edge is not always a build need, and a build need often has no card edge. The check forces waits the build does not need and still misses real ones.

payload.title: The cards-cited check counts proposed cards that carry the status decided
payload.why_not: The plan proposes its own answers under the subtree it plans, so the plan would fail its own check before anyone accepted them.

payload.why: The board log holds the cited-card versions and the move to blocked.
A stale mark on a cited card is one of the changes that counts.
A re-plan changes or keeps open tickets in place, which is how a mark clears.

payload.title: Find changed cited cards only when a later check of the plan runs
payload.why_not: Nothing runs that check at the moment of the change, so a ticket can start to build against a card that changed after the plan.

payload.title: A model reads the change and judges whether the ticket still holds
payload.why_not: The verdict is not deterministic: the same change can mark a ticket on one run and not on the next.

payload.why: A build proposes a card for a decision no card makes and goes on with it, which is why its own proposals count as recorded.

payload.title: A reviewer checks each proposed card against the card standards after the pass
payload.why_not: It catches a filler card only after the pass has written it, costs one more agent session per card, and leaves the quota that makes the filler.

payload.title: The builder prompt says that a list of values or one helper's internals is not a card
payload.why_not: The builder already reads that rule, and a quota overrides it. A rule in a prompt drifts, which is why the obligation is data in the log.

payload.title: The obligation is keyed by the ticket alone
payload.why_not: A second build of the same ticket would reuse an obligation that an earlier build closed, so it would look done before it starts.

payload.why: takes that the whole tree is the home card's page, so a turn from the tree has a card to name

payload.title: Send the whole card block on every turn
payload.why_not: It names the card, but it costs the whole block on every turn. A one-line reminder names the card for almost nothing.

payload.title: The last card heard belongs to the conversation, so a new agent gets only the reminder
payload.why_not: A new agent has no memory of the conversation, so the reminder names a card it was never shown. That is the blind state the reminder exists to prevent.

payload.title: A turn from the whole tree says that no card is open
payload.why_not: The whole tree is the home card's page. A no-card line names a state that no view has and gives the agent two names for one page.

payload.why: the committed event log is the record, which is why the chat log can stay local and disposable

payload.title: Accept any conversation name and join it to the folder
payload.why_not: A name with a separator or two dots could read a file outside the folder.

payload.why: takes the streamed and finished blocks and the end line with duration and cost that close a turn

payload.title: The pane draws a sent message only when its turn starts
payload.why_not: The person sees no sign that the message arrived while the earlier reply runs, and several waiting messages stay invisible.

payload.title: A new message stops the running reply
payload.why_not: It throws away work that the person did not ask to stop. Stopping a turn is a separate action.

payload.title: Mockup: a second message sent while a reply streams, in five steps
payload.body:
A static mockup of the chat pane. Message A "Summarise the open cards" is sent. Message B "Also list the ghosts" is sent while reply A still streams. Each step shows the pane as it was before turn names (left) and with turn names (right). An amber outline marks the parts that arrive in that step. The "reply A" and "reply B" labels exist only in the mockup.

Step 1: message A is sent, and the first part of reply A streams. Both panes are the same.

![Step 1: A and the first part of reply A](/api/image?name=werk-chat-turn-id-step1.png)

Step 2: message B is sent while reply A streams. Both panes draw B at once. On the right, B shows the waiting mark.

![Step 2: B is sent, with the waiting mark on the right](/api/image?name=werk-chat-turn-id-step2.png)

Step 3: a tool call and the rest of reply A arrive. On the left they land under B and read as the answer to B. On the right they land above B.

![Step 3: the rest of reply A lands above B on the right](/api/image?name=werk-chat-turn-id-step3.png)

Step 4: reply A ends, and reply B starts. On the left, reply B runs on from reply A. On the right, the waiting mark goes away, and reply B starts under B.

![Step 4: reply B starts under B on the right](/api/image?name=werk-chat-turn-id-step4.png)

Step 5: both replies are done. On the right, the chat reads as two question-and-answer pairs. On the left, B has three parts under it, and only the last one answers it.

![Step 5: the finished chat](/api/image?name=werk-chat-turn-id-step5.png)
payload.finding: With turn names, every part of reply A stays above message B, and B shows a waiting mark until its turn starts.

payload.why: each message goes to the input of the conversation's own agent process, so a waiting message is already inside the agent that exits
takes which exits werk retries by itself, so only the other exits end the open turns

payload.title: Send each waiting message again to a new agent after the exit
payload.why_not: It starts agent work with no action of the person, and an agent that exits at once gets the same message in a loop.

payload.title: Take a waiting message out of the thread and give its words back to the composer
payload.why_not: The message reached the agent, so it was not refused, and removing it hides that it was sent.

payload.why: takes the Markdown renderer of card text, with its safe links and boxed code

payload.title: Conductor's own Claude Code integration (inspected 2026-09-01)
payload.finding: Conductor drives Claude Code as a child process over stream-json on unix sockets. No terminal, no paste. Events land in a per-session append-only outbox file.
payload.body:
Inspected on 2026-09-01 from the process table and Conductor's application-support directory.

**How it runs Claude Code.** Conductor starts its own pinned claude binary as a child process, through a sidecar runtime. The child's stdin, stdout and stderr are unix sockets to the sidecar, not a terminal. One user turn is one JSON line written to stdin, in stream-json format. Conductor never pastes text and never simulates keystrokes. Because the sidecar owns that stdin, no other program can write into a Conductor session.

**How it stores events.** Each session has one outbox file. The file holds a version, the session id, a next-sequence counter and a list of pending events. Each pending event wraps the raw stream-json payload with a session id, a turn id and a user-message id. The queue drains into a SQLite database.

**What it confirms for werk.** The outbox is an append-only event log with a sequence number, and the database is a projection of it. werk's log and fold have the same shape, so a production app reached the same design independently. Conductor also drains the queue, which works like a snapshot. werk has no snapshot yet (see #pr-log-snapshot).

payload.title: The agent asks with its question form instead of a Next line
payload.why_not: The form needs two to four options for what is one offer, and its answer arrives as a refusal reason, not as a turn of the person.

payload.title: A command that writes a structured next-action event
payload.why_not: The agent must remember one more command every turn, so it misses as often as a skipped Next line, and it adds an event type, a verb and a renderer.

payload.title: Run the agent in process through the Agent SDK
payload.why_not: It gives the same tools and loop as a library call, but adopting it is a rewrite of a working stream reader with no defect that forces it.
