payload.title: How the host application drives its Claude Code sessions
payload.finding: The host starts its pinned agent binary (version 2.1.237) from its sidecar with: claude --output-format stream-json --input-format stream-json --verbose --thinking adaptive --thinking-display. File descriptors 0, 1 and 2 are unix sockets to the sidecar, not a terminal. A user turn is one JSON line written to that socket, so the host never pastes or simulates keystrokes. The host's command to create a message targets its cloud API. With no keychain token and local mode set, it does not reach a local session. (inspected 2026-09-01)

payload.title: Retry any exit while a turn is open, early or late
payload.why_not: A late exit may come after the agent ran a tool or edited a file, so a retry with the same message can do that work twice.

payload.title: Call an exit early only when it comes before the session id, and ignore reply parts
payload.why_not: A reply part that arrives without a session id would then be repeated by a retry. Counting any output as written is the safer reading.

payload.why: takes which exits are retried first, so a recovered crash is not a death

payload.title: Only a small dot blinks red, as for a pending ask
payload.why_not: A death can happen while the person is away, and a blink outside the place they read is easy to miss. Nothing else would tell them the conversation needs a new start.

payload.title: Count each task start up and each task end down
payload.why_not: werk must then match each end to its start, and one missed event leaves the count wrong until the agent exits. The full list gives the same number with no matching.

payload.title: werk classifies every call itself, with a shell splitter, a read-only list and a prefix matcher
payload.why_not: It copies Claude Code's engine badly: every gap needed its own patch, it asked about safe reads it did not know, and it let any script through. Kept beside the engine as a second opinion, the looser of the two wins on every call.

payload.title: The manual permission mode, which asks about the path rather than the command
payload.why_not: Auto was chosen with its measured reach accepted: the bound on the risk is that the default allowlist already lets the agent edit any file in the repository.

payload.title: Catch the denial, add the rule, restart the agent and send the turn again
payload.why_not: A restart loses the turn in progress. The control request holds the turn open while the question waits.

payload.title: A permission hook process that calls back to the pane
payload.why_not: It needs one more process and a route back to the pane. The control request on the stream werk already reads removes both.

payload.title: Rewrite the call's input on allow to carry the chosen answer
payload.why_not: werk never edits a call on approval, so a command is never changed behind the agent's back. Breaking that for one tool needs its own reason.

payload.title: Write each answered question into the map's event log as a new event type
payload.why_not: The map's log is the shared decision record that every fold replays. An ask is operational noise: every fold would pay to skip it, and local approval history would travel with the map.

payload.title: Show every tool call, fold only long output
payload.why_not: A quick build still left every read, edit and shell call visible at full length. That did not clear enough space.

payload.title: The server keeps the blocks it sent and replays what a page missed
payload.why_not: The server must keep a buffer and a position per page, and a restart loses the buffer. The chat log already holds every finished block.

payload.title: A page reads the log only when it first loads
payload.why_not: A page that loses its channel and connects again misses every block of the gap until the person reloads.

payload.title: Keep the header row on top, above the chat log
payload.why_not: The thinking indicator and the context pie then sit farthest from the text box, so the person cannot tell at a glance whether the agent is stuck.

payload.title: Return to the position the person left the conversation at
payload.why_not: A switch asks to see the conversation now. A kept position hides the messages that arrived while it was in the background.

payload.why: the open turns, from send to end line, are the span in which a switch and a clear are refused

payload.title: Use the opus and sonnet aliases
payload.why_not: An alias moves to the next release without a change in werk, so behaviour and cost change silently.

payload.why: the chat log is where quotes point, so a clear must keep it

payload.title: A clear deletes the conversation's chat log
payload.why_not: It deletes data that cannot come back, and a quote of an earlier message loses the words it points at.

payload.title: A clear writes a marker line, and readers skip every line before it
payload.why_not: Every reader of the chat log must learn a new line kind, and the pane does not read the chat log at all, so the marker serves no reader.

payload.why: the settings are saved beside the session that a restart resumes

payload.title: Recover the model from Claude Code's own session file
payload.why_not: The session file does not hold the launch settings, so the advisor and the window cannot be read back, and its format belongs to Claude Code.

payload.title: Put the settings in werk's stored session file
payload.why_not: That file holds one bare id that the resume reads as is. Adding fields changes its format and risks a wrong id passed to the resume.

payload.why: takes the id match order of the header search after a hash, with the exact id first
takes that the agent is a Claude Code process whose start event carries its command names

payload.title: The server reads the command and skill folders of the project and the user itself
payload.why_not: It repeats the agent's own lookup, misses the built-in and plugin commands, and drifts when the agent changes where it looks. Its only gain is a menu before the first message.

payload.title: Push the names to the page over the live channel
payload.why_not: A second channel for one small list is a larger interface than one read when the menu opens.

payload.why: takes that a file read gives the model a native image block, which is why the message carries a path and not the bytes

payload.title: Send the image bytes inside the message, with no upload at paste time
payload.why_not: A wrong type or an oversized image shows only at the send, and one bad image refuses the whole message. The chip has no stored file to show as a thumbnail.

payload.title: The server trusts the type that the page sends with the upload
payload.why_not: A renamed file or a wrong browser guess would store a file of another kind as an image, and the agent's read of it would fail. Reading four fixed signatures costs nothing.

payload.why: a hot reload that keeps live agent sessions lets one reload update every project safely

payload.title: One werk process per project, each on its own port, optionally behind a shared interface
payload.why_not: Each process needs its own port, browser tab and code reload, a shared interface needs a proxy to reach each one, and nothing lists the projects or switches between them.

payload.title: Compare the Origin header with the Host header
payload.why_not: Both headers come from the sender. A DNS rebinding page sends a matching pair, and a request from another machine can send no Origin at all.

payload.title: Listen on loopback only and check the Host, with no token
payload.why_not: It stops other sites and other machines, but not another program or user on the same machine, and it forbids ever opening the map from another device.

payload.title: The token alone, with no Host check
payload.why_not: One route that forgets the token reopens every path. The Host check costs one comparison and stops DNS rebinding on its own.

payload.why: each tab runs its own agent process that werk starts
Each tab is one conversation as the chat defines it, with its own live agent.

payload.title: Per-subtree focus: a conversation is bound to one subtree
payload.why_not: The map cannot enforce it and it fights normal work: a conversation that starts on one card and needs to check another is normal, not an error. Scoped context is already bought by the fork point.

payload.why: the strip sits at the bottom of the chat pane that the layout places beside the map

payload.title: A vertical conversation list, or a sidebar that collapses by itself
payload.why_not: A vertical list takes width that the chat pane does not have beside the map. A sidebar that collapses moves under the cursor, so every switch is a hover and a wait.

payload.title: Step keys only, with no key that selects a position
payload.why_not: A step needs the person to know where they are and to count. With at most five chips, a fixed position is one key press from anywhere.

payload.title: A step stops at the first and the last chip
payload.why_not: A press at an end then does nothing, so the person must look at the strip before each step. Browser tab stepping wraps, and a stop breaks that habit.

payload.why: a tab can own a card only because each conversation has a home card

payload.title: A switch of tab leaves the map where it is
payload.why_not: It splits the subject in two. The focused tab is told the card that the map shows, so a tab resumed under another tab's card works on the wrong subject. A map that does not move is worth less than a conversation that stays on its subject.

payload.why: a fork resumes the stored session id that a restart also resumes

payload.title: Every new conversation starts with an empty context
payload.why_not: It is cheapest on the first turn and worst by the fifth. The new conversation reads the same files and cards again, and it loses the shared understanding that makes the split worth doing.

payload.title: Refuse a fork of a tab with no session until it sends a message
payload.why_not: The gesture fails on the newest tab, where a person most often starts, and the person must type a throwaway message to fork.

payload.why: the fork moves the map because the map follows the focused tab
the gesture starts the new tab with a session fork
a position key returns to the earlier tab in one press, which makes a focused fork acceptable

payload.title: A plain click on a card opens a new tab
payload.why_not: The person clicks through the map all the time while a turn runs, and each click would fork. It also removes the normal case: stay in this conversation, only look.

payload.title: A Shift+click forks in the background and leaves the map where it is
payload.why_not: One gesture would move the view and the other would not, which is two rules. The conversation that the person leaves keeps running, so nothing is lost by a focused fork.

payload.title: Fork, then clear the context
payload.why_not: It takes two steps for one intent, and the fork first copies the parent's session that the clear then throws away.

payload.title: The empty start switches to a tab that already has the card as its home
payload.why_not: The press then shows an old conversation with its history, the opposite of what the person asked for.

payload.title: A second button next to plus starts an empty conversation
payload.why_not: Two small icons side by side look alike, and a rare action takes a permanent place in a narrow strip.

payload.why: parking removes chips from the strip, and must keep the order of the chips that stay

payload.title: A close that ends the conversation, with a history of closed conversations
payload.why_not: The session stays on disk either way, so closed and parked would behave the same. A second state and a history view would separate two states that do not differ. The menu of all conversations is that history.

payload.title: A close also stops the agent process
payload.why_not: It needs a check for a turn in progress and a confirmation of the stop. A park without a stop needs neither.

payload.title: A menu row shows the card's title
payload.why_not: Two tabs on one card then show two identical rows, with no way to tell them apart.

payload.why: a stopped agent comes back by resuming its stored session

payload.title: Never stop a parked agent
payload.why_not: After hours or days, every past conversation is still a live process, and memory use only grows.

payload.title: Resume a stopped agent at the next message
payload.why_not: The person types into a conversation with no process, and the message waits while the agent starts and loads the session, which is the worst moment to wait.

payload.why: the state dot sits on the chips of the strip
takes the dead state: when it starts and when it ends
takes the permission ask that is answered only in its own tab's bar
takes the next-action button whose unclicked state counts as waiting

payload.title: A shared ask queue: the ask shows inline in the focused tab, named by the asking tab
payload.why_not: Built and tried. It interrupts the tab the person reads, and the inline ask lacks the context of its own conversation, so the person cannot judge whether to stop and answer.

payload.title: The tab that asks takes the focus
payload.why_not: It defeats the feature: the person starts a background turn so it can run while they look away, and a question that pulls them out of the current conversation is worse than the wait.

payload.title: A quiet badge or a still dot only, for an ask and for a dead agent
payload.why_not: A tab that the person forgets stays blocked with no sign. A permission ask and a dead agent are the two states where nothing moves until the person acts.

payload.why: takes the question form whose open question the blue line reports

payload.title: Only the chip dot blinks for a tab that waits
payload.why_not: A person who reads another pane misses a blink on a small chip, and the waiting tab does no work until they notice.

payload.title: Every line has one color, whatever the reason
payload.why_not: The person must switch to the tab to learn whether it needs an answer, a click or a new start.

payload.why: each fork has its own session after the split, so a sibling's later turns must be pulled
a reference by card resolves through each conversation's home card

payload.title: Push a 'what changed since your fork' summary into a tab when it gets the focus
payload.why_not: It costs on every switch for a need that comes on few of them. It also repeats what the agent can look up exactly, since the map on disk is always current.

payload.title: Try a tab name first, then a session id or its start, then a card
payload.why_not: A tab keeps its name when it gets a new session, so a name can match several conversations. Trying it first lets the loosest reference decide before an exact one is checked.

payload.why: a fork is its own session with a parent session, which the line records

payload.title: One folder per tab, with a file that holds the tab's current session
payload.why_not: A tab name outlives its session. When the tab gets a new session, the file is overwritten and the earlier session drops out of the list.

payload.why: the in-place swap of a changed component comes from the chosen client stack

payload.title: Rely on server hot reload alone
payload.why_not: It keeps the server process alive, but the browser still reloads the whole page on a client edit, so every tab resets.

payload.title: A path field that completes from the server's file system
payload.why_not: It is needed only when the server runs on another machine, and werk does not support a remote server. On one machine the folder dialog is faster.

payload.title: The server also opens a Linux folder dialog, with a fallback program
payload.why_not: It adds platform code and a test for a platform that werk does not support yet. The add rule does not change when a Linux dialog comes later.

payload.why: names are unique only within the list, so a clash is found against it
the address carries the project name
dev mode decides whether the entry is present
the entry sits on top of the stored list without being written into it
the open card and the view are the parts of the address that each project remembers

payload.title: Keep every display setting per project
payload.why_not: The person would set the same theme, widths and filters again in each project.

payload.why: the second start adds its folder with a request that carries the synchronizer token

payload.title: An operating-system file lock that the kernel releases when the holder dies
payload.why_not: The runtime has no built-in call for it, and the project takes no dependencies.

payload.title: A second, short-lived lock guards the removal of a stale lock
payload.why_not: The race it closes needs two starts within milliseconds right after a crash, and the guard lock has its own stale case.

payload.title: Derive the component graph from the code, by reading its imports
payload.why_not: It maps files, not intent. A subsystem boundary is a judgement, not a directory, and an import graph cannot hold a link to a decision card, so staleness stops at the code.

payload.title: Map each diagram element to files and symbols, so the diagram shows what is built
payload.why_not: The diagram then inherits the accidents of a prototype whose shape nobody chose, and a box with no code arrow has several meanings, most of them noise.

payload.title: Use the diagram to audit the code and find the gaps
payload.why_not: It assumes the code has a chosen shape. Every difference reads as a problem, and almost all of them are prototype mess.

payload.title: Add the parts to the map as a node kind of their own
payload.why_not: Every count that reads the map would treat a part as a claim, settled or not, and give a wrong number.

payload.title: Fold the cards into the diagram as a pure data transformation, with no agent
payload.why_not: A card carries no field that names the part or level it touches. Cards about a view, a build loop and a data shape are all decided cards, and any rule that sorts them is the interpretation it was meant to avoid.

payload.title: Require one diagram edge per code route or call
payload.why_not: That is a map of the code, which the diagram is not. One server part would split into one edge per address, and every view would re-point to whichever address it calls.

payload.title: Structural: #werk-multichat, #vi-graph3d and #werk-perm-native each make diagram nodes
payload.why: Worked cases of the structural class: each card names a part a user can see or a process that runs.
payload.finding:
#vi-graph3d makes one node, the 3D graph view, and one edge from it to the state it loads. One card, one part: the plainest case.

#werk-multichat makes or co-justifies three nodes: the tab strip, the conversation manager that runs one agent per conversation, and the per-conversation transcript store. It is the case for one decision creating several parts, which is why the map and the diagram cannot be one graph (#vi-sysdiag).

#werk-perm-native makes the ask queue: the part that holds tool calls Claude Code's own permission engine could not decide. It also co-justifies the store of always-allow rules. The card reads like a policy, but the policy is carried out by a running part, so it is structural.

payload.title: Behavioural: #werk-mc-tabs and #werk-perm-mode add a citation to a node, not a box
payload.why: Worked cases of the behavioural class: each card constrains a part that a structural card already drew.
payload.finding:
#werk-mc-tabs decides where the tab strip sits and how it looks: card-id chips in the bottom control cluster. The tab strip node exists because of #werk-multichat. #werk-mc-tabs only adds its id to that node's citation list.

#werk-perm-mode decides that auto is the only permission mode and that no flag sets it. It changes how the ask queue behaves, not whether it exists, so it is a second citation on the ask queue node beside #werk-perm-native.

Both show the test: delete the card, and the diagram keeps the same boxes and edges. Only a citation goes.

payload.title: Method: #drained, #al-two and #vi-prop are rules for keeping the map and make nothing
payload.why: Worked cases of the method class: each card is a rule about how decisions are recorded, not about the product.
payload.finding:
#drained defines when a topic is finished: settled and unchallenged is zero. #al-two says a decision is never shown with one option. #vi-prop says a change marks only the next hop of dependents. None names a part, and none appears in the diagram.

They are the trap the class exists for. werk is a tool for keeping maps, so a rule for the map reads as if it described the product. #vi-prop in particular sounds like a component — a staleness propagator — and an early hand fold of the cards did map it onto the fold function. In any other project these cards would be obviously about process.

payload.title: Method and structural at once: #werk-contract is a map rule that also runs as a check
payload.why: The worked case of a card in two classes: a map rule that werk builds as a running check.
payload.finding:
#werk-contract says a card cannot become decided until a program check passes: who, depends_on, rejected options, kill criteria. As a rule, it is about keeping the map — method. But the command line runs that check before every status change, so the check is a part of the product, and the diagram cites the card on the command-line node.

It shows the class is not a property of the card's topic. It depends on whether the decision is carried out by a running part. This overlap happens in werk because the product is the planning loop (#vi-flow); a payments project would have no such card.

payload.title: A Mermaid flowchart with the card ids in a separate comment block
payload.why_not: werk draws its own picture, so Mermaid syntax buys nothing at render time. A separate block puts one fact in two places, and the two drift.

payload.title: Keep one card id per connection
payload.why_not: An id is the only path from an element back to the card that decided it, so a dropped second citation is a dead link, not a missing footnote.

payload.title: Resolve the link in the browser by matching card text to element titles
payload.why_not: It guesses back ids that are already written. Inferring links from text recovers only a small share of them.

payload.title: Mermaid draws the diagram with its own auto-layout
payload.why_not: Once connections carried labels and parts carried descriptions, the layout left large empty regions and crossing lines. Auto-layout takes placement, the judgement that makes the diagram readable, away from the author.

payload.title: The agent draws a static SVG by hand, positions and sizes included
payload.why_not: The hand arithmetic for box and label sizes caused the spacing errors, and it repeats on every redraw.

payload.title: An intent file of groups and rows, with a resolver or an object-avoiding router that places the connections
payload.why_not: The agent controls only which part sits in which row, and cannot see what the resolver produced without rendering it. The router's paths bent more and put labels on box text.

payload.title: D2 grid layout with TALA routing
payload.why_not: A D2 grid gives one width to every member of a column, and no part can span columns. The workaround is invisible spacers, which is hand-tuning under another name.

payload.title: A constrained auto-layout engine such as ELK or dagre with lane constraints
payload.why_not: A solver still chooses the positions. A constraint can forbid a bad layout but not express the one the author wants, and the author cannot read the result back before it is drawn.

payload.title: Make every hard-to-read route a build error
payload.why_not: Some hard-to-read routes are the cheapest legal route. An error would force the author to redraw a correct grid and fail a sync run that should pass.

payload.title: Penrose: Substance says what exists, Style says how it looks, and Substance holds no numbers
payload.finding: SIGGRAPH 2020, Carnegie Mellon. Three languages: Domain defines the vocabulary, Substance declares objects and relations only, Style turns them into shapes and positions. Penrose has no numeric type in Substance at all — you cannot write a coordinate there even if you want to. One Substance file renders two ways under two Style files. Positions come from minimising a badness function, which is the part that does not transfer.

payload.title: CSS grid-template-areas: the mainstream DSL that is already ASCII-art placement with a validity rule
payload.finding: Called the ascii-art method in its own docs. One quoted string per row, whitespace-separated name tokens, . for an empty cell. Two rules worth copying exactly: every row must have the same token count or the whole declaration is invalid, and a named area must form a rectangle - an L-shape makes the browser discard the entire template rather than guess. Precedent for fully-constrained-or-do-not-render. Critically, the tracks themselves are sized independently of the grid (auto, fr, fixed): the ascii art fixes topology, not pixels.

payload.title: The Kandinsky model: boxes on a coarse grid, edges routed on a finer grid
payload.finding: The standard graph-drawing model for exactly this shape. Each vertex is a box centred on a coarse grid point; each edge is an alternating horizontal/vertical run routed on a finer grid. Node size is derived from the largest number of edges attaching to one side. Extends Tamassia's orthogonal model past degree 4, and is the basis for UML and business-process layout tools. Sobering result: minimising total bends in this model is NP-complete (Bläsius, Krug, Rutter, Wagner) - an earlier min-cost-flow formulation was found incorrect by Eiglsperger, who gave a 2-approximation. Relevant because it says: do not try to make the program optimise the grid. Let the agent place, and check.

payload.title: Tiling systems / recognizable picture languages: the formal name for a 2D language defined by allowed tiles
payload.finding: Giammarresi and Restivo, 1992, then the Handbook of Formal Languages survey. A local picture language is defined by listing the authorized 2x2 tiles over the alphabet plus a boundary symbol. REC, the recognizable picture languages, is what you get by projecting a local one. This is the exact formalism for rules 1.1 to 1.7: a finite set of legal local neighbourhoods, and a picture is in the language iff every window is legal. Also characterised by existential monadic second-order logic (Giammarresi, Restivo, Seibert, Thomas 1996), so the grammar has a logic form as well as a tile form.

payload.title: svgbob, ditaa, a2s: working implementations of text grid in, styled SVG out
payload.finding: Existence proof for step 3 of the idea. svgbob (Rust, Apache-2.0) reads ASCII art and emits SVG, inferring corners, junctions and arrowheads from a character's neighbours rather than requiring them to be named. It has a scale directive that converts character cells to SVG units, plus font-size/family and colour directives. ditaa (Java) came first; a2s is a Go reimplementation, written because ditaa was verbose, rasterised, and needed a JVM per run. What none of them have: a formal grammar that rejects an invalid drawing. They are lenient parsers, not checkers.

payload.title: Keep a system font stack and approximate the width per character

payload.title: Prototype: opt0 vs opt1 against the real full-minimal diagram
payload.body:
Output-only prototype per #al-sample-build-isolation: a standalone script (no tracked file
edited) parsed and resolved .werk/diagram-grid-full-minimal.wgrid with the real gridsys code
(parseGrid/check/resolveGrid — no new parser written), then computed the pixel rectangle
opt0 and opt1 would each draw for the "mapview" (MAP VIEW) group's real cell bounds
(row 0, col 0-4), against the ground truth: resolveGrid's own member-card bounding box,
which is already built from real per-column colX/colW and is known correct.

opt0 (fixed integer scale, uniform column width assumed): right edge 146.6px short of the
real group extent, bottom edge 25.0px short. Column widths 0-4 in this diagram are
[204, 212, 141, 195, 214] against opt0's assumed average of 175.3 — not close to uniform.
A 146.6px shortfall on a group whose members span 1023px means the shape-grid outline would
NOT contain the real "diagram" card (214px wide, the group's own widest member) — the exact
containment failure #vi-sysdiag-grid-groupshape exists to prevent.

opt1 (proportional mapping via real per-column lookup, not a fraction of total extent): exact
match on all four edges, by construction — it looks up colX/colW directly instead of
assuming any distribution.

Also checked "proc" (SERVER PROCESS), a group spanning nearly the full grid width: opt0
still drifted 25.8px on the row axis, confirming the column-axis result was not a fluke of
one group's shape.

Decision: opt1. opt0 is not a simplification with acceptable rounding error — it can produce
a shape cell that a checker would need to hard-fail against, in exactly the pipeline whose
whole point is that fitting is a checked fact, not a coincidence.

/tmp/werk-proto-groupshape/ (script + rendered SVG overlay) — ephemeral, deleted after this
note, per #al-ephem.

payload.title: Dialogue Mapping and IBIS — Kunz & Rittel, Conklin
payload.finding: Introduced in 1970 to capture the reasoning behind decisions on hard planning problems. The notation is a grammar, not a set of node types: Questions respond to Ideas, Ideas respond to Questions, Arguments respond to Ideas. Two properties matter: the grammar is deliberately tiny so a facilitator can keep pace with live conversation, and the map, not the transcript, is the record of what the conversation established.

payload.title: Conversation Tree Architecture — arXiv 2603.21278
payload.finding: Flat append-only chat accumulates all context in one unbounded window, so topically distinct threads bleed into each other and degrade response quality. They call it logical context poisoning. Their framework: a tree of context-isolated nodes, each with its own local window, with rules for how context flows downstream on branch creation and upstream on deletion. Their stated gap: no mainstream LLM interface lets users manage context hierarchically.

payload.title: Guided Sensemaking: Agents in Collaborative Deliberation — arXiv 2606.02260
payload.finding: Ito et al. keep conversation state in an IBIS tree and inject facilitation messages: more comprehensive discussion, higher satisfaction. Nomura et al.: humans brainstorming with IBIS-based agents produced more ideas per person and reported less hesitation to contribute. Cites Krakauer's split: a complementary cognitive artifact coaches users toward internalising the mental model; a competitive one performs the task and transfers no skill.

payload.why_not: The span then points at a place the citer never chose.

payload.title: The citer names which occurrence to take by position
payload.why_not: The citer counts by eye, the memory step extraction removes.

payload.title: Count only non-overlapping occurrences
payload.why_not: The count says one where the words start at two places.

payload.why: The renderer links only the ids the map can open.
A message starts an agent, so it carries the synchronizer token.

payload.title: Send the raw text of the block beside its HTML
payload.why_not: The page could render it again without the server's list of ids, with unchecked links.

payload.title: Send chat messages up a two-way live channel
payload.why_not: The live channel goes one way; a second connection must be guarded and reconnected for what one request carries.

payload.title: Send chat messages to the note address with a kind field
payload.why_not: One address with two meanings: a wrong kind sends the person's words to the log or to the agent by mistake.

payload.why: Each verb that writes appends one event to the append-only log that the map is folded from.
Takes the written form of a reference in text, a hash sign before the id, which an agent copies into a command.

payload.title: A command refuses an id with a hash sign and prints the id without it
payload.why_not: The agent learns nothing it can act on except to retry. Every copied reference costs one failed command and one more turn.

payload.title: A command removes a leading hash sign from every argument, text included
payload.why_not: A title, a why or a note may start with a hash sign on purpose. Changing text corrupts what the agent wrote.

payload.title: Print listings as JSON by default
payload.why_not: Every other command prints plain text for an agent and a person to read, and no reader of a listing needs a machine format by default.

payload.why: Each agent belongs to one project of the one server, and its commands must reach that project's map.
The install places the executable on the path under the name werk.

payload.title: Write the absolute path of the running command line into the prompt
payload.why_not: The text then differs per machine and per mode, and every prompt and subagent file needs a placeholder. One plain name reads the same everywhere.

payload.title: Start a printed command with the name of the executable file that runs
payload.why_not: It prints whatever the file is called after a download or a rename, so the same fix reads differently on each machine and in each document.

payload.why: Takes the rule that every new node is a frozen ghost whose edges are held until it is accepted.
A word change on a decided card is refused because a decided card changes only through a proposal.
The required why on a depends_on link is the reason that the link must carry.

payload.title: An add refuses a card with no status
payload.why_not: A new card is nearly always open, so the agent would type the same flag every time. A refusal costs a failed call for no gain, and open is the safe default.

payload.why: The rederive is the confirm that ends the review of a marked card.
Each line under a listed card is the trace of its mark.

payload.title: One command per kind of mark
payload.why_not: A reader must run three commands to learn what needs attention. One list with a kind filter gives the same views.

payload.title: Print ids only, and read each trace with show
payload.why_not: A reader cannot rank the list without the reason for each mark, so each card would be opened one by one.

payload.title: No command; the agent reads the Flow tab
payload.why_not: The agent has a shell and no browser, so the list must exist as a command.

payload.why: Accept and discard of a ghost carry its ghost parents, options and children.
The remove, restore and removed verbs carry the removal, the reparent and its undo.
Takes the counts and the subtree that the printed rollup line shows.
A show prints the trace of each mark.
The index and the search are the two reads that each builder pass gets.
Takes which cards a find lists.
A show of a removed card names the restore because its id stays taken and it can come back.
Takes the kinds of proof that every card carries.

payload.title: The printed card lists only the ids and titles of its options and sources
payload.why_not: The agent must run one more query per item to read its reason, and it does not. The rejected reason is the part that stops a choice from coming back.

payload.title: The proof sections print only when the reader asks for them with a flag
payload.why_not: The agent does not know that it needs the proof until it has read it. The card page shows the proof every time, so the printed card does the same.

payload.why: The quote runs the verbatim extraction and refuses an inexact or repeated match.
The inbox keeps a thread by id and marks where the id was proposed again.

payload.title: Take the words of a quote in only one way, as the last argument or only with the text flag
payload.why_not: A caller with the other habit fails though nothing about its quote is wrong. Accepting both costs one refusal for the case where both are given.

payload.why: The tier flags and the refusal of the worktree tier for a sample follow the isolation rule.
The prototype verb builds one artifact per option in parallel, as the option build defines.
The target verb sets the one target repository per project, and the build verbs refuse without it.
The plan verb writes the spec and the tickets of a subtree.
The restart verb ends a subtree's unfinished work before it plans and runs again.
The gate verb passes the gate that only a person may pass.
The followed verb writes the record that closes a card obligation.
The followup verb writes the follow-up record, its class and its corrections.

payload.title: A repository flag on build, run and gate, recorded per subtree on first use
payload.why_not: The target is one fact about the project. A flag per command lets two subtrees of one project build into two repositories, and a missing flag needs a default.

payload.title: A flag on an existing verb closes the obligation
payload.why_not: The record is its own event with its own checks on the named cards. A flag on a verb with another job mixes two operations and hides the record where no pass looks.

payload.why: The move and archive subverbs make the agent's board moves that the board allows.
A restore is its own board event and puts the ticket back in the column it left.

payload.title: A verb of its own, werk ticket-check
payload.why_not: It splits the ticket operations over two help entries, and a reader looking for a ticket operation under ticket does not find it.

payload.why: The fails report computes the gates, causes, derived numbers and thresholds of the fail measure.
The rework report prints the two kinds of rework.
The cost report prints plan cost per card and per day.
The default resume and the new flag come from the resume rule.
The serve takes the one-server lock.
No permission-mode flag exists because the mode is fixed.
Takes the append-only, one-event-per-line shape and the fold of the decision log.

payload.title: Step events go into the board log
payload.why_not: The board is folded on every render, and step events outnumber ticket moves about tenfold. It also mixes build churn into the record of where a ticket is.

payload.title: One folder per build, each with its own event file and its transcripts
payload.why_not: Every reader has to read every folder, and a plan turn belongs to no build. A filter on the build id in one log gives the same events of one build.

payload.title: A summary record per pass, written beside the transcripts and not committed
payload.why_not: The summary repeats what the board log says about a pass, so the two can disagree. It has no step-level start and end for debugging, and it is lost with the worktree.

payload.title: Commit the transcripts and check output with the log
payload.why_not: One build writes megabytes of transcript. The repository would grow with every build, for detail that only debugging a recent build needs.

payload.title: The pipeline log stays local and is not committed
payload.why_not: One lost laptop or deleted worktree erases the whole measurement history. The log is small, so committing it costs little.

payload.why: A copy is needed because a plan updates the spec and the open tickets in place.

payload.title: Git history of the spec and ticket files is the copy
payload.why_not: Git does not track the ticket files, and two plans between two commits leave only the second in history.

payload.title: Git tracks the copies, beside the pipeline log
payload.why_not: A copy is debugging detail, like a transcript. A comparison is needed for recent plans, so the repository would grow with every plan for little use.

payload.why: The list holds the plan scope and its two tiers.
A log position recovers the card text because the decision log is append-only.

payload.title: The event holds a full copy of each scope card's text
payload.why_not: A scope has tens of cards, and every plan would copy them into a log that every fold reads. A position recovers the same text.

payload.title: The event holds only the count of cards per tier
payload.why_not: A count shows that the input grew, not which card changed. Two plans with the same count can read different decisions.

payload.why: Spec and ticket cost is attributed per spec.
Build cost per unit of size uses spec stories as the size.
Cost is carried on the ended events of the pipeline log.
Per-card plan cost uses the card that is open at each turn.

payload.title: Plan cost as one daily total across all chats
payload.why_not: Each conversation already has a home card and a per-turn open card, so per-card cost costs no more to collect. A daily total cannot show which cards were expensive.

payload.title: Raw token counts as the unit of cost
payload.why_not: Cache reads, cache writes, input and output tokens have different prices, and models have different prices. A token sum compares unlike things.

payload.why: The turn is written as an event of the pipeline log.
The event names the conversation and the card open at the turn.

payload.title: Read plan cost back from the Claude Code transcripts when the cost is read
payload.why_not: The transcripts expire, so the history shrinks to the retention window. A reading over a year of planning would see one month.

payload.why: The backfill writes the same plan-turn event that a live turn writes, so one fold reads both.
Code written inside a plan turn counts as the prototype step, a named step of plan.

payload.title: Count only chat-pane turns
payload.why_not: Terminal turns that wrote to the map hold several percent of past plan cost. Leaving them out drops the whole cost of the cards built from a terminal.

payload.title: Every terminal turn goes to its day
payload.why_not: Terminal sessions also build the tool itself. Code work would count as plan cost and inflate the base.

payload.title: A plan turn that changes code counts whole as card refinement
payload.why_not: Code written while a card is open is the prototype step of plan. Counting it as refinement hides what prototypes cost inside what deciding a card costs.

payload.title: Code changed inside a plan turn is not plan cost
payload.why_not: The code is a prototype for the open card, and prototype is a step of plan. Leaving it out drops a large share of plan cost from the stage that spent it.

payload.why: A past session is rebuilt from transcripts by the backfill.

payload.title: Keep the main-thread cost and mark pipeline cost as a lower bound
payload.why_not: The builder and the held-out binder, the two largest pipeline stages, stay understated by about half, and nothing says by how much.

payload.why: A pipeline session counts at its tree sum, so the total is not low.

payload.title: Count other Claude Code spend on the machine
payload.why_not: The remainder is read from transcripts at read time, so it shrinks as transcripts expire and never matches a past reading. It is also not a cost of this project.

payload.title: Record every Claude Code session on the machine in the log
payload.why_not: The log would hold work that is not the project's, and a reusable tool would read every other repository of its user.

payload.why: The fold reads the timed moves of the board log.
The measure has one row per ticket state.

payload.title: The build writes each move into the pipeline log as a step event
payload.why_not: The board log already holds every move with its time. A second copy can disagree with the first.

payload.title: The time of the last visit only, not the sum of the visits
payload.why_not: A ticket that goes back to building three times would show only its last pass, and the retries would not show in the time.

payload.why: A conflict fail comes from the merge loop.
A fail record is stored in the ended event of a pass in the pipeline log.

payload.title: The number of passes per ticket counts the builder's mistakes
payload.why_not: A fail can come from the spec, a flaky check or a false finding. Counting every fail as a builder mistake points the fix at the wrong stage.

payload.why: The next pass is a fresh agent with the failure in its brief, which lets it name the cause.

payload.title: A separate classifier agent reads each failure and names its cause
payload.why_not: It costs one more session per fail, and it sees less than the next builder pass, which reads the failure and the code in order to fix it.

payload.title: A flaky check keeps the pass red, and the rerun only sets the cause
payload.why_not: A check that fails and then passes on the same commit gives no stable verdict. A red pass for it uses up one pass of the retry cap on the check instead of the ticket.

payload.title: Collect the outcome data only when something first reads it
payload.why_not: An event that is not recorded when it happens cannot be recovered later. A reader built months later would start with no history.

payload.why: Escapes found by the person are the build-miss follow-ups.

payload.title: Each escape is its own record, written where it is found
payload.why_not: The merge result, the held-out result and the follow-up already hold every escape. A second record of the same fact can disagree with the first.

payload.why: Builder proposals are the early signal of plan misses, counted per ticket.
A rise in follow-ups per ticket uses the trend alert rule.
The spec-gap fails are an early signal of plan misses.

payload.title: The person files each follow-up and chooses its class
payload.why_not: The class is exact, but every request costs the person a form, and a request without the form is not counted.

payload.title: A review agent finds and classifies follow-ups later, from the chat, the decision log and git
payload.why_not: It writes late and guesses the request from what is left. A request after the last review is not recorded.

payload.why: A person's rejection of a gate's result is counted as a follow-up, not as a stop.
A restart of unfinished work is a kind of stop, and the run guard decides when one is needed.

payload.title: Read the kind of stop from the start of the reason text
payload.why_not: A reason is prose for a person. A reworded reason moves its stops to another kind, and three kinds of blocked ticket read as one.

payload.why: A structured question with no answer is the question form of the pane.
An unclicked next-action button is the pane's offer of a next step.
A resolved question's wait comes from the ask history.

payload.title: Count a chat-pane wait as one more kind of intervention
payload.why_not: An intervention stops an autonomous pass, and its count per ticket must go down. Counting a conversation's questions per ticket mixes two measures and makes the intervention alert fire on normal conversation.

payload.title: A text rule: a last paragraph that ends in a question mark
payload.why_not: It reads prose, so a reporting sentence that ends in a question mark starts a wait, and an ask written without one does not.

payload.title: Structured questions only
payload.why_not: It misses the next-action button, the most common way a chat-pane turn hands the next step to the person.

payload.title: A classifier reads the last message of each turn
payload.why_not: It costs a model call per turn and adds a judgement that can be wrong, where two events the pane already has give the answer.

payload.why: The cards each ticket cites, and when, come from its cite records.
The merge commit of each ticket, where the code fold starts, is recorded by the merge loop.

payload.title: Record the lines each merge adds, and watch them for changes
payload.why_not: The repository already holds every line and every later change. Asking it at read time needs no record at merge time and cannot drift from it.

payload.why: A replay run compares the cost measure.
A replay run compares escapes against the held-out set.

payload.title: Compare a variant against the production history of the current pipeline
payload.why_not: The two periods build different tickets, so a difference in cost or escapes can come from the tickets and not from the pipeline.

payload.why: werk fills the check names that this card defines.
The merge loop is werk's gate before a merge, and it runs the checks on a temporary tree with no installed packages.
It runs after the merge loop merges, and a red run becomes a follow-up ticket as a red held-out step does.
It builds and starts the one executable that this card defines.

payload.title: Hosted CI on a pull request is the gate before every merge
payload.why_not: The merge loop already merges on green checks. A hosted gate adds a push, a wait for a remote machine and a second queue to every ticket, and the merge loop then stops whenever the service is slow or down.

payload.title: No hosted CI: the merge loop's checks are the only run
payload.why_not: Every check then passes only on a machine that has already built werk. A package missing from the lockfile, or a test that reads a local file, shows up first on a user's machine.

payload.title: Git hooks run the checks before each commit
payload.why_not: An agent commits many times per ticket, and the merge loop already checks before each merge. A hook repeats the same run on every commit, and a commit can skip it.

payload.why: The React rule set is on because the client is React.

payload.title: ESLint with typescript-eslint, and Prettier for formatting
payload.why_not: Two programs with two configurations and a set of plugin packages, and the lint and format rules overlap until a third package turns the overlap off. A type-aware run is slow on every agent edit. Its one real gain is the full set of type-aware rules, such as a promise that nobody awaits.

payload.title: Oxlint for linting, with a separate formatter
payload.why_not: As fast as Biome, but linting and formatting are two programs with two configurations. Biome gives the same speed with one program.

payload.title: No linter: the type checker and a formatter only
payload.why_not: The type checker does not find unused code, wrong hook dependencies or a style that drifts across files. An agent copies the style of the code it reads, so drift grows with every change.

payload.why: Bun, the runtime from this card, runs TypeScript without a type check, so a separate check is needed.

payload.title: No separate type check: the editor and the runtime find type errors
payload.why_not: Bun and Vite never check types, and an agent does not look at an editor. A type error then reaches the main line and shows only when the code runs.

payload.title: Default strict mode, without the check on array and map reads
payload.why_not: Strict mode alone types a read from an array or a map as always present. A missing key then fails at runtime, which is the error the check exists to catch.

payload.title: TypeScript 6, the last compiler written in JavaScript
payload.why_not: About ten times slower on a full check, and werk needs none of what it still has over TypeScript 7: werk calls no compiler interface and emits no output.

payload.title: Measurement on the werk prototype: TypeScript 7.0.2 full check and the array and map read rule (Oct 2026)
payload.finding: On the prototype code base (about 80 server modules plus the browser scripts), a full TypeScript 7.0.2 check in strict mode takes 0.42 s of wall time. It reports 4 errors, so the prototype's typecheck check is red today. Turning on the rule that a read from an array or a map can return nothing adds 394 errors. Most are in a few modules that index arrays in loops: 68 in one geometry module, 20 to 25 in each of several test files. The count is the cost of adding the rule to existing code, not to code written under it from the start.

payload.title: Restart the whole process on each source change (node --watch)
payload.why_not: A restart kills the in-flight agent child processes and their session state. One session saw 8 mid-turn kills, each right after the agent edited a watched source file, so the task of improving werk keeps interrupting itself.

payload.title: Stay on Node, with vite-node as the process host for dev reload
payload.why_not: Unpatched, vite-node crashed werk's real server on an unrelated edit. With the guard both runtimes survive an edit, so the choice comes down to the release: Bun compiles werk into one executable, which Node does not match as cleanly.

payload.title: dev-pipeline-research-hmr.md: vite-node/Bun/Deno HMR vs. Agent state
payload.finding: vite-node's invalidateDepTree is transitive, not global: editing fold.ts never re-evaluates a module agent.ts doesn't import. Bun --hot guarantees globalThis survives but not the object graph across an edited boundary. Deno --watch-hmr names 'an async function currently running' as a forced-full-restart case — the exact shape of werk's failure. Node core has no HMR, only full-restart --watch.

payload.title: Prototype: globalThis-pinned child process survives edits under bun --hot and vite-node --watch
payload.finding: Built an Agent-shaped harness: a real spawn()'d child pinned to globalThis, plus an unrelated sibling module standing in for fold.ts. Under both bun --hot and vite-node --watch, editing the sibling AND editing agent.ts directly left the outer process pid, the child's pid, and the pinned object's bornAt all unchanged — only the exported marker value updated. vite-node's own --help calls --watch 'restart, similar to nodemon', but it never crosses an OS process boundary, so the globalThis guard alone was enough in both tools. This settles all three prototype items on #werk-hmr: transitive invalidation sparing agent.ts, an edit to the very state-holding file, and object-identity survival — all confirmed, for both candidates.

payload.title: Real-app test: unpatched vite-node crashes, unpatched bun --hot silently orphans
payload.finding: Ran werk's actual server.ts/agent.ts, not the toy harness, on two isolated scratch copies with a live claude child mid-task. src/cli.ts:121-124 dispatches server.listen() unconditionally at module top level with no guard, and src/agent.ts's Agent is a plain 'new Agent(...)' with no globalThis pin. Result: editing fold.ts alone (the 'safe' tier) is enough to trigger cli.ts's entry dispatch to rerun under BOTH tools, contradicting the assumption that only editing agent.ts/server.ts was risky. vite-node --watch: server.listen() fails EADDRINUSE, server.ts's own retry loop exhausts 20 tries over ~5s, then calls process.exit(1) - full crash. bun --hot: does not crash, but silently constructs a new Agent + server context on every edit. Proved with a real 25-step counting task: the already-open SSE connection kept streaming the live task uninterrupted (same claude child pid throughout, task completed normally), but a brand-new SSE connection opened mid-task saw nothing - the new Agent has no session, no child. A page refresh or new tab would silently lose visibility into a still-running task. Bun's unpatched failure mode is quieter than vite-node's crash, not safer.

payload.title: Real-app test, patched: globalThis-pin guard fixes both candidates
payload.finding: Ported the globalThis-pin from the toy prototype into the real src/server.ts: serve() now checks globalThis.__werkServe before taking the lock, constructing Agent, or calling listen(), and no-ops with a log line if the port is already being served. Repeated the exact same real-task test: 20-step counting task, edit fold.ts mid-task, on both bun --hot and vite-node --watch. Result for both: single 'hot-reloaded, reusing the live server' log line (no duplicate Agent, no EADDRINUSE, no crash), same claude child pid throughout, task completed normally, and - the decisive check - a brand-new SSE connection opened mid-task saw the live task in progress, not silence. This directly reverses the unpatched result in #werk-hmr:src2 for both candidates. The fix needed is small: one guard clause at the top of serve(), no dependency on which of vite-node or bun-hot is chosen.

payload.title: Bun vs Node as werk's shipped runtime (Sept 2026)
payload.finding: Node's native TypeScript support is stable as of 25.2.0/24.12.0 (experimental-transform-types removed in 26.0.0) - werk's 'no build step, no dependencies' premise already holds on Node, since werk uses no enums/namespaces/decorators. Bun's TS support is a superset (also runs enums) but that gain is unused today. The decisive finding: oven-sh/bun #7716 and #13811, both open, document that Bun's http.createServer does not reliably emit the close event when an SSE client disconnects - werk's src/server.ts serves SSE over plain http.createServer for exactly this pattern. child_process piping (werk's spawn+pipe of the claude CLI) is not on Bun's documented gap list but has open issues (#30831, #4670) showing the area is still being patched. Bun 1.4 (Aug 2026) was a full Zig-to-Rust rewrite shipped as a point release with an itemized breaking-change list - a materially different stability posture than Node's LTS-scheduled majors (Node 26 LTS Oct 2026 - Apr 2029). Bun's advantages (startup speed, bun build --compile) answer a distribution problem werk does not have; it ships as source, not a compiled binary.

payload.title: Direct repro on Bun 1.4.1: SSE close event fires correctly on werk's real code
payload.finding: Tested against Bun 1.4.1 specifically (the version installed and used throughout this whole investigation, and the version the runtime-migration research flagged as the big Zig-to-Rust rewrite). Added a probe to server.ts's actual /api/live handler: console.log on clients.add and inside req.on('close', ...). Opened and disconnected SSE clients two ways - a clean client-side timeout (curl --max-time) and an abrupt kill -9 mid-stream - against werk's real, unmodified route-handling code. Both cases: 'added, clients=1' followed by 'close fired, clients=0', every time, no leaked entries, no growth in server fd count (lsof) after 10 rapid connect/disconnect cycles. oven-sh/bun #7716 and #13811 are real, filed, open issues, but do not reproduce for werk's plain http.createServer + SSE + req.on('close') pattern on 1.4.1. Side finding: the globalThis-pin guard from #werk-hmr:src3 means a hot reload no longer applies code changes inside serve()'s body at all (a hot-reloaded edit to the SSE handler itself did not take effect until the process was fully restarted) - the guard trades 'my latest route-handler edit is live' for 'my live session survives an edit', which is the correct trade for the original problem but is worth naming explicitly.

payload.title: Keep the first request handler for the life of the process
payload.why_not: An edit to a route handler would not go live until a restart, and a restart kills the live chat session that the guard exists to keep. Swapping the handler costs nothing: the server, the clients and the children stay.

payload.why: The child alone takes the lock, and a child that outlived its parent would keep it.
Takes the Vite client transform that the server runs inside itself in dev.

payload.title: Stay with hand-written DOM code, and add web components or Lit for structure
payload.why_not: It keeps the no-build-step property but gives no per-component hot reload that keeps state, which the chat pane needs. A class-per-file refactor of one very large file only relabels an organisation problem.

payload.why: The client stack runs inside the Bun server with the hot reload chosen there, and avoids the rejected vite-node process host.

payload.title: SolidJS with Vite
payload.why_not: Fine-grained updates suit a map of hundreds of cards, but its hot reload has remounted components rather than kept their signals, and agents know it far less than React: the two criteria ranked hardest.

payload.title: Svelte 5 with runes, plus Vite
payload.why_not: The strongest runner-up: it compiles away and ships little script for static content. But its hot reload keeps state less reliably for a component that holds a live stream, and runes are recent enough that agents still write Svelte 4 store idioms.

payload.why: The page reads the open card's HTML again on each change signal.

payload.title: Astro with islands, React or Svelte inside
payload.why_not: Astro is page-oriented: a navigation is a document swap, which cuts the chat pane's live stream and turn in flight. Its island hot reload also tends to remount the island, which loses state where it matters most.

payload.title: React Server Components
payload.why_not: They answer progressive loading and partial hydration natively, but need Waku, Parcel-RSC or similar on a custom Bun server: very new code in the layer that must not break. Hand-made islands give most of the benefit without that risk.

payload.why: Takes the view addresses and the rule that Back and Forward move between them.
Takes the chat pane whose live stream a page load would cut.
The read ships one card's body at a time because one view shows one card.
The change signal carries no ids, so a view reads the shape again on each change.
Takes React with Vite as a client transform inside the Bun server.
The component set must support React.

payload.title: Radix Themes: a fixed set of styled components set through props and CSS variables
payload.why_not: A look outside its props needs a CSS override against styles the client does not own, and agents know it less well, so they guess more about its props.

payload.title: Mantine: a large styled library with CSS modules
payload.why_not: Its set is large and comes with its own hooks for forms and hotkeys, so an agent has several ways to build the same screen, which defeats a small fixed set.

payload.title: MUI or Chakra: styled libraries that compute styles in JavaScript
payload.why_not: Both compute styles in JavaScript on each render, which costs time on every render and fails the static CSS criterion.

payload.why: The list of view addresses comes from there; this card says when each address is added.

payload.title: Answer every listed view address with the app now, with a placeholder pane for a view not built yet
payload.why_not: It ships a screen that no card decides, and its tests pin a placeholder that the real view must then remove.

payload.why: Small modules matter because two tickets build at once only when they share no module.

payload.title: A few large modules, one per layer
payload.why_not: Every vertical slice edits every layer, so every pair of tickets shares a module and no two tickets can build at the same time.

payload.why: The build rules are cards in the map, so the file points to them instead of copying them.

payload.title: CLAUDE.md as the only instruction file
payload.why_not: It ties werk's own repository to one agent tool, and werk must become a product that runs outside that tool.

payload.title: An instruction file in each folder, beside the code it describes
payload.why_not: Each file is a second description of its folder that a code change does not update, and an agent cannot tell which one is out of date.

payload.title: A full guide to the code in the instruction file
payload.why_not: The agent reads all of it in every session, and it goes out of date with each refactor. The agent can read the code for its layout and the map for its reasons.

payload.title: A docs folder with architecture and design documents
payload.why_not: Each document repeats decisions that the map records, and nothing marks it when one of them changes. An agent then reads a document that contradicts the map and cannot tell which is right.

payload.title: Architecture decision records as numbered files in the repository
payload.why_not: They record the same thing as a decided card, with no link between dependent decisions and no mark when a decision they rest on changes.

payload.title: A glossary file of werk's terms
payload.why_not: Each term gets a second definition beside the one on its card, and the glossary keeps the old meaning when the card changes.

payload.why: It extends the make-target form set for checks to every other task.
The fix target runs the automatic fixes of the chosen linter and formatter.

payload.title: Make targets for the checks only, package scripts for every other task
payload.why_not: A newcomer then has two lists to read, and must know which kind of task is in which list.

payload.title: A dedicated task runner such as just or Task
payload.why_not: One more tool to install on every machine and in CI, while make is already on macOS and Linux and the checks already use it.

payload.why: The version check runs at the start of each make target.

payload.title: A version manager such as mise or asdf installs the pinned version
payload.why_not: Every person and every CI machine must install the version manager first, one more tool before werk.

payload.title: No pin: any recent Bun runs werk
payload.why_not: A check can pass on the builder's Bun and fail in CI or in the release build, and the failure does not say that the version is the cause.

payload.why: A rule that the configuration helps with is enforced by the checks.

payload.title: Claude Code hooks and settings enforce werk's development rules
payload.why_not: A hook runs only inside Claude Code. An agent in another harness, a script, or a person at the terminal never meets the rule, and the rule fails without a sign.

payload.why: The hook runs the chosen formatter and linter.

payload.title: No hooks: the agent sees lint errors only when the checks run
payload.why_not: The agent fixes each lint error in a second pass, after the file has left its attention, and the merge loop sends more tickets back for style alone.

payload.title: A hook runs every check when the agent ends its turn
payload.why_not: The tests and the end-to-end run take minutes, so every turn ends with a long wait, also a chat turn that changed no code.

payload.why: It allows the make targets defined there.

payload.title: No shared settings: each person approves commands on their own machine
payload.why_not: Every person and every new worktree asks the same questions about the same safe commands, and an agent waits for each answer.

payload.title: The shared settings skip every permission question
payload.why_not: An agent can then delete files outside the repository or send data over the network with no person in the loop, on every machine that checks out werk.

payload.why: A workflow is a program, not a prompt file.
A repeated workflow becomes a make target.

payload.title: Project skills for werk's common workflows, such as adding a card or running a build
payload.why_not: The steps live in prompt text that an agent may skip or change, and the skill runs only in Claude Code.

payload.title: An MCP server that exposes the map to the agent as tools
payload.why_not: The werk command line already gives the agent every map operation through the shell, with the same checks. An MCP server is a second interface to keep in step with it.

payload.why: It keeps one copy of the subagent definitions that are shipped into every project.
A definition holds a prompt only, and its steps are commands.
The link check runs as the last step of the lint check.

payload.title: Two copies, the shipped one and the repository's one, kept the same by hand
payload.why_not: A fix to one copy does not reach the other, and nothing shows the difference. werk's own agents then test a prompt that users do not get.

payload.title: A setup step copies the shipped definitions into the repository's subagent folder
payload.why_not: Every checkout and worktree needs the setup step before an agent works, and a copy made before a change is out of date until someone runs it again.

payload.title: A separate task for the link check, outside the lint check
payload.why_not: The merge loop runs only the existing check names, so a separate task does not run before a merge and a copy can merge unseen.

payload.why: React component tests run under Bun's runner with a DOM because the client is React.
A check that runs past its time limit fails as check infrastructure, which the parallel run and the limit keep away.

payload.title: Bun's runner only, with Playwright called as a bare library
payload.why_not: It saves one dependency and loses the trace viewer, the main way to read why a browser test failed. Launch, teardown and retry would be hand-written per file, and an agent gets that wrong quietly.

payload.title: Three runners: Bun's, Vitest and Playwright's
payload.why_not: Three configurations, and Vitest earns its place only if a Vite transform makes a component behave differently under Bun than in the app. Reopen if that happens.

payload.title: Run the unit test files in one process, with the runner's default per-test limit
payload.why_not: The run then takes most of the time limit of one check, and a slower machine or a few more tests fail the check for time alone.

payload.why: Takes the browser runner whose test files this card names.

payload.title: Browser tests keep the .spec.ts suffix, and the unit runner skips the browser test folder
payload.why_not: A unit test written in a skipped folder is skipped with no error, so a wrong placement goes unseen, and every new top-level folder may need the list updated.

payload.title: Browser tests keep the .spec.ts suffix, and the unit test command names the folders it reads
payload.why_not: The same quiet skip of a misplaced unit test, and the folder list moves into the command, where a coverage run and a plain run can drift apart.

payload.why: Only pure files get a coverage number, so the check judges only the files on the pure list.
The coverage gate is a check: one command whose exit code is the verdict.

payload.title: Each pure file declares itself, and the check finds the files, so no shared list exists
payload.why_not: It replaces the explicit list; while the list exists, the rule that a merge keeps every entry keeps it correct.

payload.title: Any test in the suite that runs a line counts it as covered
payload.why_not: A caller's test runs the lines of the files it calls, so a pure file passes with its own tests deleted, and the check cannot see the loss.

payload.why: It cleans the environment of Bun's test runner, whose spawn defaults are the gap.

payload.title: Only edit the program search list in the test setup
payload.why_not: Bun's spawn, program lookup and shell still read the environment the process started with, so a test that starts an agent with no explicit environment can find the real agent, silently.

payload.title: Remove a fixed list of named settings
payload.why_not: A setting can point at a real map, a real repository or the person's agent account under many names. A list of single names misses the next name, silently.

payload.why: A fresh project is a fresh map because the map is the fold of the project's own log.
The client reload test needs the copy to hold the client and the Vite config, because Vite runs inside the server.
The DOM is registered for Bun's test runner, with React from the client stack.

payload.title: All tests run in one browser-like environment
payload.why_not: Server code then calls the network, stream and timer functions of the environment, which behave differently, so a server test can pass or fail for a reason production never sees.

payload.title: Register a DOM per component test file and remove it after the file
payload.why_not: React finds a DOM only when it first loads in the process, so a DOM registered later is not the one React holds, and only the first file would be safe.

payload.why: Browser tests run under the browser test runner.
The agent reads the screenshot by the rule for reading images.

payload.title: A browser-automation MCP server, steered tool call by tool call
payload.why_not: Every screenshot returns into the main conversation, one per tool call; one session reached 920,805 cached input tokens from 57 image reads that way. It also tests nothing repeatably.

payload.title: Vitest browser mode, through the client's own Vite config
payload.why_not: Its unit is a mounted component, not a running werk: it cannot boot the Bun server, hold the live stream open or drive a live agent child, and it brings in a second runner as a side effect.

payload.title: Both: Vitest browser mode for components, Playwright for flows
payload.why_not: Two ways to write the same browser test, so the agent must pick the level on every new test, and a wrong pick is silent. Reopen if component-level browser tests turn out to be needed.

payload.title: A stored pixel baseline, compared automatically on every run
payload.why_not: A baseline over a UI being built is rebaselined on nearly every commit, so the gate teaches the agent to accept a diff rather than read it.

payload.why: Takes the binder's own folder, outside of which a write voids its report.
Takes the binder's temporary checkout, so the binder's folder never exists in a builder's checkout.

payload.title: The binder writes its own browser test settings inside its folder
payload.why_not: The settings must repeat how the product starts its server, fake agent and fixture project, and a copy that differs makes a held-out step fail for a harness reason that reads as a product failure.

payload.title: The binder's folder sits inside the product's spec folder
payload.why_not: The binder's folder would sit in the product's tree, the write check would have to special-case it, and a builder could see it in the spec tree.

payload.title: The binder names its own folder when it starts the browser run
payload.why_not: The override must keep the product's harness, and a later change to how the settings choose tests would break the binder's run with no clear error.

payload.why: v0 is the visual layer that this card names as the primary medium.
v0 includes the live chat pane.
v0 includes extracted excerpts.
v0 includes card-id link rendering.
v0 includes fenced code rendering.
v0 includes the card wording rule.
v0 includes the contract check at decided.
v0 shows the reopen reasons in the staleness view.
v0 is built to compile into one executable and follows its rules for werk's own files and name.
v0 includes the checks before and after each merge.
v0 includes the test harness.
v0 includes the start path for a person or an agent.
v0 is built on the client stack.

payload.title: v0 includes the tracker export
payload.why_not: The map is the record and the board shows the tickets, so a one-way publish to an issue tracker adds nothing v0 needs.

payload.title: v0 includes the validate stage
payload.why_not: Validate measures production. v0 has no production until it is built and in use.

payload.title: v0 includes pipeline self-measurement
payload.why_not: The build loop already records its own cost and failures in the pipeline log. A separate measurement layer duplicates it.

payload.why: It names the repository whose main branch is the main line that builds start from and merge onto.

payload.title: Extend the prototype code until each v0 item works
payload.why_not: The prototype code was written to find the shape, not to keep. Extending it carries every shortcut into v0.

payload.title: Build v0 in the prototype's repository, with the prototype on a sibling branch
payload.why_not: The two lines share one repository, its history and its map state, so a build can still start from or merge into the prototype's tree. Only a separate repository makes that impossible.

payload.why: v0 includes the spec-then-tickets plan step at full scope.
v0 includes the merge loop at full scope.
v0 includes the overseer and every card under it.
v0 includes the command-line pipeline tests.
v0's pipeline picks each agent's model from its role.
v0's builder loop grades later passes against earlier gaps and regressions.
v0's builder loop merges small gaps on the last counted pass and files them as a follow-up.
v0 runs the stages, and every gate waits for a person.

payload.title: Plan without a spec: tickets straight from the subtree
payload.why_not: The spec is where the user stories and the test seams are agreed. Tickets without it have no stories and no common whole to split.

payload.title: Builder runs checks only, with no grader and no review
payload.why_not: Checks see exit codes only. The grader and the review compare the diff with the cited cards.

payload.title: Merge queue without the held-out set
payload.why_not: The held-out set is the only bar the builder cannot see. Without it, the builder can game every check it runs.

payload.title: Overseer reacts to silence only
payload.why_not: Silence misses a loop that keeps producing events, and an ask that waits for nobody.

payload.title: No pipeline tests: test with real agent runs only
payload.why_not: The overseer's time limits cannot be tested in a usable time without a fake agent and adjustable limits.

payload.why: Every answer a plan writer gives that no card gives comes back as a proposal before the build.
Every gate v0 runs waits for the person.
The v0 board builds the board design defined there.
Takes the ticket moves an agent may make, which the command line carries: a move to blocked or ready with a reason, an archive, and a restore.
The one conversation of a project is the continuous conversation defined there.
The dead mark of the tab rules is read as a rule for the one conversation.
A dead child in another project shows on that project's switcher row.

payload.title: v0 builds the chat tabs in full
payload.why_not: Tabs, forks, parking and the idle stop add a large part to v0 that werk does not need to build the rest of itself.

payload.why: The held-out set is the part built first.
The merge loop later runs the held-out set after each merge.
The ticket checks are one operation that the plan step calls.

payload.title: Build the held-out set and the merge loop together, in one slice
payload.why_not: A red result could then come from either part, and the merge loop cannot be checked until the held-out set it calls already works.

payload.why: v0 writes the one append-only pipeline log defined there.
Transcripts and check output sit beside the log as defined there.
The retry cap reads the log to skip a pass that ended on a spec gap.
Takes the source, metric, threshold, window and minimum sample of each criterion.

payload.title: Only the state that someone records counts
payload.why_not: The recorded state and the measure disagree as soon as the data moves, and a fired criterion stays unseen until someone reads the measure.

payload.why: Takes the unit test runner whose runs it records.
Times the full replay that every read runs.
The import runs the backfill of past turns and sessions.
